P1-01.title: Porous Implants and Lattice Design
P1-01.subtitle: Connecting pore geometry, load bearing, surfaces and manufacturing through evidence
P1-01.thesis: The effectiveness of porous implants depends on accessible tissue pathways, structures that sustain loading, and surfaces that can be processed reproducibly. Research has expanded from comparing pore geometries to transport, fatigue and cleaning; design choices should be constrained by both the anatomical site and manufacturing conditions.

blocks.text: How do pore size, pore shape and connectivity affect bone ingrowth?

Bone ingrowth requires bone tissue to enter the implant and gradually form a stable connection. Pore size describes the size of the local space, pore shape determines the boundary curvature and support method, and connectivity determines the path from the outside to the inside. Even with the same porosity, the actual area that cells can reach may differ; therefore, the design must simultaneously observe geometry, transport, and tissue response. [R03]

blocks.text: This research examines design principles shared by dental implants and porous orthopaedic interfaces. Dental, spinal and joint implants differ in size and loading environment; structural comparisons therefore need to account for the specific bone-contact surface and fixation context.
How can lattice and topology design balance load-bearing capacity and stress transfer?

The load-bearing implant needs to coordinate two objectives: the structure itself must withstand repeated loads, while the surrounding bone receives appropriate mechanical stimulation. Lattice alterations change the material's spatial distribution, and topology optimization further adjusts the load-bearing path based on load and constraints. [R09]

How does multiscale surface design affect cells and the bone interface?

The surface of a printed implant combines macroscopic structure, micrometre-scale topography and finer nanoscale features. Cells encounter an interface defined by these features together with surface chemistry. Design objectives depend on location: bone-contact surfaces require bone formation and fixation; transgingival regions also involve soft tissues and bacteria; and treatments for internal pore walls must reach deep within the structure. [R12] · [R14]

blocks.text: This research emphasizes the connection between geometry and biological responses. Coating formulation, anti-infective agents, and long-term fatigue each provide relevant constraints, but the main focus here is on how to create a controllable and repeatable cellular environment for surface interaction.
N1 | Bone within pores and mechanical fixation

The 2016 study on multi-rooted dental implants involved implanting interconnected porous structures created by selective laser melting into the hind limbs of rabbits, and evaluating the implants using micro-CT, histology, pull-out, and torque testing. During the observation period, tissue gradually entered the pores and root bifurcation areas, accompanied by enhanced fixation mechanical properties. This study advanced the concept of "printing holes" to "the co-occurrence of intrapore tissue formation and mechanical connection." [R01]

The next question is what produces this effect. When external geometry, surface properties and internal pathways change together, the contribution of the pore structure itself must be isolated. Comparing pore geometries while controlling material and implantation site therefore becomes an important design strategy.

This step establishes the starting point for evaluating the collaborative work between structure and tissue. When interpreting results, it's crucial to distinguish between peripheral new bone, intra-pore bone, and trans-pore connections, and to align the direction of mechanical testing with the implantation direction. If the new bone is primarily located in non-load-bearing areas, the increase in total bone volume may not explain the fixation. Therefore, N2 requires comparing pore shapes, and N4 requires analyzing the contact surface; these two branches separately decompose the contributions of the entry path and local response.
N2 | Comparing pore geometries in a common model

A 2023 study implanted six Ti6Al4V lattices into sheep femoral condyles and compared bone ingrowth at 8 and 12 weeks using histological, image analysis, and mechanical testing. Gyroid, double pyramidal, and cubic structures maintained a high bone ingrowth ranking in this model. This result shifted the research focus from an overall comparison of "porous over dense" to the selection of different structural units. [R02]

Morphological sorting needs to be combined with the location of internal tissues. Peripheral bone and uniform ossification throughout the structure correspond to different fixation states; the same bone area proportion may also result from different distributions. Therefore, image segmentation, tissue section location, and observation time are all part of structural evaluation.

Using the same material and anatomical site in the same animal model reduces confounding between experiments, but changing the unit cell can still alter curvature, specific surface area and channel orientation together. Subsequent comparisons can keep actual porosity and characteristic dimensions similar across designs, then analyse peripheral and internal regions separately. Flow and cell-trajectory measurements in N5 provide intermediate evidence that can turn rankings of pore geometries into interpretable transport mechanisms.
N3 | Manufacturing determines actual strut geometry

Lattice performance depends on both design and manufacturing. A 2020 Ti6Al4V study compared continuous and pulsed laser scanning, together with combinations of hot isostatic pressing, sandblasting and chemical etching. Under the conditions studied, continuous scanning produced fewer defects and greater fatigue resistance, whereas pulsed scanning produced a more uniform microstructure; optimized post-processing combinations further improved fatigue performance. [R07]

This step illustrates that design comparisons require the use of the same manufacturing baseline. Even with identical component dimensions, differences in internal defects, attached particles, and grain structure can lead to different failure locations. Therefore, further optimization necessitates incorporating finished product measurements and material testing into the input.

The branch extends structural parameters from geometric files to the manufacturing state. Heat treatment primarily alters the microstructure and internal defects, while surface treatment changes both the shape and notches; the two may interact. Pairing the local strut diameters before and after treatment with the failure locations is necessary to determine which aspect contributes to the performance improvement. It provides realistic model input for N6 and also accepts the reverse constraint of the N8 cleaning requirements.
N4 | Micro/nanotopography and integration time

The microscopic topography produced by additive manufacturing provides a starting point for surface design, but the process can also leave unmelted particles and heterogeneous structures. A 2021 study of hierarchical micro/nanostructured surfaces added nanoscale features to the microrough surfaces of SLM Ti6Al4V dental implants. Surface characterization, cell experiments and implantation in rabbit femoral condyles were used together to investigate interfacial responses. [R12]

The study first broke down "surface treatment" into measurable changes: morphology, wetting, and composition, and then observed whether these changes were accompanied by alterations in cellular behavior. This avoids interpreting biological results solely based on the name of the treatment process.

The same study observed improved osteogenesis-related expression and early bone contact in the treatment group, with more mineralized bone at the early interface; towards the later stages of bone formation, the proportion of bone contact was similar to that of the control group. Its value lies in revealing that the surface may primarily alter the integration rate and early tissue maturation process, rather than continuously increasing the final amount of bone contact at all time points. [R12]

Subsequent evaluation must treat time as a design variable: initial adhesion, cell differentiation, mineralization and stable fixation occur at different stages. Only longitudinal observation can show which stage a surface accelerates and whether that benefit remains when loading begins.

This study suggests that surface action has a temporal location. The value of early adhesion improvement needs to be considered in relation to when load-bearing begins, and late-stage bone contact proximity cannot erase early differences. The next node, N9, discusses how the removal of unstable particles and the preservation of functional morphology can coexist; both require treating roughness, surface composition, and actual cell location as independent variables.
N5 | Pore transport and cell entry

A 2025 dental implant structure study compared solid Gyroids, sheet-like Gyroids, and random Voronoi networks, using tandem fabrication, micro-CT, computational fluid dynamics, and mouse bone marrow stromal cell experiments. Solid Gyroids demonstrated better fabrication control, pore distribution, and permeability in this design, and also supported better adhesion and cell entry into the pores. [R03]

The research approach moves beyond endpoint observations to examine intermediate mechanisms: actual pore channels alter fluid transport and the spaces accessible to cells, influencing where tissue formation begins. Subsequent designs should compare effective channels, local flow conditions and cell locations together to establish a continuous link between geometric parameters and biological outcomes.

Fluid analysis and cell trajectory provide a verifiable intermediate step in pore structure research. Higher permeability can improve overall flow, but it does not mean that the supply is the same everywhere; localized low-velocity areas may also alter cell residence. The inlet, neck, and depth should be observed simultaneously to identify the actual cell entry route. It imposes transport constraints on N7 and identifies channels that must be retained after cleaning on N8.
N6 | Calibrating fatigue models with as-built geometry

The 2023 study established a calibration and verification process between monotonic loading, fatigue testing, and finite element analysis for six types of porous dental implant configurations. The error was approximately 23% when using the original CAD prediction; after using micro-CT-based finished geometry or correcting the design according to actual porosity, the error decreased to approximately 14% and 8%, respectively. A crucial source of model accuracy is reflecting the true geometry after printing. [R08]

This allows the simulation to move from comparing ideal structures to product development verification: first, establishing the correspondence between geometry, load, and failure, and then verifying the predictions using independent configurations. Going forward, it's crucial to focus on whether the model can be transferred to new combinations of aperture shapes, sizes, and loads, rather than simply fitting to the samples used in the calibration.

The key contribution is to make manufacturing deviations a computational input rather than a post hoc explanation. Micro-CT geometry and adjusted CAD offer calibration approaches with different costs; selection should consider prediction accuracy, processing time and transferability to new dimensions. Optimization in N7 can therefore screen designs only within an explicitly validated range. An optimum outside that range requires additional physical validation of the relevant geometry.
N7 | Joint optimization of bone and implant

The 2025 dental implant study employed topology optimization and TPMS lattice design for internal structure, and established a finite element model using Ti6Al4V parameters obtained from mechanical testing. A bone biomechanical adaptation model was used to examine the stress on surrounding bone tissue. This study integrates stress shielding and long-term stability into the same design task. [R09]

The research questions then become more specific: which parts need to retain solid support, which areas can have their stiffness reduced, and whether the new load path will transfer stress to the thinner rod or the connection interface. Appropriate optimization should report the response on both sides of the bone and implant, specifying the load direction, boundaries, and material parameters.

Research on mandibular continuity defects used weighted topology optimization to configure lightweight support structures for different defect locations, followed by finite element analysis and dynamic fatigue testing. The tested structures reported in the paper published in a 2022 journal issue passed 250,000 loading cycles. This extends the selection of standard unit cells towards load-path design for specific defects. [R10]

Local structural optimization must then be integrated into the complete fixation system. Remaining bone, screw positions and the direction of occlusal loading alter boundary conditions; in spinal fusion cages, endplate contact and subsidence also affect overall performance. Each anatomical site therefore requires its own validation loads and failure criteria.

Both studies demonstrate that the average modulus is only one part of the design description. Porosity can reduce overall stiffness and may also concentrate loads in finite members or fixed areas; both bone-side response and device-side failure should be reported simultaneously. N5 and N6 converge here in the diagram, indicating that tissue transport and manufacturing calibration are included in the same set of constraints, with N8 checking whether this configuration allows for actual finished product cleanliness.
N8 | Depowdering constraints inform design

The interconnecting channels in the design model can only fulfill their intended function if they remain open after printing and cleaning. A 2026 powder removal study compared ultrasonic cleaning with processes involving superimposed mechanical vibration and rolling, used weighing and CT to examine residual powder in complex lattices, and discussed the cleaning and mechanical trade-offs in dental implant structures. [R04]

This step changes the order of parameter optimization: first confirm the post-manufacturing geometry and cleanability, then evaluate biological effects. For narrow or tortuous channels, reporting the CAD aperture alone is insufficient to describe the final space available to tissue. Manufacturable and cleanable pathways should be designed in conjunction with the supporting structure.

The complete research chain is therefore: define the anatomical site and loading conditions → select a topology or lattice → incorporate manufacturing deviations → calibrate finite element models → validate fatigue performance and interfaces → assess cleaning and finished-device quality. Each step informs the next design iteration, with a verifiable device structure as the final optimization objective.

Powder removal gives manufacturing implications to effective connectivity. Reducing the pore neck may increase local support but restrict particle discharge; opening sidewalls can increase cleaning paths but may also change load-bearing capacity. Therefore, a suitable optimization target is a parameter range that simultaneously achieves cleaning, mechanical, and tissue entry requirements. Feedback N3 indicates adjustments to manufacturing and post-processing, while feedback N2 indicates reselection of channel geometry; both require remeasurement rather than default validity.
N9 | Smooth substrates and active interfaces

A 2026 study combined etching and electropolishing of laser powder bed fusion Ti6Al4V scaffolds to reduce roughness and unmelted particles and form a more uniform oxide layer. Stem cells from the apical papilla formed continuous cell layers and subsequently a tissue-like matrix on the treated scaffolds. [R13]

This is not contradictory to micro/nano structures: removing unstable manufacturing residues and preserving or constructing functional textures are two tasks that can be performed sequentially. Evaluation should simultaneously report the cleanliness of the finished product, the actual morphology after treatment, and cell distribution to determine the source of the improvement.

The surface design therefore needs to distinguish between controllable textures and incidental defects. Both can increase roughness, but their stability, location, and cell contact methods differ; reporting only an average roughness cannot explain the effect. Further comparisons should be made on chemistry at similar morphologies, and on morphology at similar chemistry, with separate sampling of the inner and outer pore walls. N10 further incorporates multi-target issues involving tissues and bacteria.
N10 | Zoned tissue and bacterial interactions

A 2026 all-laser study combined laser polishing, femtosecond-laser periodic structuring and spatially guided deposition of silver nanoparticles. In vitro experiments examined fibroblasts, osteoblasts and Porphyromonas gingivalis biofilms; a canine model was then used to assess inflammation and osseointegration. Surface geometry thus helped organize both cell alignment and antibacterial-ion release. [R14]

The research objective has thus expanded from "which texture promotes osteoogenesis" to "how the same surface can accommodate the effects of different cells and bacteria." The next step is to align the textured regions, ion release sites, and actual tissue contact boundaries, and observe the duration of the effects and surface changes.

This forms the validation sequence from experiment to device: identify the contact tissue → select scale and chemistry → validate cellular and tissue responses → inspect complex finished product surfaces → evaluate sterilization, storage, and post-service performance. The final judgment should return to the design area to determine whether the expected tissue action was achieved, and whether this action can be replicated across finished products.

This node aligns interface design with tissue boundaries: regions contacting bone, soft tissue and the external environment have different tasks. Assessing functional zoning requires measurements of treatment consistency, retention of surface constituents and exposure time in each region. Convergence with N8 means that any added surface treatment must be reassessed after final cleaning on the complete device, because results from individual specimens may not cover deep pores and connecting regions.

sections.title: Evolution of Commercial Technologies and Products

blocks.text: Porous structures have become a reusable product technology.

In 2016, Stryker's announcement showcased the combination of the Tritanium PL lumbar fusion cage and the high-porosity additive manufacturing technology. The porous structure, introduced from the experimental specimen into the actual device, is responsible for designing the bone contact and fusion space. [R05]

Restor3d Current TIDAL technical documentation combines the Gyroid structure, connecting channels, and micro-surfaces into a single platform, manufactured using laser powder bed fusion. Its product presentation emphasizes consistent structural parameters and manufacturing processes, reflecting the company's strategy of packaging lattice design into cross-product capabilities. [R06]

blocks.text: The changes on the enterprise side are manifested in the co-organization of porous technology, device morphology, and surgical procedures. Existing data supports the observation of platform and product evolution; specific bone ingrowth effects require connection to the corresponding product's experimental and clinical indicators.
Truss products transform load paths into mechanical design features.

The 2016 regulatory document for 4WEB's Lateral Spine Truss System describes an open truss structure whose internal spaces support bone growth and fusion while the structure provides mechanical support. The document lists validated finite element analyses, compression and combined-loading assessments, and subsidence and expulsion tests. Its intended use includes supplemental fixation and autologous bone graft, illustrating that product validation addresses the complete use configuration. [R11]
The geometric platform organizes structure and manufacturing into a sustainable capability.

restor3d's TIDAL page combines Gyroid design, interconnected porosity and laser powder bed fusion. Compared with individual lattice specimens, a commercial platform must accommodate different shapes and sizes while maintaining alignment between technical parameters and production processes. [R06]
Enterprise Participation in Computational Verification Research

Author affiliations in the 2023 study of porous dental implant fatigue include Attenborough Dental Laboratories. The study links mechanical experiments to the calibration of numerical predictions, showing how companies and research institutions can jointly develop validation methods that reduce repeated physical testing. [R08]

These three types of records complement each other: trusses become device design, lattices become manufacturing platforms, and computational verification becomes development capabilities. They all revolve around the same engineering goal—proving that structures can reliably bear loads under actual geometric and operational configurations.
The product platform combines microscopic interfaces with macroscopic porous structures.

restor3d's current TIDAL page describes both Gyroid porous architecture and microscopic surfaces. This product strategy combines structural scales: macroscopic geometry provides open space, while the microscopic interface mediates local tissue contact. [R06]

When presenting Tritanium PL in 2016, Stryker emphasized the ability of additive manufacturing to produce highly porous structures. The company translated bone-contact spaces into a device; cellular-interface research provides further methods for optimizing those structural surfaces. [R05]
The focus of industrial evolution is the manufacturable combination of functions.

Between the enterprise technology page and the experimental papers, two different levels can be seen: the product side organizes the structure and surface into a stable production solution, while the academic side continues to explore nanotextures, cleaning processes, and controllable antibacterial functions. The most critical development step between the two is to make the multifunctional interface into a complete device capable of testing, storage, and sterilization. · [R13][R14]

In the current source, the connection between the company's porous platform and the aforementioned specific laser/silver deposition paper corresponds to a technical requirement. Products actually employing a particular formulation or process should be further linked through product documentation, manufacturing records, or collaborative research.

sections.title: Research–enterprise links through disclosed patent mechanisms

blocks.text: The industrial connection follows channels, load paths and regional interfaces. Papers identify measurable biological and mechanical variables; patents assemble them into device schemes; products supply anatomical and manufacturing constraints. TIDAL, Tritanium and 4WEB Truss provide product contexts for channels, porous interfaces and load paths, respectively. Their connection to the following patents is a correspondence of technical problems.[R05][R06][R11]
Channels and curved surfaces

Nanjing First Hospital’s CN116833425A proposes a TPMS titanium implant combining smooth surfaces, a porous ingrowth layer and self-support during additive manufacturing. Its intersection with the six-lattice animal comparison and Gyroid transport study is whether actual pore throats change deep cellular access. restor3d TIDAL supplies a product-scale context. The bridge is unit geometry and manufactured channels; the TPMS label alone does not establish osseointegration.[R02][R03][R06][R16]
Connectivity and partitioning

CN115813615A from Huazhong University of Science and Technology describes partitioning and reassembling an acetabular cup to orient the porous layer along its surface and retain connected struts. Manufactured-geometry calibration and mandibular fatigue studies supply evaluation methods; 4WEB documentation supplies compression, combined-loading and subsidence contexts. Transferable methods concern node continuity, actual strut diameter and local failure, with cup and spine contact conditions evaluated separately.[R08][R10][R11][R17]
Bone and soft-tissue sides

AESCULAP’s AU2024286530A1 separates a printed porous bone-contact surface from a coating that reduces roughness in soft-tissue contact regions. Jiasite is explicitly named in Chinese among the applicants of CN112315627A, which describes a zirconium-niobium tibial platform, proximal/distal trabecular regions and an oxide layer. Together with micro/nano-interface research, these schemes require separate measurements of openness, soft-tissue friction and oxide condition. Abstract performance statements become hypotheses for comparison against early/late bone contact and post-service surface integrity.[R12][R13][R15][R18]

sections.title: Translation and validation: variables, controls and decisions

blocks.text: Validation should link geometry, powder removal, transport and fatigue in the same manufactured batches. Hold material, nominal porosity and envelope constant while varying TPMS units, cup-surface connectivity and surface zoning; update models using measured geometry. Open CAD does not guarantee open manufactured channels, and early surface benefits may narrow later. Sampling must include internal regions and more than one time point.[R04][R08][R12] Define the ingrowth, cyclic-load and soft-tissue regions before selecting a design window, then verify their manufactured boundaries. Equal average porosity may conceal different throats/struts; equal roughness may reflect stable texture or loose particles. Register histology, cleanliness sampling and failure locations to interpret one structure rather than combine the best endpoints from different specimens.

headers: Proposed comparison, endpoints and next decision
rows: Channels

Compare TPMS with equal-porosity trusses using pre/post-cleaning microCT and flow measurements. Record pore throats, powder location and deep cell distribution. If high bulk permeability coexists with internal obstruction, revise throats and outlets.[R16]
Load bearing

Compare connected cup surfaces with conventional layers of equal mass using manufactured-geometry FE, cyclic loading and fracture mapping. If junctions fail first or subsidence increases, retain solid support and rearrange struts.[R17]
Interface

Compare porous bone zones, smooth soft-tissue zones and oxide combinations with a uniform surface. Examine treatment coverage, particle shedding and early/late fixation together. Revise zone boundaries if smoothing reaches bone regions or damages thin struts.[R15][R18]

If TPMS channels can be repeatedly cleaned at TIDAL-like product scales, a throat/outlet design window becomes plausible. Track batch pore deviations, spatial powder residue and permeability variation; size-dependent windows require size-specific rules first.[R06][R16]

If connected cup surfaces retain fatigue performance in independent geometries, partitioning could extend to new contact curvatures. Following the device-level logic of 4WEB evaluation, track fracture-location prediction, subsidence and additional testing for new sizes. Junction failure redirects work to local reinforcement.[R11][R17]

Regional interfaces warrant broader functional comparison only if location and chemistry survive sterilization, storage and cyclic loading. For the AESCULAP and Jiasite schemes, track soft-tissue response, bone-contact trajectories, particle release and batch coverage. Improvement in one region with harm in another calls for a narrower combination.[R15][R18]

blocks.text: Research priorities should follow failure location: obstruction changes channels, strut fracture changes connections, and unstable interfaces change treatment zones. Feeding these observations back into one device version distinguishes geometrical contributions from changes introduced during manufacturing and finishing.

P1-02.title: Patient-Specific Implants
P1-02.subtitle: From real anatomy and structural validation to traceable clinical delivery
P1-02.thesis: The value of patient-specific implants is extending from reproducing defect geometry to restoring function, while linking imaging, design, manufacturing, surgery and follow-up. Geometric accuracy, structural performance and clinical outcomes form a combined evaluation chain. Future competitiveness will depend on consistently delivering products that meet their designs and explaining their long-term stability or failure.

questions.question: How can patient-specific implants reconstruct craniomaxillofacial defects?
questions.focus: Distinguish cranial defect coverage, restoration of orbital space and mandibular load bearing, and explain how each task translates into geometric, fixation and outcome measures.

questions.question: How should patient-specific implants be designed for complex orthopaedic and spinal defects?
questions.focus: Design around remaining bone, the acetabular centre of rotation, vertebral endplate contact and fatigue loading together, and assess the result using postoperative positioning and longitudinal follow-up.

questions.question: How can image modeling and custom design improve implant fit?
questions.focus: Track errors arising from metal artefacts, segmentation, design generation, manufacturing and placement, using a common reference from original to follow-up imaging.

sections.title: Research Question and Industrial Implications: What Has Individualization Actually Changed?

blocks.text: Patient-specific implants first require an answer to a specific question: which patient differences must become differences in the device? Defect contours are only part of the answer. The location and thickness of remaining bone, spatial relationships to be restored, accessibility of fixation points, and differences between imaging and actual intraoperative anatomy all affect design. Personalization therefore means developing an actionable plan around patient-specific constraints and assessing whether the results satisfy them.

Craniomaxillofacial reconstruction involves distinct design tasks. Cranial reconstruction concerns defect coverage, contour continuity and fixation; orbital reconstruction must restore complex internal surfaces and volumetric relationships; and reconstruction of mandibular continuity must also address load transfer across the defect. These tasks share imaging and modelling tools but require success measures matched to their functions. Surface fit supports anatomical restoration, fatigue tests assess structural performance under specified loading conditions, and functional follow-up evaluates sustained performance in actual use. [R03][R06][R08]

A core issue in orthopedics and spine surgery is how to establish support using limited remaining bone. Acetabular design needs to simultaneously address bone volume, rotation center, and screw direction; vertebral body replacement structures must address the relationship between end-face contact and the fixation system. This leads to three sub-problems that can be investigated: does the contact area correspond to the actual bone surface? Can the planned position be achieved? Can the implanted position be maintained? Continuous recording of these three aspects is necessary to distinguish between design flaws, manufacturing deviations, and surgical execution errors. [R01][R05][R07]

blocks.text: Imaging and modelling issues run through all these settings. Achieving fit involves successive translations between original images, tissue interpretation, design files, manufactured devices and the patient; each transition requires an appropriate check. Commercial value consequently extends beyond implant supply to case collaboration, quality validation and delivery coordination. Progress means verifiably improving a weak link and carrying that improvement into actual cases through a reliable delivery process.

items: Craniofacial Issues: Is the reconstruction goal to cover defects, restore space, or connect load-bearing structures? How do fixed margins and local thickness correspond to this goal? Does improvement in symmetry on imaging simultaneously correspond to functional improvement that the patient cares about?

Orthopedic and Spine Sub-issues: Which remaining bone supports contact, and which supports fixation? How should contact area and structural stiffness be selected together? Does the actual positional deviation change the original support relationship, and at which interface will subsequent failures occur?

Modeling sub-questions: Is the determination of key bone boundaries stable? Can the reasons for the doctor's modifications to the model be recorded? What common reference should be used for digital design, finished product scanning, and postoperative imaging to compare changes in the same location at different stages?

blocks.text: N1 | Confirming bone surfaces at the surgical stage

The starting point for custom implants is to provide a real bone surface capable of contact and fixation. A 2020 acetabular study compared CT scans before and after removal of the old prosthesis in 8 out of 26 complex defects; all showed morphological changes upon reconstruction, with 3 requiring redesign adjustments. These changes involved both metal artifacts and altered bone volume during removal. The study used the Lima ProMade protocol. [R01]

The design raises a more fundamental question than segmentation accuracy: does the digital model describe the preoperative bone surface or the bone surface when the new device is implanted? If the contact area changes during debridement or removal of the old prosthesis, even if the segmentation and printing are perfectly faithful, the final product may still not support the intended area. Therefore, the image representation can be broken down into a reliable preservation area, an artifact-affected area, and a planned alteration area, each with different design constraints, ensuring that the imaging characteristics of each area correspond to the expected surgical changes.

Patient-specific characteristics should be incorporated into subsequent calculations based on these constraints. Manual verification of critical areas, preserving original slices, segmentation modifications, and clinical judgments, allows engineers to understand why a surface can bear weight. This node transmits reliable geometric boundaries to N2 and contact areas requiring postoperative verification to N5; conversely, records that could not be positioned intraoperatively should be returned to this stage to verify whether the deviation stemmed from modeling, resection, or previously unseen bone defects.
N2 | Translating clinical intent into constraints

After reliable geometry is established, design tools must still express the surgeon's fixation choices. A 2025 mandibular algorithm let surgeons select plate paths and screw positions, then generated spline interpolation, swept surfaces, integrated holes and printable files, with finite element stress assessment. Point selection took about one minute, followed by approximately 40–60 seconds for CAD generation. [R02]

This work separates clinical choices from repetitive geometric operations, providing a concrete object for understanding the value of automated design. Paths and hole positions are not decorative parameters; they determine which bone to fix to, surgical accessibility, and how the load crosses the defect. The algorithm then stabilizes these choices into a computable model. Therefore, when evaluating speed, input preparation, automated generation, physician review, and rework should be timed separately, avoiding treating the speed of local modeling as the entire case cycle.

From a research perspective, automatic generation must converge with structural verification at N3: printable morphology does not equate to proper load transfer. More informative follow-up experiments compare the number of design modifications, final hole placement differences, and the location of errors under the same defect and operator task. If multiple rapidly generated designs pass basic checks, it's necessary to explain which one improves surgical accessibility or preserves bone volume; this makes the computational tool a verifiable expression of clinical intent and preserves design versions for N8 workflow traceability.
N3 | Fatigue testing lightweight structures

The mandibular reconstruction advances morphological restoration to address the stress issues across the defect. This study established a geometric basis using 105 mandibular images, combined with finite element analysis and weighted topology optimization. The three types of structures achieved a weight reduction of 54.3%–69.7% compared to a solid design. The additive manufacturing reconstruction piece passed 250,000 dynamic loading cycles. The study also observed fracture or loosening of traditional bone plate configurations. [R03]

The design principle is to arrange internal supports according to different occlusal loading conditions rather than remove material uniformly. External shape serves anatomical relationships, whereas internal beam positions and dimensions serve load paths; these can have different optimization objectives. Finite element analysis estimates stress under specified boundary conditions, while bench tests establish whether the manufactured structure and its connections retain function under cyclic loading. Together, the methods can reveal problems that static peak values alone do not explain.

The next question arising from this is whether the boundary conditions can represent the usage scenario. The weakest point may shift when the bite position, muscle action, screw constraints, and bone contact change. A more suitable method for verifying parametric designs is to select edge combinations of geometry and load ranges, and then check whether the failure location matches the calculated expectations. This node merges with N2 at the design level and transmits the requirements to N4: only when the actual beam thickness, pore geometry, and connection area realize the design can the calculation and fatigue results have a clear correspondence; actual failure can then provide feedback to modify the support and fixation schemes.
N4 | Manufacturing variability for the same design

Manufacturing is an independent link in the evidence chain. A 2024 study had seven companies manufacture the same Ti6Al4V pelvic design by powder bed fusion and examined geometry and microstructure. Specimens from two companies had no defects in the features examined; the others had different defects, including local deviations of up to 5 mm, broken lattice elements, and pores or cracks. [R04]

The fact that the same input produces different outputs indicates that design documents cannot replace finished product verification. Different regions require different criteria: bone contact surfaces affect positioning, screw holes affect fixation, beam intersections affect local stress, and internal defects affect crack initiation during cyclic loading. While the average error across the entire surface helps describe the overall morphology, it may dilute significant deviations in a few critical areas. Therefore, inspection should begin by functionally locating the area, followed by selecting geometric measurements, imaging, or materials testing.

This node translates the design propositions of N2 and N3 into release-ready finished product requirements. Defects identified in manufacturing studies can pinpoint the locations and limiting configurations to be tested in the next stage, while clinical follow-up further examines the relationship between these characteristics and failures. Cross-enterprise comparisons should also retain printing orientation, post-processing, and measurement procedures to explain where differences originate. After entering N5 to N7, finished product scans should be saved so that post-operative deviations can be broken down between manufacturing and placement; after entering N8, these checks must become executable, not incidental, research procedures for every case.
N5 | Acetabular planning and maintenance of position

Acetabular reconstruction requires linking design intent to postoperative spatial position. An observational study of 10 aMace cases compared planned, postoperative and one-year CT data. Median deviations in inclination, anteversion and rotation were 3.6°, −2.8° and −1.2°, respectively; migration during follow-up was small, with no re-revision during that period. The study assessed achievement and early maintenance of position in severe acetabular defects. [R05]

The key to the method is distinguishing between two time lags: from planning to postoperative measurement achievement, and from postoperative to follow-up measurement maintenance. Directly comparing the plan with one-year imaging results in a mix of initial surgical deviations and post-implantation migration, making it impossible to pinpoint the areas requiring improvement. Co-registration methods and measurement repeatability are equally important, as displacements near measurement noise and clearly measurable migrations have different interpretations. Positional indicators should also be aligned with the original contact and fixation intentions to determine the direction of deviation.

This node builds on bone-surface confirmation in N1 and finished-device inspection in N4, but positional stability alone does not explain functional recovery. Remaining bone quality, fixation and case management also influence outcomes and should be recorded in subsequent consecutive cohorts. If rotational deviations alter expected loading, the design process can return to N2 to revise hole locations and guidance; if placement difficulties relate to imaging discrepancies, it can return to N1. This creates feedback that identifies causes rather than reporting only a successful reconstruction endpoint.
N6 | Restoring orbital surfaces and volume

The orbital branch emphasizes spatial support rather than mandibular trans-defect bearing. A retrospective study of 40 cases using TnR mesh compared preoperative and six-month CT scans. The volume ratio of the affected to healthy side decreased from 109.0% to 100.6%, and the median root mean square distance of the morphology decreased from 3.426 mm to 1.073 mm; the device used was a composite material of PCL and β-TCP. [R06]

Volume and local surface distances provide complementary information. Two shapes may have similar volumes but differ through local depressions in important support regions; conversely, improved local distances may not fully describe restoration of the overall space. Measuring both links the volumetric objective to surface fit. Mirroring the contralateral side provides a within-patient reference, allowing assessment of restoration after unilateral defects without assuming one standard orbital shape for every patient.

Compared to N5, both studies established a mapping from planned or reference morphology to postoperative images, but the indicators must be subordinate to the function of each site. Further research on the orbit needs to link volume and curvature restoration with changes in eyeball position, diplopia, and material support over time. Future studies could pre-define key support areas, analyze where geometric residual errors are concentrated, and then determine whether they are caused by edge design, placement channels, or local deformation. Such feedback can be returned to N2 to modify the curvature and boundaries, or it can proceed to N8 to develop a follow-up plan.
N7 | Vertebral endplates and long-term support

Vertebral reconstruction branches place the load-bearing problem between adjacent bone surfaces and the fixation system. A prospective four-case study in 2025, using individualized reconstruction after en bloc vertebral resection, combined with biomechanical testing, pain and functional assessments, and two years of CT scans, reported stable positioning with no subsidence or fixation failure. [R07]

Endplate fit has two roles: determining where support occurs and the area over which loads are transferred. A design that merely reproduces the external shape can still create local contact pressures that initiate failure, whereas maximizing contact area alone may make implantation harder. Assessment must combine geometric contact, material stiffness and posterior fixation conditions, and relate intended contact regions to changes in adjacent bone during follow-up. Mechanical tests should therefore preserve system-level load paths.

This connects computational and physical validation in N3 with clinical maintenance of position in N5: the mandible requires evaluation under cyclic occlusal loading, the acetabulum requires migration assessment, and vertebral reconstruction requires axial support and subsidence assessment. Four cases provide longitudinal observations for a particular surgical approach. The next priority is stratification by endplate bone volume and contact configuration to identify the constraints governing stability. Subsidence concentrated in certain regions should inform endplate-contact and support design, rather than simply increasing overall stiffness; N8 should preserve versions and imaging throughout.
N8 | Traceable in-hospital delivery

A 2026 PEEK in-house study incorporated quality management, manufacturing execution, risk analysis, process validation, and monitoring into a common framework. The paper details two craniofacial applications, with a timeframe of 3-5 days from imaging to sterilization and delivery, requiring no intraoperative modifications; the institution's reporting framework has supported the production of over 40 implants. [R08]

The research focus expands from a single device to the organizational process that delivers it repeatedly. Delivery time is directly relevant to surgical scheduling only if it includes image receipt, design discussion, printing, inspection and sterilization. A deeper question is whether decisions remain explainable when the process deviates: how inadequate images are returned, out-of-tolerance critical dimensions are handled, design changes reach manufacturing, and produced devices are managed after surgery is cancelled. These relationships must be preserved when the first seven nodes become a routine service.

Therefore, the clinical value of process validation lies in turning abnormalities into learnable records. If repeated cases show in-situ modifications in the same area, one can return to N1 to examine the bone surface or to N2 to examine the design expression; if the deviation only occurs under a certain manufacturing condition, one should return to the N4 revision process. Future cross-institutional replication should compare the first-pass yield, complete cycle, and follow-up acquisition rate under the same definitions, and retain undelivered cases. The feedback arrows in the figure represent this research task, supporting the tracing of causes from results and then narrowing the scope of the validation design with new validation.

Comparisons across anatomical sites can use a common data structure for contact regions, fixation regions and load paths while retaining site-specific endpoints. Acetabular rotation and migration, mandibular cyclic load bearing, and vertebral endplate subsidence can then be interpreted separately while sharing traceability from design version to finished device and follow-up imaging. The central aim is to relate each case outcome to explicit geometric and manufacturing parameters.

sections.title: Enterprise Roadmap: From Customized Products to Manufacturing Capabilities

blocks.text: BioArchitects' 2015 milestone illustrates patient-specific structures entering a defined product scope. K151692 records cranial/craniofacial titanium plates manufactured by electron beam melting. Materialise aMace organizes complex acetabular reconstruction around bone-volume analysis, position planning, fixation design and case collaboration. The original study evaluates the product's clinical position, while the official page describes the current service workflow; these sources address application outcomes and delivery capabilities, respectively. [R09][R10][R05]

LimaCorporate and HSS's 2022 announcement further changed the manufacturing location: the ProMade commercial facility located on a hospital campus has already provided the first implants for hip and shoulder reconstruction. This signifies a reduced distance between engineering and clinical collaboration, and "located in a hospital" itself does not determine the regulatory path. Manufacturing by a commercial entity near a hospital versus manufacturing by a medical institution for internal use requires separate explanations of liability. [R11]

blocks.text: The two 3D Systems pathways should be distinguished. VSP PEEK Cranial Implant received FDA clearance under K231834 on 4 April 2024, followed by a company announcement on 15 April. It is a non-load-bearing PEEK cranial implant manufactured by material extrusion. The company describes segmentation and modelling, the EXT 220 MED, material and a predefined production process together, showing an expansion from supplying a product to providing a controlled workflow. [R12][R13]

The 3D MAC Titanium Cranial Plate System received FDA clearance under K253116 on 18 June 2026, with the U.S. Army Medical Department as the applicant. A 28 July announcement describes 3D Systems' support for quality management, design validation and the submission. The implantable component is an EBM-manufactured Ti6Al4V titanium plate; an SLA resin cranial reference model supports fit checks and positioning. The components serve distinct functions through different materials and manufacturing processes. [R14][R15]

blocks.title: Product clearance and in-house production: distinct pathways
blocks.text: K253116 identifies BioArchitects K151692 as its predicate device, establishing a specific regulatory reference. The 2026 in-house PEEK paper organizes internal institutional production under the Article 5(5) framework. FDA product clearance, in-house production arrangements and clinical research provide evidence about device regulation, production organization and clinical outcomes, respectively. [R14][R08]

sections.title: Research–enterprise links through disclosed patent mechanisms

blocks.text: Patient-specific implants must turn preoperative anatomy into a placeable, fixable and traceable device. Metal-artifact research, the seven-manufacturer comparison and acetabular positioning follow-up expose errors in imaging, manufacturing and surgical execution. Patents help locate the design step addressing each error. Materialise aMace, Lima ProMade and 3D Systems cranial products supply distinct delivery settings with their own materials and anatomical sites.[R01][R04][R05][R10][R11][R12]
Mirroring is an intermediate step

US2018113992A1, with ORTHOPEDIX/MOSAIC named as applicants, describes contralateral segmentation, inversion, surgical connection features and comparison with ideal anatomy. This complements metal-artifact research: the opposite side supplies missing shape, while residual bone determines fit. Planned/achieved position and one-year migration in aMace cases supply downstream observations. Record which surfaces arise from mirroring, residual bone or manual reconstruction.[R01][R05][R10][R16]
Custom ceramics and internal architecture

CERHUM’s EP4454614A2 describes an additively manufactured synthetic biocompatible ceramic implant with TPMS-defined cavities, a specific disclosure by the company associated with MyBone. Orbital reconstruction supplies surface/volume outcomes, while manufacturing comparisons motivate internal-integrity checks. External fit, cavity continuity and fixation regions in a brittle structure are separate acceptance objects; an external scan cannot substitute for internal measurement.[R04][R06][R17][R20]
Delivering tools with the plan

Chulalongkorn University’s AU2018316389A1 treats small-joint patient-specific implants and surgical tools as a system. Beijing Dapu3D’s CN105982722A describes CT reconstruction, reduction, screw-hole planning and simulation on printed models. These extend surgeon-led jaw design from shape generation to operative sequence. Lima ProMade and 3D Systems point-of-care delivery provide organizational contexts: revisions should update tools, fixation plans and release records together.[R02][R11][R15][R18][R19]

sections.title: Translation and validation: variables, controls and decisions

blocks.text: The validation unit is a complete case version: imaging time, resection boundary, implant, tools and manufacturing record. Proposed comparisons separate mirroring from local reconstruction on identical residual-bone models, then compare matched guidance tools during simulated placement and apply the same geometry/fatigue checks across batches. Follow-up should link planned deviations, actual fixation and migration rather than infer stability from contour similarity.[R03][R04][R05] Manufacturing release and surgical usability are separate. A conforming contour may still need revision because of insertion path, soft-tissue obstruction or screw access. Simulate complete fixation, record unplanned contact, tool interference and revision reasons, and obtain independent checking. This locates the next change in contact surfaces, tools or imaging/resection interfaces.

headers: Proposed comparison, endpoints and next decision
rows: Geometry source

Compare mirroring with residual-bone-constrained reconstruction for one defect; measure gaps, hole positions and placeability. If artifacts change critical contact surfaces, reacquire data or revise planning before manufacture.[R16]
Internal/external agreement

Compare cavity layouts with identical ceramic envelopes using CT, scanning and fixation-region loading. Track shrinkage, voids and fracture sites. If thin-wall defects cluster at screw holes, revise fixation before comparing tissue entry.[R17]
Plan execution

Simulate placement using matched and generic tools; record insertion path, final pose, contact and revisions. If a tool blocks insertion or loses fit after resection, revise tools and implant together.[R18][R19]

If imaging versions and surface provenance are traceable, aMace/ProMade-like workflows can distinguish reconstruction from placement error. Track revision reasons, critical hole deviations and planned/achieved pose. If artifacts dominate, improve input quality first.[R10][R11][R16]

If CERHUM-type cavities can be reproduced across shapes, site-specific craniofacial inspection could develop. Track post-sintering connectivity, fixation cracks and batch shrinkage maps. Geometries outside prior experience require additional site-specific validation.[R17]

Point-of-care revision becomes reliable delivery only if tools, implants and release versions remain aligned. In 3D Systems/ProMade contexts, track total delivery time, simulated placement deviations, remakes and follow-up migration. More intraoperative adjustment despite faster production redirects work to planning interfaces.[R11][R15][R18][R19]

blocks.text: The most valuable record links each contact surface or hole to its design origin, manufactured measurement, operative adjustment and follow-up state. This separates the contributions of image reconstruction, cavity design and matched tools and identifies which experience can transfer to the next case.

sections.title: Observational Indicators and Research Priorities: Establishing Data That Can Explain the Results

blocks.text: The observation system is set up along a six-ring chain, retaining common case identifiers. The input end records image adequacy and model revisions; the design end records time and version updates; the manufacturing end records errors in key areas and rework; the surgical end records actual location and adjustments; and the follow-up end records stability and re-intervention. Only when the indicators correspond to each other can areas needing improvement be identified.

items: Priority 1: Establish a registration study of original images—design—finished product—postoperative images. Select relatively consistent defect types, distinguish the introduction and correction of errors at each stage, and avoid attributing all final errors to the design.

Priority 2: Conduct cross-manufacturing condition validation around key areas. In addition to overall deviations, predefine acceptable ranges for contact surfaces, hole locations, and weak connections, and document the impact of post-processing and inspection methods on the results.

Priority 3: Link design parameters to follow-up failures. Organize multi-center continuous cohorts according to remaining bone, fixation method, and reconstruction task, save planned and actual locations, and interpret the conditions for migration, subsidence, or structural failure.

Priority 4: Compare the complete case cost and time of delivery models. Include incomplete, reworked, and delayed cases, distinguish between direct production, system maintenance, and fixed inputs, and prevent evaluating economics solely based on printing material consumption.

blocks.text: These studies should prioritize data interpretability before sample expansion. A single failed case in a consecutive cohort, if its design, manufacturing, and placement records are preserved, may be more effective in driving improvement than multiple successful cases lacking procedural information. For improvements in clinical function, the reconstruction method and case conditions should also be documented to distinguish the contribution of individualized design from surgical and other treatment factors.

Research priorities should also reflect process dependence. If the input bone surface is unreliable, directly increasing the complexity of structural optimization may only refine the error boundary; if deviations in key manufacturing components are not yet controlled, expanding the clinical sample will not be able to explain design differences. A more effective sequence is to first identify the main sources of uncertainty, then narrow down the scope using local validation, and finally test functionality and cost in consecutive cases to generate feedback that can revise the design.

Based on the verification evidence from 2020 to 2026, the most noteworthy change is the gradual expansion of verification responsibility to cover the entire delivery process. The next stage of maturity will be marked by an organization's ability to consistently answer three questions: Why was this design adopted? Did the final product achieve the design? And can follow-up performance be explained by these choices? Only such evidence can enable patient-specificity to evolve from a single successful production to a continuously improving clinical service.

P1-03.subtitle: From osteogenic surfaces to sequential repair in infected environments
P1-03.thesis: Osseointegration and infection control must be evaluated at the same tissue interface over time. Structural support, surface treatment and local delivery have distinct roles; the relationships among reduced bacterial burden, immune changes and bone attachment determine whether an approach supports continuous repair.
