P2-02.title: Denture Accuracy and Patient Experience
P2-02.subtitle: From tissue-surface trueness to patient-perceived stability and convenience
P2-02.thesis: Digital dentures require evaluation at four levels: geometry, mechanics, clinical adaptation and manufacturing efficiency. Denture-base accuracy, framework retention and patient satisfaction answer different questions. Linking error locations, interventions and patient experience within the same workflow can explain which process improvements yield practical benefits.

questions.question: How to evaluate the precision and fit of the digital denture base?
questions.focus: Compare regions of the denture-base intaglio surface, distinguishing trueness, repeatability, seating gaps and intraoral fit.

questions.question: How do different manufacturing processes affect the efficiency of denture production?
questions.focus: Record clinical and laboratory working time, rework and delivery appointments separately to determine how workflow changes affect acceptable output.

questions.question: How do printed dentures affect retention, comfort, and patient experience?
questions.focus: Measure dislodgement force, stability, pain, speech and patient-reported outcomes together, tracking adaptation after delivery.

questions.question: How can the framework of a removable partial denture balance precision and function?
questions.focus: Evaluates the framework shape error, abutment tooth stress, clasp fatigue, and ease of insertion and removal within the same design.

blocks.text: The "fit" of a denture is both a manufacturing issue and a matter of mutual adaptation between the patient and the device. The base needs to replicate the shape of the tissue surface, the edges need to coordinate with oral activities, and the dentition needs to maintain the designed occlusal relationship; the partial denture framework also needs to utilize the remaining teeth and mucosa to bear the load. Printing technology can control the manufacturing geometry, but actual retention, stability, and comfort are formed by the entire device and its usage environment.

Accuracy assessment first requires a defined reference. Trueness describes deviation of a finished denture from its digital design, while precision describes agreement among repeat manufactures. The gap between a base and a model is another fit measure; intraoral responses add deformable mucosa, saliva and muscle activity. Paired measurements across these levels can establish whether smaller manufacturing deviations explain less local tenderness, more stable seating or fewer adjustments.

Manufacturing efficiency involves the redistribution of tasks between clinics and laboratories. Digitalization can change the number of impressions, designs, fittings, and deliveries, and may also increase initial design reviews or equipment handling. When comparing, it's best to use a single denture that meets delivery requirements as the unit, accumulating the time spent at both ends, rework due to failure, and patient trips. This allows you to determine at which stage savings occur and whether they are accompanied by changes in the patient experience.

The scientific challenges of removable partial dentures, particularly those involving precision and mechanics, are paramount. Clasps need to provide sufficient retention while allowing for patient insertion and removal; rests and connectors must distribute loads according to design, as manufacturing deformation can impose additional constraints on abutment teeth. Therefore, this study retains two branches—the denture base and the metal framework—which converge in the evaluation of the overall workflow's experience and efficiency. Both branches ultimately aim for a stable, comfortable, and easily maintainable delivery.
N1 | Tissue-surface comparison across seven systems

A 2024 study compared two milling and five printing systems, producing 10 maxillary denture bases per group and scanning them after seven days in artificial saliva at 37°C. The tested milling groups showed better intaglio-surface trueness and precision, while results varied among printing systems. [R01]

The significance of comparing multiple systems within the same study lies in reducing the differences caused by varying case designs and measurement methods. Materials and equipment are still used as a complete assembly in the experiment, so the results are suitable for identifying the bias characteristics of a particular workflow. The palatal, marginal, and alveolar regions of the denture base have different curvatures and thicknesses; the overall root mean square value can be used for overview, while local error maps are better suited for interpreting potential placement or compression problems. These two representations complement each other, preventing a large area from masking the bias in critical small areas.

Repeated scanning and storage measurements can be designed separately to estimate contributions from the scanner, registration and environmental changes. Stable regional biases suggest targets for parameter adjustment; large batch variation instead requires tracing materials, supports and post-processing. The next node treats support layout as an intervention, moving from system comparison to process explanation.
N2 | Support reduction and deformation

A study published online in 2023 and in a 2024 journal issue produced 80 maxillary denture bases and compared four support conditions: no reduction, reduction at the palate, reduction at the margins, and reduction at both. Printing time and resin consumption were recorded. Support settings affected accuracy and regional deviations; the fully supported control had a smaller overall error. [R02]

The support restricts displacement during printing and also increases removal, trimming, and material consumption. Reducing the support in a certain area may change the direction of local errors; therefore, resource optimization should be analyzed together with error distribution. Inferring a region's closer fit to the model from the color map can lead to a retention hypothesis; further measurements of actual dislodgement forces and local pressures are needed to link geometric changes to function. This sequence allows manufacturing experiments to provide both efficiency information and a clear clinical validation task.

The study can be conducted after printing, unsupporting, and post-curing to examine whether deformation occurs during manufacturing or after constraint release. Support schemes should also be repeated across different palatal vaults and alveolar morphologies to determine if a single setup can cover diverse cases. This stage branches towards patient experience and resource accounting, as the same support change can simultaneously affect finishing time, surface quality, and local fit; all three factors jointly determine its worthiness.
N3 | Clasp fit and insertion/removal

The 2022 study categorized clasps into eight groups based on manufacturing method, abutment tooth type, and undercut depth, with 10 cobalt-chromium clasps in each group. Fitting and retention changes were measured after up to 7200 insertions and removals. Initial retention and fit were generally similar between SLM and cast clasps, with regional and design factors contributing to performance. [R03]

The clasp needs to elastically deform during insertion and removal, and then regain retention after being in place. Therefore, the maximum dislodgement force in a single instance only describes the initial state. Repeated insertion and removal introduce cumulative deformation and wear, which can identify whether a design trades faster retention decay for a larger initial force. Different undercuts and tooth profiles change the deformation path of the clasp. Studies should record both its geometric parameters and the manufacturing surface condition, so that the results can be applied to the specific design rather than the manufacturing label.

After a single clasp is inserted into the complete framework, multiple retention and support elements interact and constrain each other. A tighter fit of a clasp may increase the overall placement resistance of the framework and may also alter the force on adjacent abutment teeth. Therefore, the next step employs a constraint-sensing model to connect the fit of individual components with the mechanical behavior of the entire framework. Clinical translation can further observe patient difficulties in insertion and removal, local pain, and the number of adjustments required, supplementing the functional implications of framework fatigue.
N4 | Constraint forces in complete frameworks

A 2023 study produced 60 cobalt-chromium removable partial denture frameworks with different designs and measured constraint and dislodgement forces on a model with horizontally movable abutment teeth. Mean horizontal constraint forces were similar for SLM and cast frameworks, but SLM results were less dispersed; the tested SLM groups met the study's retention target. [R04]

The advancement of this method lies in not only asking how much the framework surface deviates, but also observing how the deviation drives the abutment tooth. Flexible support allows deformation after placement to be converted into force, thus creating a measurable intermediate variable between geometry and function. Horizontal constraint and dislodgement force serve different purposes: the former reflects the additional load after placement, while the latter reflects the resistance during removal. Using both side-by-side helps identify whether high retention is accompanied by unnecessary continuous constraint.

Further research could increase vertical load and mucosal support, simulate load distribution for different tooth loss types, and pair the same framework scan data with the forces acting on each abutment tooth. If local dimensional deviations stably correspond to abnormal forces, manufacturing tolerances specific to that area can be established. Research on the reinforcing rods of titanium frameworks advances along the branches controlling manufacturing deformation, aiming to reduce structural mismatches that have already formed before entering the oral cavity.
N5 | Reinforcement bars for titanium frameworks

A 2025 study compared four reinforcement-bar configurations for commercially pure titanium SLM frameworks on a Kennedy Class I model. Reinforcement improved trueness in some regions, with different effects on clasps, rests and distal regions. Simple connecting or separate posterior reinforcement arrangements performed more favourably. [R05]

The reinforcing bar restricts structural displacement during manufacturing and leaves the final support structure after removal. Its design involves constraint location, stiffness, and release sequence; therefore, more material or a more complex arrangement does not necessarily result in smaller final deviations. Long, thin connecting structures can be scanned after printing, heat treatment, and bar removal to track deformation, separating residual stress release from original forming errors. These measurements help explain why one area improves while neighboring areas change.

Moving from regional trueness to function requires testing whether improved clasps and rests reduce whole-framework constraint forces and clinical adjustment. Geometry can serve as an intermediate endpoint, followed by the mechanical model in the preceding node and then representative patient studies. Reinforcement bars would thereby become a measurable manufacturing strategy whose benefit appears in seating, adjustment time and abutment loading rather than only in deviation-map colours.
N6 | Crossover trials distinguish workflow convenience from patient experience

A 2022 randomized crossover trial compared conventional and digitally printed dentures, recording multiple dimensions of satisfaction, quality of life, visits and adjustments. Conventional dentures performed better for speech, ease of cleaning, stability, comfort and overall satisfaction, while the digital route reduced some visit-related measures. [R06]

Experiencing two different dentures on the same patient helps control for differences between anatomy and general expectations, but the wearing sequence and adaptation process should still be included in the analysis. The value of multidimensional scales lies in explaining where the overall evaluation comes from: stability and comfort may be related to tissue surfaces, speech may be related to palatal thickness or tooth position, and ease of cleaning is related to surface and morphology. Breaking down these results allows feedback to be transferred to the corresponding design and fabrication stages.

Efficiency and experience become parallel outcomes at this stage. Fewer visits reduce patient burden, but the final choice depends on the quality of wear and subsequent adjustments. The next step is to integrate patient time costs, lab time, and adjustment records with sub-satisfaction levels into the same case file and track the impact of proficiency on both. The research figure thus separates resource accounting and fixation measurements, explaining the contributions of process and function respectively.
N7 | Clinical performance and costs

A retrospective study in 2025 compared 60 patients, 30 of whom received conventional dentures, and the digital group consisted of 15 patients who underwent milling and 15 who underwent printing. There were no significant differences in occlusal force and masticatory performance between the groups at six months, but the digital group had lower chairside time and laboratory costs. [R07]

Studies like supplement controlled trials with information on workflow organization. Time should be broken down into impression taking, design communication, trial fitting, delivery, and follow-up visits to determine if savings come from reduced steps, shorter single-step operations, or different case arrangements. Cost considerations should take into account staff experience and equipment utilization, as the same process may require different inputs in novice and experienced laboratories. Case allocation rules should also be clearly defined to analyze whether complexity affects route selection.

Presenting costs and outcomes together explains value better than a price per denture alone. When clinical outcomes are similar, compare total time per acceptable delivery; when experiences differ, present those differences alongside savings. This node combines denture-base and framework manufacturing questions and calls for records of rework for complete dentures and individual components, testing process benefits at the level of the whole prosthesis.
N8 | Measure objective retention and quality of life together

A randomized crossover study in 2026 compared the retention and oral health-related quality of life of thermocured, printed, and injected polyamide complete dentures. No significant differences in retention were observed in the printed and thermocured groups at different time points, while the polyamide group showed differences compared to the other two groups. [R08]

Simultaneous measurement of dislodgement force and patient reports can verify whether subjective stability aligns with the mechanical retention direction. Discrepancies between the two can be further analyzed based on factors such as marginal movement, pain, saliva production, and patient adaptation. Force measurement itself requires a fixed dislocation direction, loading position, and number of repetitions; otherwise, differences in the testing apparatus may be mistaken for differences in denture performance. Longitudinal repeated measurements can distinguish between initial delivery and post-adaptation performance.

Establishes a verifiable bridge between this node and multi-system geometric studies: by first recording tissue surface deviations in identical dentures, and then measuring intraoral dislodgement forces and individual patient experiences, it's possible to explore which areas of error have practical functional significance. Research should build models around this paired design and test them in another group of patients, ultimately feeding interpretable correlations back into design or support rules. Patient experience thus becomes one of the endpoints for manufacturing improvements, rather than an additional questionnaire after final product testing.
N9 | Experience in another workflow

A crossover randomized trial of in 2024, involving 18 participants, compared a different workflow for printed and traditional complete dentures, reporting comparable oral health-related quality of life and satisfaction. The study focused on the devices resulting from the materials used, their design, and the clinical procedures employed. [R09]

Compared with earlier trials, shifts the research question to which workflow conditions explain differences in experience. Material updates, trial-and-place strategies, tooth position recording, and operator experience can all be considered as factors to be examined, rather than simply attributing the publication year to technological advancements. Multicenter replication of the same workflow, or comparison of manufacturing methods under fixed clinical procedures, can progressively isolate these factors. Consistent definitions of individual experience and objective retention facilitate comparable results between different trials.

Feedback can be organized around patient events: investigate intaglio-surface deviations for local tenderness, clasp and whole-framework forces for insertion/removal difficulty, palatal form and tooth position for speech problems, and workflow organization for repeated visits. The feedback links represent these next research tasks, connecting accuracy to experience and specifying the clinical burden each manufacturing improvement aims to reduce and how it will be assessed.

sections.title: Evolution of Commercial Technologies and Products

blocks.text: BEGO launched WIRONIUM RP Complete in 2025, combining SLM metal frameworks, printed saddles and teeth in a modular digital workflow. Its official documentation emphasizes unified design and locating connection structures and lists exocad PartialCAD and material combinations. [R10] Partial-denture digitization thereby extends beyond an isolated metal framework to integrated components, requiring assessment of accuracy across their interfaces.

Carbon released DB 4000 baseplate resin in August 2026, targeting the M-series platform and employing a matching single-curing process. The company prioritizes fracture energy, printing accuracy, and production economics in its product development. [R11] This approach incorporates both baseplate material toughness and process repeatability into the product definition. The research and evaluation can then simultaneously design the shape, aging, and fracture tests of the complete baseplate, and further examine how these improvements affect post-delivery use.

Formlabs' current digital denture guideline presents Denture Base V2, Premium Teeth, assembly, and post-curing as a complete process, including repair and relining. [R12] It corresponds to the operational path of continuous production and maintenance in the laboratory. Base support, printing direction, and assembly method are no longer independent options, but rather jointly determine the manufacturing conditions of tooth position, tissue surface, and material condition.

The three routes respectively emphasize the synergy between metal and resin components, the performance of base material, and supporting manufacturing services. The enterprise timeline can track actual product changes accordingly: what materials were added, how the design entry point was altered, whether post-processing was changed, and which maintenance tasks received support. For procurement and R&D, the most valuable comparison is how many qualified deliveries these changes resulted in, what adjustments were reduced, and what personnel and equipment configurations are needed in actual production.

sections.title: Research–enterprise links through disclosed patent mechanisms

blocks.text: Denture accuracy connects with experience through tissue surfaces, framework restraint and occlusal adjustment. Base-system, clasp-cycling and framework studies supply intermediate geometric/mechanical endpoints; randomized trials show that these do not necessarily move patient experience together. BEGO WIRONIUM RP, Carbon DB 4000 and Formlabs supply metal-framework and resin-base contexts. Patents turn scanning, reinforcement and occlusal revision into testable operations.[R01][R03][R05][R06][R10][R11][R12]
Rescan after model-side preparation

Peking University Stomatology’s CN109223217A describes designing the partial denture and printed preparation guide, preparing teeth on the model with that guide, rescanning the prepared model, redesigning/manufacturing the denture, and delivering the guide with the denture for clinical use. Clasp-fit research connects the planned model, prepared model and eventual clinical tooth surfaces. BEGO supplies a framework context. Test transfer of model-side preparation to clinical surfaces through seating, restraint and adjustment.[R03][R04][R10][R13]
Reinforcement requires placement control

SIRONA’s CN111372536A describes digitally subtracting an internal reinforcement volume, printing the lower part, inserting reinforcement and printing above it. The patent retains internal reinforcement; R05 studies temporary bars during titanium-framework manufacture. Both address location-dependent deformation, with different retention states and materials. Carbon/Formlabs bases provide tissue-surface requirements: reinforcement needs checks for local warping, residual stress and tissue contact; flexural strength alone cannot establish comfort.[R02][R05][R11][R12][R14]
Occlusal redistribution and experience

Guangdong Jishu’s CN116350371A describes calculating tooth contact areas, adjusting digital occlusal surfaces and partly printing teeth/base together. Retention/quality-of-life trials and cost research motivate a full-workflow question: can contact design reduce adjustment while retaining retention, speech and chewing? Formlabs provides an assembly context. Separate assembly from occlusal changes to identify the source of patient benefit.[R07][R08][R09][R12][R15]

sections.title: Translation and validation: variables, controls and decisions

blocks.text: Validation should link tooth inputs, manufactured tissue surfaces, seating forces, occlusal changes and patient feedback. Compare preparation and reinforcement on controlled models before matched follow-up. Match material, tooth arrangement and operator; record initial insertion, after-adjustment and adapted states. Reduced global RMS with worse rest/distal deviations requires regional maps rather than a single accuracy conclusion.[R01][R04][R06] Clinical value includes adaptation and maintenance burden. Easy first insertion does not establish later stability; fewer adjustments can reflect follow-up schedules. Record speech, chewing, pain and overall satisfaction separately from seating force/contact, alongside actual wear time. Accuracy gains with discomfort prioritize contact/occlusal analysis over further reduction in global error.

headers: Proposed comparison, endpoints and next decision
rows: Model-to-clinic transfer

Compare planned/prepared model geometry, then check clinical tooth surfaces, rest gaps, clasp force and adjustments. An additional intraoral rescan is a proposed comparison branch. Dominant transfer error prioritizes guide positioning or preparation design.[R13]
Reinforcement position
Compare unreinforced and reinforced positions in one material for regional fit, bending and pressure. Higher stiffness with worse fit requires relocation.[R14]
Occlusal revision
Compare original and redistributed contacts on matched bases for adjustment, retention, chewing and discomfort. Faster adjustment with worse experience requires revised targets.[R15]

Traceable versions of model preparation, model rescanning and joint guide/denture delivery could enable model-to-clinic transfer assessment in BEGO-like production. Track planned/prepared model deviations, guide positioning, clinical rest gaps and initial seating. Unstable transfer prioritizes positioning/preparation design.[R10][R13]

Inspectable reinforcement without compromised tissue surfaces could support durability/pressure comparisons with Carbon/Formlabs-like bases. Track placement, warping and insertion-cycle changes. Coupon-only advantages do not support whole-denture expansion.[R11][R12][R14]

Contact redistribution that reduces adjustment across operators while preserving experience could yield reusable case rules. Track adjustment time, remakes, retention and quality of life by material/assembly. Accuracy without experiential gains prioritizes adaptation and occlusal targets.[R15]

blocks.text: Translation asks where fit improves, whether stability follows and whether patients benefit. Patent variables separate causes; clinical comparisons determine which changes merit retention. Both require records from the same denture.

The priority research is a paired cohort of denture base errors and clinical adjustments. Each denture will be preserved through design and final scanning. Adjustment areas, time taken, and pain locations will be marked at delivery and recorded repeatedly during the adaptation period. Deviations in the palatal, marginal, and alveolar regions will be modeled separately to analyze which errors can explain patient events. The study will also record tissue conditions and occlusal relationships to allow for separate estimation of manufacturing and case-related factors.

The second priority is whole-framework functional testing of removable partial dentures. Compare manufacturing and reinforcement strategies using the same partially edentulous model, measuring seating constraints, dislodgement, repeated insertion/removal and deformation under loading. Link geometry and force data from the same framework to identify sensitive regions before small clinical studies. For multicomponent designs, measure before and after assembly to isolate contributions from the metal framework, resin saddles and assembly.

Priority Study Three is a multicenter comparison that combines objective function, subjective experience, and process time. The primary endpoint can focus on the time required for patients to achieve stable wear, supplemented by retention, local pain, speech, and ease of cleaning. Randomization or pre-defined allocation helps reduce the influence of case selection; operator experience and production batch are used as stratification factors. The analysis preserves the patient's maxillary-mandibular association and explains the specific reasons for discontinuation of wear and loss to follow-up.

Priority Research 4 focuses on economic accounting with qualified delivery as the denominator. It incorporates equipment depreciation, consumables, labor, reprints, clinic adjustments, and patient travel into the same cycle, reporting the institutional and patient-borne costs separately. It examines changes in production scale and labor costs, and under what conditions test results remain valid. Such a model can explain why large, centralized laboratories and small clinics make different choices and identify the most worthwhile steps to reduce.

The focus of future data accumulation is to ensure that each measure of "more accurate" is linked to a specific usage outcome, and that each measure of "more efficient" indicates where resources are being reduced. Trade-offs are permissible between accuracy, retention, comfort, and efficiency; the task of research is to measure these trade-offs and translate them into selection criteria that can be used for design, manufacturing, and clinical delivery.

graph.title: Research pathway: denture-base and framework accuracy converge in patient experience and efficiency
graph.summary: Denture-base research moves from comparisons across systems to support optimization, while metal-framework research progresses from clasps to whole-framework loading and deformation control. Clinical crossover trials and workflow studies combine geometry, retention, adaptation and resource use to inform manufacturing and design.

nodes.title: Tissue-surface comparison across seven systems
nodes.question: Can different digital systems reproduce tissue surfaces consistently?
nodes.evidence: Ten specimens each from two milling and five printing systems were scanned after artificial-saliva storage; the milled groups showed better trueness and repeatability.

nodes.title: Support reduction and deformation
nodes.question: Can reducing supports balance accuracy and material use?
nodes.evidence: Eighty denture bases were compared after reducing palatal or marginal supports; accuracy and local deviation patterns changed with the strategy.

nodes.title: Clasp fit and insertion/removal
nodes.question: Can initial retention survive repeated insertion and removal?
nodes.evidence: Eighty SLM or cast clasps were compared across undercuts and tooth shapes, measuring gaps and performance through 7,200 insertion/removal cycles.

nodes.title: Constraint forces in complete frameworks
nodes.question: How does framework fit translate into forces on abutment teeth?
nodes.evidence: Sixty frameworks of different designs were tested on a flexible abutment model for horizontal constraint and dislodgement forces; mean constraint was similar for the two processes.

nodes.title: Reinforcement bars for titanium frameworks
nodes.question: How do temporary reinforcement bars affect regional deformation?
nodes.evidence: Four reinforcement-bar designs were compared in Kennedy Class I titanium frameworks; arrangement affected the trueness of clasps, rests and distal regions.

nodes.title: Early patient experience
nodes.question: Does reducing fabrication steps improve patient experience?
nodes.evidence: A randomized crossover trial compared several satisfaction measures and visits; conventional dentures performed better on some experience measures, whereas digital workflows required fewer visits.

nodes.title: Clinical performance and costs
nodes.question: How do workflow resources change when clinical outcomes are similar?
nodes.evidence: A retrospective comparison of conventional, milled and printed dentures in 60 participants found lower chairside time and laboratory costs in the digital groups.

nodes.title: Retention and quality of life
nodes.question: How do retention measurements and patient outcomes change together?
nodes.evidence: A crossover trial of three workflows found no significant retention difference between printed and heat-cured dentures; the polyamide group differed.

nodes.title: Experience in another workflow
nodes.question: Can patient outcomes be reproduced across specific workflows?
nodes.evidence: A randomized crossover trial in 18 participants found comparable quality of life and satisfaction for the tested printed and conventional dentures.

P2-03.title: Restorative Materials and Durability
P2-03.subtitle: Linking washing, polymerization, surfaces and environmental changes in a durability chain
P2-03.thesis: Printed dental resin properties depend on both the material and the complete post-processing workflow. Initial strength, fracture mode, dimensional stability, color and surface responses operate over different timescales. Research is moving from single-property comparisons to process interactions and performance retention after environmental exposure; complete devices and clinical events must validate practical value.

questions.question: How do flexural strength and fracture behaviour vary in printed resins and occlusal splints?
questions.focus: Distinguish strength, stiffness, toughness and fatigue damage, relating them to build orientation, local thickness and fracture paths.

questions.question: How do aging and the oral environment affect color and surface properties?
questions.focus: Use combinations of exposure media, thermocycling and surface treatments to explain concurrent changes in colour, roughness and retention of mechanical properties.

questions.question: How do different materials and post-treatments affect the reliability of restorations?
questions.focus: Include cleaning, drying, curing equipment and atmosphere in the material definition, linking version-tracked workflows to evaluation of complete devices.

blocks.text: Dental restorations and occlusal splints, after molding, still undergo cleaning, drying, curing, support removal, and surface finishing. Each step can change the dimensions, surface, and polymerization state; therefore, the material name is only the starting point for performance interpretation. Reliability studies need to specify at which processing stage the performance was measured, in what environment the sample was subjected, and for which task within the complete device it corresponds to.

Bending strength describes the maximum stress that the device can withstand under a specified load; bending modulus reflects the ease of deformation; fracture toughness relates to the conditions required for crack propagation; and hardness focuses on local surface response. These parameters can be improved simultaneously or independently. Occlusal plates need to maintain contact and withstand repeated loads; denture bases need to withstand overall bending and localized impacts; and crowns also involve wear, discoloration, and cementation. Evaluation should select the primary endpoint according to the device's function and retain auxiliary measurements that can explain the failure.

Changes in the oral environment include temperature, moisture, staining media, cleaning, and mechanical effects. Controlled experiments can alter these factors individually or construct combined challenges; the interpretability of the study is defined by the applied environment and load. Accelerated experiments are suitable for screening relative sensitivity, while clinical follow-up provides real-world usage events. The most valuable connection between the two is to examine the mechanism through specialized experiments after similar failure locations or response patterns have been observed.

The main theme of this research direction is "performance formation—performance retention—usage events." Cleaning and curing studies answer how materials are formed, aging and surface studies answer how they change, and complete device and clinical studies answer whether these changes increase the need for intervention. Product development also follows the lines of materials, supporting equipment, and maintenance processes. Research needs to preserve versions and processing conditions so that different tests can accumulate evidence for the same specific combination.
N1 | Curing and dimensional time courses

A 2021 study applied no post-curing or post-curing for 5, 15, 30 or 60 minutes to printed maxillary and mandibular denture bases and measured dimensions over 28 days. Shorter curing was associated with greater subsequent changes; mandibular bases were more sensitive, and changes were particularly pronounced during the first day. [R01]

The value of time series analysis lies in separating the shape immediately after leaving the device from its subsequent steady state. Post-curing can continue to alter the polymer network while simultaneously inducing or releasing deformation throughout the device; the different geometries of the upper and lower jaws mean that the same treatment may not produce the same response. Studies can use area scanning and key distances to track shrinkage, bending, and localized warping, and then correlate this with the degree of sample reaction to determine whether a change is primarily determined by continued material reaction or geometric constraints.

In the next round of experiments, the interval between manufacturing and measurement should be fixed, and the storage medium and temperature should be recorded. The waiting time before clinical delivery can also be used as a workflow variable to verify whether adjustments are reduced after dimensional stabilization. This step does not propose a uniformly extended curing scheme, but rather establishes a process window that matches the material, geometry, and stabilization time. Cleaning studies follow from here, tracking the impact of surface residues and solvent exposure before curing on subsequent geometry.
N2 | Interactions between atmosphere and printer

A 2022 study combined LCD and DLP printing with flash post-curing in air or nitrogen, assessing flexural properties, hardness, fracture toughness, degree of conversion, water sorption and solubility in hard occlusal-splint materials. Curing atmosphere and printing method affected several endpoints, but toughness and other measures did not all change in the same way. [R02]

The atmosphere test introduces surface reaction conditions into material evaluation. It helps verify whether the surface polymerization state is consistent with the overall mechanics, but the combined changes in hardness and bending results still require direct chemical or microscopic evidence for explanation. If a treatment only improves the surface without altering crack propagation, it may suggest that different properties are controlled by different structural scales. Measuring the fracture surface, surface layer, and internal network separately allows this difference to become a verifiable hypothesis for further investigation.

For actual occlusal splints, the surface will undergo grinding and polishing. Studies can compare the original surface, the surface after thin-layer removal, and the re-treated surface to observe whether advantages are retained. The combination design of atmosphere and equipment also suggests that, in addition to post-curing time, spectra, temperature, and processing methods need to be recorded. The next stage of equipment cross-experimentation expands this problem, allowing the "same resin" to be broken down into different reaction and manufacturing conditions.
N3 | Washing-induced geometric changes

The 2025 study used two printers to fabricate a three-unit bridge and compared five cleaning strategies, including ethanol, isopropanol, and a combination of these with ultrasound. Geometric library registration analysis showed that equipment differences, along with evaluation methods such as angle and distance, collectively influenced the observed deformation response. [R03]

The three-unit structure is more effective than simple specimens in revealing local displacement and span variations. By fixing one end and comparing the position of the other, the angular shift that might be amortized by the overall best fit can be revealed. Therefore, the cleaning task thus includes two aspects: removing unreacted residues and maintaining the designed shape during processing. Interactions may exist between solvent, sonication, and drying, making it suitable for measurement in controlled combinations, rather than relying solely on cleaning time as the sole explanation.

Retain scans before and after cleaning and after final curing, together with mass changes and surface-residue analysis, to separate removal effects from deformation. A faster cleaning method may not reduce total workflow cost if it increases subsequent deviations. This node branches into surface and orientation studies: residual surface state affects coatings and colour, while layer orientation may influence thin-wall sensitivity to cleaning and stress release.
N4 | Crossed equipment comparisons reveal processing effects in the same resin

A 2025 study crossed two DLP printers and two curing devices using the same fixed-restoration resin, measuring dimensions, fracture strength and degree of conversion by FTIR. Performance differed among combinations, with particularly notable effects of the post-curing device on several outcomes. [R04]

The cross-design allows for the separate consideration of the printing and additional polymerization stages. Observing degree of conversion and strength together can verify whether the material response is consistent with changes in load; dimensional changes also remind researchers to retain geometric constraints. It should be noted that different devices simultaneously alter the spectrum, energy distribution, and temperature; therefore, device names are merely identifiers of the combination. Further measurement and control of these actual physical quantities are needed to extract a general mechanism.

By combining the node with the dimensional time series, a more complete process window can be defined: the processing range that achieves stable shape, sufficient reactivity, and required load-bearing capacity under given material, thickness, and equipment conditions. Validation should cover different locations within the equipment and multiple batches of material, observing the sensitivity at the window's edges. Once these conditions are saved in the clinical product version record, subsequent fractures or surface changes can potentially be traced back to the specific manufacturing process.
N5 | Combining orientation and duration

In 2025, 180 NextDent Ortho Rigid specimens were prepared, with three orientations and three curing conditions used to compare flexural strength, modulus, and microhardness. Post-curing improved the measured properties; a 45-degree combination with extended curing resulted in higher flexural strength, and the orientation altered the treatment response. [R05]

The relationship between the lamination direction and the load direction means that the same material may exhibit different weaknesses at different structural locations. A complete occlusal splint contains bending zones as well as areas of localized contact and support removal; therefore, the optimal orientation of the strip specimen needs further verification through device geometry. The manufacturing orientation can be changed while maintaining consistent thickness and occlusal contact, allowing for the measurement of localized strain, fit, and fatigue crack locations, and observation of whether directional effects are retained in the material specimen.

Extended curing can also lead to changes in time, color, and size; therefore, optimal conditions should be set around multiple outcomes. Studies can incorporate the main load-bearing targets, allowable deformation, surface requirements, and production time into the optimization problem, and repeat this process with independent batches. This node connects to environmental studies because the initially high strength only holds true for long-term service tasks after hydrothermal treatment, abrasion, and repeated loading.
N6 | Glazing and thermal cycling in coffee

A 2025 study used 180 specimens of conventional and four printed denture-base materials to compare mechanical polishing with VITA AKZENT LC glazing, followed by 5,000 thermocycles in coffee. Effects on strength, hardness, roughness and colour depended on the material; the glaze did not improve all outcomes together. [R06]

This result elevates surface finishing from a mere aesthetic step to an integral part of the material system. Coatings can alter roughness, protect the outer layer, or introduce new interfaces, and their effects are influenced by the wetting and bonding states of different substrates. To explain why a certain combination improves hardness without improving color, one can consider surface morphology, coating thickness, and interfacial integrity after aging. Improvements at a single endpoint cannot replace observations of other functions; therefore, multi-endpoint design is directly relevant here.

Researchers can further simulate clinical grinding and repolishing to examine whether the coating has been locally removed and whether performance can be restored. The coffee thermal cycle provides a scenario where coloring and temperature act simultaneously; setting coloring and thermal cycling separately helps identify their respective contributions. This branch ultimately leads to patient appearance and maintenance events, joining another branch of mechanical aging to explain when device intervention is needed.
N7 | Multiple properties after thermal cycling

A 2025 study of 72 specimens compared heat-cured and printed denture-base polymers, measuring strength, hardness and colour after thermocycling. Flexural strength, tensile strength and hardness of the tested printed materials were affected by ageing, highlighting the need to assess initial properties and retention after environmental exposure separately. [R07]

Simultaneous observation of multiple mechanical parameters can distinguish between surface softening and changes in overall load-bearing capacity. Tensile and bending parameters differ in their sensitivity to defect location and stress state, and hardness primarily describes the local surface layer; therefore, inconsistencies in these parameters can help pinpoint the scale of change. Further integration with water absorption, dissolution, and chemical characterization can examine candidate mechanisms such as plasticization, residual reactions, or interfacial changes, rather than attributing all performance degradation to a single explanation.

For materials, it is advisable to provide both absolute values before and after aging, as well as the retention rate. High initial values accompanied by a significant decrease, versus lower initial values that remain stable, may correspond to different application choices. For complete devices, performance margins also need to be determined by considering thickness, local stress, and allowable deformation. The next step is to expand material screening through different hydrothermal environments to verify whether the initial ranking is maintained under different environmental challenges.
N8 | Hydrothermal screening in artificial saliva

A 2026 study placed four types of occlusal splint materials in artificial saliva at 60 degrees Celsius and evaluated them at 24, 48, and 72 hours. The hardness, modulus, strength, and failure strain of the different materials showed varying changes; this condition was defined as an accelerated model for comparing hydrothermal sensitivity. [R08]

Using a fixed medium and temperature helps identify the relative response, while continuous time points show whether the change occurs rapidly and then stabilizes, or continues to progress. Different mechanical endpoints can show different time trajectories, indicating the need to focus on both structural deformation and failure. Mechanism verification can incorporate water absorption mass, dissolution analysis, thermal analysis, and fracture surface observation to determine whether the response is consistent with network or surface changes. Strength curves alone can only suggest candidate relationships between these mechanisms.

When advancing the to real-world use, it's advisable to first introduce longer observations and cyclic contact at commonly used temperatures before selecting the complete occlusal splint geometry. The research's connection objective is to verify whether environmental sensitivity predicts clinical deformation, cracking, or replacement, rather than directly converting acceleration hours into years of use. Comparing clinically retrieved devices with experimental samples from the same batch offers the opportunity to identify the most critical environmental and loading combinations for real-world use.
N9 | Single-crown responses during use

2026 Two-year follow-up report of 30 printed resin-based composite posterior single crowns: 93% retention and 87% success rate, with recorded debonding and some color changes. [R09] This study provides observation of specific material, geometry, post-treatment, and cementation combinations in patient use.

Clinical events reorganize previously scattered material indicators. Color changes may trigger cosmetic interventions, debonding involves bonding and preparation, and fracture or wear is related to material and stress. If follow-up records include manufacturing details, local thickness, and treatment methods, corresponding experiments can be developed for each type of event. Occlusal plates and baseplates need to establish their own usage cohorts, using definitions of deformation, fracture, relining, and replacement that match their functions.

Clinical-to-experimental feedback can use event-driven designs: identify where and when changes occur most often, then select corresponding specimens, environments and cyclic tasks. Improvements in polymerization and surface treatment can then be evaluated by whether they reduce actual interventions. The final convergence retains distinct material categories and uses while sharing version tracking and event-based analysis, creating reproducible links between durability development and patient use.

sections.title: Enterprise Material and Post-processing Route Evolution

blocks.text: VITA's 2024 product documentation lists AKZENT LC and other systems for individualizing polymer-restoration surfaces, incorporating stains and glazes into digital restorative workflows. [R10] A 2025 independent experiment directly used AKZENT LC on different printed denture-base materials, showing why surface treatments must be evaluated with their substrates. [R06] The company supplies a usable treatment, while research explains its effects in specific combinations.

A NextDent document issued in 2025 provides a material–printer compatibility table with a November 2024 status date, distinguishing validated combinations from those still being evaluated. [R11] This treats materials as equipment-linked systems rather than isolated resin bottles. Compatibility status can guide testing, but specific curing, cleaning and geometric conditions must still be documented for reproducible manufacturing.

Carbon released its DB 4000 baseplate resin in August 2026, emphasizing fracture work, precision, and a single-curing process for its M-series platform. [R12] The product description shows a focus shifting from initial strength to damage tolerance and the manufacturing process. Corresponding independent evaluations can compare fracture work after aging, the location of intact baseplate failure, and actual rework, and track material updates and process updates separately.

Formlabs' current digital-denture guide covers separate-component assembly, surface finishing, repair and relining. [R13] Including maintenance means that properties of newly manufactured materials must be assessed alongside colour, bonding and load bearing after reprocessing. Product timelines can therefore track changes in initial manufacturing and repair protocols, asking whether they reduce repeated work and patient downtime over the service period.

These enterprise approaches collectively reflect a shift in product organization: materials, equipment, surface treatment, and maintenance are increasingly being delivered as a package. Observable aspects of industry competition include package validation coverage, process time, batch repeatability, and post-failure recovery methods. Different organizations achieving different performances using the same materials can trace the reasons along these records, rather than attributing all differences solely to printers or resin formulations.

sections.title: Research–enterprise links through disclosed patent mechanisms

blocks.text: Durability depends on the final material state. Cleaning, atmosphere, post-curing, glaze and storage jointly alter shape and properties. NextDent compatibility, Carbon DB 4000 and Formlabs denture workflows supply device–material contexts; VITA AKZENT LC supplies finishing context. Patents define regional properties, color forming and presintering infiltration as research variables.[R02][R03][R04][R10][R11][R12][R13]
Regional curing and properties

Shanghai Zhouge’s CN121101779A describes a photopolymer shell with parameter-dependent regional mechanical properties for orthodontic appliances. Atmosphere, orientation and curing studies share the conversion/property question. For restorative-material research, test whether regions differ in hardness and water uptake. NextDent compatibility helps bound combinations; the patent does not establish denture/crown durability, so regional repeatability comes first.[R02][R04][R05][R11][R14]
Color formation and residue

Jiaxing University/Jiaxing Yabao’s CN113416071A describes ink/slurry co-curing with regional color/transparency. Glaze and coffee-thermocycling research asks whether color derives from bulk, surface layers or aged adsorption. VITA provides a surface-color context. Compare before/after finishing and wear while examining density/cracks to determine whether optical stability accompanies structural retention.[R06][R07][R10][R15]
Thermal processing changes internal structure

Peking University Stomatology’s CN118078643A describes presintering, liquid infiltration, drying, final sintering and polishing of zirconia, controlling microstructure/phases through infiltration and thermal schedules. It parallels curing-equipment research methodologically: finishing determines final state. Comparisons with Carbon/Formlabs resin routes can share dimensional, wet-strength and color endpoints while interpreting polymer conversion and ceramic phases separately.[R01][R04][R12][R13][R16]

sections.title: Translation and validation: variables, controls and decisions

blocks.text: Use a state matrix after manufacture, cleaning, post-treatment and hydrothermal/wear exposure. Match thickness and regions, retain unaged controls and alternative finishing combinations, and distinguish dimensional from material deterioration. Artificial-saliva screening identifies mechanisms/ranking before device/use-condition confirmation. Two-year crown debonding and color changes remain separate endpoints.[R03][R08][R09] Trace aged changes to pre-exposure states. Strength may reflect conversion, pores or thickness; color may reflect adsorption or bulk change. Retain repeated regional measurements and matched destructive-test specimens, recording polishing, glaze and cleaning versions. Changed processing requires rechecking rankings rather than transferring durability judgments by trade name.

headers: Proposed comparison, endpoints and next decision
rows: Regional resin
Compare uniform/regional parameters in one resin for conversion, hardness, uptake and relaxation. Interregional cracking or storage drift narrows parameter differences.[R14]
Optical origin
Compare bulk/surface coloring before/after aging for color, roughness and strength. Color removal by polishing or uneven wear exposure requires depth/finishing revision.[R15]
Infiltration/sintering

Compare infiltration variants from equal green bodies for phases, translucency, pores and fatigue. Better translucency with cracks/wet deterioration redirects infiltration and thermal processing.[R16]

Compatibility records retaining complete finishing versions could support regional state maps. Track device, atmosphere and cure-duration effects. Pronounced regional drift prioritizes narrower property windows.[R11][R14]

Distinguishable aging mechanisms in colored ceramics and VITA-like finishing could support color-source-specific maintenance. Track color, wear and cracks jointly. Optical gains cannot offset structural deterioration; selection remains site-specific.[R10][R15]

Infiltration/sintering retaining wet mechanics in whole crowns could support indication-matched resin comparisons. Track fatigue, margins, debonding and repairs, separating bulk and bonding interfaces. Extend to thin walls/bridges after process stability.[R16]

blocks.text: Material selection must explain when, where and after which exposure properties change. Linking state matrices to device failure determines whether to revise resin curing, ceramic structure or surface maintenance.

sections.title: Observation Indicators and Priority Research Tasks

blocks.text: The first priority is joint material–process design. Hold device geometry constant while controlling build orientation, cleaning, curing equipment and atmosphere. Measure dimensions and polymerization in stages, then compare load bearing after environmental exposure. Factorial designs identify interactions, and independent batches test consistency. The output should be reproducible processing ranges and the principal sensitivities that lead to nonconforming devices.

The second priority task is to separate the environment from the surface mechanism. Individual and combined treatments using water, coloring media, thermal cycling, and mechanical abrasion are employed to compare the original, polished, glazed, and maintained surfaces. Roughness, color, water absorption, hardness, and cracking are measured simultaneously to analyze which changes occur first. This sequence allows for the determination of whether surface changes are the primary cause of failure, accompanying phenomena, or early indicators that can predict subsequent damage.

Priority Task Three is fatigue and deformation at the device level. For occlusal splints, the focus is on the contact area, thin walls, and repeated insertion and removal; for denture bases, the focus is on arch bending, local thickness, and impact; and for crowns, the focus is on local loads and cementation. Primary endpoints are set for each application, and experimental crack locations are compared with clinical events. Local strain and fracture surface recordings help interpret whether material improvements truly alter the structural failure path.

Priority Task Four is to track usage and maintenance by product version. Upon delivery, record material batches, equipment, processing, and critical dimensions. During follow-up, record deformation, cracks, color interventions, repairs, and replacements. Link manufacturing and events through case-level data to select the most worthy process hypothesis for validation. Replacement reasons and loss to follow-up are kept in separate categories, allowing for separate explanations of material usage periods and patient selection.

The evaluation of material advancements ultimately boils down to four indicators: repeatability of qualified manufacturing, performance margin after environmental impact, time to first intervention, and continued use after maintenance. These correspond to process, material, device, and service levels, respectively. Only when these levels form a verifiable link can durability studies provide a clear basis for material formulation, equipment configuration, and clinical application.

P2-04.title: Denture Bonding and Integration
P2-04.subtitle: From Manufacturing Integration to Long-Term Use and Maintenance
P2-04.thesis: The value of integrated dentures lies in reducing manufacturing errors and improving reliability throughout the entire lifespan. Current evidence has shifted the focus from whether the teeth and denture base can bond securely to assembly deviations, material transition zones, repair structures, and long-term patient use; commercial systems have also entered the regional delivery phase. The next stage of competition will depend on whether manufacturing simplification can continue to translate into fewer adjustments, lower failure rates, and easier maintenance.

questions.question: How to improve the bonding strength between artificial teeth and denture base?
questions.focus: Track combinations of denture teeth, base material, bonding agents and ageing conditions to explain changes in both strength and failure location.

questions.question: Can integrated printing reduce assembly errors?
questions.focus: Separate tooth-socket design, linked-tooth arrangements, continuous material forming and post-processing to establish how each affects tooth position and occlusal relationships.

questions.question: How can denture relining and repair interfaces remain reliable?
questions.focus: Evaluate reline interfaces, fracture-repair structures and subsequent ageing separately, relating each to clinical intervention events.

sections.title: I. Research Questions and Industrial Significance: Placing delivery and maintenance on the same quality chain

blocks.text: This chapter focuses on research published up to November 3, 2026, on tooth-base connections, fabrication integration, and subsequent maintenance. The evaluation focuses on a denture delivered to a patient, designed for continued use and maintenance. Material samples reveal local properties, digital models describe geometric changes, and complete devices and clinical observations link these changes to actual use. The main research thread is to establish a testable chain of evidence connecting initial connection strength, fit location, post-aging load, and patient intervention events.

The connection problem involves both mechanical and geometric dimensions. The connection area needs to transfer loads, while the tooth position determines whether the design relationship can be retained in the finished product. Thickening the binder or changing the positioning method may affect both strength and tooth position simultaneously; therefore, optimizing only one indicator may not improve the final delivery. Existing cyclic loading and tooth position experiments have revealed these two dimensions respectively, and also suggest that subsequent comparisons should incorporate material composition and manufacturing processes into the same design. [R01][R02]

Integrated dentures can be categorized into three levels based on their manufacturing content. The first level consists of a single resin-printed monolithic geometric model, used to answer whether canceling assembly changes position; the second level comprises continuously formed structures of different colors or materials, involving the joint realization of tooth and denture functions; and the third level comprises clinically deliverable commercial dentures, including supporting materials, post-processing, and scope of use. These three levels correspond to geometric, material, and instrumentation issues, respectively, each providing different types of evidence and preserving material differences between different commercial systems. [R02][R03][R04]

The industrial implications of extend to the entire delivery process. Laboratories need to determine if the savings in labor are sufficient to cover equipment, materials, and rework costs; clinics need to assess whether adjustments and repeat visits are reduced; and patients are more concerned with the longevity of their dentures. The interests of these three parties can align, or they can shift: faster initial delivery, but requiring a complete remake after partial damage; fewer manufacturing steps, but more finishing and color treatments. Only by considering both these inputs and results can the total cost change resulting from simplified manufacturing be assessed.

blocks.title: Main evaluation framework
blocks.text: Uses the entire process of each denture, from design to the point where intervention is needed again, as the comparison object. The precision at delivery, failures during use, restoration after repair, and eventual disuse constitute a continuous but distinct hierarchy of outcomes.
N1 | Material combinations and fatigue

A study by Löscher et al., published online in 2024 and included in the 2025 issue, used 11 combinations of artificial teeth with the same tooth shape and connection area, with 8 pieces in each combination. The artificial teeth, denture bases, and connection methods were varied, and then thermomechanical cycles and destructive loads were applied. The duration of cycles and destructive forces differed among the combinations, with some milled, pressed, and prefabricated systems showing better performance. [R01]

This design answers the question of which component in the system becomes the weakest point first. A uniform geometry reduces the interference of tooth shape on stress, while variations in the combination of tooth structure, base, and connector help identify compatibility issues that cannot be detected by evaluating materials individually. Fatigue survival and final failure force serve different purposes: the former observes damage accumulation, while the latter describes the remaining load-bearing capacity. Only by considering both side-by-side can one determine whether a particular combination will detach early or withstand a higher load after cycling.

Failure location and strength must be interpreted together. A stronger interface can shift cracks into a tooth or the base, changing load transfer and subsequent repair options. At the same failure load, a readily replaceable tooth failure and a deep base fracture have different service consequences. Research therefore branches into retaining separate components with better positioning and bonding, or changing manufacturing to reduce assembly. Both approaches should ultimately be compared using common outcomes over the service period.
N2 | Tooth-socket geometry and linked-tooth arrangements define assembly constraints

A 2025 study compared tooth-socket and linked-tooth arrangements in 80 dentures, alongside other manufacturing routes. Three-dimensional tooth-position analysis found the smallest deviations in a semi-conventional flask-and-press group; among relevant separately printed combinations, a full-arch linked dentition with a grooved socket design performed better. [R09]

Tooth sockets accommodate bonding agent and constrain displacement. Larger clearance permits seating but also tooth movement; too little clearance can cause local interference and incomplete seating. Research should therefore examine clearance, depth, locating surfaces and channels for excess bonding agent rather than simply choose a groove or flat socket. A full-arch linked dentition can also convert local displacement into overall deformation, requiring assessment of anterior and posterior regions together.

These interpretations propose a further distinguishable competitive mechanism. If the error originates from assembly gaps, increasing positioning constraints should improve repeatability; if the error mainly stems from the warping of the connecting teeth themselves, excessive constraints may store stress. Scanning at three stages—post-printing, post-trial assembly, and post-bonding—can verify which interpretation aligns with the changed location. The next step, eliminating the assembly stage, forms a mechanism reference, allowing design optimization and manufacturing integration to enter a common geometric evaluation framework.
N3 | Geometric effects of eliminating assembly

A 2026 in vitro study divided 60 dentures into four groups of 15. Two were printed as monolithic units using either model resin or tooth-coloured provisional-crown resin; the other two used separately printed bases and complete or segmented tooth arches bonded afterwards. Three-dimensional matching showed smaller full-arch and regional tooth-position deviations in the monolithic groups. [R02]

The value of a single-piece reference lies in eliminating the manual assembly step, thereby helping to pinpoint the source of finished product deviations. It also alters the material and molding state, so subsequent experiments should control resin shrinkage, support positions, and curing conditions within the same design. Retaining scanned files for each processing node allows observation of whether errors gradually increase or are partially offset during subsequent processing. Preserving data from all six zones provides a better chance of identifying localized anomalies related to occlusal contact than simply reporting the overall arch average.

This research line translates the geometric benefits of integration into testable clinical questions: whether reduced deviations improve initial placement, adjustment time, and occlusal reconstruction. Individual trials of the model or temporary crown resin handle error attribution, while the final material denture handles delivery evaluation. Connected by a common digital design, measurement coordinates, and tooth area definitions, these two levels avoid mixing differences caused by different resins or different cases in comparisons of manufacturing routes.
N4 | Load bearing across continuous material regions

The 2023 study used Stratasys J55 and Vero series materials to print the tooth color and baseplate color areas as continuous units, comparing damage, water absorption, and geometric performance after thermal cycling. The experiment found some favorable load-bearing and shape properties, but also observed high water absorption. [R03]

Continuous forming reduces subsequent assembly while still retaining different functional areas. The teeth need to resist occlusion and wear, while the denture base needs to adapt to tissue surfaces and overall curvature; both have different requirements in terms of thickness, color, and localized loads. Therefore, it is necessary to observe how stress is transferred in material transition areas, whether the dimensions change after environmental water absorption, and from which region the final crack originates. Only by incorporating both geometric and material consistency can it be determined whether the benefits of continuous manufacturing come from reduced interfaces or the material system itself.

The Vero specimen provides the structural concept and testing methodology in this chain. When moving towards deliverable materials, the same loading methods should be maintained, and water absorption, dissolution, and mechanical retention should be remeasured. In this way, the relationship between the preceding and following studies is one of problem-method continuity, while specific properties follow their respective material systems. The next step is to conduct direct experiments on TrueDent to supplement the commercial material's response after surface treatment and environmental aging.
N5 | Surface aging of commercial materials

A 2024 TrueDent material study compared three surface treatments in 90 specimens and included 5,000 thermocycles. Ageing reduced flexural strength, while the glazed group retained strength and surface hardness more favourably. Surface finishing after material jetting was treated as an independent variable. [R04]

Post-treatment can simultaneously alter surface defects, water absorption channels, and outer layer load-bearing capacity, making it suitable for evaluation in conjunction with material formulation. If strength changes only occur under specific surface conditions, the contributions of surface protection and specimen size changes should be further differentiated. Fracture observation, surface roughness, and changes in mass before and after aging can serve as intermediate measurements connecting mechanical results with possible mechanisms. For complete dentures, it is also necessary to consider whether wear or grinding has removed the surface layer, thus altering the initial advantages with use.

This node merges with the geometric branch during the delivery phase. Accurate shape but unstable post-processing, or stable material properties but tooth misalignment, can both increase the need for clinical intervention. Therefore, tooth position, material samples, and surface finish can be recorded simultaneously within the same production batch, using operator and equipment batches as analytical factors. These manufacturing records are then correlated with patient events to examine whether a particular surface or curing step truly shortens or extends the time to no intervention.
N6 | Re-establishing reline interfaces

A 2025 DentaBase study compared mechanical and chemical pretreatments in 90 specimens. Median tensile strength was 25.9 MPa in the intact control, 11.5 MPa in the untreated relined group and 19.7 MPa after sandblasting plus monomer treatment. All relined groups failed at the base–reline-material interface. [R05]

The relining restores tissue surface adaptation, thus the research task differs from the primary tooth-base connection. The original base has already formed a cross-linked network, and the new material needs to establish continuous load transfer on its surface. Roughening increases the contact path, and chemical treatment may improve wetting or surface bonding; the combination of these two deserves further differentiation using surface morphology and chemical characterization. The results of different treatment groups also indicate that a monotonic relationship should not be assumed between the number of complex steps and the connection effect.

Subsequent validation of the complete device can begin with thickness and edges: the same interfacial strength may result in different crack propagation under varying relining thicknesses, baseplate flexibility, and load locations. Edge sealing, localized peeling, and bending loads should be included in the experiments first, followed by recording when patients require a second intervention. This step, along with the repair step, advances manufacturing reliability to post-maintenance reliability and defines relining as an independent event for the clinical registry.
N7 | Repair reinforcement and aging

A 2026 repair experiment compared a complete control, simple resin repair, and metal and thin/thick glass fiber reinforcement. After zero or 10,000 thermal cycles, three-point bending was performed. The thick glass fiber group showed the greatest improvement; the strength after cycling was not significantly different from the complete control, and the failure morphology also changed with the reinforcement method. [R06]

This design evaluates bonding interfaces and reinforcement in the same specimen, separating bonding fractured surfaces from restoring load-bearing capacity. Reinforcement thickness, length and location govern load transfer across the repair; stiffness transitions may shift stress into adjacent regions. Restored flexural strength therefore needs to be interpreted alongside crack location and complete or incomplete fracture. For devices intended to be repaired repeatedly, the structure retained after fracture also affects the feasibility of another repair.

Complete dentures can be further modeled using representative midline, alveolar, and marginal fractures to compare the effects of the same reinforcement method at different locations and record the original material that needs to be removed for repair. Statistical design can pre-define acceptable load-bearing differences and, with a sufficient sample size, evaluate the degree of restoration. Combined with relining studies, clinical follow-up can differentiate between fitting maintenance, structural repair, and complete denture fabrication, avoiding merging interventions of different natures into a single repair rate.
N8 | Patient outcomes test the acceptability of technical workflows

A crossover randomized trial in 2024 enrolled 18 edentulous patients to compare oral health-related quality of life and satisfaction between 3D-printed and traditional complete dentures. The tested printing workflow yielded patient-reported results comparable to traditional dentures. [R08]

A crossover design lets the same patient experience both options, reducing differences in anatomy, prior experience and general expectations, while requiring analysis of wearing order and adaptation. It translates manufacturing measures into experience: are smaller geometric deviations perceptible, and do changes in material or weight affect comfort and willingness to wear the denture? Patient-reported outcomes, adjustment and repair events should be recorded separately because appearance, function and continued use need not change together.

In the chain of evidence, randomized comparisons test early acceptability after delivery, while extended observation tests durability and maintenance. Both can use consistent scales and event definitions, allowing time-varying performance to be interpreted as the same device performing at different stages of use. The option for continued use by follow-up subjects should also be preserved to explain which patients enter long-term observation and whether discontinuation is related to breakage, fit, or personal preference.
N9 | Two-year use and interventions

The prospective study, conducted in 2026, followed 18 patients with 36 printed dentures, of whom 12 patients (24 dentures) completed the two-year observation period. Four maxillary dentures fractured in the first year, and two patients subsequently discontinued use; the reported two-year cumulative success rate and survival rate were 88% and 87%, respectively, with patient-reported outcomes generally stable. [R07]

This study separates the structural event requiring intervention and discontinuation of use into two endpoints, clearly distinguishing between "device malfunction" and "treatment losing its value." Dentures that are continued to be worn after restoration retain their benefits but incur a maintenance burden; discontinuation requires analysis of both device- and patient-level reasons. Since the upper and lower jaws are from the same patient, their correlation should be preserved during analysis, and cumulative indicators should be understood by combining loss to follow-up and different observation periods.

Provides clear feedback to previous nodes through long-term observation: fracture location, critical thickness, material version, and post-treatment records are reconnected to fatigue testing, allowing for the selection of geometry and loads that more closely approximate the event distribution; re-incident events after repair are reconnected to reinforcement and relining experiments. The feedback arrows in the study diagram indicate the next round of experimental tasks accordingly. This allows both integrated and modular approaches to undergo four levels of evaluation: delivery, use, maintenance, and decommissioning, and translates product improvements into specific, repeatable measurable issues.

sections.title: III. Enterprise Evolution: Three Paths Revolving Around Different Process Constraints

blocks.text: Stratasys' strategy centres on multicolour monolithic dentures. TrueDent and its J5 DentaJet workflow were launched in February 2023; TrueDent-D entered Europe as a CE Class I product in January 2025; and TrueDent resin received CE Class IIa certification on 17 March 2026, expanding the corresponding scope of use. Market entry and the later certification-class change represent distinct stages in European development. [R11][R12][R13]

3D Systems' NextDent roadmap comprises a multi-material jetting system consisting of Jet Base, Jet Teeth, and NextDent 300. The company announced a full commercial launch in the US on July 29, 2025; and on April 28, 2026, announced that the portfolio had obtained EU MDR IIa certification, stipulating that it would be available in Europe from May 4th. These milestones record the commercial and certification progress of the specific product portfolio. [R14][R15]

Formlabs retains separate manufacturing and assembly. Its current guide describes bonding Denture Base V2 and Premium Teeth and includes surface repair, fracture repair, tooth replacement, and soft and hard relining. [R16] This approach covers initial manufacture and subsequent local maintenance. Its value can be assessed through the clarity of material and procedural choices and whether laboratories can perform maintenance tasks consistently.
