blocks.text: The common goal of the three routes can be stated as reducing uncertainty in delivery, but the control methods differ. Integration places more emphasis on the unified control of materials, equipment, and printing tasks, while modular manufacturing retains component selection while requiring stable connection processes. Therefore, product competition will occur simultaneously at both the process automation and service support levels; which route is more economical will be determined by laboratory output, equipment utilization, and maintenance structure.

The enterprise timeline records the process of a product entering a specific market and workflow, while comparative studies are used to evaluate the performance of each route. After commercial release, the correspondence between material versions, laboratory implementation methods, and patient cohorts is particularly worth tracking. If the resin or post-processing method is subsequently changed, early results correspond to that specific version, and results for the new version need to be accumulated separately. Continuous tracking helps determine whether performance improvements stem from material updates, operator proficiency, or a combination of both.

sections.title: Research–enterprise links through disclosed patent mechanisms

blocks.text: Denture integration separates geometric, material and maintenance continuity. TrueDent/TrueDent-D and NextDent jetting remove some traditional assembly steps; Formlabs supplies a separate-print/bond workflow. Patents describe processing of physically corrected try-in substrates, repeat positioning and secondary curing as manufacturing links. Monolithic geometry, water uptake and reline/repair studies require evaluating delivery accuracy together with serviceability.[R02][R03][R05][R06][R11][R12][R14][R16]
Retaining physical try-in correction through machining

Aidite Qinhuangdao’s CN116849850A describes oral data, CAD design, a printed try-in, physical correction to obtain a qualified substrate, and machining of the final complete denture. Tooth-socket/splinting and monolithic-position studies ask how confirmed relationships survive the substrate and machining stages. TrueDent/NextDent supply assembly-error contexts. Compare processing after physical correction with digital forming for tooth position, contact and rework.[R02][R09][R11][R14][R17]
Repeat positioning as a connection

Shenzhen Icorewin’s CN110974461A describes a printed cavity box with repeat-positioning accessories, thermal/pressure joining of teeth and denture material, and CNC processing. Bonding research extends the question to datums, joining and thermal history. Formlabs provides comparison logic. Measure positioning error, interfaces and aged behavior separately; integral appearance does not eliminate joint failure.[R01][R16][R18]
Secondary curing connects teeth/base

Carbon’s US2022168077A1 describes a dual-cure flexible partial-denture base, acrylic tooth insertion and heat curing with retained resin for bonding. Bond fatigue, reline and repair papers create a chain from initial joining through aging to old/new-material interfaces. Carbon FP3D supplies a flexible-partial-denture and dual-cure industrial context; implementation still requires validation by material, indication and cure version.[R01][R05][R06][R19][R20]

sections.title: Translation and validation: variables, controls and decisions

blocks.text: Separate final tooth position, original joining and post-repair joining. Match tooth arrangement/base geometry across bonding, repeat-positioned processing and secondary curing; monolithic multimaterial products retain matched workflows. Measure fit/occlusion before hydrothermal/cyclic tests and classify tooth loss, base fracture and material-region failure. Maintenance testing needs aged devices rather than newly bonded coupons.[R01][R04][R05][R07] Case series help identify design choices used clinically. Record socket design, tooth assembly and processing together. Original-joint failure, post-reline debonding and base fracture are different events; report their timing and interventions needed to restore use. Less assembly with greater maintenance requires selection based on patient needs and repair access.[R10]

headers: Proposed comparison, endpoints and next decision
rows: Correction retention

Compare the pre-correction try-in, corrected substrate and machined device for retained tooth/tissue-surface relationships. Digital return can be a separate proposed comparison. Loss of physical correction during processing prioritizes positioning/machining datums.[R17]
Positioning
Repeat fixture cycles and compare pre/post-joining tooth position, datum drift and aged bonds. Strong bonds with misplaced teeth prioritize positioning accessories.[R18]
Cure/maintenance
Compare dual-cure and matched bonding for conversion, aged joints and reline/repair. Better original joints with impaired repair interfaces require maintenance-material redesign.[R19]

Physical try-in corrections retained through Aidite-type substrate machining could support initial-delivery comparisons with TrueDent/NextDent. Track tooth positions before/after correction and machining, tissue contact and remake causes. Changed confirmed relationships prioritize positioning/datum retention.[R11][R14][R17]

Stable positioning/thermal joining could enable maintenance comparisons with bonded dentures. Track fixture drift, tooth/base joining, aged fracture and repair work. Better geometry with difficult maintenance favors serviceable interfaces.[R18]

Aged joint/reline stability in Carbon-type secondary curing could justify broader partial-denture comparisons. Track tooth loss, base fracture, repairs and discontinuation separately. Complete and partial dentures need independent long-term evidence.[R19]

blocks.text: Define integration by which errors disappear and which maintenance capabilities remain. Geometric continuity does not eliminate material interfaces; positioning/cure variables should feed back with whole-denture repair records.

blocks.text: The priority research is a design-based error tracking experiment. Split and integrated dentures will be manufactured separately using the same batch clinical design, and scans will be performed at key processing points. The major dental regions, registration methods, and occlusal evaluation methods will be pre-defined, and operator time will be recorded. The research objective should be to explain which steps alter tooth positions and examine the relationship between deviations and adjustments. It is suitable to conduct cross-batch experiments first, followed by clinical delivery comparisons, to avoid attributing differences caused by different designs to the manufacturing process.

The second priority is comparing repairs in complete dentures. Use representative fracture sites and damage severity to compare local repair, structural reinforcement and digital remanufacture, followed by environmental ageing and cyclic loading. Alongside failure load, record changes in failure location, how much original material must be removed and whether another repair remains possible. This can guide maintenance choices and provide clear categories for clinical registries.

Priority Study Three is a multi-center cohort registered by product version. At delivery, resin, equipment, processing procedures, critical thickness, and previous denture status are recorded; during follow-up, damage, relining, repair, re-fabrication, and discontinuation are recorded separately. Analysis is organized at both the patient and device levels to avoid treating the upper and lower jaws of the same individual as completely independent. After product upgrades, the old version cohort is retained, and which issues can be compared across versions are pre-defined.

Clinical comparisons require prior specification of case allocation rules. If more complex cases fall into a particular route, directly comparing rework rates may introduce case differences. Randomization comparisons can be conducted among patients suitable for both approaches, or the factors influencing choice can be recorded and adjusted within the observation cohort. Sample size should be estimated around the difference requiring a change in decision-making, while allowing for loss to follow-up; scan points, independent devices, and independent patients should be processed as different levels of data, ensuring appropriate units of analysis for both geometric precision and clinical outcomes.

Priority Study Four involves cost accounting conducted concurrently with clinical research. For each case, the total cost is calculated by accumulating laboratory and clinic inputs, rework due to failure, and subsequent maintenance, without using material unit prices to represent the total cost. Production volume and equipment utilization can be used as scenario variables to examine when labor savings are sufficient to cover additional inputs. This selection criterion is applicable to large laboratories and also explains why smaller institutions might make different decisions.

Cost studies can simultaneously present costs and effects: first, list the cost of qualified delivery, time to use without intervention, and time to patient discontinuation, then examine whether the choice changes under different weights. If a certain route is only superior under extremely high yield or extremely low maintenance probability, this condition itself is an important result. Publicly disclosing calculation methods, material versions, and event definitions allows other laboratories to recalculate using their own workloads and identify how the benefits of a single institution change in other environments.

Research priorities should follow the principle of "first identifying the locations of errors and failures, then comparing the net benefits of the entire denture." In the short term, the most valuable actions are reproducible assembly and repair protocols; in the medium term, multi-center results for specific product versions; and in the long term, linking design, manufacturing, and maintenance records. Each step should make the next choice clearer: which cases are suitable for which approach, how to restore the denture after damage, and what the total cost is to achieve stable results.

P2-05.title: Clinical Comparisons
P2-05.subtitle: Linking survival, patient experience and maintenance burden through stratified comparisons
P2-05.thesis: Clinical evidence for printed restorations supports specific judgments by material, device use and workflow. Complete dentures, resin single crowns, resin bridges and zirconia crowns have different outcomes. Progress requires distinguishing success, survival and continued use, linking patient experience to intervention costs, and using systematic reviews to identify comparable evidence and subsequent research tasks.

questions.question: What are the differences between printed and traditional dental crowns in terms of clinical survival and complications?
questions.focus: Compare resin and zirconia restorations, single crowns and bridges separately, recording fracture, debonding and biological events while retaining patient- and restoration-level data.

questions.question: What are the differences in patient outcomes between printed dentures and traditional dentures?
questions.focus: Link early patient experience in randomized comparisons to maintenance events during long-term follow-up, assessing function, satisfaction and continued wear.

questions.question: How should systematic reviews assess clinical evidence for digital restorations?
questions.focus: Organize evidence according to the same purpose, control, material version and follow-up length, and examine the impact of bias, heterogeneity and outcome definition on the overall judgment.

sections.title: Research Task and Clinical Comparison Framework

blocks.text: Clinical comparisons first require clarifying what is being chosen. "Printed" and "conventional" are names of manufacturing routes; what patients actually receive is a treatment process comprised of materials, device design, clinical documentation, and post-processing. The main tasks of complete dentures include stability, comfort, and continuous wear; single crowns involve retention, structural and tissue response; and three-unit bridges further increase connectors and span load-bearing capacity. Only by stratifying these tasks can research results be translated into clear selection criteria.

Survival, success and continued patient use are related but distinct outcomes. A recemented restoration may remain in the mouth after requiring intervention; repaired dentures may recover function while adding maintenance costs; and patients may stop using an intact device because of comfort or appearance. Define each outcome level in advance and record event timing and management so that technical problems and patient choices can be interpreted separately.

Clinical comparisons also include resource evaluation. Fewer patient visits, shorter chairside procedures, or less material consumption can reduce the burden on one party; however, if subsequent adjustments are made, the overall investment for the treatment cycle may differ. Therefore, patient experience, device events, and costs should be observed within the same timeframe, clarifying the respective contributions of initial manufacturing, delivery, and maintenance.

Systematic reviews bring together comparable clinical questions and explain differences in findings. They should retain materials, manufacturing versions, case conditions, study designs and follow-up duration rather than group studies only as digital or conventional. Original research provides specific observations, while evidence synthesis examines consistency across conditions; together, they guide subsequent trials.
N1 | Early denture-experience comparisons

A 2022 randomized crossover trial compared conventional and digitally printed dentures, recording satisfaction with speech, cleaning, stability and comfort alongside visits and treatment processes. Conventional dentures performed better on some experience measures, while the digital workflow reduced some visit-related measures. [R01]

The crossover trial allows the same patient to undergo two procedures, reducing discrepancies between individual anatomy and general expectations. The study also explains the need to preserve treatment sequence, adaptation periods, and prior prosthetic experience, as the later approach may be influenced by the initial learning phase. Multidimensional scales help differentiate overall evaluations based on appearance, stability, speech, or treatment convenience, thus linking patient feedback to specific manufacturing and clinical steps.

This node proposes a dual task for subsequent comparisons: firstly, to observe whether the process saves on patient visits; and secondly, to examine whether the wearing experience can be maintained after the savings. The primary outcome most important to patients can be pre-defined, while adjustments and intermediate events are recorded, avoiding simply asking for an overall score at the final follow-up visit. It compares workflow conditions with the next randomized study using a common scale and at the same time points, progressively explaining differences in conclusions.
N2 | Randomized testing of another workflow

2024 18-person crossover randomized trial report, the measured quality of life and satisfaction of printed and traditional complete dentures are comparable. [R02] The study subjects are two denture processes formed by specific design, materials and manufacturing steps.

Places this result alongside earlier studies, and the most valuable question is what conditions changed. Clinical records, fitting methods, materials, tooth position, and operational experience can all influence the experience, and these should be progressively separated through research design. A manufacturing comparison under the same clinical steps can be used, or the complete process can be preserved while detailed records of differences can be kept. The former is more suitable for mechanistic attribution, while the latter is more suitable for treatment selection; the two designs answer different questions and can complement each other.

Short-term patient outcomes also need to be linked to objective retention and long-term events. Similar satisfaction levels may indicate similar function, or patient adaptation may offset different mechanical performances. The next two branches therefore add retention measurements and extended follow-up, respectively, extending early acceptability to reliability during use. Retaining the reasons for selection and withdrawal when the same patients continue observation can indicate the composition of the long-term cohort.
N3 | Measuring retention and experience together

The 2026 crossover trial compared thermo-cured, printed, and injected polyamide complete dentures, while also recording retention and oral quality of life. There were no significant differences in retention between printed and thermo-cured dentures at any observation interval, while the polyamide group differed from both. [R03]

Objective measurements offer mechanistic clues beyond patient perception. Dislodgement-force measurements require standardized loading direction and position, while quality of life captures broader experience. If they change differently, investigate pain, movement at denture borders, saliva and occlusal conditions as additional influences. Longitudinal patient data can establish whether retention and adaptation change at different rates.

Clinical comparisons can thus move from "which is better" to "what explains which outcome." Proposing a hypothesis about the association between fixation and stability in advance, and validating it in independent patients, helps determine which areas should be prioritized for control in manufacturing evaluations. Subsequently, when combined with resource studies, it can also be examined whether reducing steps affects patient experience through some measurable functional change.
N4 | Two-year interventions and continued use

A 2026 prospective cohort followed 18 patients with 36 printed dentures; 12 patients with 24 dentures completed two years of observation. Four maxillary dentures fractured during the first year, and two patients subsequently discontinued use. Success and survival were reported separately, with cumulative estimates of 88% and 87%, respectively. [R04]

Stratifies events to preserve the clinical value of continued use after repair while also presenting the maintenance burden. The initial fracture, repair, recurrence, and discontinuation can form a continuous path; different paths require different resources and affect patient confidence and normal usage time. For maxillary and mandibular dentures from the same patient, the analysis should preserve their association, and follow-up duration and loss to follow-up should be handled using an appropriate time-to-event approach.

This observation extends the early randomized trial into a real-world usage process, but the continued wear choice within the cohort is itself an outcome. Future multicenter designs could include all recipients at initial delivery, continuously recording choice changes and interventions. This would allow for assessment of whether changes in materials, geometry, and clinical manipulation reduced events, and determine appropriate observation periods and primary endpoints for subsequent comparisons.
N5 | A single-crown cohort records survival and success separately

A 2026 study observed 30 VarseoSmile Crown Plus posterior single crowns for two years, reporting a 93% survival rate and an 87% success rate, with some instances of debonding and partial color changes. [R05] The scanning, printing, post-processing, and bonding procedures used have clearly identified materials and equipment.

A single-arm cohort describes which events occur in a defined workflow, when they occur and how they are managed. Debonding, fracture, secondary caries and aesthetic interventions should be separated because they involve different mechanisms. Recemented crowns contribute to restoration survival but also treatment burden; patient satisfaction adds their experience of events and maintenance. Endpoints should therefore extend beyond whether the restoration remains in place.

The next round of controlled studies can allocate treatment within similar preparement heights, periodontal status, and opposing and occlusal conditions, and record cementation materials and treatments. This separates the fabrication route from case conditions. Fixed prosthetic branches are then developed according to pediatric use and zirconia materials, emphasizing that clinical selection is jointly defined by dentition, material, and structural tasks.
N6 | Paediatric split-mouth studies retain differences beyond function

A comparative study of 50 primary molars from 25 children in 2026 showed that printed resin and precast zirconia were similar in retention and multiple functional indicators, but the printed group showed worse results in terms of plaque, gingival indices, wear, and color changes. The observation period was 12 months. [R06]

The contralateral design leverages the shared living environment of the same individual to reduce some differences, while still needing to preserve pairing relationships in statistical analysis. The remaining useful life of deciduous teeth, preparation methods, and gingival margin positions constitute independent application scenarios. Studies can simultaneously record surface condition and cleaning behavior, analyzing whether changes in tissue parameters are consistent with material surface or local geometry. Placing functional retention alongside surface and biological outcomes prevents overall success rates from masking other potential burdens faced by patients.

This node establishes a shared requirement for adult-crown and bridge studies: define multidimensional outcomes and specify clinically decision-relevant differences. Set separate thresholds for wear, colour acceptability and interventions, then examine whether they alter treatment choices. Uses may assign different weights, but clear recording enables later evidence synthesis.
N7 | A randomized zirconia comparison holds material category constant

A randomized trial in 2025 compared NPJ-printed versus milled zirconia single crowns in 48 posterior teeth from 43 participants. At 12 months, the primary aesthetic, functional, and biological parameters were generally similar, with one fracture occurring in each group. [R07]

Comparing manufacturing routes within the same material category helps reduce the interference of material differences on interpretation. Randomization and concealed allocation further reduce the influence of case selection, while standardized evaluation criteria improve endpoint comparability. Studies still need to retain actual forming and heat treatment conditions, as well as adjustments and bonding information at delivery, as these steps can all affect the same clinical outcome. After linking manufacturing data with clinical case numbers, it's possible to further explore which step the discrepancies originate from.

When a between-group difference is not statistically significant, effect estimates and confidence intervals indicate the range of differences still compatible with the data. Demonstrating that a difference is sufficiently small requires prespecified clinically acceptable margins and an appropriate sample size. Longer follow-up with adjustment and resource measures can then compare clinically similar routes in efficiency and maintenance.
N8 | Follow-up of resin three-unit bridges

A 2025 study followed 68 three-unit printed resin-composite posterior bridges in 49 patients for a mean of 22.36 months. Mechanical failures were concentrated at connectors, and estimated cumulative survival accounting for mechanical and biological events was 36.2%. The longest observation exceeded three years. [R08]

This result makes the structural distinction between single crowns and bridges clinically relevant. Connectors, span and multiple supports alter load transfer, so restorations described as resin composites still require use-specific validation. Failure sites linked to connector cross-sections, local thickness and occlusion can generate experimental hypotheses. Because the studies use different materials and cases, comparisons should identify tasks added by bridge use rather than directly infer manufacturing superiority from separate cohorts.

Future bridge studies should distinguish repairable damage, failures requiring remanufacture and events requiring abutment treatment, retaining repeat events and clustering within patients. Changes in both event location and cumulative occurrence after redesign would help explain its clinical effect. This node feeds evidence synthesis by separating printed restorations into specific material–use combinations.
N9 | Clinical outcomes and resources

A retrospective study of 60 participants in 2025 compared traditional, milled, and printed complete dentures. Overall functional outcomes at six months were similar, with the digital group having lower chairside time and laboratory costs. [R09] The study also recorded clinical outcomes and treatment-related inputs.

While reviewing the data can reflect established workflows, it's necessary to explain case selection, staff experience, and cost metrics. Timeframes should be divided into pre-production documentation, trial use, delivery, and subsequent adjustments; costs should retain the components of equipment, materials, and labor, allowing other institutions to incorporate their own resources. Patient travel and downtime can also be listed separately, demonstrating which approach actually benefits in clinically similar cases.

When economic analysis is conducted concurrently with clinical trials, mismatches between different cases and timeframes can be reduced. Pre-defining the observation period and accumulating failures and retakes helps verify whether initial savings can be maintained. This stage provides a resource dimension to the overall system and also reminds subsequent randomized studies to simultaneously measure cost and effect, ensuring that treatment options are not limited to a single satisfaction or retention value.
N10 | Systematic synthesis and stratification

The 2025 review of printed and milled dentures included four studies, showing no significant difference in retention and satisfaction, and exhibiting high heterogeneity. The 2026 review included 25 randomized trials, but no clear advantage of the manufacturing route was shown in the important patient outcomes, and the certainty of the evidence was generally low. [R10][R11]

A comprehensive interpretation of the system requires returning to the study subjects. Different materials, trial procedures, control types, and follow-up times may lead to different treatment protocols; these factors can be stratified before pooling. Crossover and parallel trials require appropriate effect estimates for each, and multiple publications on the same cohort need to be identified to avoid duplication. Prioritizing important patient outcomes helps link statistical differences to actual experience, intervention, and continued use.

The most actionable output of the review is clarifying how to reduce uncertainty in the next round of trials: standardizing the definitions of success and retention, recording by product version, extending observation, incorporating maintenance costs, and selecting differences that can change decisions. The feedback edges in the diagram thus return to the original research design. Adding new trials will only make the overall judgment clearer than simply increasing the number of papers if it complements these specific tasks.

sections.title: Timing of commercial product development and clinical evidence

blocks.text: BEGO released the VarseoSmile Crown plus permanent single crown material in 2020, followed by prospective clinical observations surrounding the material and its associated procedures. [R12][R05] There is a time lag between the proposed use of the product and the maturation of clinical results. Studies should retain the actual version used and the delivery date, distinguishing between information resulting from product updates and extended observation periods.

As of 2026, Formlabs' official permanent-crown guide organizes manufacturing around BEGO VarseoSmile TriniQ and associated equipment such as Form 4B. [R14] This new material–platform combination is a distinct research object that can use established single-crown outcomes. Crown plus observations help identify important endpoints; evidence for the TriniQ workflow must come from its actual clinical use.

Carbon released DB 4000 denture-base resin in 2026, emphasizing work of fracture, printing accuracy and manufacturing economics. [R13] This update shares questions with denture trials and maintenance cohorts: do material or accuracy improvements reduce fracture, adjustment and discontinuation? Release records identify the version's starting point; subsequent case registries establish whether improvements reach actual use.

The enterprise timeline can simultaneously record changes in materials, software, equipment, post-processing, and indications. Clinical evaluation treats each version as a traceable, complete process, which helps explain differences in trials across different years. If multiple stages are updated simultaneously, process controls can be conducted first to identify key contributions, followed by a complete process clinical comparison, avoiding attributing all changes to a single material name.

sections.title: Research–enterprise links through disclosed patent mechanisms

blocks.text: Clinical comparisons must turn patent mechanisms into patient-important questions while retaining indications. Dentures, resin crowns, zirconia crowns and multiunit bridges fail differently. BEGO, Carbon DB 4000 and Formlabs TriniQ supply product/process contexts; retention microstructures, gradient resins and slurry optics are explanatory variables requiring mechanism checks before indication-matched clinical comparisons.[R04][R05][R07][R08][R12][R13][R14]
Retention and experience together

Sichuan University’s CN121370420A describes integral polygonal micropillars on tissue surfaces for capillary/friction retention. The retention/quality-of-life crossover trial asks whether initial gains survive saliva, insertion cycles and chewing while benefiting patients. Carbon DB 4000 supplies a base context; match materials/cleaning. Mucosal, cleaning and continued-use outcomes must test comfort statements.[R02][R03][R13][R15]
Separate gradient material and shape

Air Force Medical University’s CN121818392A describes voxel-level mixing of two resins into wear-resistant outer and tough inner layers. Crown/bridge follow-up supplies endpoints: gradients may alter crack paths, while debonding and connector geometry remain separate. BEGO/TriniQ provide crown references. Start with crowns, tracking wear, color, debonding and fracture; abstract toughness statements cannot override bridge failures.[R05][R08][R12][R14][R16]
Ceramic forming and follow-up

Foshan Xianhu’s CN112745120A describes nano-zirconia photopolymer slurry addressing scattering. It shares a material category with the zirconia randomized trial, not its NPJ process. Fit/fracture assessment methods are transferable. Primary-molar research adds wear/gingival questions. BEGO resin products may be indication-matched comparators after specifying material, thickness and case conditions.[R06][R07][R12][R17]

sections.title: Translation and validation: variables, controls and decisions

blocks.text: Start with mechanism/manufacturability checks, followed by indication-specific controls. Denture crossovers should address adaptation/order; crown studies stratify material/site and separately record repair, debonding, fracture, discontinuation and experience. Reviews do not establish a uniform patient-important advantage. Prespecify primary outcomes and retain withdrawal/missing-follow-up reasons.[R01][R04][R10][R11] Resource comparisons should include all interventions from initial delivery: adjustment, rebonding, repair, remake and extra visits, with withdrawal/discontinuation reasons. These explain survival/success differences. Fewer visits with similar experience may matter if necessary follow-up remains intact. Clear material, assembly and follow-up versions make patent hypotheses clinically testable.

headers: Proposed comparison, endpoints and next decision
rows: Micropillars
Compare matched bases with/without pillars for wet retention/cleaning, then mucosa, comfort and wear time. Retention gains with cleaning difficulty or pain require texture revision.[R15]
Gradient
Compare uniform/gradient crowns of equal shape for fatigue, wear and bonding; distinguish success from survival after repair. Bonding failure requires inner-layer/adhesive revision.[R16]
Zirconia
Match preparation/thickness for printed/milled comparison; assess fit, cracks and separate endpoints. Batch effects exceeding route differences prioritize process stability.[R17]
Micropillar retention surviving wet/cleaning conditions could justify limited Carbon-like comparisons. Track retention, mucosa, cleaning burden and preference across adaptation phases.[R13][R15]
Reproducible gradient effects in crown fatigue could support BEGO/TriniQ-matched studies. Track cracks, debonding, wear and repair. Bridge progression depends on connector evidence.[R12][R14][R16]

Stable zirconia processing with adequate follow-up could support resource/patient-outcome selection. Track repairs, function, visits and missing follow-up. More interventions require lifecycle reassessment.[R17]

blocks.text: Clinical comparisons should identify which patients, restorations and stages benefit. Patents supply mechanisms, products define combinations, and follow-up establishes real-use burden. These levels need linked records.

The primary task is to establish a core outcome set based on usage. For complete dentures, at least quality of life, sub-satisfaction, retention, initial intervention, and discontinuation should be recorded; for fixed restorations, at least fracture, debonding, biological events, aesthetic intervention, and final replacement should be recorded. The timing, severity, and management of each event should be clearly defined, and patient feedback on outcomes should be retained to allow different studies to pool the same endpoint.

Priority Task Two is a clear multicenter comparison of material versions. For applications with early feasibility, assign manufacturing routes under the same case conditions and clinical procedures; if comparing complete workflows, record procedural differences in detail. Estimate sample size based on meaningful clinical differences, account for loss to follow-up, and report effects and intervals. Establish a new hierarchy after product upgrades to avoid misalignment between results from the old and new versions.

The third priority is maintenance and time-to-event cohorts. Preserve design, thickness, connector dimensions and processing at delivery, then link specific damage to its management during follow-up. Record continued use after the first event, repeat events and permanent discontinuation to evaluate the value of repair. Combine retrieved-device examination with experimental failure analysis to identify material and geometric factors most worth improving.

Priority Task Four is concurrent economic research. This involves cumulatively analyzing laboratory, clinic, and patient inputs on a case-by-case basis, presenting total costs, time to no intervention, and patient experience over the same period. Scenario analyses are conducted based on institution size, labor costs, and equipment utilization rates to illustrate under what conditions changes should be made. The results can be used both for treatment procedures and to determine which burdens should be prioritized for reduction in R&D investment.

The hallmark of mature evidence is the reduction of decision-making uncertainty through both primary trials and comprehensive studies. New data can clarify which materials and workflows are suitable for which patient groups, when maintenance is needed, and the total investment required to achieve stable results. By addressing these answerable questions in each round of research, clinical comparisons can shift from name-based debates to concrete treatment choices.

P2-06.title: Prosthetic Sockets
P2-06.subtitle: Digital fitting from residual-limb geometry and interface loading to years of use
P2-06.thesis: The key advance in prosthetic sockets is a closed loop connecting modifiable geometry, validated load bearing and ongoing feedback from wear. Printing accuracy, weight reduction and patient comfort each require appropriate tests for interpretation.

questions.question: How can residual-limb scanning and digital design improve prosthetic socket fit?
questions.focus: How do scanning and clinical shape rectification jointly define the contact surface?

questions.question: How can prosthetic sockets reduce local pressure and improve wearing experience?
questions.focus: How to cross-validate pressure measurement, simulation, and patient experience?

questions.question: How can socket materials and lattice structures provide adequate load-bearing capacity?
questions.focus: How can materials, fibres and lattices form load-bearing designs that can be independently checked?

blocks.text: The socket is the component that provides continuous contact, load transfer, and fixation between the residual limb and the prosthesis. Its digital value depends on whether three issues can be addressed simultaneously: whether the shape of the contact surface is suitable for the specific residual limb, whether the local tissue can withstand the load, and whether the shell and its distal connections can remain intact during repeated use. Scanning, printing, and lattice work each alter a part of these aspects; therefore, the evaluation unit needs to cover the entire fitting process from acquisition to follow-up examination.

This paper treats upper limb and lower limb studies as two related but independent design scenarios. Upper limb sockets need to accommodate hand devices, control components, and grasping activities; lower limb sockets also bear weight transfer, gait cycles, and ground action. Even with the same material grade and similar weight reduction ratios, interpretation needs to be based on the corresponding stress scenarios. Geometric studies focus on contact area errors, structural studies focus on damage and deformation under specific loads, and clinical studies focus on wearability, activity, skin, and maintenance. [R02][R07][R08]

Research has progressed from preserving external shape to recording rectification decisions and testing their effects through pressure measurements and long-term cohorts. The central value of digital sockets is making modifications and their consequences traceable within a fitting episode. Faster delivery, lower local pressure and lighter devices are distinct benefits; linking them in the same user creates knowledge for the next design.
N1 | Testing deep-region errors with smartphone photogrammetry

A 2021 study optimized smartphone photogrammetry using an existing transtibial socket and a printed solid reference, comparing reconstructed volume, surface area, height and internal wall thickness. Overall height and surface area approached the reference, but deep internal surfaces showed substantial distortion. A visually complete reconstruction can therefore still misrepresent the contact surface. [R01]

This node first addresses the issue of digital input fidelity. For the prosthetic socket, the easily accessible surface near the opening and the deeply obscured area have different visibility; a single overall error will average both. Therefore, the design analysis should preserve the spatial location of the error and observe the distal end, bony protrusion area, and rim of the cavity separately. Replicating an existing prosthetic socket also requires distinguishing between the inner and outer surfaces; the wall thickness assumption will translate the shape reconstruction error into actual contact differences.

From this node, the path to digital reshaping begins, and the research variables change accordingly: first, scanning errors are recorded, then the amount of clinically active modifications are recorded, and both are saved separately in the data. When local discomfort occurs in the new prosthetic socket, it can be reviewed whether it is due to input shape deviation or whether the designer intentionally increased or decreased the space. This arrangement also provides a clear quality threshold for remote acquisition, ensuring that the value of low-cost equipment lies in repeatable contact geometry, rather than simply being measured by the number of images or whether the model is closed.
N2 | Linking automated pediatric upper-limb design to materials

The 2021 AutoMedPrint study used a scan of one three-year-old child's upper-limb residual limb to compare PLA and TPE, connection designs and printing parameters. Thirty-six sockets were manufactured and assessed for geometry, roughness and compressive performance. Most met strength requirements, but fit and comfort varied among combinations. [R02]

The methodological contribution lies in breaking down automated modeling into verifiable choices. For the same residual limb contour, using harder and more elastic materials will alter the wearing/removing deformation, edge contact, and connection/fixation methods. Recording both design and material parameters simultaneously can explain why a particular design, while strong enough, is inconvenient to wear. Children also have growth and activity needs; therefore, remanufacturing speed and adjustability should be evaluated along with the initial mechanical results.

This branch provides a transferable experimental organization method for subsequent structural research: first, compare materials under fixed geometry; then, modify the stress path under determined materials; and finally, submit the assembly to actual trial wear. For the upper limb prototype, the strength results correspond to the tested connection and compression scenarios. When moving to lower limb design, it is necessary to redefine the load, fixed end, and cyclic conditions, while retaining the original geometry and contact evaluation, so that load-bearing enhancement does not come at the cost of discomfort.
N3 | Manual versus digital rectification under matched manufacturing

A 2024 feasibility study in nine people with transtibial amputations compared manual casting and rectification with scanning followed by digital rectification; both routes ultimately used printed sockets. Geometry, comfort and workflow time were recorded. Comfort was similar, scanning saved time, and digital rectification took longer. [R03]

The key to this comparison lies in the shared manufacturing process. It focuses clinical questions on "how to determine the contact shape," avoiding attributing all results from simultaneous changes in scanning, software, materials, and printers to digitization. Manual experience, including palpation and assessment of soft tissue deformities, needs to be expressed in software through anatomical marking, local reduction, and spatial addition. Whether these operations are fully recorded determines whether these judgments can be reused among different prosthetists.

At the location shown in the diagram, node represents both the algorithm and interface mechanics. The algorithm needs to learn the modified shape, while the mechanics model needs to understand which contact area has been altered. Subsequent comparisons can retain three surfaces within the same user: the initial residual limb scan, each step of modification, and the final device, while incorporating a unified walking task. This approach not only pinpoints specific differences but also identifies necessary manual adjustments for comfort, thus representing a realistic digital adaptation workload.
N4 | Learning historical shapes for independent-user fitting

A 2025 study developed a transtibial socket-shape algorithm from historical data for 116 patients, then compared algorithm-based and manual routes in 10 participants. Mean predicted-shape deviation was 2.51 mm. Eight algorithm-generated and all 10 manually designed sockets met the criteria for home trials, followed by comfort and professional fit assessments. [R04]

This design allows data learning to bypass model similarity evaluation and move into the selection of practically wearable devices. Historical designs are the result of clinical practice, incorporating prosthetist preferences, patient body types, and specific suspension conditions. Therefore, a small average shape error initially indicates approximation to an existing design distribution; whether the local space meets the needs of a new user still needs to be determined through trial fitting and independent fitting evaluation. The algorithm can be set to provide a starting point, with human modifications then serving as analyzable results.

The next step in the study could be to establish joint endpoints based on the initial protocol acceptance rate, modification location, modification time, and final comfort changes. Protocols that failed to reach home trial settings should still be included in the process evaluation, as the trial and redesign time they consumed impacts actual service efficiency. This would allow for identification of which types of residual geometry the algorithm is stable in, in which situations more professional intervention is needed, and abnormal shapes would be fed back into the data for updates, rather than simply comparing the average scores of those who completed the trial.
N5 | Calibrating interface finite element models with a rollover simulator

The 2025 study integrated a load measurement unit into the outer wall of a printed prosthetic socket, sensing the internal force through the piston interface and comparing it with predictions from finite element methods at seven locations on a rolling simulator. The results show that the accuracy of the geometric description has a crucial impact on the prediction of interface pressure. [R05]

The node places the validity of the computational model within a repeatable experimental context. Simulating residual limbs, prosthetic sockets, and rolling trajectories allows for repeatable load inputs, enabling observation of whether the error originates from material constitutive modeling, contact assumptions, or geometry. The load element measures the normal force at the corresponding location, and the model should output the quantity at the same location, area, and time point. Comparing the maximum stress across the entire field with the local average pressure, even if the numbers are close, fails to verify the prediction mechanism.

This model, along with the scanning nodes, forms a crucial convergence: geometric errors are amplified into pressure errors through contact relationships. Subsequent digital modeling can first predict the direction of change, then compare the before and after modifications using the same device to establish local design rules with clear inputs and results. When transferred to the human body, tissue condition, padding, and suspension conditions must also be recorded. In this way, the pressure model can help interpret the modeling, while patient-reported pain, stability, and activity remain the endpoints of the actual outcome.
N6 | Textile pressure-sensing socks: establish measurement stability before clinical interpretation

A 2026 study integrated textile sensing elements into a prosthetic sock, first testing sensitivity, repeatability and drift, then loading a simulated residual limb made from silicone and printed components. Elements detected changes equivalent to 5% of maximum load and changes in pressure distribution under a 600 N simulated-gait condition. [R06]

This work changes the way measurements enter the prosthetic socket. The sock-like shape more easily covers curved surfaces, but fabric elongation, wrinkles, repeated putting on and taking off, and humidity can also affect the signal. Therefore, even after achieving a stable unit response, the repeatability of the sensing point relative to the anatomical position still needs to be evaluated. The thickness and stiffness of the measurement system itself can also alter the original contact; a comparison before and after inserting the sensing sock can identify this interference effect.

Moving from benchtop use to daily life, the wearing process can be marked for standing, walking on flat ground, walking on slopes, and prolonged sitting, and then correlated with the time of discomfort occurrence. Adaptation decisions may focus on prolonged load in a certain area or the emergence of new focal points throughout the day, rather than the lowest point of a single peak. In the diagram, this node, along with the structural design, ultimately merges into the long-term cohort to determine whether measurable load changes are accompanied by more stable wear and fewer skin problems, and to provide specific locations for the next refit.
N7 | Continuous fibers reinforce load paths

A 2024 study of continuous-fibre-reinforced transfemoral sockets combined material testing, gait finite element analysis and print-path planning to place fibres in load-bearing regions. The tested reinforcement reduced weight by approximately 28% relative to the unreinforced resin design and passed three million loading cycles, illustrating joint design of shape and load bearing. [R07]

The core of this branch is placing reinforcing materials where they can function effectively. The distal connection, local curvature, and rim of the prosthetic socket determine how the load enters the shell, while the fiber orientation affects tensile and bending capacity. Therefore, "fiber addition" needs to be further specified in terms of orientation, continuity, bends, and interlayer connections. Material samples provide basic parameters, and whole-piece cyclic testing verifies whether these parameters remain effective along the actual path and at the connection locations.

The results support staged validation: confirm material-batch properties, verify manufacturing quality along the print path, then test complete sockets in worst-case loading configurations. Weight comparisons should specify whether adapters, liners and outer coverings are included so that system boundaries match. Long-term damage records should return to this node, using actual crack locations to determine whether reinforcement covers the principal failure regions.
N8 | Field-driven upper-limb lattices connect computation and manufacturing

A 2026 field-driven study combined residual-limb reconstruction, elastoplastic homogenization and stress-field mapping to generate spatially varying lattices for upper-limb sockets. Full-size PA12 prototypes were manufactured by Multi Jet Fusion and compared with designs using quasi-static testing and CT. The studied prototype weighed approximately 25% less than the solid design. [R08]

This node extends individualization from external shape to internal material distribution. Local rod diameters and densities are controlled by stress requirements, and the lattice is described using equivalent materials during calculations, then the equivalent results are translated into a manufacturable structure. There are two dimensions that need to be connected here: how the overall shell deforms, and whether the tiny connecting rods can be shaped as designed. CT scans provide an additional physical basis between these two, identifying whether computational performance is built on geometry that doesn't actually exist.

This application targets upper limb devices that connect to wrist components. The research logic can provide a methodological reference for lower limb structures, but the load system needs to be reconfigured according to the task. Further research can compare homogeneous and gradient lattices while maintaining the same shape and suspension, and observe local compliance, clean accessibility, and post-damage propagation. In the figure, it complements fiber branching: the former distributes spatial density, and the latter distributes directional enhancement; the common goal is to bear a defined load with a verifiable structure.
N9 | Rural cohort tracks use and damage

A Sierra Leone cohort study, published online in 2025 and in issue 2026, followed nine lower leg amputees for 2.5 years. Six sockets were damaged during follow-up, and others were replaced due to size issues; the median daily wearing time at the last recorded point was 12.4 hours. The study simultaneously measured activity, function, and quality of life. [R09]

This node adds time to service evaluation. Continued wear shows integration into daily life, while damage and remanufacture reveal the support needed to sustain use. Separate the lifetime of the initial socket, replacement devices, repair waiting time and eventual wear so that high activity after replacement can be interpreted. Activity exposure also matters: the same months of use may represent different step counts and loading cycles.

The two feedback loops in the diagram are thus formed. Size changes are returned to scanning and reshaping, requiring the preservation of the limb's state at each stage; damage location is returned to materials and reinforcement paths, requiring the recording of the fracture area and manufacturing batch. The evaluation of service accessibility further incorporates transportation, remanufacturing, and temporary alternatives. By integrating these records into a single archive and digitizing them, each replacement can become the basis for the next design iteration, and longer effective wear time can be used to verify whether manufacturing efficiency truly improves rehabilitation.

sections.title: Academic Evolution: From Shape Copying to Interpretable Adaptation

blocks.text: Early digital research focused on demonstrating that inputs could become manufacturable three-dimensional surfaces. Subsequent research began separating the roles of shaping and manufacturing, then integrating mechanical simulations, sensing tools, and actual wearable devices into the same object. This shift can be observed at research endpoints: localized pressure emerges after geometric deviations, overall wear cycles after material strength improvements, and damage time and continuous use follow after initial comfort. These new endpoints add different dimensions of information and require older endpoints to retain sufficiently detailed records.

A layer of clinical interpretation is needed between geometry and comfort. The surface of the residual limb is not a static, rigid body; the sampling posture, volumetric state, and padding thickness all alter the contact. Accurately replicating a scan does not equate to creating a space suitable for the load. Digital modification studies therefore play a pivotal role: they receive scans, user feedback, and output practical designs to the load-bearing model. Treating modifications as independent research subjects allows for the accumulation of experience on which areas need to release space and which regions bear support.

Materials and structural studies, particularly those involving, require a unified definition of load. While fiber reinforcement and lattice-based weight reduction seem to share the goal of "lighter and stronger," their actual mechanisms differ: fibers depend on orientation and continuity, while lattices depend on rod diameter, connectivity, and overall distribution. Common endpoints for comparison include cyclic durability, permanent deformation, failure location, and manufacturing dispersion per unit system weight. These endpoints are only suitable for supporting design choices if loads, geometry, and connectivity are identical. [R07][R08]

Future clinical comparisons are better suited to using explicit adaptation strategies as interventions. For example, maintaining the same foot components and suspension methods, comparing conventional and pressure-assisted modifications; or maintaining the same shape, comparing different structural strategies. The learning process for participants using the new device should also be documented, with pre-set adaptation periods and measurement sequences. This makes it easier to attribute differences and corresponds to steps that service providers can actually take to improve.

sections.title: Research–enterprise links through disclosed patent mechanisms

blocks.text: The socket connection follows how shape becomes pressure and load bearing. Scanning/design define inputs, sensors/models explain local loads, and materials/paths define structure. The actual iFab, MyFit and PROTEOR evidence is retained below; patents turn local revision, modular replacement and printed walls into testable objects. Initial comfort, continued use and structural life require separate records.[R03][R04][R05][R09]

Ottobock's iFab organizes scanning, digital modification, and centralized manufacturing into a service process, allowing customer platforms to transfer data and order products. The company also describes a future direction of improving subsequent processes using centralized documentation. Its productization significance lies in expanding "documents can be printed" to "orders that clinical institutions can submit, modify, and reorder," with the service system handling the multiple communications involved in traditional processes. [R10]

Current MyFit TT documentation specifies PA12 Multi Jet Fusion, digital upload and suspension options, and includes stable residual-limb volume among fitting conditions. The page's detailed MyFit TF section describes online geometry adjustments and ordering of diagnostic sockets. [R11] These show different roles for digital tools in definitive load-bearing devices and trial fitting: consistent delivery of a defined device versus rapid assessment of shape changes.

PROTEOR's definitive-socket workflow combines ORTEN software, ICARUS printers and KyronMAX material and explicitly describes printing outside vase mode. [R12] Materials and equipment form a complete process package. The strategy emphasizes in-house manufacturing, shorter order waits and more options for structural paths; actual delivery data can assess these goals.

The differences in enterprise routes also correspond to the choice of service capabilities. Centralized manufacturing is beneficial for aggregating equipment and process control, while in-house manufacturing is beneficial for shortening waiting times after modifications. However, both require clearly defined document versions, qualification criteria, maintenance records, and rework entry points. Optional items in product descriptions should be converted into actual fields in the order, such as suspension type, adapter location, flange shape, and local modifications, rather than simply uploading a mesh file whose origin cannot be explained.

Once the technology platform matures, the focus of competition may shift to the ability to handle abnormal situations. Changes in volume, skin discomfort, localized damage, and equipment downtime may all require rapid redesign. The ability to retain older versions and indicate changes in newer versions facilitates collaboration between prosthetists and manufacturers. When companies publicly disclose clinical usage data, separating statistics by initial delivery, modifications, repairs, and replacements will provide a more accurate picture of service performance than simply showcasing printing speed.
Pressure feedback changes local thickness

Zhejiang Lab’s CN120531531A describes stump-model calibration, point-cloud processing and flexible-sensor-guided thickness changes. Roll-over FE and textile-sensor studies connect measurement position, registration and drift with design decisions. MyFit online adjustment supplies the order interface. Compare geometry-only and calibrated-pressure revisions while measuring stiffness changes and neighboring load transfer.[R05][R06][R11][R13]
Replaceable interfaces and volume changes

EXTREMITI3D’s US2018243112A1 describes exchangeable panels/distal cups whose geometry/material change support, pressure and comfort. Manual/digital feasibility and rural follow-up studies supply adaptation/replacement questions. iFab archives provide version context. Compare remaking a socket with replacing modules for edge pressure, junction durability, restored wear and revisions; interchangeability does not itself establish fewer visits.[R03][R09][R10][R14]
Walls and distal reinforcement define load paths

PREC VALVE & AUTOMATION’s US2022370202A1 describes single-nozzle-pass solid perimeters and radial distal stiffeners. Continuous-fiber research supplies load-directed paths/cyclic validation; lattice research supplies geometry/CT methods. PROTEOR non-vase definitive sockets provide a different path-selection context; this patent does not validate the KyronMAX combination. Distal junctions, interlayer bonding and thickness are shared observables.[R07][R08][R12][R15]

sections.title: Translation and validation: variables, controls and decisions

blocks.text: Use one residual-limb model and clinical shaping target. Calibrate pressure/geometry before comparing relief, module replacement and wall structure; recheck neighboring pressures and global stiffness after each change. Defined training/follow-up should separately record skin, comfort, wear time and device damage. Deep scan distortion and sensor drift require known input uncertainty before automated revision.[R01][R05][R06]

headers: Proposed comparison, endpoints and next decision
rows: Feedback
Compare calibrated pressure-driven and geometry-driven revisions for pressure, drift and comfort. Position-dependent conclusions require registration/repeatability repair.[R13]
Modules
Compare panel replacement and whole remakes for edge pressure, joint fatigue and return to wear. Local relief with edge irritation requires boundary/transition revision.[R14]
Structure
Compare single-pass walls and alternative paths in equal envelopes for thickness, distal fatigue and damage. Distal cracking after weight reduction requires reinforcement before wear trials.[R15]

MyFit-like revisions retaining pressure locations/versions could create interpretable feedback records. Track repeatability, revision sites and initial fit. Input drift favors reviewed local revision first.[R11][R13]

Modules retaining edge comfort/durability after volume changes could be compared with iFab-like socket reorders. Track remakes, module damage, restored wear and skin, separating task from total delivery time.[R10][R14]

Walls/stiffeners retaining cyclic performance across body types could support definitive-socket expansion. In PROTEOR-like contexts, track fracture, repair, wear time and replacement reasons. Activity-clustered failures narrow design scope first.[R12][R15]

blocks.text: Socket value lies in timely restoration of safe, tolerable wear. Pressure, structure and service records should identify the same version, making local benefits/trade-offs traceable and retention dependent on subsequent use.

The focus of cavity research is shifting from replicating individual body shape to maintaining individual fit within defined stress and life situations. Scans provide recordable input, shaping expresses clinical judgment, pressure measurements examine contact changes, fibers and lattices provide structural choices, and long-term follow-up reveals the persistence of these choices in real life. These nine nodes form a recurring and up-to-date research process.

The most valuable achievement of in this direction is ensuring that each modification leaves an interpretable record, and that these records correspond to actual device versions and usage results. By establishing common data interfaces around geometry, load, structure, and maintenance, academic research can propose more specific design rules, enterprise platforms can implement and correct them more quickly, and users can receive more stable wearable support in continuous service.
