P2-07.title: Prostheses and Orthoses
P2-07.subtitle: Organizing personalized devices around tasks, gait and wearing experience
P2-07.thesis: Printing enables individual anatomy to become modifiable structures whose function can be tested through defined tasks. Upper-limb, lower-limb, orthotic and maxillofacial applications have distinct endpoints, while sharing a pathway from user feedback to the next design iteration.

questions.question: How can printed upper limb prostheses improve grasping and daily functions?
questions.focus: Match residual motor ability and grasp configurations to daily tasks.

questions.question: How do printed lower limb prostheses and orthoses affect gait?
questions.focus: Match shape and stiffness to the functional demands of each gait phase.

questions.question: How can patient-specific orthoses combine fit and accessibility?
questions.focus: Evaluate donning and doffing, assisted movements and resources required for complete delivery.

questions.question: How can maxillofacial and ocular prostheses combine appearance with patient-specific fit?
questions.focus: Evaluate geometry, colour, soft-tissue contact and repeat fabrication.

blocks.text: Prostheses, orthotics, and external maxillofacial restorations share the need for personalized manufacturing, but they serve different purposes. Prostheses replace missing parts, orthotics work in conjunction with preserved limbs, and prosthetic eyes and facial prostheses reconstruct shape and contact soft tissue. This article organizes by task: upper limbs focus on grasping, holding, and releasing; lower limbs focus on support and rolling; orthotics focus on positioning or assisting movement; and maxillofacial restorations focus on appearance, wearing, and care.

Personalization includes both form and function. Scanning aligns shells with individual anatomy, while joint orientation, local stiffness, connections, actuation and surface treatment determine their function. Endpoints must therefore be device-specific: grasp success, gait measurements and appearance scores answer different questions. Sustained use additionally requires observation of donning and doffing, training, maintenance and refitting. [R03][R04][R10]

Ten nodes cover the key aspects from structural configuration to clinical experience. The diagram shows both the design progress within similar devices and the connections between different devices sharing evaluation methods. The intersection of academia and industry lies in the fact that design documents can be updated with feedback, manufacturing processes can be executed stably, and users can experience improvements that align with their goals.
N1 | Body-powered fingers in personal tasks

Two finger amputation cases reported in 2022 utilized the open-source Knick Finger design, which assisted flexion and extension by preserving the metacarpophalangeal joint movement and using linkages and traction structures. After one month of training, both participants showed improvement in personal goals such as cooking and computer typing, and reported satisfaction. [R01]

This study focuses on residual motor function as the starting point for structural design. Defects with the same appearance may have different joint ranges of motion, strength, and contact tolerance; therefore, the traction path and fixation method of the device need to be determined in collaboration with the user. Individual goals can also differentiate task requirements: holding cutlery stably, touching a keyboard, and lifting heavy objects all place different demands on fingertip position, movement speed, and contact friction.

Moving from case studies to comparative studies allows for simultaneous recording of standard and personal tasks, observing changes before and after training. Standard tasks facilitate comparison between different devices, while personal tasks explain whether the device alters daily life. It's also important to record which tasks the device is chosen to wear, when it is actively removed, and maintenance needs each day. This ensures the benefits of body-driven design correspond to specific usage scenarios and provides directional feedback for subsequent improvements to joint range of motion, fingertip surfaces, and retainer rings.
N2 | Separating grasp variables through thumb configurations

The 2022 study compared four low-cost prosthetic hand configurations, observing grasping and retention performance using AHAP and simplified SHAP. The combination of thumb opposition, abduction/adduction, and flexion/extension affects the manipulation of different objects; independent control provides more options while increasing the number of control components. [R02]

The node indicates that the number of degrees of freedom needs to be interpreted in conjunction with the motion organization. The thumb's ability to move does not guarantee it will provide adequate counterforce when contacting an object; a fixed thumb, if properly oriented, may stably complete tasks involving large objects. During testing, it should be observed whether the object is grasped, whether the posture matches the target, whether the hand can maintain its position after rotation, and how many repositionings are required. Each failure corresponds to a different design reason.

The design iteration can fix the other fingers and actuators, changing only the thumb's direction, range of motion, or control coupling, and then comparing the results using the same set of objects. This distinguishes configuration effects from surface friction, manufacturing quality, and operator skill. The feedback returned here by subsequent bench comparisons in the diagram precisely transforms certain types of grip failures into modifiable parameters. User training is then arranged after the mechanism's performance stabilizes, ensuring that the added control capabilities ultimately serve to reduce operational burden and achieve more reliable movements.
N3 | A common prosthetic-hand test bench isolates mechanical grasp differences

A 2024 study used a standardized AHAP bench setup to compare three printed and three commercial prosthetic hands, adding published data for four existing printed designs. Printed specimens generally performed worse in cylindrical, diagonal volar, extension and spherical grasps. The results identified targets for improvements in mechanisms or manufacturing quality. [R03]

Bench tests examine hand–object contact while reducing variation from socket fit and myoelectric control. They assess whether a mechanism can hold an object after a grasp pattern is selected and permit repeat testing after component or material changes. Report separate scores for each grasp because an overall mean may conceal weakness in a key daily task.

When conducting user studies, the testing tasks should also include autonomous grip selection, arm positioning, and bimanual coordination. Bench performance forms the structural basis for this type of evaluation, while user outcomes reintegrate control and training. A two-stage comparison can be used, first the bench and then the user, reporting object retention, task time, erroneous actions, and usage preferences on the same version. This provides companies with a concrete list of actionable improvements, and clinical selection can be based on the match between the user's primary tasks and the device's capabilities.
N4 | Scan-customized AFOs in individual gait tests

A 2011 study used laser scanning, computer design, and rapid prototyping to create two individual ankle-foot orthoses, which were then compared with prefabricated polypropylene devices in one subject. The observed gait function was similar, and the digital route enabled adaptation to individual anatomical features. [R04]

This node establishes the basic chain from the body surface to the supporting device. The contact area, edges, and in-shoe space of the ankle-foot orthosis affect whether it can be worn comfortably, while its restriction and support effect on the joint depends on stiffness. When simply replicating the shape, these two layers of effects may be mixed; research designs can compare materials under the same geometry, or change the support range under the same materials, gradually identifying the morphological and mechanical contributions.

Gait assessment should follow the intended treatment goal. For foot drop, assess toe clearance and ankle position during swing; for joint instability, assess weight-bearing phases and asymmetry. Record footwear, walking speed and adaptation time to interpret repeated measurements. Digital records can then guide changes targeted at observed walking problems and support within-person comparisons with the first design.
N5 | Optimizing prosthetic feet for nonlinear toe stiffness

The 2021 prosthetic foot research used finite element analysis to simulate the final support phase, linking the forefoot curve, flexion space, concave structure, and flexion zone to optimize the moment-angle relationship and stress in the toe. The paper resulted in a computational design for a printable structure; physical fabrication and further verification are planned as subsequent steps. [R05]

The question is how one component can provide different responses at different deformation levels. Propulsion demands are not captured by one fixed stiffness; geometry can progressively increase mechanical resistance. A target moment–angle curve shifts design from resembling a foot to producing specified behaviour during a defined gait phase, while a maximum-stress constraint addresses load-bearing capacity.

The model transitions from calculation to actual device implementation, requiring the incorporation of material orientation, interlayer bonding, and printing errors into mechanical verification. This can be achieved by first measuring the actual torque-angle curve, then conducting cyclic and multi-directional load tests, and finally examining the user's rolling propulsion and performance at different speeds. Each stage retains the same design version, allowing simulation, bench testing, and walking to be mutually interpretable. This node, along with the ankle-foot brace, emphasizes that individualized stiffness should be selected according to specific movement goals, and its applicability should be verified through real-world tasks.
N6 | Open-source wrist-driven orthoses: joint iteration by users and fabricators

A 2018 open-source wrist-driven orthosis study incorporated feedback from three people with spinal cord injury and six orthotics students and published dimensions and assembly methods. Material costs were approximately US$15–20 depending on size, and manual assembly took about 1.5 hours. Benefits varied across personal tasks, and feedback informed changes to structure and fasteners. [R06]

This study breaks down accessibility into observable steps. Easy material availability is just the starting point; manufacturers also need to understand sizing modifications, joint assembly, and fitting methods, while users need to be able to put on and take off the garment and maintain stable contact. Modifications to the straps, magnetic connections, and finger supports extend the research from mechanical movements to everyday operations. For individuals with limited hand dexterity, independent wearability is itself an important functional endpoint.

Future evaluation should record the full pathway from measurement to first use, including printing waits, manual assembly, clinical adjustments and remanufacture. Pair reasons for modifications with task outcomes to determine whether simpler assembly affects reliability or easier donning and doffing supports continued use. Versioned open-source documentation enables replication across institutions and feedback from local needs, supporting transition from low-cost prototypes to sustainable rehabilitation services.
N7 | Testing immediate hand function with a myoelectric orthosis

A 2019 study used a printed structure, electromyographic input, and active actuation to construct a hand orthosis, comparing participants with and without the device on the same day in 10 participants with chronic cervical spinal cord injury. Improvements were observed in hand function tests and eating-related performance, while changes in fine object manipulation and other self-care tasks were limited. [R07]

This node shifts evaluation of active assistance from actuator output to the user's ability to complete tasks. Greater grip strength may help lift a cup, but dressing and washing also depend on trunk control, joint movement and bimanual coordination. Report self-care tasks separately, alongside device size, weight, adjustment and wearing requirements, to identify the tasks most directly improved by mechanical assistance.

Longer-term studies can include adaptation before examining whether learning expands task benefits or added control increases fatigue. Hold the device version constant and record myoelectric calibration and daily use to distinguish training from redesign. Feedback to the wrist-driven node represents shared questions of donning and doffing, fit and task matching. Choices between body-powered and active assistance should follow residual abilities and daily-life goals.
N8 | Silicone powder binder jetting: soft prostheses require a complete material process

A study published in a 2022 journal issue used PVB-coated silicone powder for binder jetting, followed by sequential pressure–vacuum infiltration with silicone and solvent to produce final components. Particle size, coating, surface treatment and infiltration conditions jointly influenced the mechanical properties of printed preforms and finished structures. [R08]

Soft facial prostheses must combine shape, thin margins and compliant contact, unlike rigid shells. Conversion of a printed porous preform into an infiltrated component can change dimensions, porosity and material continuity. Printing and post-processing should therefore be assessed as one workflow, with measurements of both the preform and final state to identify sources of appearance or strength deviations.

As this approach is further developed, areas of varying thicknesses can be designed for localized features such as the ear and nose, allowing for comparison of changes after edge tearing, repeated bending, and cleaning. Color and surface detail also need to be evaluated in the final material state, as impregnation and curing alter optical properties. Digital manufacturing provides repeatable geometry, while patient fit determines the suitability of edges, softness, and fixation. The research findings can provide a comparable comparison between mold forming and direct printing.
N9 | OCT and color models generate ocular prostheses

A 2024 study used anterior-segment OCT to capture eye-socket information, a statistical shape model to complete the fitting geometry and calibrated images of the fellow eye to generate appearance. Ocular prostheses were made by multicomponent colour printing and post-processing. Initial clinical applications in 10 patients were presented, with final shapes still fitted and adjusted by an ocularist. [R09]

The individualization here is accomplished through two types of data: geometric description of the spatial relationship between the eyelid and the contact surface, and color description of the appearance of the iris, sclera, and blood vessels. Both need to be consistent across the same coordinate system and production version; otherwise, adjusting the shape may alter the iris position or visible area. The statistical model is responsible for forming a usable initial shape from limited scan information, which is then confirmed by clinical adaptation.

Repeat fabrication is an important endpoint. Appearance data can be retained for the same patient, but eye-socket conditions and preferences may change, so remanufacture should permit colour preservation with independent adjustment of the contact surface. Evaluate automated generation time, manual modifications, fitting attempts and final appearance consistency. Feeding ocularists' adjustments back to the model could improve initial fit and reduce professional work per completed case.
N10 | A randomized ocular-prosthesis comparison separates comfort and microbiological outcomes

A 2023 randomized study randomly assigned 22 participants to either a printed prosthetic eye or a traditional PMMA prosthetic eye, with a three-month follow-up. No significant differences were found in microbiological results between the two groups. The printed group reported better comfort levels, and there were no significant differences between the groups in terms of secretions, tearing, and lubrication frequency. [R10]

This node breaks down the measurement of prosthetic eye performance. Aesthetic acceptance, contact comfort, and microbial colonization can be influenced by various factors, including posterior surface adaptation, polishing, care, and wearing habits. Therefore, the study needs to pre-define the measurement time and methods for each endpoint to avoid using any single factor to represent the entire effect. Actual infection, surface colonization, and subjective discomfort should also be recorded as separate outcomes.

This node provides feedback for automated design: local discomfort informs shape changes, care requirements inform surface and cleaning procedures, and colour changes inform appearance materials. Longer follow-up can record insertion/removal frequency, polishing and replacement reasons. As in hand and gait research, separate endpoints link manufacturing to actual experience and trigger traceable design updates.

sections.title: The Evolution of Academic Approaches and Common Methods

blocks.text: The changes in this research direction are primarily reflected in more specific task descriptions. Hand research has progressed from assessing the flexion and extension capabilities of the mechanism to conducting sub-tests on different grips; gait research has evolved from conforming to the shape to assessing stiffness response during movement; and prosthetic eye research has progressed from aesthetic manufacturing to contact and care. Technological advancements are demonstrated by the new questions that can be answered, rather than by the complexity of the printed parts or the quantity of research conducted.

A second development is preserving shared conditions in comparisons. Prosthetic-hand bench tests reduce effects of control and socket fit to isolate mechanism differences; within-user tests with and without orthoses assess immediate assistance; randomized ocular-prosthesis comparisons place manufacturing routes in a shared follow-up framework. Each addresses part of attribution, together informing the roles of structure, fit and learning. [R03][R07][R10]

Feedback is also becoming stored design information. Open-source wrist-driven orthoses translate users' donning, doffing and grasping difficulties into component changes, while data-driven ocular prostheses retain clinical fitting after automated shape generation. [R06][R09] Recording each modification's location, magnitude and reason creates a comparable version history. Frequent changes can identify parameters suitable for automated adjustment and those still requiring in-person assessment.

Research organizations also need to preserve population differences. Amputation level, residual joint mobility, muscle signals, and trunk control influence device selection; walking ability and footwear affect lower limb support; and orbital morphology and care capabilities affect prosthetic eye use. Stratification is not about increasing reporting complexity, but about ensuring clear applicability of technical conclusions. The same device exhibiting different benefits in different tasks can serve as a basis for design differentiation.

More informative research can use sequential validation: first hold materials and mechanisms constant for bench comparisons, then identify fitting issues through short-term use, and finally assess training, maintenance and long-term choices. Shared version numbers and records of modifications link laboratory and patient results, giving manufacturers specific targets for iteration.

sections.title: Research–enterprise links through disclosed patent mechanisms

blocks.text: Prostheses/orthoses connect retained capability, mechanical adjustment and tissue contact through distinct tasks. Actual product workflows are retained below; three patents connect regional hardness, ankle stiffness and ocular shape/color. Studies supply task/tissue-response methods, patents define adjustable variables and companies show how measurements become revisable deliveries.[R01][R03][R04][R07][R09][R10]

Naked Prosthetics' PIPDriver is a body-driven finger product that revolves around preserving proximal interphalangeal joints and residual finger conditions. It uses nylon and titanium components and is individually manufactured using advanced printing. The product's positioning shares the idea of "complementing movement with preserved capabilities" with finger case studies, with joint alignment, residual finger length, and contact stability as the core adaptation principles. [R11]

Open Bionics' official timeline states that the Hero Arm was launched in 2018, and in 2020, the early PLA hand and frame were updated to laser-sintered nylon 12, while the inner liner and outer casing connections were improved. This technological evolution encompasses three aspects: structural materials, residual limb interfaces, and user operation, indicating that product updates are gradually revolving around long-term user experience. [R12]

Spentys' current ankle-foot orthosis process incorporates weight, activity level, clinical type, scan source, support shape, local thickness, and manufacturing location into the order. Dynamic models also allow selection of joint configuration and activity requirements. This platform transforms clinical choices into fields that can be passed to both design and manufacturing, enabling individualization beyond physical dimensions and allowing institutions to choose between centralized printing or local manufacturing. [R13]

ActivArmor's provider workflow connects mobile phone scanning, custom design based on clinical positioning and instructions, and in-house manufacturing. Its product service focuses on the delivery of fixation and protection devices, with open structures and adjustable fixation providing operational space for follow-up examinations. [R14] Evaluating this type of platform can focus on observing acquisition success rates, design round trips, initial wear, and adjustments after volume changes to understand how same-day manufacturing goals are achieved within the complete clinical workflow.

Regarding prosthetic eyes, Fraunhofer IGD's 2024 translational data connects Cuttlefish-related technologies, Moorfields clinical applications, and Ocupeye's specialized manufacturing. Software, manufacturing, and clinical fitting are handled by different participants, forming a reusable production chain. [R15] The importance of this organizational approach lies in assigning geometry and color processing, post-printing surface treatment, and final fitting to their respective stages, while connecting them using the same patient data.

These pathways demonstrate how companies are expanding from selling single finished products to providing organizational adaptation services. Body-driven fingers, myoelectric prosthetics, dynamic ankle-foot braces, fixation devices, and prosthetic eyes have different delivery requirements, but all require clearly defined inputs, versions, and subsequent modification entry points. Product comparisons can therefore simultaneously present device capabilities and service capabilities: the former determines what can be done, and the latter determines how quickly usable devices can be restored in case of problems.
Regional hardness

US2016235158A1 names Clemson University and ABILITY PROSTHETICS & ORTHOTICS and describes local hardness through cell void volume/material. AFO gait and wrist-driven orthosis studies show why equal contours may provide different support/contact. Spentys weight/activity/thickness fields supply inputs; ActivArmor supplies posture/open-structure context. Evaluate pressure, tasks and donning alongside hardness.[R04][R06][R13][R14][R17]
Stiffness needs gait targets

Michigan’s US2022339017A1 describes separate printed footplate/cuff and a prefabricated strut with width/thickness for ankle stiffness and shoe fit. Nonlinear prosthetic-foot research extends average stiffness to moment–angle/task-phase response. Spentys dynamic AFOs supply activity context. Test struts, joints and whole devices, distinguishing assistance from junction fatigue; component stiffness alone does not establish gait benefit.[R04][R05][R13][R18]
Shape/color still need tissue validation

CN115923122A from Aier Sichuan/Chengdu Shumou describes healthy-eye OCT, affected-side modeling, reverse design and texture/color mapping for ocular prostheses. Data-driven ocular research shares the acquisition/design chain; the randomized trial supplies comfort/microbiological endpoints. Fraunhofer/Cuttlefish, Moorfields and Ocupeye supply software/manufacturing/fitting roles. Compare acquisition, finishing and fitting revisions beyond visual similarity.[R09][R10][R15][R16]

sections.title: Translation and validation: variables, controls and decisions

blocks.text: Stratify validation by task. AFO bench tests establish moment–angle, pressure and fatigue before within-user gait comparison. Hand assessments retain common tasks, training and retained capability; orthosis results cannot establish hand-prosthesis performance. Ocular tests confirm geometry/color/surface before fitting, comfort and tissue contact. Retain input/material/joint/finishing versions for every revision.[R02][R03][R07][R10]

headers: Proposed comparison, endpoints and next decision
rows: Hardness zones
Compare uniform/regional cells in equal contours for hardness, pressure and wear tasks. Relief causing collapse or lost stability requires transition redesign.[R17]
Ankle stiffness
Fix plate/cuff and vary strut dimensions; measure moment–angle, shoe volume and joint fatigue before gait comparison. Joint failure despite suitable stiffness prioritizes interfaces.[R18]
Ocular chain

Compare acquisition/finishing versions within patients for shape/color, fitting revisions, comfort and conjunctival response. Better appearance with discomfort redirects edges, polishing and fitting.[R16]

Inputs mapped to local hardness in Spentys/ActivArmor-like systems could create prescription/structure records. Track hardness repeatability, pressure and initial adjustments. Operator drift narrows adjustable scope.[R13][R14][R17]

Struts retaining whole-device fatigue/shoe fit could support task-specific AFO options. Track moment–angle retention, junction damage, gait and wear time. Better gait with poorer durability pauses stiffness expansion.[R13][R18]

Reproducible ocular design/finishing across institutions could support full-delivery comparisons of Fraunhofer/Ocupeye-like chains. Track acquisition failure, manual finishing, tissue response and reorder consistency. Technician-dependent quality retains specialist fitting.[R15][R16]

blocks.text: The common value is interpretable adjustment and restored use after problems. Mechanical assistance, appearance and tissue tolerance need their own endpoints linked by user/version. Revision and maintenance also determine service maturity.

Research in this area has formed multiple executable chains, from individual input and structural design to task evaluation. Upper limb devices focus on residual abilities and grasping mechanisms, lower limb devices focus on staged mechanical responses, orthotics focus on support and independent operation, and maxillofacial restorations focus on appearance and tissue contact. Together, they drive individualization from size matching to designs with clear functional justifications.

The most noteworthy aspect to observe in the next phase is whether each chain can retain complete feedback: task failures return to the mechanism, gait changes return to stiffness, donning and doffing obstacles return to the fixation method, wearing discomfort return to the contact surface, and maintenance issues return to materials and services. By preserving these feedbacks as comparable versions, academic trials and enterprise deliverables can continuously improve around the same user goals.

P3-01.title: Personalized Oral Dosage Forms
P3-01.subtitle: Co-designing dose, release and use
P3-01.thesis: Personalized oral dosage forms align digital geometry, actual drug content and patient use. Geometry and multi-ingredient studies provide design capabilities, pediatric and rare-disease studies define practical constraints, and low-dose comparisons translate capabilities into measurable quality benefits.

blocks.text: This research direction organizes evidence based on specific application tasks, placing formulation design, measurable quality, and actual usage conditions within the same research chain. Geometric adjustments provide design freedom, but each adjustment requires explanation of which physical processes it affects; the usage scenario determines which changes are valuable, and the original questions are addressed accordingly.
How can printed tablets achieve personalized doses?

Personalized dosing must match both the prescription and actual drug content. Tablet volume adjusts total quantity, but formulation uniformity, extrusion or sintering, drying and individual-tablet mass all affect the final dose.
Therefore, the problem has two aspects: how to manufacture multiple dosage strengths, and how to prove that each strength is stable, accurate, and suitable for administration.
How do dosage-form shape and internal structure affect administration and release?

Tablet shape, size, porosity and internal cavities alter liquid pathways, diffusion distances and erosion, while affecting handling, swallowing and splitting. The same drug amount can have different structures, and similar appearances can conceal different release mechanisms.
This question considers structure as part of the formulation's function, focusing on how it affects release and its connection to patient needs.
What do children and special populations need from personalized dosage forms?

Children may require dose adjustments with weight and disease status and may struggle with swallowing or bitter taste. Some patients need tube feeding, while others take several formulations long term; caregivers also perform preparation and record keeping.

Therefore, individualization requires simultaneous consideration of dosage, form, taste, route of administration, and care process. Different populations cannot be distinguished solely by age or tablet size.
How can fast-dissolving oral films and new dosage forms support personalized administration?

Fast-dissolving oral films must be easy to handle, disperse rapidly and retain an accurate drug quantity. Locally adhesive films must remain at a specified site. Both are thin, but their intended uses differ.

The printer allows for adjustable membrane area, thickness, number of layers, and composition distribution. Its practical value lies in adapting dosage or function as needed while maintaining stability in packaging, handling, and drug delivery processes.
How can printed capsules and combination formulations support personalized treatment?

Combination formulations must accommodate several active ingredients while addressing dose ratios, compatibility and release. Required combinations may change with treatment, so customization extends beyond placing drugs in one shell.

This issue includes printing multi-chamber, layered formulations, and printing capsules that synergize with liquid or granule dispensing. They reduce manufacturing limitations between ingredients in different ways.
N1 | Geometry couples dose and release (2015)

A 2015 study printed acetaminophen-containing polyvinyl alcohol filaments into five geometries and found that release correlated with surface-area-to-volume ratio. Dimensional changes can alter both dose and release, so personalized design must control both outcomes. [R01]

Comparing the geometry within the same material system allows for a better separation of compositional and shape changes. Surface area determines the initial interface with the liquid, while volume determines the total amount to be released; therefore, the ratio of the two is closer to the mass transfer task than considering area alone. This conclusion imposes a constraint on individualized dosing: scaling up the volume typically does not increase the interface proportionally, and changing the dosage may simultaneously alter the release rate.

The next step in the research needs to differentiate between external shape, internal structure, and material behavior. If the goal is similar release at different doses, it's advisable to maintain the critical mass transfer length or use a combination of multiple small units, and use measured curves to determine whether this is achieved. N2 and N3 offer two decoupling approaches for the shell and membrane area, respectively, while N9 returns to actual content verification, ultimately linking numerical dimensions to quality evidence.

Causal explanations in geometric studies require a distinction between initial surface area and dynamic surface area that changes with erosion. If the difference in the curves occurs later, the initial shape index may only be a surrogate variable; a time-series characterization of structural evolution can verify whether the model truly captures the controlling process.
N2 | Capsule shells and liquid dispensing (2018)

A 2018 study combined FDM printing of polymer shells with liquid dispensing to load theophylline solution or dipyridamole suspension. Shell material and thickness affected release, while dispensed volume determined drug loading, enabling separate optimization of thermally processed structures and liquid-drug handling. [R02]

Separating shell fabrication from liquid filling allows processing conditions and functions to be optimized for different materials. The shell controls liquid retention and diffusion paths, the dispenser controls the quantity of contents, and their junction provides sealing. Assessing both fill quantity and shell structure shows that personalization need not subject every ingredient to the same thermal or mechanical history.

This modularity raises two new questions: whether the liquid alters the shell properties over time, and whether different filling states change the release. Therefore, validation needs to cover the interaction of fill level, seal integrity, and shelf life, rather than relying solely on fill volume linearity to determine the equivalence of the entire product. N4's hierarchical system further demonstrates that the digital spatial boundaries must also be examined in conjunction with the actual drug distribution.

The capsule system allows for the observation of the independent effect of fill weight on release using controls with different fill levels but identical shells. Conversely, changing the shell while maintaining the fill weight allows for the identification of barrier contributions. This two-way comparison quantifies the advantages of modular manufacturing, rather than remaining solely at the device configuration level.
N3 | Film area linked to drug content (2019)

The 2019 warfarin membrane study used semi-solid extrusion to produce flexible oral membranes with adjustable drug content. The designed dimensions showed a good linear relationship with drug content, making membrane area a dose-adjusting variable. For low-dose formulations, it is crucial to validate this relationship in conjunction with uniform distribution and actual dimensions. [R03]

The oral membrane simplifies a three-dimensional dosage form into a thinner plane, making area a design quantity that is easily adjustable. For changes in area to correspond to changes in dosage, both thickness and drug distribution per unit area must be stable; if different deposition or drying behaviors exist at the membrane edge and center, the overall linear relationship may still mask local inhomogeneities. Therefore, this method selection offers advantages in both manufacturability and testability.

The application tasks of film also include integrity after peeling, handling, and wetting. Thinning facilitates dispersion but may increase operational breakage; increasing the area, while increasing content, may also alter the user experience in the oral cavity. Patient preference studies of N6 provide design feedback suggesting that dosage, strength, and size need to all fall within an acceptable product range, rather than pursuing an extreme value for any one of them.

The area-content relationship requires reporting the prediction interval as well. A high correlation coefficient indicates a consistent trend, but does not directly suggest that the absolute error of each small membrane is sufficiently low; especially in low-drug-loaded units, the proportion of edge loss increases, and both ends of the dose range should be included in independent testing.
N4 | Layering does not ensure ingredient isolation (2019)

In 2019, a six-component photopolymerization study fabricated a multilayer structure, and Raman microscopy was used to examine the distribution. Although independent printed layers were formed, some drugs still diffused across layers, and the differences were related to the drug state. This indicates that the layering in CAD must be confirmed through actual component distribution. [R04]

The choice of Raman microscopy is crucial: ordinary photographs prove the appearance of layers, but cannot prove that each drug remains at the target location. Composition maps link spatial design with chemical distribution, revealing how amorphous or crystalline states and material compatibility can affect migration. Therefore, the focus of research on multi-component formulations shifts from the number of chambers to the actual boundaries of components during manufacturing and storage.

If interlayer migration changes local concentrations, neighboring materials can also influence each ingredient’s release, so simple addition of single-drug results may fail. Comparing single layers, adjacent bilayers and complete combinations can locate interactions at contact interfaces or whole-structure wetting. This converges with patient combination needs in N7: reducing administration frequency requires interpretable, reproducible multi-ingredient quality.

The validation of multi-drug combinations should also consider the selectivity of the detection. Total content or a single spectral peak cannot identify all components; spatial analysis and component-by-component quantification each have their own tasks. Both types of evidence together form the basis for judging the interlayer isolation and the correctness of the combination.
N5 | Validating sustained use in rare disease (2019)

A 2019 isoleucine chewable-formulation study used a single-center prospective crossover design to examine personalized compounding and acceptability in patients with maple syrup urine disease. Evaluation moved from formulation specimens to patients requiring ongoing treatment adjustment, bringing dose, taste and administration together. [R05]

The study uses patients as a comparative context between different formulations, establishing a practical link between continuous dosage needs and manufacturing capabilities. The significance of chewable dosage forms lies not only in changing appearance, but also in changing the patient's action of completing a single dose. Clinical monitoring, taste feedback, and prescription records need to be analyzed in parallel to identify whether observed differences stem from formulation quality, usage behavior, or concurrent disease management.

This small-scale study sets the stage for a reasonable task of further expansion: testing more ingredients, more preferences, and long-term reusability. N7 extends this to six children and a combination amino acid formulation; N9 examines the accuracy of low-dose units at the pharmacy level. The two lines of investigation, one focusing on willingness to use and the other on accurate availability, will ultimately converge in a comprehensive evaluation of the personalized oral product.

The crossover order and time effect in the patient study are also worth observing. Familiarity with the new dosage form may improve later acceptance, and changes in growth and routine management may also alter monitoring indicators; continuous recording can help interpret these factors and provide a basis for designing more targeted comparisons later.
N6 | Children’s preferences alter design constraints (2020)

The 2020 Children's Visual Survey examined the appearance preferences of different printed tablets. It incorporates shape, color, and recognizability into formulation development, but visual preference alone cannot answer questions about actual swallowing or long-term acceptability. [R06]

This survey compares similar sizes and shapes manufactured using different processes to minimize interference from macroscopic geometric differences. Informing children that the formulation is chewable alters their preferences, indicating that children's choices are influenced by both visual perception and expectations of the method of administration. Design decisions that prioritize surface smoothness may overlook usability attributes that make the formulation more acceptable. [R06]

Therefore, preference studies should be designed separately for visual selection, actual user experience, and continuous use. These are at different stages of the behavioral chain and cannot be substituted for one another. For N1 and N3, patient feedback provides the boundaries for shape and size; for N7, it provides the basis for choosing flavor and combination. Future research questions include whether these choices are stable after repeated use and whether caregiver and child evaluations are consistent.

Child studies can further analyze tasks by developmental stage, rather than just by age group. The ability to independently grasp, understand labels, and complete swallowing are different skills; which skill a product needs to be adapted to should be defined in advance. This will change the way acceptance questions are asked and the actual evaluation process.
N7 | Combining multiple ingredients with patient feedback (2024)

The 2024 study developed different amino acid chewable formulations, including two-component combinations, for six children with rare metabolic diseases in a hospital and collected feedback on taste and usage. Target amino acid levels were maintained, and the combination formulations reduced the frequency of administration. Individualization moved from single-dose adjustments to combined adjustments of ingredients, taste, and dosing burden. [R07]

The study expanded from a single manufacturing specification to a portfolio of products catering to multiple patient needs, with ingredient and flavor adjustments incorporated into the actual hospital medication dispensing process. The introduction of mobile phone feedback increased the observation time dimension, allowing receptiveness to go beyond a single interview. Fewer dosing sessions logically reduce preparation steps, but sustained adherence still requires linking feedback to actual usage records.

The benefits and adjustment costs of the combination are intertwined. Whether the entire combination must be remanufactured when one component needs to be changed, whether the release of other components can be maintained, and how to identify different strengths all affect long-term usability. N4 indicates the need to track component distribution, and N9 indicates the need to examine unit content; only by considering both factors and patient burden can it be determined which combination is worth continuing development.

Combination formulations may reduce the identification burden, but they may also increase the complexity of component adjustments. Studies should record the frequency of prescription changes and the number of units replaced to determine whether reducing one administration action is worthwhile by adding an overall preparation task.
N8 | Alternative administration routes redefine disintegration (2024)

An efavirenz study in the same year used laser sintering to prepare porous dispersible tablets for children requiring enteral feeding tubes. Polymer and loading conditions affected dispersion. This development shows that tube-feeding design must consider dispersion volume, residues and blockage risk, beyond simply producing a tablet. [R08]

The tube feeding scenario further refines the concept of "disintegration" into the ability to form a transferable system within a limited liquid and practical apparatus. Porous structures facilitate liquid entry, but matrix dissolution is also constrained by solvent capacity; increasing the polymer content may hinder complete dispersion under certain conditions. The differences observed in this study therefore indicate that porosity and hydrophilicity need to be considered in conjunction with environmental assessments.

Subsequent designs should independently assess device residues, drug-content recovery after dispersion and passage through the device to identify losses in containers or tubing. The task is to establish product tests consistent with intended use. This returns to N1: when the end-use task changes, appropriate geometric metrics also change, and ordinary dissolution tests cannot be extrapolated directly.

Losses in specific pathways are location-dependent. Residues in containers, interfaces, and pipelines reflect different mechanisms; segmented recovery analysis helps distinguish between adsorption, sedimentation, and mechanical retardation, and provides specific feedback for material selection and shape optimization.
N9 | Low-dose comparisons test benefits (2026)

A 2026 metoprolol study compared low-dose units obtained by manual halving, manual quartering and automated printing. Printed formulations met the relevant content-uniformity requirements at two hospital pharmacies and one compounding pharmacy, while manually split units varied more. The study addressed dose quality and established direct comparison with current practice. [R09]

This comparison shifts the value of individualization from design freedom to actual dose error distribution. Manual fracturing relies on fracture behavior, while printing relies on material homogeneity and deposition control; the error mechanisms of the two differ. Using the same content detection framework can identify which mechanism produces greater fluctuations under low-dose conditions and provide a basis for selecting suitable printing tasks.

The next step should be to compare quality benefits with preservation, patient identification, and delivery time in the same way. Personalization can only be transformed from a single-sample service to a repeatable service if stability across different pharmacies is supported by continuous data. This node provides feedback on N1 and N7: the digital dosage range should be defined by validated quality and usage; exceeding this range requires new product studies.

For multi-site comparisons, intra-site and inter-site variability should be estimated separately. The same average content does not necessarily mean that all sites are stable; stratified data by batch, date, and operator can reveal the sources of error that most need to be controlled when scaling up individualized manufacturing.

sections.title: Evolution of Commercial Technologies and Products

blocks.text: How can printed tablets achieve personalized doses?

Aprecia announced the launch of SPRITAM in 2016, using rapidly disintegrating structures formed by powder bonding for industrial pharmaceuticals. It demonstrates that printed formulations can become finished products, but its value lies primarily in dosage form and manufacturing, rather than in the ability for pharmacies to arbitrarily adjust dosages. [R10]

CurifyLabs' dispensing platform and 2026 metoprolol study enable the direct integration of enterprise equipment into small-dose preparation scenarios in hospitals and pharmacies. FABRX offers various printheads, weighing and spectral attachments to support formulation and batch adjustments. [R09] [R11]

The enterprise roadmap has expanded from printing equipment to a combination of prescription execution, formulation, manufacturing, and testing tools. The competitive focus in small-batch, individualized production is shifting towards accurate delivery, not just speed of production.
How do dosage-form shape and internal structure affect administration and release?

Aprecia's SPRITAM combines a porous, rapidly disintegrating structure with high drug loading to create an easily dispersible, industrially viable product. The geometric value chosen by the company is very specific: improved formulation disintegration and administration. [R10]

The FABRX platform supports different printing processes and multiple printheads, providing structural adjustment capabilities for research and small-batch manufacturing. Its quality-control accessories allows for the integration of single-piece weighing and process information into manufacturing. [R11]

These represent different commercial endpoints: one fixes a particular structure into a stable product, while the other provides tools to change structures. Academic principles become reproducible in both settings when incorporated into formulation, process and testing requirements.
What do children and special populations need from personalized dosage forms?

The FABRX equipment and formulation development work has entered into hospital-based individualized research, and its platform supports different extrusion processes, multiple printheads, and quality accessories. This corresponds to the pharmaceutical team's ability to select and execute specific formulation protocols. [R11]

For enterprises, the product value of extends beyond a single printer to include available dosage forms, formulation tools, and consistent workflows. For specific populations, the most meaningful product metrics include applicable dosage range, actual route of administration, and pharmacy processing time.
How can fast-dissolving oral films and new dosage forms support personalized administration?

These enterprise capabilities correspond to formulation and process inspection in the academic chain. For oral films, the real determinants of application also include drying, peeling, single-sheet processing, and packaging, not just the printing path.

If companies can organize the area-dosage relationship, drying conditions, and testing methods of a specific formulation into an executable protocol, they can reduce the workload of developing each item individually. Different drugs still require corresponding formulation validation.
How can printed capsules and combination formulations support personalized treatment?

The expansion of enterprise capabilities is reflected beyond printing: ingredient allocation, process switching, batch recording, and quality inspection together determine whether compound preparations can be remanufactured.

The focus of productization has therefore shifted from "how many drugs can be printed" to "which combinations can be stably executed." Different formulation combinations require corresponding formulation compatibility, content, and release validation.

sections.title: Academic–enterprise links: mechanisms to executable schemes

blocks.text: The industrial interface is a reproducible rule connecting prescribed dose, structure and administration. Geometry research supplies structural variables, pediatric and rare-disease studies define patient tasks, and the low-dose metoprolol comparison supplies actual content as an endpoint. Patents specify implementations of dose-to-volume conversion, unfolding capsules and drug-bearing films; equipment must execute these inputs with quality records.[R01][R05][R07][R09]

headers: Academic evidence, patent scheme and enterprise role
rows: Dose to geometry

Guangdong Pharmaceutical University’s CN106821755A sets formulation density and radius-to-height ratio before dose input, modelling and pharmacist confirmation. This connects geometry and tablet-splitting research to FABRX M3DIMAKER preparation and weighing. The link is a testable prescription-execution scheme: formulation changes require recalibrating effective density versus drug amount; shape cannot substitute for assay.[R01][R09][R11][R12]
Structure to use

Zhejiang University’s CN108635336A discloses near-field electrospun drug-bearing meshes with different spacing, folded into a capsule and unfolded after shell dissolution. It shares spatial-organization questions with liquid-capsule and polypill research. Aprecia SPRITAM is a product comparator with a different target: rapid disintegration versus proposed retention and release control. Printability alone cannot unify their evaluation.[R02][R04][R10][R13]
Film to task

Sahmyook University’s industry-academic foundation discloses aripiprazole/biocompatible-resin filament and an orodispersible film in KR20230114255A. This is a materials and area-dose comparison with warfarin films; FABRX supplies a multi-process equipment reference. Pediatric preferences and tube-administration research require separate handling, oral dispersion and tube-passage tests rather than one thickness metric.[R03][R06][R08][R11][R14]

sections.title: Translation and validation: variables, controls and decisions

blocks.text: Translation should fix one drug, dose range and administration task before testing transfer of a design rule. Link prescribed dose, model volume, deposited mass, assayed content and delivered amount to locate conversion, mixing, printing or use errors. Include the low-dose end and routine handling variation, retaining independent chemical assays: weighing detects missing material but not segregation. Use conventional compounding or splitting at the same prescription as the practical comparator.[R09][R11][R12]

Separate prescription changes from manufacturing changes. Material lots, drying or deposition can change volume/content at one prescription, while a formulation change can alter dose at one volume. A prescription database therefore needs formulation version, measured effective density, model rule and review, beyond a shape file. If low-dose error comes from substrate/packaging residues, finer printing may not help; reduce transfers and assay the amount actually taken.[R03][R09][R12][R14]

headers: Variables, controls, endpoints and failure decisions
rows: Volume conversion

Vary dose with formulation and aspect ratio fixed across days; compare splitting and compounding. Measure content, uniformity and rework causes. If density drift changes amount per volume, narrow the formulation window before extending prescriptions.[R09][R12]
Folded mesh

At equal drug amount compare spacing and unfolded controls; record deployment, integrity and release curves. Separate shell-dissolution time from mesh behavior. Unstable deployment or fold damage calls for structural redesign rather than dose escalation.[R02][R13]
Film use

Compare area and thickness against content, peeling loss, dispersion and packaged integrity; assay handling residue at low doses. Separate oral and tube-use comparators. If strength gains impede dispersion, revise material and packaging before simply increasing area.[R03][R08][R14]

blocks.text: Patient evaluation should inform manufacturing choices. Color/appearance preferences help acceptance but do not establish swallowing or accurate handling; caregiver preparation, dispersion vessels and tube rinsing affect delivery. For titration, first confirm that resizing does not simultaneously change dispersion/release. Enterprises can organize successful prescriptions and failure causes into restricted options specifying when to retain structure or change material/form, for pharmacist confirmation.[R05][R06][R07][R08][R11][R12][R13]

For 2027–2029, follow the prescription–structure–delivery chain. Observable enterprise progress comprises validated drug/dose combinations, exception records and actual use outcomes; the number of shapes only describes design space. Pediatric and rare-disease expansion should feed caregiver preparation time and error causes into formulation versions.[R05][R06][R07][R11]

rows: If FABRX-type equipment closes volume conversion against independent assay, build cross-day batches for established drugs and tasks. Track low-dose failures and pharmacist review effort; content drift despite passing mass checks requires chemical release testing and revised mixing.[R09][R11][R12]

Reproducible capsule deployment and film handling could support task-matched evaluation. Compare dispersion with SPRITAM and delivery/release with conventional capsules. If patient actions add variability, retain simpler dosage forms as alternatives.[R10][R13][R14]

Consistent conversion, content and use across operators/sites could justify incremental library expansion. Track revalidation after version changes, rejected units and remakes. If expansion requires extensive manual correction, concentrate on a small set of high-need prescriptions.[R07][R09][R11][R12]

blocks.text: Decisions should run from patient task back to manufacturing: choose the administration problem, then film, tablet or capsule, then equipment and release tests. These patents make dose conversion, deployment and film materials concrete engineering questions linking research and products through shared failure causes.

P3-02.title: Drug Release Control
P3-02.subtitle: From geometric adjustment to mechanism-constrained release design
P3-02.thesis: Printed release control requires distinguishing the roles of geometry, drug solid state, material responses and actual exposure conditions. Different mechanisms can produce the same curve; combining structural characterization, independent controls and validation across conditions is necessary for reusable digitally designed release strategies.

questions.question: How can materials and structures enable sustained and controlled release?
questions.focus: Sustained release prolongs release; controlled release also adjusts rate, onset or stages. Printing offers geometric freedom, while water uptake, dissolution, diffusion and structural changes jointly govern release.

questions.question: How can dissolution and immediate release of poorly soluble drugs be improved?
questions.focus: Poorly soluble drugs need improved dissolution; immediate release requires rapid release from the dosage form. Tablet disintegration, drug dissolution and eventual absorption are connected but distinct steps.

questions.question: How can multidrug and layered structures provide staged release?
questions.focus: Staged release includes different ingredients released at different rates, repeated release of one ingredient, or sequential onset of different drugs. Compartments separate space; timing also depends on barrier dissolution, liquid entry and drug-loaded materials.

questions.question: How can gastrointestinal targeting or stimulus responses control release location?
questions.focus: Gastric retention keeps a dosage form in the stomach, whereas intestinal targeting avoids premature release and delivers in a specific segment. Buoyancy, shape change, time barriers and pH responses act through different mechanisms.
