blocks.text: This research direction organizes evidence based on specific application tasks, placing formulation design, measurable quality, and actual usage conditions within the same research chain. Geometric adjustments provide design freedom, but each adjustment requires explanation of which physical processes it affects; the usage scenario determines which changes are valuable, and the original questions are addressed accordingly.
How can materials and structures enable sustained and controlled release?

Sustained release prolongs release; controlled release also adjusts rate, onset or stages. Printing offers geometric freedom, while water uptake, dissolution, diffusion and structural changes jointly govern release.
This question focuses on how design variables affect the release mechanism, and which research stages need to be connected when entering product development from the in vitro curve.
How can dissolution and immediate release of poorly soluble drugs be improved?

Poorly soluble drugs need improved dissolution; immediate release requires rapid release from the dosage form. Tablet disintegration, drug dissolution and eventual absorption are connected but distinct steps.
This question focuses on how materials and structure work together to improve release, and how these studies can be incorporated into formulation platforms and actual products.
How can multidrug and layered structures provide staged release?

Staged release includes different ingredients released at different rates, repeated release of one ingredient, or sequential onset of different drugs. Compartments separate space; timing also depends on barrier dissolution, liquid entry and drug-loaded materials.
This problem focuses on analyzing how spatial structure becomes temporal arrangement, and gradually connects in vitro release with in vivo absorption.
How can gastrointestinal targeting or stimulus responses control release location?

Gastric retention keeps a dosage form in the stomach, whereas intestinal targeting avoids premature release and delivers in a specific segment. Buoyancy, shape change, time barriers and pH responses act through different mechanisms.

The positioning of also needs to be combined needs of the drug itself: some drugs require local action, and some active ingredients need to be protected before passing through the gastrointestinal environment. The design needs to specify the location, time, and drug state simultaneously.
N1 | Incorporating geometry into release equations (2015)

A 2015 study of drug-containing tablets of different shapes showed that the surface area to volume ratio could explain the release differences in the studied systems. Geometry therefore became a design variable beyond formulation. [R01]

This method holds material composition constant while changing shape, allowing the independent explanatory value of geometry to be tested. Surface area represents the liquid-contact interface and volume the total quantity to be released, so their ratio provides an initial scale measure. Boundaries move during release, however, and initial geometry cannot replace observations of water uptake and erosion. The node establishes a testable structural hypothesis whose material-specific validity must then be examined.

N2 examines dynamic porosity, and N3 tests whether correlation can lead to prediction. The two branches respectively add mechanism explanation and design applications. More informative comparisons should include samples with the same surface area to volume ratio but different shapes: if the release still differs, curvature, path connectivity, and local mass transfer need to be incorporated into the model.

This approach of controlling variables can also prevent the misconception that smaller tablets release faster because a certain shape is inherently superior. When designing comparisons, it's essential to first define the objective: is it to accelerate early release, prolong overall release, or maintain the curve during dose changes? Different objectives can yield opposing evaluations of the same geometric change.
N2 | Dynamic porosity and matrix changes (2021)

A 2021 study used swellable, erodible polymers to fabricate different porous structures by hot-melt droplet deposition. Porosity was examined in a dynamic material environment: the initially printed structure absorbed water and changed during drug release. [R02]

Printed pores are not static liquid channels. Water absorption can expand the polymer volume and compress the pores, while erosion can open new interfaces; therefore, there is no universal one-to-one correspondence between initial porosity and effective mass transfer area. Choosing swellable and erosive materials allows for proactive testing of the coupling between structure and material response, rather than simply comparing the appearance of dry tablets.

Compared to N1, this study requires incorporating time into the structural description. Subsequently, mass loss, dimensional changes, and release can be recorded simultaneously to determine when diffusion or erosion is dominant. If the geometric predictions of N3 differ across different materials, the reasons should be sought within these processes, and features should be reselected rather than simply increasing regression complexity.

Drug release profiles can be similar but controlled by different mechanisms, and this similarity may disappear after storage or changes in the medium. Therefore, priority should be given to studying perturbations that can distinguish mechanisms, such as changes in medium conditions and structural scale, and observing whether the model parameters remain consistent.
N3 | From correlations to unseen geometries (2021)

The release prediction study of the same year used surface area to volume ratio to organize experimental data and establish a design-release correlation for specified drugs and formulations. The purpose of the prediction is to screen structures that may meet the target, which are then confirmed experimentally. [R03]

The study used previously unprinted geometry for validation, separating the fitting from the prediction. The average dissolution time compresses the curve information, while the complete curve equation preserves the differences between early and late stages; both scales jointly examine whether the geometric features support the design. The juxtaposition of soluble and inert matrices allows for comparison of the applicability of geometric relationships based on the release mechanism. [R03]

The design inversion requires more than just optimal prediction; it also necessitates an acceptable margin of error. Multiple geometric possibilities correspond to approximate release curves, making manufacturing strength, swallowability, and dosage additional conditions for solution selection. This node, combined with the multi-specification instantaneous release of N9, transforms the model from interpreting existing samples to screening candidate products.

The next key validation units are new material batches and new dosage ranges. Successful interpolation within similar shapes alone does not necessarily indicate predictability after scaling down to micro-units or changing drug loading conditions; stratified external validation can clarify at which level the model should be recalibrated.
N4 | Measuring porosity and drug solid state together (2021)

A 2021 lumefantrine study combined water-soluble ingredients with lattice structures. Lower-infill designs achieved rapid release, while higher infill slowed release; micro-CT and Raman analysis linked accessible porosity and drug state to dissolution. [R04]

The release of poorly soluble drugs is influenced by both the openness of the matrix and the drug's own dissolution behavior. Micro-CT observes internal pathways, Raman spectroscopy provides information on drug distribution or state, and dissolution reveals the final outcome; these three types of measurements correspond to different stages, helping to distinguish between "water not being able to enter" and "drug not being able to dissolve." Changing only the filling rate without observing the solid state will incorrectly attribute changes caused by thermal history to porosity.

Therefore, subsequent studies should construct controls with similar structures but different solid states, and similar solid states but different structures. If low filling improves early release but is still limited by dissolution in the later stages, the benefits of simply continuing to increase porosity may be limited. N9's shift to multi-specification and excipient co-design is precisely to put pore research back into the overall formulation task.

Rapid disintegration and rapid dissolution also need to be measured separately. Large particles formed after tablet breakage may still dissolve slowly, especially under incomplete dissolution conditions; this dictates that experiments should report particle formation and eventual dissolution, rather than just the disappearance time.
N5 | Actual chemical boundaries in multilayers (2019)

In a 2019 study of a six-component photocurable compound, Raman microscopy was used to observe the distribution of the drug, revealing that some drugs diffused across layers. The printed independent layers do not automatically form independent drug regions; the material and drug states require joint verification. [R05]

Placing drugs in separate layers is intended to assign distinct release tasks to different materials, but interlayer migration can change that division. Spatial Raman analysis makes digital boundaries observable as chemical distributions, showing that material compatibility and drug state also control structural function. For staged release, both initial positions and positions after storage affect which ingredient contacts liquid first.

The hybrid molding of N8 further materializes the division of labor among different materials. The key issue between the two is maintaining boundaries and ensuring predictable interface behavior, rather than simply increasing the number of layers. Research should compare single-component modules, bi-module contacts, and complete multilayer formulations to identify whether changes in release originate from interfacial migration, overall barriers, or differences in component solubility.

The release curves of each component need to be quantified independently. Even if the total release mass meets the target, it may still mask the offsetting effect of premature release of one component against delayed release of another; the criteria for multi-component systems must be consistent with their respective design objectives.
N6 | Testing enzyme activity and targeting separately (2022)

2022 Alkaline phosphatase research used powder bed printing to print enzyme-containing preparations, employing an intermediate layer and colon-targeting coating. The study examined enzyme activity and simulated gastrointestinal release, ensuring that "activity remained" and "released in the target environment" were integrated into the same validation chain. [R06]

Biomacromolecules add an independent endpoint to release studies: whether the substance remains active upon reaching the medium. Content analysis, enzyme activity assays, and release labeling each answer different questions; none can be used to deduce the whole picture. Studying the formation, coating, and storage as separate observation stages helps pinpoint at which stage activity loss or barrier failure occurs.

This node contrasts with N7: both external coating and dual-material printing attempt to provide an environmental response barrier, but their structural interfaces and defect sources differ. The next step should be to compare pre-response leakage, post-trigger release integrity, and activity recovery to further evaluate which manufacturing organization is more suitable for small-batch variations.

The simulated gastrointestinal system supports a localized release task within a specified environmental sequence. The actual location is also related to transport time, local environment, and pathological state. Studies require linking controllable variables (in vitro) with observable locations (in vivo) to explain inter-individual differences.
N7 | Organizing responsive layers from two materials (2023)

The 2023 dual-nozzle study evaluated the feasibility of colon-oriented delivery using a combination of an HPMCAS outer layer and a PVA internal structure containing 5-aminosalicylic acid. The acid-base responsive layer and drug-containing zone, through printing, reduced the limitations of relying solely on homogeneous formulation designs. [R07]

The dual-nozzle selection allows the barrier and drug delivery zones to use polymers suitable for their respective tasks. External environmental responses alter the degree of pathway opening, while internal structure determines dissolution area and drug diffusion; openings allow for release even in the early stages. Therefore, "colon localization" should be broken down into two aspects: pre-leakage and post-acceleration, rather than a simple binary label.

Compared to the coating method used in N6, the overall printing of increases geometric freedom but introduces problems such as interface adhesion, pinholes, and machining accuracy. Microscopic and tomographic imaging were used to confirm the actual structure before interpreting release differences. The next step in the research should be to incorporate manufacturing deviations into the release model to determine which dimensional errors truly alter the target curve.

Environmental response experiments need to consider changes near the threshold; it's not advisable to select only two conditions with significant differences. Observing the response transition region and its repeatability can estimate the product's sensitivity to physiological fluctuations and provide a basis for robustness across different patient conditions.
N8 | Dividing tasks between printing and injection molding (2024)

2024 bilayer tablet research combines droplet deposition and injection molding to address the rheological and structural requirements of different formulations. The printed portion allows for adjustable porosity, while the overmolded portion forms a denser structure. The combination of these two methods broadens the range of manufacturable formulations and release combinations. [R08]

Combining two forming methods means materials need not suit every manufacturing process. A high-viscosity formulation may be unsuitable for one deposition method yet work in overmolding. Process selection can therefore follow product function rather than allowing one machine to constrain the entire design. Comparing release from porous and dense structures connects manufacturability with performance targets.

A new challenge in hybrid manufacturing of lies at the interface: the two layers have different thermal histories, shrinkage, and wetting behaviors, potentially leading to separation during storage or release. Future research should examine the interface strength in conjunction with single-component release, and use cross-sectional structure analysis to determine whether curve changes originate from delamination or alterations in the diffusion barrier. This node feeds back the manufacturing boundary to N9, aiding in the selection of a scheme capable of stably covering multiple specifications.

Economic considerations also need to be evaluated within the product family framework. Disposable molds and variable printing sections may be suitable for tasks involving repeated changes to local structures, while frequent changes to the entire formulation increase cleaning and validation costs; scientific design and drug delivery organization should jointly determine module division.
N9 | Maintaining immediate release across strengths (2024)

In 2024, the cabozantinib study combined water-soluble polymers, excipients, and geometric design to investigate rheology and establish a calculation method for the required dimensions at different dosages. It advances the problem from the rapid release of a single sample to whether a single formulation can cover multiple strengths. [R09]

This study transforms immediate release from a single-sample attribute to a requirement met by multiple specifications. Dimensional calculations address the geometry corresponding to the target drug dosage, rheological and excipient studies determine whether a stable structure can be formed, and dissolution tests whether the target is retained after dimensional changes. These three factors are interdependent; dose linearity cannot replace release consistency.

N1 to N8 provide design variables such as geometry, dynamic porosity, solid state, interface, and environmental response; N9 consolidates these into a constrained product selection. Subsequent validation of the minimum, maximum, and intermediate specifications is recommended to identify which variable dominates with dimensional variations, and the saved performance should be incorporated into the same judgment.

The final design space should be expressed as conditional relationships: given the material state and manufacturable structure, which dosages maintain the target release, and which changes need to be re-examined. This is how the predictive model is connected to product development, creating a feedback loop from requirements to experimentation and back to digital design.

sections.title: Evolution of Commercial Technologies and Products

blocks.text: How can materials and structures enable sustained and controlled release?

AnelleO uses printing to develop long-acting vaginal rings. Its ANLO102 page targets approximately 28 days of progesterone release and lists studies intended to support subsequent regulatory submissions. The development task combines release duration, local use and device integrity in one program. [R11]

The two approaches target long-term local use and gastrointestinal positioning, respectively, showing that the industrial application of structure-controlled release depends on the clinical setting. Development objectives and completed validation should be shown separately on the timeline.
How can dissolution and immediate release of poorly soluble drugs be improved?

Aprecia's SPRITAM utilizes a porous rapid-disintegration structure to improve dispersion and administration, demonstrating that specific dosage form characteristics can become a core value of industrial products. [R10]

The shared mission of enterprises and academia is to ensure the reproducibility of formulation performance. The maturity of rapidly disintegrating products does not automatically mean that the dissolution problem of any poorly soluble drug has been solved; each active ingredient still has corresponding material and stability requirements.
How can multidrug and layered structures provide staged release?

These enterprise capabilities provide tools for ingredient allocation and batch execution. OPERA's manufacturing tasks primarily focus on composition preparation and quality, while phased release studies further require independent validation of timing controls.

The key to advancing the industry is to incorporate module assembly, formula switching, and the quality of each component into a unified record system. The ability to identify whether other modules maintain their intended release after a change in a module is fundamental to configuration flexibility.
How can gastrointestinal targeting or stimulus responses control release location?

This corporate roadmap connects structural design to specific development projects and human evaluations. The timeline should distinguish between platform construction, research licensing, positioning results, and subsequent efficacy studies, with each node representing a different stage of work.

Academic research can provide material-response and structural mechanisms for this development, while companies’ in vivo localization results help select in vitro evaluations closer to intended-use conditions.

sections.title: Academic–enterprise links: mechanisms to executable schemes

blocks.text: Release control connects measurable area, porosity and material response to manufacturable structures. Geometry and area-to-volume studies supply structural hypotheses; poorly soluble drugs and compartmental devices make material state and boundary conditions equally important. The patents add gastric-floating and intestinal pH-response implementations. Aprecia rapid-disintegration products and AnelleO ring development provide distinct rapid-release and long-term local-use references.[R01][R02][R03][R04][R07][R10][R11]

headers: Academic evidence, patent scheme and enterprise role
rows: Cavity–release coupling

Guangdong Pharmaceutical University’s CN111920775A discloses a clarithromycin outer layer and polymer/inorganic-carbonate core that becomes hollow after drying. Porosity research becomes two separable variables: outer-layer transport and core buoyancy. Aprecia is a technical comparator: similar low density serves opposing timing tasks, so rapid disintegration cannot establish gastric retention.[R02][R10][R12]
Loading and matrix

CN111956623A from the same university discloses floating sustained-release tablets using a water-soluble gel matrix, release modifier, binder and poorly soluble drug. Bilayer deposition/moulding and immediate-release cabozantinib studies likewise require loading and material state to be assessed with geometry. Aprecia provides a high-loading manufacturing reference; sustained flotation remains a separate patent hypothesis.[R04][R08][R09][R10][R13]
Response and location

Jilin University’s CN115068408A discloses polymer/carbomer/model-drug honeycomb hydrogel processed by freezing and ambient standing. Proposed hydrogel contraction in the stomach and swelling in the intestine provide a mechanism comparison with ileocolonic and dual-compartment delivery. AnelleO ring development adds integrity and anatomical-use questions for long release.[R06][R07][R11][R14]

sections.title: Translation and validation: variables, controls and decisions

blocks.text: Validation should identify the source of release before establishing location. Vary cavities or infill at equal dose and fixed material state to isolate geometry; vary material at fixed geometry to test swelling, erosion or diffusion. Assay each component in layered combinations. Flotation, medium release and in-vivo location are separate endpoints; earlier results should determine subsequent models and comparators.[R03][R05][R12][R13][R14]

Area-to-volume ratio explains some geometry effects but is not a universal cross-material predictor. Uptake, swelling and erosion change exposed area; cavities may lose shape during release. Record initial dimensions separately from evolving structure at matched time points. Similar initial ratios with different curves first call for tests of wetting, material state and internal connectivity before more complex modelling.[R01][R02][R03][R12][R14]

headers: Variables, controls, endpoints and failure decisions
rows: Cavity route

Compare cavity/no-cavity units at equal dose and outer thickness; measure drying shrinkage, density, flotation/loss and dissolution. Coupled buoyancy/release drift after collapse requires drying and support redesign.[R02][R12]
Matrix route

Vary loading/gel ratio at matched shape, with nonprinted composition-matched controls; measure uptake, erosion, solid state and release. If crystallinity dominates, include material state in release criteria.[R04][R08][R13]
Response route

Sequential media compare honeycomb/solid and responsive/nonresponsive materials; measure swelling delay, recovery and stage-specific release. Early leakage or response mismatch calls for material revision before location studies.[R06][R07][R14]

blocks.text: Dose expansion may change the mechanism: more drug in an outer layer can increase thickness, matrix loading can alter pores/wetting, and combination ingredients can affect local medium. Group validation by invariant mechanisms rather than labels. A company should state which structures, material ratios and tests a dose change preserves; otherwise treat it as a new configuration and compare separately with established fixed-dose products.[R04][R05][R08][R09][R10][R12][R13]

Scenario progression depends on when a structural rule transfers to another dose or drug. Cavity flotation and pH response have different success conditions; track integrity, release reproducibility and location evidence separately. Aprecia and AnelleO provide manufacturing/use references. Continue a patent scheme when mechanism tests explain failures, rather than because it shares a printing label.[R10][R11][R12][R14]

rows: If repeated batches separate buoyancy and release contributions, establish cavity/matrix design windows. Track drying variation and loss of flotation. If loading disrupts structure, simplify and compare nonprinted composition-matched forms.[R02][R04][R12][R13]

Reproducible honeycomb response across sequential media could inform site-relevant models alongside ileocolonic and bicompartment studies. Track response timing and early leakage; disagreement between location and release favors coating or compartment alternatives.[R06][R07][R14]

Predictable release and integrity after dose changes could support restricted structure families. Track cross-dose prediction error, rejected batches and long-use integrity. Failed transfer favors focused fixed-product or single-local-use development, as illustrated by Aprecia and AnelleO.[R03][R10][R11][R13][R14]

blocks.text: Continue when material–structure–location relations are explainable. Reproducible manufacture with unpredictable release requires renewed material/geometry controls; stable in-vitro curves with unstable location require anatomical-condition work. This converts patent design freedom into maintainable product rules.

sections.title: Observation Indicators and Priority Research Tasks

blocks.text: Release studies for first need to distinguish three time points: the time when the formulation begins to release, the time when the drug is completely released, and the time when the drug reaches the target site or enters circulation. Barrier structure primarily alters the first two, while gastrointestinal transport and the tissue environment also alter the third. Conflating these three factors into a single "sustained-release time" can lead to an overly strong clinical interpretation of identical in vitro curves. Subsequent studies should select appropriate observation methods based on the specific product, ensuring a gradual alignment between structural design and actual targets.

The priority of comparative studies is to establish controls that can distinguish mechanisms, rather than continuing to add uncompared geometries. Keeping drug dosage and materials the same while changing porosity, keeping porosity similar while changing drug solidity, and keeping external geometry the same while changing internal pathways—these address different questions. Only after these independent changes are identified can the synergistic effects in complex multi-material systems have an interpretable reference.

Observable metrics should include curve shape and variability, rather than the average release percentage at a single time point. Early leakage, start-up time distribution, late release integrity, and batch-to-batch variability correspond to different failure mechanisms. For multi-component systems, component-by-component analysis is also required; for sensitive loads, activity recovery should be measured simultaneously; for localized systems, results must be reported under a defined environmental sequence. These metrics constitute the evidence set for the product mission.

The research priorities for digital models are external validation and uncertainty representation. Models can narrow down the range of candidate structures, but manufacturing deviations, material aging, and changes in the medium can cause the input to differ from the actual product. Incorporating these perturbations into model evaluation helps determine whether the prediction error primarily originates from geometric measurements, release experiments, or the model itself. For designers, knowing when retesting is necessary is more valuable than simply obtaining a target dimension accurate to a decimal point.

Commercial development maps to these mechanistic tasks. Aprecia’s rapidly disintegrating products use industrially manufactured porous structures for a defined dosage-form need; AnelleO’s ring platform under development reflects the geometric and barrier requirements of long-term local release. Validation is organized around rapid oral disintegration and sustained local delivery, respectively. Academic papers provide structural principles, while each product requires performance evidence for its materials, use location and manufacturing system. [R10][R11]

In 2027, the focus should be on observing whether multiple specifications can simultaneously maintain content and release. In 2028, the focus should be on whether the structural predictions remain usable in new batches and new equipment. In 2029, it depends on whether the positioning or exposure evidence of in vivo can be linked to the design parameters. If these conditions are met, printing may form a transferable release module; if only in vitro has abundant curves, applications will still mainly rely on product-by-product development and testing.

The most valuable data to prioritize is not the best release curve, but rather the design failure boundaries: what kind of porosity leads to structural brittleness, what interfaces cause early leakage, and what type of dimensional changes turn immediate release into confinement. These failure boundaries can constrain subsequent reverse engineering, reduce repeated exploration of unstable solutions under unmanufacturable or operational conditions, and ensure that feedback from the research graphs truly influences the next round of material and structure selection.

P3-03.title: Printing Quality and Stability
P3-03.subtitle: Jointly validating material compatibility, manufacturing repeatability and storage quality
P3-03.thesis: The quality of printed formulations is determined by materials chemistry, processing history, deposition repeatability, and structural changes during storage. Research is translating printability experience into measurable properties and unit-by-unit evidence; thermal stability, forming accuracy, and content uniformity are measured separately to explain the final release and delivery quality.

questions.question: How do printing heat and light affect drug stability?
questions.focus: Printing may involve heating, shear, photoinitiated reactions and drying. Drug content, crystalline state and drug–polymer interactions can change separately, affecting storage and release.

questions.question: How can printed formulations ensure content uniformity and dose accuracy?
questions.focus: Drug content per tablet depends on dosage-form mass and drug distribution. Consistent mass suggests stable deposition but does not establish consistent drug concentration. These factors require separate testing, particularly for low-dose and multi-ingredient formulations.

questions.question: How do formulation and process parameters affect printability?
questions.focus: Pharmaceutical materials must feed into equipment, flow consistently during deposition, retain structure after forming, and meet drug-quality and release requirements. Filament, semi-solid and photocuring systems impose different material requirements.

blocks.text: This research direction organizes evidence based on specific application tasks, placing formulation design, measurable quality, and actual usage conditions within the same research chain. Geometric adjustments provide design freedom, but each adjustment requires explanation of which physical processes it affects; the usage scenario determines which changes are valuable, and the original questions are addressed accordingly.
How do printing heat and light affect drug stability?
Printing may involve heating, shear, photoinitiated reactions and drying. Drug content, crystalline state and drug–polymer interactions can change separately, affecting storage and release.
This problem requires distinguishing between chemical degradation and intentional changes in physical state, while also connecting changes during processing with storage before use.
How can printed formulations ensure content uniformity and dose accuracy?

Drug content per tablet depends on dosage-form mass and drug distribution. Consistent mass suggests stable deposition but does not establish consistent drug concentration. These factors require separate testing, particularly for low-dose and multi-ingredient formulations.
This question focuses on the quality chain from ingredient preparation to piece-by-piece output, and how small-batch manufacturing can maintain reliable judgment while reducing destructive sampling.
How do formulation and process parameters affect printability?

Pharmaceutical materials must feed into equipment, flow consistently during deposition, retain structure after forming, and meet drug-quality and release requirements. Filament, semi-solid and photocuring systems impose different material requirements.
This question uses printability as a connection point to analyze how formulation parameters affect the process, and how the process affects the final formulation.
N1 | Material blending meets two functional needs (2016)

2016 polymer blending research attempted to improve the processability of FDM solid dispersions while regulating release. Material composition affects both filament feeding and drug release, shifting formulation optimization from a single mechanical objective to a multi-objective equilibrium. [R01]

Using polymer blends for printability exposes a tension between pharmaceutical materials and mechanical feeding: filaments must resist feeding pressure yet disintegrate after fabrication according to product targets. Comparing whole-matrix disintegration with strip peeling brings interlayer fusion into explanations of release. Printability is therefore a relationship among material, equipment and final performance, rather than a single intrinsic material label. [R01]

Subsequent measurements should cover solid feed, melt flow, and post-cooling interlayer bonding. Optimizing only one stage may transfer defects to another stage; for example, easy-to-feed material may fail to maintain its shape after ejection. N4 translates these empirical judgments into measurable mechanical and rheological variables, while N3 examines the impact of this processing history on chemical stability.

The reference used for material screening should be matched with the target process. The same formulation may perform differently under different gear pressures, nozzles, or paths, so method development should preserve equipment conditions so that the observed material advantages can be accurately reproduced in the next study.
N2 | Photoreactions reveal compatibility limits (2020)

A 2020 four-component photocuring study found a reaction between amlodipine and a diacrylate component, confirmed by infrared spectroscopy and NMR. The issue arose from a specific drug–resin chemical interaction, showing that reduced heat exposure cannot replace formulation-compatibility studies. [R02]

Photocuring can reduce some heat exposure, but it introduces reactive components. The combination of infrared and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) provides evidence of chemical structure, which is more indicative of changes in the original drug than appearance and total peak intensity. The significance of this study lies in using specific functional group interactions as a failure mechanism, demonstrating that "low temperature" cannot encompass the pharmaceutical suitability of the entire process.

This discovery necessitates addressing two issues simultaneously in the screening of N5 resins: whether they can form the target structure, and whether the target chemical composition can be retained after the addition of a specific drug. These two require different experiments and different criteria. When selecting a formulation, it is advisable to compare pure drugs, single resins, and coexisting systems to separate the contributions of light, material contact, and the polymerization reaction.

Compatibility also includes a time dimension. Residual reactive components after printing may continue to come into contact with the drug, therefore immediate content and post-storage impurities should be linked. This node merges with the N3 thermal aging branch, forming an examination of the complete manufacturing history.
N3 | Processing history links to storage changes (2021–2022)

A stability study published online in 2021 simulated heat treatment and storage conditions, finding different drug-polymer combinations yielded different results: some combinations exhibited protective effects, while others showed instability and chemical changes. The study specified process selection as formulation combinations and the conditions they underwent. [R03]

Treating extrusion and reprinting as a continuous thermal history explains why measuring only the thermal decomposition temperature of the raw material is insufficient to determine formulation stability. The molecular environment changes after the drug enters the polymer; interactions may delay these changes or introduce new incompatibilities. Different combinations in the study showed different results, indicating that ranking the heat resistance of pure drugs cannot directly replace formulation-level evaluation.

This method links the process to time, raising shelf-life quality issues with N8. Stability studies should observe different levels of active ingredients, impurities, crystallinity, and functional performance to identify the properties that change first. If chemical content remains stable but releases changes, further examination of moisture, pores, or matrix rearrangement should be conducted, rather than attributing all aging to degradation.

The explanatory power of simulation studies depends on whether they cover the main stresses in the actual process. Besides temperature, residence time distribution, mechanical shear, and humidity may also affect the sample. Subsequent verification of simulation conclusions with real manufactured samples can determine which preliminary screening results have predictive value.
N4 | Mechanical and rheological properties predict quality (2023–2024)

The study, published online in 2023, prepared twenty-three types of filaments and used mechanical and rheological parameters to predict processability and tablet property consistency. Its contribution was transforming the empirical judgment of "too brittle or too soft" into a measurable variable, helping to narrow down the experimental scope. [R04]

Feeding is a solid-state stress problem, while ejection and deposition are melt flow problems; therefore, multiple measurements are closer to the manufacturing process than a single hardness measurement. The study uses multivariate regression to connect material properties and output, and points out that the feeding model is equipment-dependent. This result gives a concrete boundary to the "portable model." With the same material parameters but different equipment forces, the failure threshold may change. [R04]

Subsequent validation should hold out data by equipment and material type to determine where model transfer fails. Feeding failures suggest a mechanical-interface problem; changes in tablet width or release consistency require tracking deposition and cooling. Unit-by-unit weighing in N6 provides production outcome signals that link offline models to actual output.

The regression coefficients should also be understood in conjunction with the correlation between variables. Hardness, elasticity, and viscosity may all change with the formulation simultaneously; the variables selected in the model may not be the sole cause. Targeted changes to a single factor and subsequent analysis of the output are key to advancing statistical prediction into process understanding.
N5 | Systematic screening of photocuring windows (2024)

The study in 2024 screened 156 resin formulations, examining the effects of initiators, polymer molecular size, and liquid fillers on molding. This provided a basis for narrowing down the range of manufacturable formulations; subsequent compatibility and residue evaluations of the selected drugs are also necessary. [R05]

The significance of the system screening lies in simultaneously examining multiple factors, rather than attributing all changes to a single component after repeated substitutions. Photopolymerization rate, viscosity, and network formation jointly determine the molding process, while liquid fillers influence the optical and flow environments. Placing different variables within a common experimental framework allows for the identification of areas requiring joint control and reduces trial-and-error.

N2 reminds users that this formability window must intersect with the drug compatibility window. If a formulation prints optimally but still causes a drug reaction, it is still not within the usable range of the target product. Subsequent considerations include residue, release, and shelf-life performance, and the results should be screened through independent sample testing, rather than using appearance scores as the final quality conclusion.

The window boundary is more suitable for production than a single optimum. Actual materials and equipment fluctuate, and if an optimum is too close to the failure zone, daily operation may be unstable. Studies should report performance changes after perturbations to help select a solution with acceptable tolerances.
N6 | Unit-by-unit weighing captures startup deviations (2024)

The 2024 study integrated an analytical balance into a printer to automatically record the tablet-by-tablet mass of hydrocortisone formulations and compare it with an external balance. The system identified manufacturing deviations in the first tablet, demonstrating that online weighing can capture unit problems that are easily masked by average batch results. [R06]

The tablet-by-tablet record preserves the production sequence, allowing observation of differences during start-up, continuous operation, and termination phases. The output of semi-solid materials can be affected by loading conditions and flow recovery; an abnormal unit may have a small impact on the batch average but a direct significance for the unit's dosage. This explains why quality data must be at the unit level, and not just total yield and average tablet weight.

The weighing feedback, combined with the property prediction of N4, can determine whether a certain type of filament or ink is more prone to temporal drift. However, identical mass does not guarantee identical drug content; N7 further introduces component-sensitive spectroscopy. Only by combining these two methods on the same unit can output quantity deviations be separated from mixing or composition deviations.

When integrating the instrument, vibration, environmental factors, and stabilization time must also be considered. If the measured values are related to the printing action, seemingly realistic process fluctuations may occur. Comparing and verifying measurement repeatability with independent references helps determine whether the anomaly originates from the product or the measurement system.
N7 | Cross-site verification of unit drug content (2025)

A 2025 study applied miniature near-infrared and Raman spectroscopy to tamoxifen formulations produced at Gustave Roussy Hospital. Calibration samples were prepared at the research center, while the hospital collected spectra and validated local products. Material sources were kept consistent, and both open-capsule measurements and measurements through closed shells were examined. [R07]

This design directly addresses the most challenging aspect of knowledge transfer in decentralized manufacturing: the center possesses analytical and development capabilities, while the hospital controls the actual production environment. The outer shell alters the optical path and background, thus closed-shell prediction requires verification that the sampling information represents the internal drug. The complementarity of the two spectra stems from their different physical responses; the choice should not solely rely on goodness of fit but also depend on detection time, packaging interference, maintenance, and the connection to production records.

Compared to N4, N7 is closer to external applications, but the same supply source still constitutes a clear migration condition. The next stage should use raw material batches, operators, and equipment as stratification factors to observe how deviations accumulate; if different institutions are outside the validation set, the central model needs to be updated or partially calibrated. This issue advances the testing research to multi-site comparisons at N9 and reinstates version management requirements to the quality system of the quality validation system.
N8 | Fresh-product conformity and storage performance (2025)

The 2025 furosemide study combined semi-solid extrusion with a near-infrared partial least squares model, and used infrared, diffraction, and surface characterization to explain formulation performance. Fresh samples met the requirements of content uniformity, but the two formulations showed different release characteristics after six months, although the observed drug crystal structures remained intact. [R08]

The results from reveal that quality attributes are not interchangeable. Chemical content and crystalline stability do not guarantee that pores, moisture migration, or matrix wetting conditions remain unchanged; therefore, release changes can occur without clear evidence of chemical degradation. Surface morphology provides candidate interpretations, but still requires confirmation of which process controls dissolution through measurements of water absorption, erosion, and internal structure. Quality studies are shifting from single-point-of-life acceptance to the behavior of products under predetermined storage conditions.

The preservation study provides feedback to N7 regarding model validity: if spectral changes are caused by both content and aging, the model must distinguish between the two sources. It also connects to the comparative design of N9, requiring comparisons between printed and conventional dispensing methods at the same storage stage; directly comparing freshly printed formulations with long-term stored flakes would confound process and time differences.
N9 | Direct comparison with current tablet splitting (2026)

A 2026 metoprolol study compared manual tablet splitting with automated printing at two hospital pharmacies and one compounding pharmacy, using validated liquid chromatography to measure drug content. Printed units had mean content near the target and acceptance values below 15; some manually split low-dose units showed greater variability. [R09]

Direct comparison adds workflow-level explanatory value beyond showing that printed samples meet specifications: improvement occurs in a step already used in practice. Low-dose tablet splitting is particularly sensitive to fracture position and fragment loss, whereas automated dispensing shifts error sources toward mixing uniformity and deposition repeatability. Further work should separate within-site from between-site variation, because a favorable overall mean can conceal one site running high and another running low.

Evidence supports dose-quality benefits for specified formulations and under studied conditions. It provides a manufacturing-level response to the material and performance requirements proposed in N1 and raises maintenance requirements for the quality validation system: does the original comparative advantage still exist after equipment replacement, raw material changes, and software upgrades? Long-term studies should include batch deviations, rework, and pharmacist time to determine whether stable quality is achieved with an manageable workload.

sections.title: Evolution of Commercial Technologies and Products

blocks.text: How do printing heat and light affect drug stability?

The practical value of these capabilities lies in expanding the range of optional processes and preserving process parameters. Whether a formulation can remain stable still depends on the specific drug, temperature, and storage results.

The connection between this direction and industry therefore occurs in process selection and validation services: equipment provides manufacturing conditions, academic research establishes the response laws of drugs and materials, and pharmaceutical development organizes the two into reproducible schemes.
How can printed formulations ensure content uniformity and dose accuracy?

The FABRX platform offers weighing, near-infrared, and pressure accessories, combined with software for batch recording; online balances and hospital spectroscopy studies are directly linked to its related technologies. [R10][R06]

The enterprise roadmap has evolved from "automatically outputting tablets" to "outputting tablets and their manufacturing records." The platform's value depends on its ability to promptly identify anomalies, prevent the delivery of non-conforming units, and retain traceable data.
How do formulation and process parameters affect printability?

The versatility of the enterprise platform means that processes can be selected based on drugs and materials, rather than requiring all formulations to fit the same equipment. Academic models help select process windows, while process sensing helps confirm actual operation.

True product capability lies in delivering the right formula, parameters, and inspection methods together. Adjusting equipment parameters is only the starting point; stable manufacturing requires clearly defined permissible ranges of variation.

In January 2026, CurifyLabs released the PharmaPrinter Aurum, focusing on built-in weighing, cleaning and calibration, ease of loading, and software traceability as key product updates. Its connection to the furosemide study in 2025 and the metoprolol study in 2026 lies in the device's entry into specific formulation validation and multi-site quality comparisons; these studies and product announcements provide quality evidence and product functionality information, respectively. [R08][R09][R11]

The FABRX product configuration aligns with the 2024 balance integration study and the 2025 hospital spectroscopy study, forming a roadmap from deposition to unit-by-unit detection. Enterprise involvement facilitates easier integration of detection and equipment control, while academic evaluation requires continued quantification of detection errors, true anomaly detection, and cross-site migration. The product configuration can support the detection methods, and validated formulations and models determine which products the methods are effective in. [R06][R07][R10]

sections.title: Academic–enterprise links: mechanisms to executable schemes

blocks.text: Quality links academia and enterprise through material history and unit-level output. Blends, compatibility and filament rheology require joint selection of printability and stability; unexpected photopolymer–drug reactions show that acceptable shape can conceal chemical failure. Weighing and miniature spectroscopy connect inspection to individual units. The patents disclose filament formulation, cartridge testing and formulation/cartridge combinations, giving FABRX and CurifyLabs monitoring concrete risk sources.[R01][R02][R03][R04][R06][R07][R10][R11]

headers: Academic evidence, patent scheme and enterprise role
rows: Formulation–thermal history

UCL BUSINESS PLC’s WO2017134418A1 discloses drug, polymer, lubricant and optional plasticizer extruded into filament before FDM. Blend/processability studies therefore meet FABRX process selection through two separate thermal exposures. FABRX process options can be compared through impurities, solid state and dissolution after the two thermal exposures.[R01][R03][R04][R10][R12]
Cartridge–deposition consistency

YANG WEN’s CN113865852A prints binder onto a support and combines mass/image data for cartridge performance and viscosity-related indicators. It complements integrated-balance and spectroscopic dose studies: deposition diagnosis versus drug assay. FABRX weighing, pressure and NIR options provide an equipment reference; neither image nor mass independently establishes chemical stability.[R06][R07][R10][R13]
Formulation–consumable combination

MB THERAPEUTICS’ WO2025247979A1 discloses an extrusion-printable formulation, cartridge and preparation of solid/semi-solid unit doses. The abstract does not reconstruct composition, but treats formulation and cartridge jointly. Compare this with CurifyLabs Aurum loading, weighing and traceability, using furosemide/metoprolol studies for drug-specific evaluation.[R08][R09][R11][R14]

sections.title: Translation and validation: variables, controls and decisions

blocks.text: Map signals to failure mechanisms rather than accumulating sensors. Thermal routes prioritize degradation/phase state, light routes reactions/residuals, and semisolids deposition/drying. Resin screening and unexpected-reaction studies inform process choice. Online-model training needs real faults, raw-material batches and storage states, with independent assay/dissolution references; correlation may otherwise merely distinguish mass.[R02][R05][R07][R12][R13][R14]

Separate amount from material-state signals. NIR can reflect content, moisture, density and surface state; images can detect missing layers without seeing drug reactions. Hold out material lots, manufacturing dates or storage states and test equal-mass/different-content and equal-content/different-state samples. Failure to distinguish these confines the model to process monitoring, with independent assay/dissolution deciding finished status.[R02][R05][R06][R07][R13]

headers: Variables, controls, endpoints and failure decisions
rows: Thermal history

Compare feedstock, filament and printed units while varying residence time at fixed formulation; assay impurities, solid state, mechanics and dissolution. Extra degradation after reheating calls for process or exposure changes.[R03][R04][R12]
Deposition diagnosis

Perturb viscosity, cartridge state and material supply; classify mass/image faults against independent assay. Report false release/rejection. Formula-specific detection should restrict the cartridge–material combination.[R06][R07][R13]
Consumable stability

Follow loading, waiting, printing and packaged storage against fresh formulation/conventional compounding; measure uniformity, extrudability and stored dissolution. Restart first-unit bias requires a defined restart procedure and clearance verification.[R08][R09][R11][R14]

blocks.text: Manage stability by material history rather than equipment label. Filament extrusion/storage/printing and cartridge loading/waiting/restart can alter flow/uniformity; packaged moisture or relaxation can change dissolution. FABRX/CurifyLabs-type systems benefit from unit-linked lot, time/temperature, deviation and final-test data. Their linkage distinguishes narrow formulation windows, excessive waiting and models requiring reconstruction.[R03][R04][R08][R10][R11][R12][R14]

Annual progress is the range of failures correctly detected and handled. FABRX attachments and CurifyLabs integration supply implementation; papers and patents define inspection targets. A model confined to fixed formulations can still support a useful library. Multi-process expansion requires chemical and physical faults to map to corrective actions.[R06][R07][R10][R11][R12][R13][R14]

rows: Independently characterized thermal/waiting risks could establish stability windows for fixed formulations. Track impurity and dissolution drift. Chemical failure behind acceptable appearance requires material/process revision before online-release expansion.[R02][R03][R12][R14]

Agreement of mass/image diagnosis and NIR in faulty batches could support cross-lot models on FABRX/CurifyLabs-type platforms. Track false release, recalibration and review burden. Failed transfer favors formulation-specific models and destructive sampling.[R07][R08][R10][R11][R13]

Traceable formulation/cartridge/equipment changes with predictable revalidation could scale quality services with libraries. Track closure of deviations and cross-site revalidation effort. New chemical reactions favor retaining a few well-validated combinations.[R02][R09][R11][R12][R14]

blocks.text: The deliverable is a bounded quality rule: compatible materials/processes, signals for specific defects, and actions outside the window. Patents specify risk sources, academic measurements make rules falsifiable, and platforms apply validated rules to units and records.

sections.title: Quality Attributes, Level of Evidence, and Research Priorities

blocks.text: Quality assessment requires defining the failure first, followed by instrument selection. Insufficient content, increased related impurities, interlayer delamination, and release shift correspond to different mechanisms and require different reference methods. Even if a spectral model accurately predicts content, it may not be sensitive to low-level impurities; a tablet with intact weight may also have localized delamination compensated for by excessive deposition in other areas. The study design should ensure that each critical failure has at least one directly observable chain of evidence.

The primary priority is to establish a localizable error budget across materials, processes, and products. At the material level, batch composition, moisture content, and flow behavior are observed; at the process level, deposition and energy interactions are recorded; and at the product level, content distribution, mechanical integrity, and release are examined. If a deviation occurs in the final product, the most probable source should be traceable using records from the same unit or batch. This design avoids attributing all anomalies to equipment inaccuracies and helps determine where sensors should be placed for maximum value.

The second priority is to study the non-steady-state phases at the beginning and end of the process. Many screening experiments select samples from continuous, stable phases, easily overlooking deviations at start-up, pauses, replenishment, and restart. Weigh-by-piece studies have shown the value of preserving the production sequence. These phases should be included in the validation scope, and it should be clarified whether the calculated overall pass rate includes the first or last piece manually rejected; otherwise, the quality performance of different studies will lack a common denominator. [R06]

The third priority task is to distinguish between measurement noise and actual product variation. Repeated measurements of the same unit primarily describe instrument repeatability; multiple units within the same batch describe intra-batch variation; multiple batches describe production robustness; and multiple devices and locations describe migration capability. These four types of repetition correspond to different scientific questions. Increasing the number of scans on the same piece can stabilize the signal, but it cannot replace increasing the number of independent batches; resources should be allocated to the layer of variation with the greatest uncertainty during the design phase.

Stability evaluation should consider both chemical and functional aspects. Processing can introduce amorphous states or alter component contact, while storage can lead to rearrangement, hygroscopicity, and interfacial changes. The fact that the drug is still detectable is only part of the chain of evidence. By juxtaposing impurities, crystalline state, content uniformity, and release time series, it's possible to determine whether changes in product performance precede chemical degradation, and to select key variables for packaging and storage studies accordingly. [R03][R08]

For machine learning and regression models, truly reusable outcomes are predictive relationships with applicable scope. Randomly splitting the same batch of data, which often shares materials and environments, can easily underestimate future production uncertainties. Reserving data by batch, date, and location allows for more meaningful validation and makes model update conditions clearly visible. Anomaly identification should also report missed detections and false rejections, not just overall accuracy; these two types of errors affect quality and drug supply differently.

The most likely progress for in 2027 is the combined use of unit weighing and formulation-specific spectroscopy for a limited product range; this is contingent on sufficient reference analysis and outlier samples. In 2028, the key is ensuring calibration remains consistent after batch, machine, and site changes, with key indicators including external prediction bias and model update workload. A strong scenario for 2029 is the integration of material selection, process monitoring, and stability data into a unified change management system, allowing for specification adjustments within clearly defined boundaries.

The relationship between product quality and equipment quality will become clearer. Equipment validation demonstrates that actions and measurements conform to design, while product validation requires demonstrating that specific materials produce predetermined properties after these actions. When software updates change pathways, raw material batches change flow, or detector replacements change signals, the affected layers of evidence differ. Mapping changes to quality attributes allows for focused validation and reduces irrelevant duplication of testing.

Cross-enterprise comparisons should ideally focus on shared product tasks and employ common reference analysis. Equipment resolution, printing speed, and configurable modules each describe different capabilities and cannot individually represent pharmaceutical quality. More comparable endpoints include the percentage of qualified deliveries within a specified specification range, post-storage performance, anomaly traceability, and total verification time. Such comparisons can also help researchers determine whether to prioritize improvements in material compatibility, mechanical stability, or testing information.

Priority shared data should include corresponding records of normal and failed samples, reference analysis results, and material and equipment background. Having only failure labels without root cause analysis makes it difficult to guide the next round of formulation improvements; having only successful samples without perturbation tests also makes it difficult to describe the stability window. Organizing both types of data together allows modeling, mechanism research, and equipment development to focus on the same quality issue.

P3-04.title: Microneedle Delivery
P3-04.subtitle: The chain of evidence from needle tip precision to actual tissue delivery
P3-04.thesis: Microneedle printing connects manufacturable geometry, insertion mechanics and drug disposition. High-resolution molds, direct printing and active infusion provide complementary routes. Translation depends on reproducible tissue delivery and retained function after storage, rather than single-needle appearance or total loading.

questions.question: How can microneedle structures balance strength and skin insertion?
questions.focus: Microneedles must be sharp enough to enter skin and strong enough to withstand insertion forces. Height, tip geometry, spacing, material and base all contribute; single-needle mechanics differ from whole-array performance.

questions.question: How can drug-loaded microneedles control transdermal delivery and release?
questions.focus: Microneedle delivery can use surface drug coatings, infusion through hollow channels, or drug loading within dissolving needles. The three routes differ in loading capacity, release mechanism and use.

questions.question: How can molds and printing improve microneedle fabrication accuracy?
questions.focus: Key microneedle dimensions include tip geometry, height, channels, spacing and base. Direct printing and replication from printed master molds have different error sources; nominal equipment resolution alone does not represent final geometry.
