blocks.text: This research direction organizes evidence based on specific application tasks, placing formulation design, measurable quality, and actual usage conditions within the same research chain. Geometric adjustments provide design freedom, but each adjustment requires explanation of which physical processes it affects; the usage scenario determines which changes are valuable, and the original questions are addressed accordingly.
How can microneedle structures balance strength and skin insertion?

Microneedles must be sharp enough to enter skin and strong enough to withstand insertion forces. Height, tip geometry, spacing, material and base all contribute; single-needle mechanics differ from whole-array performance.
This question focuses on how geometric design, through manufacturing and mechanical testing, ultimately translates into effective insertion depth and delivery capability.
How can drug-loaded microneedles control transdermal delivery and release?

Microneedle delivery can use surface drug coatings, infusion through hollow channels, or drug loading within dissolving needles. The three routes differ in loading capacity, release mechanism and use.
This question focuses on how drugs cross the skin barrier and what step printing actually plays in the final delivery chain.
How can molds and printing improve microneedle fabrication accuracy?

Key microneedle dimensions include tip geometry, height, channels, spacing and base. Direct printing and replication from printed master molds have different error sources; nominal equipment resolution alone does not represent final geometry.
This question focuses on how digital design maintains critical dimensions through multiple processes and how this precision is linked to puncture, flow, and drug delivery functions.
N1 | Separating needle fabrication and protein coating (2018)

In 2018, research was conducted on printing conical and pyramidal microneedle needles, followed by inkjet coating with insulin and carbohydrate-protective components. Drug structure was examined using spectroscopy, and release was evaluated using a Franz diffusion assay on porcine skin. Printing is responsible for the needle body, while coating is responsible for drug loading and protection; these two steps together determine delivery performance. [R01]

Separating the needle body and drug-loaded layer allows the needle body selection to primarily conform to mechanics and geometry, while the coating selection primarily conforms to drug stability and release. Circular dichroism and Raman spectroscopy are used to observe protein conformation, and porcine skin diffusion assays are used to observe delivery; these two methods correspond to biomolecular states and tissue barrier penetration, respectively. The research design thus breaks down successful manufacturing into two tasks that must be met simultaneously, rather than simply focusing on the integrity of the needle tip.

The coating may alter the needle tip radius, and insertion may leave some load on the skin surface, so the loaded amount needs to be distinguished from the actual amount inserted. The next step should be to connect post-insertion residue, tissue distribution and permeated drug in a mass balance. N2 uses a geometric template for enhanced control, while N3 reduces dependence on surface coating capacity through hollow channels, forming two distinct delivery branches.

The stability of the same drug in different coating materials does not mean that different biomolecules can utilize the same protective relationship. A more suitable approach is a segmented validation method: first confirm the active structure, then confirm shaping and puncture, and finally confirm tissue delivery. Simultaneously, the geometry and load-bearing capacity before and after coating should be compared to determine whether the drug loading step, in turn, weakens the structural function. This creates a two-way feedback loop between pharmaceutics optimization and microstructure optimization.
N2 | Molds isolate geometric variables (2020)

A 2020 two-photon polymerization study fabricated seven master molds with different heights, shapes, base widths and spacing, then replicated them into dissolving and hydrogel microneedles. Needle geometries produced different insertion depths in skin models, broadly corresponding to delivery of a model drug. Molds made geometry a controlled comparison variable. [R02]

The value of the high-precision template lies in making needle formation a repeatable variable. The final material is provided by replication molding, avoiding the need to readjust the high-resolution printing process for each drug-loaded formulation. The study simultaneously compares insertion depth and drug delivery, establishing a relationship between geometric effects and effective intradermal contact, going beyond mere microscopic appearance.

Different geometries result in different insertion depths, which may improve delivery by increasing the drug-load volume entering the tissue; they may also alter the mechanical damage and dissolution environment. To differentiate these explanations, it is necessary to compare the actual needle volume entering the tissue with the delivery amount per unit entry volume. N5 further examines the effect of manufacturing orientation on the needle tip, while N7 and N8 transfer the template capability to different soluble materials.

The repeatability of the template does not mean that the final product will automatically repeat. Negative mold filling, drying shrinkage, and demolding deformation can all alter the needle tip. Quality evaluation should track three stages: the master mold, the negative mold, and the final needle body, to identify at which step the error increases. The center needle and edge needles in each array may bear different loads; spatial distribution is more indicative than average insertion depth of whether some needles have not entered.
N3 | Hollow microneedles with active control (2020–2021)

The hollow-microneedle MEMS study, published online in 2020, combined a printed needle with a control system to observe intradermal fluid distribution in real time and evaluate insulin administration in diabetic animals. The study advanced from passive dissolution and release to a controlled infusion process. [R03]

The hollow structure of the needle separates the drug-load capacity from the needle volume, while the control system makes delivery a time-varying process. The inclusion of real-time imaging is particularly important because not all pumped fluid necessarily reaches the target tissue; channel resistance, contact state, and tissue backpressure can all alter the distribution. Research has shifted from passive release to monitorable infusion, allowing for cross-verification of controlled doses with actual tissue results.

Animal blood glucose monitoring connects the infusion device to the biological response, but drug absorption and distribution remain between the two. Future studies should simultaneously record flow rate, tissue distribution, and drug efficacy time series to identify whether changes in response originate from delivery or physiological processes. The N6 local disease model raises another question: the target of control could be local exposure, rather than a systemic response.

Compared to the soluble microneedle, the active system of adds flow paths, drive components, and connecting parts; therefore, the reliability of the entire device requires a joint evaluation. A single needle's ability to penetrate only indicates that the flow path inlet is adequate; continuous operation also depends on sealing, blockage, and contact stability. The control system's setpoints require independent flow or mass references to rule out situations where commands are executed correctly but actual liquid delivery is insufficient.
N4 | Geometric errors in direct printing (2021)

The 2021 DLP hollow needle microneedle study compared the effects of printing angle on geometry and examined curing and mechanical performance. The actual shape of the needle tip and channel may deviate from the CAD design, thus manufacturing parameters are incorporated into the puncture design, not just production settings. [R04]

The internal channels of the hollow needle complicate manufacturing issues compared to solid needles: over-curing can shrink the opening, and cleaning and residue can alter the actual flow path. The printing orientation affects both stair-stepping, support, and localized exposure; therefore, the actual needle tip and channels should be measured, not just the nominal resolution. Geometric error studies provide interpretable input for subsequent puncture and infusion.

N5 connects this input to the puncture force, demonstrating that manufacturing parameters can become functional variables. For hollow systems, the channel cross-section also needs to be connected to flow resistance; as the orifice size decreases, needles with seemingly identical shapes may exhibit significantly different infusion performance. Studies should combine structural observation and functional measurements to avoid judging structures that do not allow liquids to pass as acceptable solely based on appearance.

Post-curing can also alter material stiffness and residual composition, potentially improving load-bearing capacity while changing brittleness. The quality window should include post-puncture integrity and chemical residue, rather than using maximum hardness as the sole optimization objective. Exposure variations may also exist between different locations within a printing batch; examining a single optimal sample is insufficient to represent the geometric consistency of the entire manufacturing area.
N5 | Build orientation changes insertion (2023)

A 2023 study compared different printing tilt angles, finding that the 45-degree angle required less puncture force than the zero-degree angle in the DLP system used. The results linked process direction, tip formation, and puncture performance, indicating that optimization needs to be based on actual equipment and materials. [R05]

The tilt angle study links digital geometry, printed needle tips, and measured punctures. Its methodological focus is on making the manufacturing orientation a controlled variable, then comparing functions under uniform mechanical conditions. This is more convincing than simply demonstrating the sharpness of a single needle tip, because minute appearance differences only gain practical significance through the response of the tissue or standard model.

The puncture force of the needle is determined by the needle tip, tissue deformation, and array synergy; the advantages of a single needle are not necessarily retained in a dense array. Subsequent observations should be made on multiple skin samples and at different array locations to determine whether the improvement originates from the needle tip rather than overall substrate deformation. The N6's flexible substrate incorporates these array contact issues into its product design.

Different printers have different pixel sizes, optical systems, and material responses, so improvements brought about by manufacturing direction need to be reproduced on a system-by-system basis. A more transferable conclusion is to examine the relationship between the actual needle tip and the puncture, rather than treating a certain angle as a universal process choice. The reduction in puncture force should also be compared with the needle body damage threshold; only by retaining sufficient load-bearing margin can a lower applied load be meaningful for product stability.
N6 | Flexible arrays for localized disease (2023)

In the same year, the flexible hollow microneedle study used a printed master mold and double molding to adjust the needle size and substrate characteristics, and evaluated local delivery in a mouse psoriasis model. The design expanded from a single needle to the overall relationship between the array and skin contact. [R06]

The flexible substrate addresses the fit between the entire array and the skin's curvature, while the needle body handles puncture and delivery; both require different mechanical properties. Dual molding makes it possible to design these two types of requirements separately. Mouse disease models further connect local delivery with tissue response, shifting the evaluation from creating holes to actual effects on specific lesions.

Local application of medication involves a different exposure pathway compared to oral administration; therefore, the results should be interpreted through a combination of local concentration, systemic distribution, and tissue response. The study suggests that delivering the drug to the target location may alter the required overall exposure, rather than directly estimating the dosage for human use. Dynamic distribution imaging of N3 can provide a complementary approach to this, helping to explain the relationship between array adhesion and local exposure.

During the translation process, stability under activity and prolonged contact should also be observed. Flexibility improves adhesion but may also alter the direction of force on the needle; whether skin movement causes local withdrawal or uneven insertion needs to be investigated as part of repeated delivery studies. Tissue response evaluation should separate changes caused by drug action from those caused by the puncture itself; blank arrays and identical material controls help identify their respective contributions.
N7 | Vacuum compression forms drug-loaded needles (2025)

The 2025 rivastigmine study combined DLP and Free-D Molding to examine the finished product's structure, mechanics, and skin permeability. Vacuum compression molding provides another method for drug-loaded materials to enter complex microstructures; accuracy needs to be confirmed on the final needle body. [R07]

This route uses high-precision printing for precursor geometry, followed by vacuum compression of the final material, avoiding the need for the final drug delivery system to be compatible with photopolymerization. Multiple microscopic observations and skin permeability tests are used to examine replication accuracy and functionality, allowing the value of the molding technology to be assessed at the product level. MeltPrep personnel are involved in the research, also establishing a direct link between equipment suppliers and pharmaceutical development. [R07]

The dissolving system requires both dry-state load bearing and wet-state release to occur simultaneously, both of which may be affected by the water content and storage conditions. Insertion, dissolution, and tissue drug recovery at different storage stages should be compared to determine whether the material softens prematurely due to moisture absorption. The N8 PVA/PVP system presents a similar task, but with different material mechanisms; therefore, a shared evaluation framework is more valuable for transfer than replicating individual processes.

The molding cost should also be calculated based on the qualified final array. Reusing the master mold reduces the burden of single-cycle geometry development, but missing needles, air bubbles, and demolding losses may dominate yield; recording these failures can help identify the areas that truly need optimization during manufacturing expansion. Comparisons of ex vivo permeability require maintaining the same skin source and integrity conditions to avoid sample barrier differences overshadowing the influence of the molding method.
N8 | Mechanical support and release in dissolving carriers (2026)

The 2026 pregabalin study involved converting the printed master mold into a PDMS negative mold, followed by the fabrication of a bilayer PVA/PVP microneedle, and examination of morphology, insertion, and release (in vitro). This demonstrates that the accuracy of the master mold and the performance of the final formulation need to be jointly verified; the entire manufacturing chain cannot be evaluated solely based on the master mold image. [R08]

Dissolving microneedles use the carrier material itself as the source of release, tightly coupling mechanics and mass transfer. Dry-state compression and model insertion test load bearing before use; swelling and in vitro release assess behavior after wetting. Linking the two shows whether a structure can enter first and then release its payload. Model insertion provides early evidence for this chain.

The amount of drug in the in vitro release medium is still far from actual intradermal delivery. The next step should be to determine the load destination based on tissue stratification recovery and needle residue after puncture, and to examine whether the two-stage curves originate from matrix dissolution or drug at different locations within the sample. N8 informs the geometric design in N2: if effective delivery primarily occurs at the needle tip entering the skin, additional drug loading in the base may not necessarily improve product efficiency.

This node merges the template, mechanics, and release branches into a material selection problem. Evaluation priorities should shift from total load to the repeatability of actual delivery, while also considering duration of retained activity, humidity sensitivity, and post-use structural integrity, thus defining product boundaries for specific applications. Results from multiple independent preparations and different die locations can supplement single-batch averages, revealing whether the replication route has a basis for stable scaling-up of production.

sections.title: Evolution of Commercial Technologies and Products

blocks.text: How can microneedle structures balance strength and skin insertion?

The core capabilities lie in high-precision geometry manufacturing and template processes. Academic research further provides insertion, material, and delivery verification, enabling the precision structures to be integrated with specific applications.

The choice of product route requires consideration of both accuracy and quantity: direct printing is suitable for exploring complex structures, while master mold replication allows for the transfer of designs to more materials and batch production. The final needle body must be examined for different routes, not just the master mold.
How can drug-loaded microneedles control transdermal delivery and release?

Nanoscribe provides high-precision manufacturing capabilities for complex microneedle models and master molds; MeltPrep's Free-D Molding connects the printing of prototypes, negative molds, and vacuum compression molding, supporting the production of complex dosage form prototypes with small amounts of material. The 2025 rivastigmine research directly adopts this molding route. [R09][R10][R07]

Enterprise capabilities here are divided into manufacturing segments: precision printing determines the geometry, molding allows the target drug and polymer to enter the final needle. Active infusion also requires the joint participation of pumps, flow channels, control, and bonding systems.
The key link between devices and therapeutic products is to combine these components with a defined formulation and usage method, and to validate the final dosage.
How can molds and printing improve microneedle fabrication accuracy?

MeltPrep’s Free-D Molding converts printed engineering-material prototypes into negative molds, then uses vacuum compression to form prototypes in the target material, providing micromolding tools for high-value formulations available in small quantities. [R10]

These two types of companies have complementary capabilities. The choice between direct printing and master mold replication should be based on the final material, required quantity, channel structure, and quality control, rather than simply comparing printing speed.

sections.title: Academic–enterprise links: mechanisms to executable schemes

blocks.text: Microneedles must translate microfabrication into repeatable penetration and delivered dose. Insulin, hollow-system and dissolving-needle studies use different loading and actuation modes; tilt/parameter studies show that tip, lumen and material state exceed nominal dimensions. Nanoscribe Quantum X and Free-D Molding provide template/forming references. The patents connect channel machining, reservoir actuation and soluble-needle/backing functions to specific delivery bottlenecks.[R01][R02][R03][R04][R05][R07][R08][R09][R10]

headers: Academic evidence, patent scheme and enterprise role
rows: Channel fabrication

CN118061534A, jointly filed by Beijing Institute of Technology-related applicants and CHONGQING MOFANG, prints solid needles by projection curing then drills through-holes with a femtosecond Bessel beam. It separates shape printing from pore machining. Nanoscribe two-photon templates are an alternative reference; compare open-channel yield, resistance and strength rather than minimum size alone.[R02][R04][R09][R12]
Reservoir and actuation

Sun Yat-sen University’s CN112587790A discloses hollow needles, anti-leak ring, sponge reservoir and conductive film, driven by pressing or iontophoresis. Hollow MEMS and flexible psoriasis studies become contact, sealing and actuation tasks. Nanoscribe is a fabrication reference; delivered dose also depends on assembly and skin interfaces.[R03][R06][R09][R11]
Needle and backing

BIT’s CN119606857A discloses a polymerizable eutectic hydrogen-bond network with soluble needles and a flexible recyclable backing. Rivastigmine/pregabalin studies share forming/dissolution tasks; Free-D Molding supplies a replication-route comparison. Backing recycling is a materials scheme requiring separate dose, residue and cycle-performance measurements.[R07][R08][R10][R13]

sections.title: Translation and validation: variables, controls and decisions

blocks.text: Move from structural integrity to skin interface and delivered amount. Drug-free/tracer tests first identify broken tips, blockage and leakage; then compare delivery/residue at equal loading. Hold array density while varying tilt, contact and pressing to distinguish manufacture from use. Hollow routes emphasize patency/actuation, soluble routes insertion/dissolution/residue; both require post-removal integrity records.[R04][R05][R11][R12][R13]

Partition nominal loading into reservoir amount, channel entry, surface loss, needle residue and delivered amount. Pressing may merely move fluid onto skin, and soluble-needle shortening may reflect dissolution outside skin. Appearance/reservoir mass alone cannot prove delivery. Reconcile material destinations under matched tasks and link blockage, backing lift and contact variation to delivery curves to locate design-correctable losses.[R01][R03][R06][R07][R11][R13]

headers: Variables, controls, endpoints and failure decisions
rows: Machining control

Compare direct printing and post-laser machining at equal shape; measure lumen continuity, resistance, debris and post-penetration damage. Better patency with weaker needles requires machining-window revision.[R04][R12]
Actuation control

Compare passive, pressed and electrical modes with matched arrays; measure outflow, surface leakage and delivered amount after penetration. Reservoir depletion with surface retention requires sealing/contact redesign before dose customization.[R03][R06][R11]
Soluble control

Compare virgin/reprocessed backing under the same needle layer; assay loading uniformity, dissolution and residue. If recycling alters mechanics or residues, restrict backing reuse and validate delivery layers separately.[R07][R08][R13]

blocks.text: Distinguish printed parts contacting drug/skin from replication templates. Two-photon templates transfer tips into another material; direct photocured needles carry curing/processing state into the device, and laser holes add surfaces/cleaning. Compare Nanoscribe/Free-D routes through template reproducibility, replication losses and finished inspection, not template detail alone. Blunted tips or altered channels after replication require finished-part measurements.[R02][R04][R09][R10][R12]

Annual scenarios should separate microfabrication, assembly and drug evaluation. Nanoscribe/template routes contribute reproducibility and template stability, not skin-delivery outcomes. Machining, actuation and recyclable backings may combine only after their separate failure gates are resolved; integration introduces assembly and user variation.[R09][R10][R11][R12][R13]

rows: Cross-batch patency/integrity could justify comparing Nanoscribe templates with projection/laser routes. Track open channels, damage and replication consistency; precision gains with defects favor a reproducible size range.[R02][R09][R12]

Explainable dose under skin-interface controls could support one-drug/site device evaluation. Track surface loss, user variation and removal integrity; actuation-related variability favors passive or moulded soluble alternatives.[R01][R03][R06][R10][R11]

Stored needles retaining penetration/delivery and unaffected backing material could support limited recycling evaluation. Track cycle residues, rejects and needle-layer consistency; excessive recovery burden favors disposable backing and stable forming.[R07][R08][R13]

blocks.text: Advance when manufacture is explainable and delivery measurable. Fine dimensions without reliable skin delivery require interface/actuation work; repeatable delivery with frequent defects requires narrower geometry. The shared object is the delivery task, not a resolution record.

sections.title: Translational Validation and Research Priorities for 2027-2029

blocks.text: A common challenge with and microneedle technologies is connecting five quantities: load capacity, releasable capacity, actual inserted load, tissue recovery, and effective amount reaching the target. These five quantities have different denominators. Coated routes may leave residues on the surface, hollow routes may experience backflow, and soluble routes may leave loads in the substrate that haven't penetrated the skin. Therefore, overall mass balance is more helpful in selecting a product route than simply increasing the loading rate.

Structural comparison requires distinguishing between single-needle and array-based designs. The sharpness of a single needle facilitates localized penetration, while increased array density can cause skin deformation, altering the effective load on each needle. A flexible substrate further affects load distribution. Therefore, the evaluation should simultaneously consider single-needle load-bearing capacity, array puncture, and insertion location distribution to determine whether a particular geometry still holds an advantage in actual array applications.

The model hierarchy should be selected according to the specific problem. Homogeneous membranes facilitate screening and reproducibility, ex vivo skin more closely approximates the stratum corneum and tissue structure, and animal studies allow for observation of local responses and systemic distribution. The evidence provided by different models is complementary in the research chain. Migration from standard membranes to tissues should be compared using the same apparatus and the same evaluation metrics to clearly identify what changes occur with increased biological complexity, rather than directly merging results from different models.

The industrial route can be divided into direct manufacturing of the final needle and replication after mold manufacturing. The former reduces geometry transfer steps, while the latter expands the choice of final materials and facilitates repeated replication. Nanoscribe lists the high-resolution microneedle array and master mold manufacturing as applications, demonstrating the platform's support for geometric research; MeltPrep Free-D connects the printing precursor with vacuum compression forming, emphasizing small-scale prototyping. [R09][R10]

Commercial technology should be tracked by task rather than product counts. Two-photon mold studies in 2020 showed repeatable geometric replication; DLP studies in 2021 and 2023 linked build orientation to function; a 2025 study involving MeltPrep connected replication to specific drug-loaded microneedles. These include both equipment use and company participation; similar processes alone do not establish that all papers belong to one product-development chain. [R02][R04][R05][R07]

For industrial scale-up, the most important metrics are qualified array yield, channel open ratio, needle tip size distribution, drug loading distribution, and final delivery variability. Printing speed only describes one step; if post-processing, duplication, assembly, or inspection becomes a bottleneck, speeding up printing may not improve overall output. Recording failure locations to individual needles or arrays can identify whether investment should be made in printing accuracy, die life, or final inspection capabilities.

The priority study for in 2027 is the consistency of the same product across different skin models and multiple independent batches. For coated, soluble, or hollow systems with clearly defined uses, it is advisable to validate their respective primary dose loss pathways. Evidence triggering further translation should be stable actual delivery rates and that the drug and structure retain their intended function after storage, rather than just a single successful puncture.

A key condition for in 2028 is incorporating application methods and usage scenarios into the design. Skin curvature, movement, different operators, and contact states can affect the number of array entries; device design needs to mitigate the fluctuations caused by these factors. Research can use controlled-change measurements to assess the system's sensitivity to usage differences, feeding the results back to the choice of substrate, needle spacing, or feedback detection.

The stronger scenario for 2029 is the development of an evidence package that can explain actual delivery volume, local tissue response, and long-term product stability, demonstrating its value relative to existing methods in specific drug missions. The weaker scenario involves increasing precision in microstructures, while issues of dose delivery and reusability remain unresolved. The difference between the two depends on whether mechanistic studies can extend to real-world application endpoints.

Research priorities also include a systematic analysis of failed samples. Channel blockage, tip bending, replicated bubbles, and moisture softening each correspond to different improvement directions; if only the most complete array is shown, the manufacturing window will be overestimated. Introducing failed samples into structural, mechanical, and delivery tests can clarify which types of defects have functional significance, thereby determining reasonable inspection priorities.

For cross-route comparisons, a common endpoint consistent with the target should be used. For local skin diseases, priority should be given to the distribution of intratissue exposure and local response; for systemic delivery, the amount entering circulation and changes in time should be considered. This preserves the characteristics of various microneedle types and avoids substituting practical application value with a conveniently measurable in vitro release ratio.

Reusable research findings should also specify the inspection locations of the mold and final product, the background of the tissue sample, and the estimation method for the actual needle insertion. Differences in results obtained by different teams using the same digital model but different tissue or metrological definitions may not necessarily stem from manufacturing level. Establishing common geometric and dosage representations allows subsequent comparisons to focus on genuine material and mechanistic differences and reduces redundant prototype exploration.

P3-05.title: Implantable and Local Delivery
P3-05.subtitle: Local exposure is determined by structure, time, and tissue interface.
P3-05.thesis: The research value of printed local drug delivery lies in transforming shape, reservoir, and barrier into measurable exposure controls. Infection response, tumor rhythm, wound contact, and mucosal retention each impose different constraints, and future competition will depend on whether the design parameters can remain predictable across manufacturing batches and usage environments.

edges.label: From sustained release to environmental response

blocks.text: The core task of the local drug delivery printing device is to deliver drugs to target tissue at the appropriate location, duration, and spatial range. Shape, channels, reservoirs, and barriers are not merely packaging; they collectively determine the functional structure of the exposed tissue. This research focuses on implants, dressings, tumor and infection devices, vaginal rings, and ocular inserts, comparing the roles of geometric control, material control, and tissue environment control.
How does the printed implant provide continuous local drug delivery?

Implantable delivery places drugs near the target tissue and releases them through diffusion, degradation, or layered structures. The device must not only carry the drug but also adapt to the implantation location, tissue movement, and subsequent removal or degradation processes.
This problem focuses on localized ear, infected implants, and peritumoral delivery, analyzing how printing can link spatial morphology with drug delivery time.
How do printed dressings and hydrogels support local wound care?

Wound treatment involves moisture, exudate, bacteria, and tissue regeneration simultaneously. Printing allows for adjustable pores and shapes, and the placement of drug-loaded particles, proteins, or cells into different areas.
This question focuses on dressings and hydrogels, distinguishing between three modes of action: drug release, the bioactivity of the material itself, and replacement of living cell tissue.
How can local delivery devices be combined with tumor and infection treatment?

Both tumor lesions and implanted infections may require high local drug concentrations while controlling exposure to surrounding tissues and the whole body. Printing provides spatial partitioning, drug storage, and release rhythm design, but the biological goals of the two diseases differ.
This question compares how antibacterial and tumor devices connect drugs, structures, and lesion responses.
How do vaginal rings and eye inserts achieve local drug delivery?

Local mucosal drug delivery requires maintaining the device for a sufficient duration while ensuring comfort, drug stability, and release. The spatial and mechanical requirements of vaginal rings differ significantly from those of small inserts under the eyelids.
This question compares two types of devices along the path of "materials—geometry—release—tissue exposure—use".
N1 | Ear-implant geometry (2022)

Triacca and colleagues used flexible levofloxacin-loaded material to fabricate stereolithographic ear implants, assessing geometry, mechanics, in vitro release and antibacterial activity. The prototype combined local anatomical fit with drug delivery, rather than demonstrating printability and drug activity separately. [R01]

The constraints of the ear space make flexibility and shape integral to delivery: the device must be close to the target area while maintaining a placeable and stable state. The significance of choosing photopolymerization lies in providing a comparative tool for finely shaped devices; however, changing the shape also alters the liquid contact area and diffusion distance. Therefore, release differences cannot be directly attributed to "individualization"; the geometric effects under the same loading capacity should be separated from the diffusion resistance of the material itself.

The causal chain established by node is that structural changes alter the contact boundary, which in turn alters mass transfer. This leads to two subsequent tasks: infection devices need to address drug resistance selection during continuous exposure; mucosal devices need to ensure mechanical stability during tissue contact. Both require methodologically linking the static release profile to the usage environment. Comparable endpoints should include post-release structural integrity and whether the dynamics remain consistent before and after structural deformation, not just the longest release duration.
N2 | Dual-drug nanoparticle hydrogels (2023)

The 2023 study placed PLGA nanoparticles carrying rifampicin and vancomycin, respectively, within GelMA-printed layers to organize dual-drug delivery using alternating layers, and compared single-drug, combined, and antibacterial performance. The authors combined sustained release of nanoparticles with macroscopic printing layout to address the problem of drug-resistant bacteria. [R02]

The choice of a two-stage carrier is to separate two control scales: nanoparticles regulate the rate at which individual drugs leave the carrier, and the printed layer regulates the spatial proximity of the two components. If only the overall antibacterial effect is considered as the result, it's impossible to determine whether the advantage comes from the combination itself, overlapping release times, or local initial concentrations. Therefore, the interpretation should begin with individual release, then move to the common exposure zone, and finally to the bacterial response.

For infection treatment, similar total release amounts can still lead to different selective pressures. It is necessary to compare whether the exposure tail exhibits a time window with only one component remaining, and the changes in the bacterial population after multiple rounds of challenge. This problem leads research to the N3 environmental response barrier: sustained release provides time extension, while infection response provides timing modulation; the two address different tasks, and their convergence should simultaneously measure trigger selectivity and post-trigger combinatorial integrity. To address this issue, a discriminative study should maintain macroscopic geometry while adjusting the release of the two carriers, and then, while keeping the carriers unchanged, adjust the interlayer layout. Two rounds of comparison can identify the respective contributions of chemical temporal control and spatial organization, and examine whether their combination produces a reproducible interaction effect.
N3 | Infection-responsive metal implants (2024)

A 2024 Scientific Reports study incorporated vancomycin-loaded hydrogels and PCL membranes into printed porous titanium rods, regulating release through bacterial lipase-related membrane degradation, and evaluated the results using imaging, blood, and pathological methods in a Staphylococcus aureus rabbit femoral infection model. [R03]

This design uses a metal to perform the structural tasks, a hydrogel to provide the reservoir, and an outer membrane to act as an environmental recognition and mass transfer barrier. This division of labor reduces the difficulty of requiring a single material to simultaneously bear, store, and respond, but introduces the issue of continuity across the three interfaces. If the membrane is damaged during insertion, subsequent rapid release may originate from mechanical damage rather than biological triggering; therefore, the uninfected movement control and the infected condition control have different interpretative value.

The animal infection endpoint pushes material phenomena to the tissue level, but local bacterial load, bone response, and implantation stability should be considered together. Simply reducing bacterial load may be accompanied by disruption of normal repair, and better imaging does not necessarily indicate the continued effectiveness of long-term drug reserves. The next step in design feedback should return to the most variable membrane interface: correlating initial defects, insertion damage, environmental triggering, and post-release bone ingrowth separately is necessary to determine whether the benefits of intelligent response outweigh the added complexity.
N4 | Time-programmed tumor drug release (2024)

In 2024, Myung and Kang proposed a minimally invasive implantable printed device that incorporates the pulse timing program of local chemotherapy into the structure. They compared tumor growth, metastasis, and drug resistance-related responses in a triple-negative breast cancer experimental system. The study used time density within the same drug delivery framework as a design variable. [R04]

This approach differs from the logic of simply prolonging release. While sustained platforming focuses on controlling exposure stability, pulsed platforming attempts to program drug peaks and intervals into events. Selecting structural barriers has the potential to avoid frequent external manipulation, but any swelling, diffusion, or destruction of these barriers can shift peak time. Evaluation should first determine whether each pulse can be retained under manufacturing reproducibility, and then investigate how tissue clearance further alters the actual concentration peak.

Local delivery timing and systemic drug delivery timing are not the same variable: drugs released from the device outlet need to cross the tumor stroma, and delays and attenuation are more likely to occur with greater distance from the device. When research is connected to an enterprise tumor bed platform, the key issue is whether coverage and local exposure can be simultaneously satisfied, rather than simply pursuing longer durations. This also provides feedback for the infection branch: release should be designed according to the timescale of disease response, rather than letting the release curve achievable by printing technology define the treatment target.
N5 | Open dressings and protein carriers (2023)

In 2023, Nano Convergence research constructed open and closed dressings using alginate and zinc oxide tetrapods, investigating protein adsorption, antibacterial performance, and ex vivo skin compatibility. In open structures, the contact state between the particle arms and the surface makes geometry a functional variable. [R05]

Wound dressings deal with a constantly changing, moist interface. Choosing open pores simultaneously alters fluid pathways, gas pathways, and particle exposure; therefore, optimal porosity cannot be solely determined by a single antibacterial outcome. Protein adsorption to a carrier does not equate to retaining the desired biological activity upon reaching the tissue; adsorption capacity, post-release structural integrity, and receptor-level function should be considered as separate but continuous pieces of evidence.

This node represents a shift in local delivery from closed reservoirs to large-area dynamic contact. Compared to N2, both use gels to carry functional components, but wound application requires addressing exudate, dressing changes, and local shape variations. Future research could consider disease progression as an external factor, comparing the performance of the same material under different contact and fluid exchange conditions to determine whether to adjust the structure, surface properties, or release program. Such comparisons help avoid attributing all changes to material formulation.
N6 | Freeform vaginal rings (2019)

In 2019, Welsh and colleagues used plastic freeforming to fabricate dapivirine-containing vaginal rings, creating drug-loaded annular structures through high-pressure jetting of molten thermoplastics. This placed ring-delivery systems, previously more dependent on fixed forming processes, in a digitally adjustable manufacturing framework. [R06]

The ring device presents a unique design contradiction: the ring needs to be flexible enough to deform, yet it also needs to regain its shape to maintain its position. Material deposition alters internal pathways and interlayer bonding, potentially changing drug migration pathways as well. Therefore, successful printing only addresses the morphological issue; actual formulation research requires determining whether mechanical circulation and release functions are coupled. Surface continuity and internal pores cannot be simply considered as aesthetic indicators.

This study provides a common starting point for regulating the reservoir structure of N7 and the internal filling of N9. Two subsequent approaches, respectively adjusting transmembrane diffusion and the effective stiffness of the entire ring, are suitable for answering different questions. Changing the ring's perimeter by individual dimensions may affect drug loading, surface area, and compression response; it is necessary to first clarify which performance characteristics are desired to be maintained, and then determine which dimensions the digital model allows to be altered, resulting in a bounded, individualized design.
N7 | Flexible reservoir rings for multiple payloads (2022)

A 2022 study used fused deposition modeling to fabricate flexible polyurethane vaginal reservoir rings, testing how membrane thickness, infill and other structural factors affected release of different active ingredients. Payloads spanned small molecules, proteins and particulate systems.[R07]

The significance of choosing the reservoir architecture is to separate the device body from the drug space, so that each type of payload does not have to undergo the exact same body manufacturing process. However, different molecular sizes, hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity, and interfacial interactions will alter transmembrane transport, so the same shape does not imply the same release mechanism. The platform's versatility should be demonstrated by identifying which parameters remain effective under different payloads and which parameters require recalibration.

Compared to N6 direct drug delivery systems, the reservoir offers new decoupling opportunities while simultaneously increasing the requirements for sealing and long-term integrity. Its research focus is not solely on increasing the number of drug types, but on finding reproducible parameter mappings. Only if membrane thickness variations can stably predict the transport of a class of molecules can a size design range be established; if protein adsorption is significantly affected, then activity recovery, rather than dissolution mass, should be used as the core subsequent reading. The reservoir should also be evaluated before and after mechanical cycling. If deformation only alters short-term diffusion without compromising the seal, the problem falls under the category of modelable usage perturbations; if irreversible leakage occurs, it is necessary to return to seam and structural design, rather than simply masking a few failures with average release curves.
N8 | Factorial design of ocular inserts (2022–2023)

An ocular-insert study combined hot-melt extrusion and FDM, using a full factorial design to analyze structural variables alongside in vitro release, ex vivo corneal and antibacterial evaluations. Published online in 2022 and in a 2023 journal issue, it examined biodegradable ciprofloxacin-hydrochloride inserts. [R08]

The full factorial design is valuable because thickness and infill can influence each other: increasing thickness extends the diffusion distance but may also increase the load; reducing infill increases the contact area but weakens integrity. Statistical interaction terms help distinguish whether these variations can be independently explained, rather than replacing design principles with a seemingly ideal prototype. For finite sample studies, the model scope should be defined by the actual combination of structures tested.

The ocular surface is subject to rapidly changing fluid and mechanical disturbances, resulting in multiple loss paths between device release and corneal reach. Ex vivo evaluation moves the issue from container release to the tissue barrier, but the next step still needs to connect retention, comfort, and actual contact area. This branch, along with the vaginal ring, illustrates that the successful unit of a local device is "a system that maintains proper exposure in the correct position," where geometry participates in both formulation function and user behavior.
N9 | Personalized rings by droplet deposition (2024)

The 2024 study on droplet-deposited vaginal rings examined the individualization of filling and internal structure, considering quality properties such as compression, resilience, geometry, porosity, and release. The study shows that the impact of design parameters needs to be considered in conjunction with both mechanical response and delivery performance. [R09]

The node merges the two previous research lines: the external shape is responsible for adaptation, while the internal structure is responsible for adjusting effective stiffness and mass transfer. Different deformation behaviors can occur under the same outer diameter, but the user experience cannot be directly represented by a single compressive force. Cyclic load, recovery rate, and material changes after long-term contact jointly determine whether the device maintains its original design state; therefore, the individualized evaluation object should be the performance trajectory during use.

The principle fed back to N1 from here is to first define the acceptable contact and exposure windows, and then select the parameters that need to be individualized. For enterprise R&D, this can lead to product families with fixed materials and infrastructure, and geometry that varies within the verification boundary; for academic research, the priority should be to reveal the trade-offs when a parameter simultaneously affects multiple endpoints. Only when this coupling is quantified can complex structures be transformed from manufacturing demonstrations into interpretable delivery designs.

sections.title: Evolution of Commercial Technologies and Products

blocks.text: Freeformed vaginal rings in 2019, reservoir rings in 2022 and droplet-deposition studies in 2024 established three design capabilities: directly drug-loaded structures, separation of drug and device body, and internal-structure adjustment. These expand the design space, but commercial development must select stable base materials and limited strengths or sizes so that performance can be reproduced in production, storage and actual use.

AnelleO’s official product page lists its first infertility-related vaginal ring as under development and states that IND-enabling studies began in 2025, targeting approximately 28 days of release. Its development focuses ring-based delivery on a specific women’s-health application, with subsequent pipelines extending to other hormones and local diseases. [R11]

The key focus of this product evolution is shifting from a processable ring structure to a verifiable product identity. For companies, size adaptation is only part of the value; more importantly, it's about whether a reliable release range, shelf life, and user experience can be achieved for a given drug and indication. If each size introduces a new release mechanism, specification expansion will rapidly increase the validation burden; only if geometric changes fall within a unified model will the platform's value increase with the increase in specifications.

BioSapien’s website describes MediChip as a biodegradable printed local-delivery device placed in the tumor bed, designed for approximately 28 days of release after a single placement. Its 2026 news section records approval to conduct a Phase I trial in Abu Dhabi and progress in clinical development, while the page also indicates patient recruitment. [R10]

The tumor bed platform's industrial roadmap connects surgical accessibility, local delivery, and drug development. Compared to the pulsed device described in the paper, the company's publicly stated sustained release target uses a different timeline; this parallel development suggests that product value needs to be assessed through spatial coverage of specific lesions, local tolerability, and clinical procedures. Observable phase changes should include study initiation, enrollment completion, exposure and safety outcomes, and whether the manufacturing system supports consistent supply across centers.

Infected metal implants and wound dressings are currently primarily driven by academic prototypes in this evidence set. A more suitable industrial connection would be to embed functional layers into existing device manufacturing and quality processes, or to create combo products around specific wound types. The commercial challenges extend beyond additional material costs; they also include additional storage requirements, pre-use preparation, placement damage, and the predictability of post-replacement function.

sections.title: Academic–enterprise links: mechanisms to executable schemes

blocks.text: Implanted/local delivery co-designs a drug-bearing structure that functions after placement. Ear, antibacterial hydrogel and titanium-rod studies connect local amount to shape, transport or support; breast, ocular and ring studies define site-specific conditions. Patents specify layering, degradation and release mechanisms. MediChip and AnelleO provide industrial references for local delivery/rings; results cannot transfer automatically across sites.[R01][R02][R03][R04][R06][R07][R08][R10][R11]

headers: Academic evidence, patent scheme and enterprise role
rows: Core–membrane roles

EP3501543A1 from DELIM COSMETICS & PHARMA/STRUSI discloses drug-loaded TPU core surrounded by TPU membrane. Freeforming, FDM and droplet-ring studies become core/membrane interface questions. AnelleO ANL0102 provides a vaginal-ring development reference for comparing membrane integrity, ring deformation and long-term release.[R06][R07][R09][R11][R12]
Ocular scaffold

Baylor College of Medicine’s WO2024258996A1 discloses ocular devices including 3D-printed antifibrotic drug scaffolds for corneal conditions. Ciprofloxacin inserts provide site/contact comparisons with different drugs and targets. MediChip provides a local-delivery device reference for placement, local release and device condition after use.[R08][R10][R13]
Degradation–release coupling

Changzhou University’s CN112932737A discloses drug-loaded PLA sinus stents with proposed parallel degradation/release. Ear implants, coated titanium rods and protein dressings share the influence of material change on delivery. Local-device development exemplified by MediChip should jointly evaluate retention of structure, release and post-placement handling; proposed healing benefits need direct endpoints.[R01][R03][R05][R10][R14]

sections.title: Translation and validation: variables, controls and decisions

blocks.text: Fix the anatomical task rather than judging every device by cumulative release. Rings require deformation/membrane integrity, ocular structures contact/local injury, and sinus stents support during degradation. Antibacterial/tumor studies supply local-action endpoints, separated with equal-dose free drug, unloaded structure and conventional-device controls. Structural exposure changes must align with tissue response before clinical-task benefits are inferred.[R02][R03][R04][R08][R12][R13][R14]

Beyond cumulative fraction, identify the release face and receiving tissue. Complete ring membranes versus defects create different pathways; ocular scaffolds and dressings differ in contact/fluid exchange. Equal cumulative release can hide an early burst/depletion or sustained low output, with different irritation/exposure implications. Record sampling time, local retention and remaining drug, using unloaded structures to distinguish material from drug response.[R02][R05][R06][R08][R12][R13]

headers: Variables, controls, endpoints and failure decisions
rows: Ring

Compare membrane presence/thickness at equal dose; measure release, interface defects and integrity after deformation against nonprinted same-material rings. Deformation-induced bursts require core–membrane/path revision.[R06][R07][R09][R12]
Ocular structure

Use unloaded scaffold, free drug and insert comparators; measure retention, local amount and contact response, separating antifibrotic action from irritation. Increased exposure with injury requires contact/release redesign.[R08][R13]
Degrading stent

Measure mass loss, support, degradation products and release together against coated and unloaded PLA. Premature support loss or drug-bearing fragment shedding requires revised degradation/loading and use duration.[R01][R03][R14]

blocks.text: Implant tasks determine when structure must persist or may change. Sinus support/degradation must match recovery, ocular inserts require end-of-use state, and rings usable overall shape. Include placement, deformation, movement and completion of use beyond factory dimensions. For MediChip/AnelleO-type development, track whether tasks become design inputs and failures feed material/structure versions, beyond platform provision.[R01][R08][R09][R10][R11][R12][R14]

A feasible 2027–2029 route builds restricted site-specific families before sharing manufacturing/QC. AnelleO and MediChip reference long-term local use and implanted delivery; patents identify interface/degradation variables. Deposition, records and inspection may transfer across sites; tissue tolerance, residence and clinical endpoints require separate evidence.[R10][R11][R12][R13][R14]

rows: Reproducible structure–release coupling could narrow ring/stent materials and paths. Track deformation leakage, support loss and batch differences; unexplained release returns development to material state and drug distribution.[R07][R09][R12][R14]

Site-relevant exposure and tolerance could justify comparison with ocular inserts. Track residual drug, retention and tissue response; benefits attributable only to greater total dose favor simpler carriers or conventional local dosing.[R08][R10][R13]

Cross-batch mechanics/release within one site could expand long-term-ring or local-implant development. Track stored performance and placement failures. If moving sites rebuilds the entire evidence base, retain a single-site focus.[R10][R11][R12][R14]

blocks.text: Task requirements should determine complexity: location, suitable exposure and completed use over the required interval. Core–membrane, ocular and degrading-carrier disclosures define testable interfaces connecting research to product decisions.

P3-06.title: Pharmacy Compounding and Quality Control
P3-06.subtitle: From single-tablet qualification to verifiable pharmacy manufacturing network
P3-06.thesis: Pharmacy printing connects patient needs, material shaping, nondestructive testing and accountability systems. Low-dose comparisons and hospital-based spectroscopic validation provide concrete evidence; transfer across batches, storage performance and recovery from deviations determine whether individual projects can become sustained services.

questions.question: How can hospitals and pharmacies implement on-demand printing of formulations?
questions.focus: The question of "How to implement on-demand printing of formulations in hospitals and pharmacies" first involves the service recipients and the supply rhythm. Rare diseases requiring continuous dosage adjustments, low-dose needs lacking suitable specifications, and combination formulations in trials all have different batch sizes and change frequencies. The study design needs to map each need to a preparation unit: a single prescription, a set of prescriptions with the same formulation, or a continuous supply cycle. Only by clearly defining this unit can batch pass rates, turnaround times, and workload have comparable denominators.

questions.question: How can rapid detection and quality control of printed formulations be achieved?
questions.focus: Rapid testing and quality control of printed dosage forms require distinguishing measured signals from the attributes to be demonstrated. Balances measure mass, cameras measure visible structure, and near-infrared and Raman spectroscopy measure signals related to composition and physical state; drug content, impurities, release and storage performance are product-quality attributes. The scientific task is to establish reproducible mappings and identify changes that invalidate them. Integrating a detector into equipment determines where data are acquired; calibration scope and handling of deviations remain scientific questions. [R02][R03][R04][R06]

questions.question: How do regulation and scaling affect pharmacy applications?
questions.focus: "How Regulation and Scale Impact Pharmacy Applications" encompasses two extensions: higher output at a single point, and production of the same controlled product across multiple locations. The former requires studying process bottlenecks, while the latter necessitates research into knowledge and responsibility transfer. The UK's field manufacturing framework, implemented in 2025, connects multiple production points through control centers and product master files, providing a concrete example of treating the manufacturing network as a governance object. [R12]
