sections.title: Translation and validation: variables, controls and decisions

blocks.text: Retain image, segmentation, plan, mesh, print and post-sterilization versions in common coordinates. Known geometry tests algorithms before real cases test segmentation/contact; independent repeat planning separates algorithm and observer effects. Navigation must distinguish tracking loss from guide movement. Clinical comparisons need reasons for revisions/intraoperative changes so final error maps to an actionable step.[R08][R10][R11][R14][R19][R20][R21]

Preserve error direction and coordinates. Imaging, segmentation, smoothing, shrinkage and seating can compound or accidentally cancel at one endpoint; summing published mean errors is uninformative. Measure stages within the same case/coordinates, separating translation, rotation and local deformation. A correct final position despite large intermediate shifts does not justify wider process limits because cancellation may not recur.[R02][R08][R10][R11][R19][R20]

headers: Variables, controls, endpoints and failure decisions
rows: Tracking interface

Vary reseating, occlusion and loading against independent navigation; measure registration drift/target error. Stable tracking with guide–bone motion requires contact verification.[R13][R15][R16][R19]
Model processing

Vary denoising/contact extraction at fixed images/plan; compare meshes before printing and after sterilization. Smoothing-induced seating change requires protected anatomical regions and bounded processing.[R02][R08][R10][R20]
Automatic planning

Compare automated, expert and corrected plans across deformity/image quality; measure parameter errors and revisions. Misclassified abnormal anatomy requires human review/exit rules, beyond mean design time.[R07][R17][R18][R21]

blocks.text: Automation and navigation need independent references. Compare automated landmarks with expert-confirmed anatomy, not another automated version; compare navigation with bone/external measurement, not tracker stability alone. Raw inputs, algorithm versions, edits and final plans distinguish image insufficiency, recognition error and strategy change. Records also guide preoperative versus intraoperative route selection rather than forcing one automation workflow.[R07][R13][R16][R17][R18][R19][R21]

Track automation together with correction cases. Version chains, landmark planning and different decision timing can share revision/error endpoints. AR/navigation should detect previously unobserved displacement rather than merely add display; fixed guides with conventional checks may remain preferable for some cases.[R06][R07][R15][R16][R17][R18][R19][R21]

rows: Traceable image-to-part changes could establish stepwise error budgets. Track segmentation edits and sterilization change; processing-dominated errors require algorithm/anatomical-region constraints.[R02][R10][R11][R20]

Anomaly-aware, editable landmark plans could be compared with preoperative workflows for total preparation time/consistency. Fast generation with repeated revision favors semiautomation and explicit exits.[R06][R07][R17][R21]

Tracking that distinguishes registration drift from seating motion could justify hybrid-navigation evaluation against intraoperative adjustment. Track added tasks, detected faults and rescue; no reduction in unseen errors favors simpler verification.[R14][R16][R18][R19]

blocks.text: Transferable planning shows which error-chain segment each change affects. Patents define navigation, metal manufacture and automation interfaces; studies measure error and workflows preserve versions/review. Automation gains come from less rework and earlier detection.

sections.title: Priority Research Tasks and Evaluation Framework

blocks.text: The first task is to create a local error map. Contact areas, guide channels, grooves, and areas adjacent to hazardous structures are selected, and corresponding markers are used in imaging, design, physical models, and postoperative status. The results should indicate at what stage the error occurs, in what direction it propagates, and which parameter adjustment is most likely to be effective.

The second task is to separate soft tissue deformation from rigid body positioning. While bony surfaces can be represented using rigid body pose, tissues such as breast tissue also require consideration of body position and pressure conditions. Studies should select acquisition and placement conditions close to those used in surgery and verify the stability of the relationship between the internal target and the external surface. Different tissue conditions should not be treated with the same surface matching threshold.

The third task is to compare the error recovery capabilities of various guidance methods. Given the same plan, scenarios such as guide misalignment, reference marker movement, or intraoperative target changes are set up to observe whether the team can identify, interpret, and correct the problems. Error recovery quality may be a better differentiator between systems than minute differences in precision under ideal conditions.

The fourth task is to establish a closed loop from research to service. This involves incorporating interim errors, design versions, and reasons for clinical modifications into a traceable record, and regularly analyzing recurring issues. If a product version improves local biases in the model but does not reduce clinical conversions, exposure conditions and workflows should be further examined; if conversions are significantly reduced, cross-personnel and cross-institutional reproducibility should be further validated.

Research priorities should be determined by the magnitude and consequences of uncertainty. Tasks near critical structures, requiring multiple adjustments, or relying on soft tissue morphology should prioritize obtaining independently validated information. For already stable processes, resources should be allocated to weaker interfaces to simultaneously improve overall accuracy and clinical usability.

P4-03.title: Surgical Guide Stability and Safety
P4-03.subtitle: Continuous verification of material handling, geometric preservation, and intraoperative fixation
P4-03.thesis: The stability and safety of the guide plate are determined by the final material handling condition, structural constraints, and patient contact conditions. Manufacturing, cleaning, curing, sterilization, and storage should be validated as a continuous process, and the positioning function should be confirmed under actual loads to ensure that geometric, mechanical, and tissue contact properties correspond to each other.

blocks.text: How do guide materials and structures affect mechanical stability?

Guides experience different loads during seating, fixation, drilling and cutting. Material stiffness governs deformation, span and thickness affect loading, and post-processing changes final performance.
The study links the material properties of standard specimens with the functional stability of actual surgical guides and observes their compatibility with tissue contact requirements.
How do sterilization and storage affect guide dimensions and safety?
From printing to use, surgical guide may undergo cleaning, post-curing, packaging, storage, and sterilization. Each step can affect the geometry, mechanical properties, or surface condition.
The study focuses on how these changes affect adaptation and use, and distinguishes the questions that disinfection, sterilization, and material performance testing each answer.
How do intraoperative fixation and contact surfaces affect guide stability?

Surgical guide stability requires limiting undesirable translation and rotation while maintaining an accessible placement path. Contact area, anatomical features, fixation screws, and intraoperative exposure all contribute to the outcome.
The research focuses on whether the surgical guide can maintain the planned posture from the first positioning to the completion of drilling and cutting.

Stability includes unloaded positioning, retention after fixation, and pose control under drilling loads. Safety involves material contact, treatment effectiveness, and whether geometric failure occurs during operation. These three research questions therefore need to be answered together: materials and structures limit load-bearing capacity; sterilization and storage alter the final state; and intraoperative contact and fixation determine whether these properties can be translated into positioning functionality.

The usability of the surgical guide is limited by several conditions. Too soft a plate may alter tool orientation, while too hard a plate with improper contact may make positioning difficult; excessive coverage may facilitate positioning but hinder exposure and removal. Research should clearly define critical loads, permissible displacements, and necessary operating space, ensuring that material selection and structural design serve the same objective.

This approach uses the final use state as a common benchmark. If geometric scanning, mechanical testing, and cell evaluation occur at different processing stages, the results are difficult to correlate directly. Allocating the same manufacturing batch to different tests and maintaining the same cleaning, curing, sterilization, and storage history allows for a more reliable chain of evidence.
N1 | Post-curing and cellular responses (2017)

A 2017 study compared the effects of Clear and Dental SG resins on cells at different processing stages. Printing and post-curing reduced the impact on cell viability, indicating that the final product state is a better representation of the actual contact material than the raw material name. [R01]

The contact properties of material are gradually formed during printing and post-curing. The study addresses questions at different stages by examining the cellular results obtained from uncured raw materials, initial prints, and final products. Distinguishing these stages helps explain why the same product name cannot substitute for specific cleaning and curing conditions, nor does it represent the same level of treatment for all geometries.

For guides containing narrow channels or varying thicknesses, post-processing accessibility should be incorporated into the design. Evaluation should utilize complete parts that have undergone actual processes or representative hard-to-process areas, combining extraction and direct contact methods to differentiate between releasable components and surface contact effects. The subsequent goal is to link processing conditions, material state, and functional performance, ensuring that biological response and mechanical validation correspond to the same batch of final products.

This logic also aligns material screening with hospital procedures: samples are first prepared using practically feasible post-processing conditions, then cellular and mechanical properties are compared. If cleaning or curing steps need to be changed, the finished product status should be re-examined, and the changes recorded in the corresponding batch. Such comparisons can determine whether the performance stems from the material formulation or from differences in post-manufacturing processing.
N2 | Sterilization and mechanical properties (2022)

A 2022 study tested standard SLA and DLP specimens and complete guides, comparing mechanical properties after disinfection and steam treatment at two temperatures. Heat treatment changed tensile, flexural or load-bearing performance, showing that sterilization is part of the material-processing history. [R03]

Heat treatment can further alter the solidification state and may cause softening, stress release, or dimensional changes, the outcome of which depends on the material and manufacturing process. Therefore, changes in load-bearing capacity cannot be simply summarized as "sterilization damage"; the elastic range, fracture mode, and permanent deformation after loading should be observed separately. The performance of the intact surgical guide is also affected by the geometry of the connecting arm and guide hole.

The standard specimen is suitable for comparing the material itself, while the actual surgical guide reveals the amplification of the load on the structure. Both types of tests should use the same treatment history and be analyzed correspondingly under loads close to the operating direction. If the specimen strength changes little but the surgical guide shifts significantly, geometric deformation and local buckling should be examined; if the shape is maintained but fracture occurs prematurely, attention should be paid to material embrittlement and critical joint areas.
N3 | Loaded fit and deformation (2023)

A 2023 study placed guides on an implant-referenced model before and after sterilization to compare accuracy and fit. Material and sterilization affected results, while seating load also influenced measurements. Free-state scans and actual fit therefore describe different properties. [R09]

This study connects the free form after sterilization with the stress-bearing placement, revealing the significant impact of measurement methods on the conclusions. A larger load reducing the gap does not necessarily mean the surgical guide has returned to its original stress-free shape. The additional load borne by the fixation point and the contact tissue, as well as whether the direction of the guide channel has changed, all need to be examined simultaneously.

For, actual acceptance testing can use displacement curves within the specified loading range, rather than simply measuring whether it is tightly fitted at a single moment. If the surgical guide requires significantly greater force to be in place, it may mean that the deformation has affected the usability window. Using positioning force, post-fixation position, and unloading recovery as a set of indicators can distinguish between acceptable elastic fit and geometric mismatch requiring rework, and prevent operators from habitually masking material differences.
N4 | Local coordinates and storage (2024)

A coordinate measuring machine study conducted in 2024 revealed that the main dimensional deviations of the tested surgical guide were concentrated in the upward bending at the free end. Besides the overall average deviation, localized issues arose with the cantilever and span, requiring evaluation by functional area. [R04]

Local coordinate measurement is suitable for discovering structural problems that are easily hidden by the overall surface average. Upward tilting of the free end indicates that the deformation has direction and spatial distribution, which may change the contact sequence or the sleeve axis. For dental arches or long surgical guides, even end deviations occupying only a small surface area can determine whether wobbling occurs during positioning.

Two-week storage observation of in this experiment mainly showed minor additional changes, which should be distinguished from the initial deviations formed during printing. A more complete design would fix the measurement benchmark, track the same indicators at various time points after processing, and record environmental conditions. If the changes persist over time, further observation should be conducted to see when they stabilize; if they exist from the beginning, priority should be given to optimizing the printing orientation, support, and post-curing.
N5 | Equipment and one-month storage (2025)

2025 SG01 Resin Study: Comparison of three LCD devices, and observation of dimensions after printing, one month of storage, sterilization, and re-storage. Equipment and processing stages both affect the results; even with the same material name, different finished product performances may occur. [R10]

The fact that the same resin yielded different finished products on different equipment illustrates that exposure, light field, support, and post-processing all jointly determine the actual state. Comparing equipment solely based on nominal pixels or layer thickness easily overlooks the degree of polymerization and residual stress. Including a month of storage and sterilization in the same experiment allows for continuous observation of equipment differences throughout the delivery cycle.

For product development, what needs to be defined is the combination of equipment, materials, and processes, rather than a resin name that can be arbitrarily transferred. Results from different geometric specimens should also be interpreted according to functional regions: long spans, pore sizes, and thin walls may have different sensitivities. Validation can be performed by selecting the most unfavorable geometry as representative, and then confirming this representativeness using a real surgical guide, reducing the burden of repeating the entire experiment for each case.
N6 | Hospital workflows and ten materials (2025)

A 2025 study compared the dimensional changes of extruded polymers from ten materials after cleaning, disinfection, and hospital sterilization processes, using a tibial osteotomy guide incorporating freeform surfaces and fine features. The materials' thermal response and hygroscopic properties jointly influenced the results. [R05]

Hospital processing involves continuous chemical contact, humidity, and temperature exposure to the printed material, which may alter the material's quality ranking immediately after printing. The study uses a real osteotomy surgical guide, allowing freeform surfaces and fine features to participate in the evaluation. The local maximum deviation and the overall root mean square error after processing carry different information; both should correspond to the contact and grooving functions.

Material screening should first determine the stable processing conditions that the hospital can perform, and then compare geometric retention and mechanical properties under those conditions. If a material requires additional equipment or special packaging, its delivery cost and process consistency should also be taken into account. Subsequent comparisons of multiple items within the same batch and across batches can be added to determine whether the observed changes are repeatable systematic shifts or unpredictable discrete deformations.
N7 | Bone-surface location and positioning ambiguity (2017–2018)

A 2017 online study using a radius model compared proximal, midshaft, and distal contact and found that positional changes resulted in positioning errors. Lateral extension improved some indicators, but midshaft rotational errors may increase, suggesting that the identification characteristics of the contact surface are more important than the area itself. [R11]

The positioning features provided by the bone surface are directional. Smooth bone shafts may allow rotation, and prominent protrusions can improve identification, but may also cause insertion interference. Increased contact area does not necessarily translate to a proportional increase in stability; the real goal is to constrain key degrees of freedom with exposed structures and make it difficult for erroneous locations to form stable contact.

Design validation should include blinded repeatable positioning, allowing different operators to find a stable position without relying on pre-defined posture cues. After measuring the error distribution, it can be determined which contact structure is most prone to causing directional ambiguity. When connecting to material nodes, it is also necessary to check whether slight warping after sterilization alters the contact sequence, as geometric changes may transform what was originally a unique positioning state into multiple approximately stable positions.
N8 | Supports and metal sleeves (2018–2019)

A spinal cadaver study published online in 2018 improved simplified guides by adding hooks, cross-linked supports and metal inserts. Drilling accuracy improved, directly linking structural support to functional stability.[R02]

In spinal drilling, stability derives from the synergy of bone surface support, connection stiffness, and the tool interface. Cross-linked structures alter the relative motion between the left and right sides, hooks increase anti-slip constraints, and metal sleeves affect wear resistance and instrument fit. These changes correspond to different failure mechanisms, and a comparative design, either item-by-item or in groups, is necessary to determine which factor truly reduces trajectory deviation.

For drilling, the actual drilling process should record the advance, retraction, and eccentric loading processes, not just the position before and after the operation. The surgical guide may experience a brief displacement during operation and then recover; static inspections may miss this change. Connecting the instantaneous pose to the final hole axis allows identification of the roles of flexible deformation, contact slippage, and sleeve clearance, providing a direct target for structural optimization.
N9 | Mucosal support under pressure (2021)

A 2021 in vitro edentulous-jaw study showed that mucosal elasticity affected guide stability. Displacement of soft tissue under pressure created differences between the statically scanned surface and the loaded state.[R12]

Soft tissue support allows for a deformable interface between the surgical guide and the patient. While the surgical guide itself is rigid enough, it cannot guarantee maintaining the same position under varying degrees of pressure. The order of the fixation pins, the operator's pressure direction, and mucosal thickness all affect the contact state; therefore, loading and support conditions need to be clearly defined in stability experiments.

A rigid support model can be paired with a controllably elastic covering layer, keeping the surgical guide geometry unchanged while gradually changing the interface conditions. If the error changes significantly with the elasticity of the microstructure, priority should be given to optimizing the fixation and stress distribution; if similar deviations occur under different interfaces, then the focus should return to manufacturing or sleeve factors. This comparison avoids conflating material stiffness with overall stability.
N10 | Bone support and cochlear receiver beds (2022)

A 2022 cadaveric study of cochlear implantation used nine head specimens and eighteen ears to locate the stimulator's bone bed using a surgical guide with bone support and screw fixation. Different deviations were observed in different directions, suggesting that three-dimensional translation and rotation still need to be checked after fixation. [R13]

The positioning of the bone bed for the cochlear receiver stimulator requires simultaneous control of spatial position and orientation. Deviations in different directions persist even after screw fixation, indicating that while fixation reduces free movement, it cannot eliminate differences between the placement, bone bed preparation, and device installation stages. The surgical guide position, bone bed preparation, and final implant position should be checked sequentially to identify at which step the error occurred.

This study brings the principle of bone support to new anatomical and instrumentation tasks. As we move towards clinical application, flap exposure, bone surface curvature, and implant morphology can all alter the actual procedure. Evaluation should preserve deviations and outliers in all directions and observe whether fixation affects removal and subsequent installation. The ultimate goal is to establish a system that is both stable and easy to perform, rather than simply increasing the number of fixation points.

sections.title: Evolution of Commercial Technologies and Products

blocks.text: How do guide materials and structures affect mechanical stability?

Formlabs' Surgical Guide Resin clearly links compatible printing equipment, cleaning, post-curing, and sterilization processes. The company documentation describes material properties under specified manufacturing conditions, reflecting the complete product form based on the entire process combination. [R06]

Materialise provides stability analysis on the design side and provides an instruction manual entry point for the osteotomy guide. Material processing and patient contact design together constitute the device delivery. [R07] [R08]

Competition among companies therefore involves materials support, manufacturing consistency, and design services. For hospitals or manufacturing partners, repeatable processes are just as important as single-batch material specifications.
How do sterilization and storage affect guide dimensions and safety?

Formlabs provides manufacturing guidelines and usage instructions for surgical guide resins, including connection equipment compatibility, cleaning, post-curing, and applicable sterilization processes. Materialise's osteotomy guide instructions are available in region-specific versions. [R06][R08]

The value of a company's products lies in organizing processing conditions into executable processes, enabling different manufacturing sites to achieve the expected final state. Both hospital production and centralized delivery require the management of processing records and storage cycles.
The market comparison should therefore extend from material prices to process stability, documentation support, and delivery qualification rate.
How do intraoperative fixation and contact surfaces affect guide stability?

Materialise's osteotomy guide service explicitly includes Guide Stability Analysis, designed directly around patient bone surface adaptation. Mighty Oak's FIREFLY regulatory record shows that patient-specific screw-guided devices have formed a product roadmap. [R07] [R16]

The two types of enterprise capabilities respectively highlight patient anatomical design and specialized instrument delivery. Academic research provides interpretations between contact, fixation, and trajectory, enabling products to select structures based on different anatomical sites.
More valuable enterprise data includes duplicate positioning, intraoperative availability, and reasons for design modifications, which reflect true adaptability.

The company roadmap can be observed along three levels: material package, instrument design, and instructions for use. The 2017 resin research brought the then-current Clear and Dental SG materials into cell experiments; the current Formlabs Surgical Guide Resin data connects the materials with specified post-printing processing. Materialise's 2021 instructions for use specifically specify surgical guide adaptation, fixation, sawing fit, and processing requirements; the current product page continues to emphasize contact stability analysis. [R01][R06][R07][R08]

The resulting product capability is the transformation of design freedom into a controlled scope. Which contact areas must be retained, which channels require metal sleeves, and which structures can be adjusted for patient needs should all correspond to validation criteria. For hospital production, equipment availability is only the starting point; cross-batch consistency and delivery records determine whether the same quality guides can be consistently provided.

sections.title: Academic–enterprise links: mechanisms to executable schemes

blocks.text: Guide stability/safety jointly maintains geometry, material and contact. Cell-response studies evaluate processed materials, sterilization/storage studies dimensional and mechanical change, and radius/spine studies seating-to-trajectory transfer. Patents identify controlled structures: tracking-to-bone fixation, standard-frame/custom-contact assembly and degradable support. Formlabs workflows, Materialise instructions and FIREFLY records provide product/use references.[R01][R02][R03][R04][R05][R06][R08][R10][R11][R16]

headers: Academic evidence, patent scheme and enterprise role
rows: Relative stability

SURGITEC’s CN111388088A combines bone fit with guide/carrier tracking surfaces. Deformation and radius-contact studies ask whether the tracked object remains on the correct bone. Materialise stability analysis and Mighty Oak FIREFLY are design/product references; stable tracking still requires independent guide-to-bone checks.[R04][R07][R11][R16][R17]
Frame–contact roles

Changmugu and co-applicants’ CN113081157A discloses a conventionally made frame, mounting holes and detachable printed contact columns. It separates strength from patient matching. Sterilized-material studies and Formlabs/Materialise processing references test the assembled state; frame compatibility does not establish custom-component compatibility.[R03][R05][R06][R08][R18]
Support–material action

Peking University School of Stomatology’s CN106859817A discloses a defect-contact cage/soft-tissue contour lid and proposed magnesium release on degradation. Cell-material and mucosa-supported-guide studies offer different contact-task comparisons. Formlabs/Materialise provide process management references; this degradable graft cage additionally requires sustained-support, degradation and tissue-contact evaluation.[R01][R06][R08][R12][R19]

sections.title: Translation and validation: variables, controls and decisions

blocks.text: Validate the cleaned, cured, sterilized, stored and assembled instrument. Coupons screen risks but omit walls, channels, columns and joints. Follow actual processing order with dimensions, stiffness, contact and residues, then repeat under load; untreated and isolated-step controls locate changes. Cochlear fixation/mucosal-support studies inform stability endpoints beyond single seating images.[R01][R03][R09][R10][R12][R13][R17][R18][R19]

Interpret material safety and structural stability in the same finished state. Washing/curing alter residues and dimensions; steam changes stiffness/joint clearance; storage can further change thin walls/columns. Biological and accuracy tests with different processing cannot combine into product evidence. Link residues, cell response, dimensions and mechanics to one batch/configuration and identify the step causing conflict before selecting a window.[R01][R03][R05][R06][R09][R10][R18]

headers: Variables, controls, endpoints and failure decisions
rows: Contact/tracking

Repeat seating with occlusion, incomplete contact and operating loads against bone coordinates; measure guide motion, tracking drift and trajectory. Undetected loosening requires mechanical checks or contact redesign.[R02][R04][R11][R17]
Hybrid assembly

Compare whole-unit, separate-component and assembled processing; measure clearance, torsion and reseating. Passing materials with loosened joints require connector/process-order revision.[R03][R05][R08][R18]
Degrading support

Compare material controls and cage/lid structures over time for shape, mechanics, degradation medium and cell response. Coupled release/support loss requires matching degradation to the tissue task; ion release alone does not establish regeneration.[R01][R12][R19]

blocks.text: Safety also depends on visible errors. A guide can appear seated despite interference, a hybrid frame look intact with loose joints, and tracking lose bone correspondence. Test foreseeable faults, operator detection, recovery and backup needs. Instructions on contact/fixation/tools should map to these tests. Faults visible only retrospectively favor design/workflow changes over more training text.[R07][R08][R11][R13][R16][R17][R18]

Track usable post-processing state and failure handling. Formlabs combinations and Materialise instructions reference complete workflows; Changmugu hybrid frames add interface management. Data need real storage/use order, and material properties require matching finished conditions. If customization changes load interfaces each time, validation becomes the scaling constraint.[R06][R07][R08][R10][R17][R18][R19]

rows: Explainable deformation/stiffness after full processing could define material/minimum-structure windows. Track seating/load motion; coupon success with finished-part failure favors geometry/post-processing changes.[R03][R05][R06][R18]

Stable frame–column interfaces could support hybrid/whole-guide comparisons in limited anatomy. Track assembly mistakes, post-sterilization loosening and seating; interface risk may favor whole structures.[R07][R08][R11][R18]

Independent tracking/contact checks could embed stability in navigation-assisted instruments. Degradable cages advance after support/tissue timing aligns. Track missed motion and degradation failures; unclear decision value favors simple fixation and established materials.[R04][R13][R16][R17][R19]

blocks.text: The result is a stability rule for specified geometry, processing and use. Patents locate interfaces, studies explain change and enterprises encode rules. Every new material, connector or tracking function should address an observable failure and action.

sections.title: Research Priorities and Continuous Evaluation Indicators

blocks.text: The first priority is to establish supporting evidence for the final product. For each combination of materials, equipment, and treatments, local geometry, mechanical function, and contact material evaluations should be simultaneously developed. All tests should use a consistent treatment history so that variations in one stage can be interpreted in other stages, and to clarify which results apply to which guide geometry.

The second priority is quantifying the uniqueness of placement. Different operators repeatedly place the surgical guide within the actual exposed area, recording the position distribution, required pressure, and drift after fixation. The focus is on observing whether multiple seemingly stable positions exist and which structural changes can eliminate this ambiguity. This task directly connects the design software with clinical use.

The third priority is to measure the load throughout the entire process. Drilling, cutting, and continuous traction each have different stress modes and cannot be uniformly replaced by a single static fracture load. Displacement and tool orientation during critical operations should be recorded first, and then the material stiffness, wall thickness, connection method, or sleeve settings should be adjusted accordingly.

The fourth priority is to study the delivery cycle. Incorporate changes in storage time, packaging support, transportation, and surgical scheduling into representative validation, and check whether the surgical guide still meets the original geometry in actual use. For combinations with minor variations, a simple routine acceptance can be established; for time-sensitive combinations, materials or handling strategies should be reselected.

The continuous evaluation should simultaneously include local maximum deviation, repeatability dispersion, in-situ force, post-treatment mechanical changes, and actual conversion causes. This set of indicators connects materials science, structural design, and clinical feedback. If an improvement only increases specimen strength but does not improve positioning under load, interface constraints should be further investigated; if improved stability compromises operating space, structural objectives need to be rebalanced.

P4-04.title: Clinical Workflows and Outcomes
P4-04.subtitle: Stratified Evidence for Efficiency, Precision, and Functional Outcomes: Cross-Specialty Clinical Comparison
P4-04.thesis: Surgical guides can provide three distinct types of benefit: geometric control, operative efficiency and patient outcomes. Comparative studies show that these benefits do not necessarily occur together. Evaluation should combine patient selection, learning, whole-workflow resources and actual utilization to identify the surgical tasks best suited to guides.

questions.focus: Record preoperative work, operative stages and imaging dose separately to distinguish work shifted earlier from actual efficiency gains.

questions.focus: Compare geometry, perioperative burden and recovery under shared planning conditions, linking learning and long-term follow-up.

questions.focus: Set specialty-specific task endpoints and record plan execution, intraoperative conversion and whole-workflow resources.

edges.label: From complex preparation to efficiency assessment
Connect actual use to task endpoints

blocks.text: Can surgical guides reduce operating and fluoroscopy time?

The surgical guide may reduce intraoperative probing, repeated fluoroscopy, and temporary shaping, but it also increases the steps of positioning, fixation, and verification. The key research focus is on which tasks are eliminated, which are brought forward, and whether the added steps offset the savings.
The duration of surgery, duration of anesthesia, number of fluoroscopy sessions, radiation dose, and preparation time for the entire case are different indicators and should be explained separately.
How do guide-assisted and conventional surgery compare in outcomes?

The surgical guide primarily affects positioning and cutting, and only then can it influence implant placement, tissue damage, healing, and quality of life. Research needs to clarify the causal connections at each step to avoid using a single postoperative angle to represent the overall treatment outcome.
The study focuses on comparisons with conventional surgery, emphasizing the distinction between geometric outcomes, perioperative burden, and long-term patient outcomes.
How do guides perform in actual use across specialties?
Patient-specific guides serve different goals in drilling, bone cutting, sampling and reconstruction. Contact sites, exposure, fixation and soft-tissue interference alter their actual effects.
The study placed real-world applications within specific surgical procedures to observe when the surgical guide could successfully complete its task and when adjustments or replacements were needed.

The three original questions can be organized into a clinical decision chain. First, identify which operational steps the guide alters; then examine whether these changes produce measurable time, imaging, or accuracy benefits; finally, observe whether the benefits are meaningful for patient recovery. Different specialties have different goals, but this mechanism-to-outcome evaluation sequence can be used for all of them.

Surgical time should include clearly defined start and end points. The time from skin incision to suturing, bone manipulation, anesthesia time, and operating room occupancy reflects different resources; the number of fluoroscopy sessions, exposure time, and dosage also carry different information. These definitions must be clearly defined in the study design to ensure the results can be used for hospital scheduling and cost analysis.

Case complexity is an important context for evaluation. Patient-specific devices are more likely to prove effective in tasks where routine positioning is difficult, spatial relationships are complex, or multiple confirmations are required. Therefore, comparisons should define anatomical and procedural characteristics in advance, investigate which patients gain incremental benefits, and whether these benefits change with team experience.
N1 | Complex fractures and incremental value (2021)

The 2021 study of intra-articular radius fractures used patient-specific instruments in 7 patients. Postoperative joint step and space improved, but the researchers believed the benefits were insufficient to offset the additional investment. This suggests that even if individualized localization techniques are feasible, their incremental value relative to conventional methods needs to be demonstrated. [R08]

There is a significant difference between geometric restoration and procedural benefits in complex fractures. While the location of fragments can be described by digital models, the ability to move, reduce, and fix them in the same sequence during surgery depends on soft tissue connections and exposure conditions. Case series are well-suited for uncovering these implementation details, translating "planning feasibility" into "which steps during surgery are challenging."

This study included additional input as part of clinical judgment, suggesting that evaluation should record design and manufacturing wait times, as well as the additional work the surgeon incurs for the adapter. The next step could be to set up comparison groups according to fracture complexity and time requirements, and pre-define the rotational deformities most likely to benefit. If a subgroup shows more significant geometric improvement and the preparation time can be absorbed by surgical scheduling, its application value may differ from the average of all cases.

The study should also include patient waiting time in the outcome. For fractures requiring immediate treatment, the delivery cycle itself influences the choice of treatment plan; for elective orthopedics, there is more opportunity to complete design communication and validation. The value of the same technology can therefore change in the two processes.
N2 | Preoperative organization of maxillofacial reconstruction (2022–2024)

A maxillofacial reconstruction study,, published online in 2022 and in the journal in 2024, compared 13 patients, 8 of whom used virtual planning and printed cutting guides, and 5 of whom used conventional methods. The small-scale series reports reduced surgical time. Its workflow pre-determines fibular segmentation and cutting locations, reducing intraoperative remeasurement and adjustments. [R01]

Fibular flap reconstruction involves donor site cutting, recipient site resection, and multi-segment assembly. Preoperative planning can complete in advance some spatial reasoning and measurements. The time-saving mechanism should be examined through staged recording, such as separately measuring the time spent on cutting, segment positioning, and fixation, to determine which part is truly affected by the surgical guide.

The two groups of cases have relatively small numbers, and comparisons need to retain specific conditions such as defect extent, number of bone segments, and team configuration. A more interpretable subsequent design would be to continuously record cases from the same team and stratify complexity. Intraoperative time, ischemic time, and preoperative time each have different meanings; presenting them separately allows us to determine whether the savings come from work transfer, proficiency in procedures, or substantial improvements in geometric positioning.

For hospital resource evaluation, preoperative tasks can often be completed in parallel, while operating room time is more difficult to extend. Research can use this to calculate the actual input of different positions and observe whether additional procedures, delays, or redundant preparations should be reduced, so that efficiency gains correspond to specific service capabilities.
N3 | Foot osteotomy and imaging frequency (2023)

The 2023 study on rigid clubfoot included 20 patients and 25 feet. The surgical guide group had shorter operation time and fewer radiological examinations, but no significant difference in final functional scores between the groups. This suggests that efficiency gains can precede measurable functional differences. [R02]

Rigid foot deformities involve multiple joints and osteotomy surfaces. The surgical guide transforms the spatial plan into a predetermined operational sequence, potentially reducing repeated measurements and confirmations. Functional recovery is simultaneously influenced by soft tissue condition, fusion, and rehabilitation; therefore, the discrepancies in surgical time and functional scores have an explainable mechanism.

The study design should further break down the number of imaging examinations into exposure time, dosage, and examination purpose. A single image taken to confirm the final correction and a repeated examination due to surgical guide misalignment reflect different procedures. For patients with both feet, the correlation within the same patient should also be considered to ensure that the statistical units are consistent with the actual treatment subjects.

Further validation can be stratified according to the main plane and severity of the deformity to check whether the time benefit is concentrated in multi-planar correction. If conventional methods are already efficient in simpler cases, the incremental value of the surgical guide may mainly appear in cases with more planning difficulties and repeated intraoperative confirmation.
N4 | Prospective high tibial osteotomy comparison (2025)

The 2025 prospective study of high tibial osteotomy randomly assigned 30 patients to different groups. Reports indicated reduced operation time and intraoperative radiographic exposure, but no corresponding advantage in corrective effect or functional outcomes. Time savings and treatment efficacy are two separate outcome chains that need to be validated. [R04]

High tibial osteotomy has a clear corrective goal and a relatively standardized procedure, making it suitable for comparing surgical resources and patient recovery simultaneously. Prospective randomized studies, measuring time and imaging exposure separately from correction and function, suggest that the value of the guide may primarily lie in its efficiency. For resource-constrained day procedures, this benefit needs to be evaluated in conjunction with delivery costs.

Further research should use the same imaging plan, fixation protocol, and rehabilitation pathway to minimize variability beyond the implementation tools. Correction angles should be reported simultaneously with target values, actual values, and outlier distributions; function should be observed at pre-defined time points, and preoperative levels should be recorded. This allows for assessment of whether similar average results mask the reduction in complex cases or poorer outcomes.

The evaluation should also track cancellations, postponements, and temporary conversions. If the saved intraoperative time is offset by production wait times, service capacity may not necessarily improve; however, if production is stable and intraoperative fluctuations are reduced, scheduling may become more predictable, creating another quantifiable benefit.
N5 | Randomized instrument comparison in total knee arthroplasty (2024)

The 2024 randomized trial of total knee replacement enrolled 102 patients, with both groups using AI-assisted preoperative planning. The patient-specific instrument group showed improvements in partial osteotomy and alignment parameters, but the operation time was longer. The surgical guide did not automatically eliminate the time required for learning, placement, and examination. [R03]

Both groups underwent AI-assisted planning, making the comparison closer to the independent contribution of the executing device. Improvements in partial sections and alignment, coupled with increased operation time, suggest that more precise execution may be accompanied by new inspection and placement steps. Pairing these two types of results helps in understanding the actual performance of the product during the learning and process integration phases.

The total time should be broken down into surgical guide exposure, fitting, fixation, cutting, and routine supplementary steps, and adjusted according to the cumulative number of cases observed. If the additional time mainly occurs in the initial learning phase, the benefits for experienced teams may differ; if it comes from necessary steps added by the device itself, then optimization of the structure or process is needed.

Regarding patient outcomes, the role of geometric improvement should be observed through appropriate follow-up. Pain, function, complications, and reoperation each have different mechanisms of formation. Short-term geometric outcomes can serve as intermediate endpoints, and a clearer patient selection rule can only be formed after establishing a link with long-term recovery.
N6 | Unicompartmental replacement and functional signals (2026)

A retrospective study of unicompartmental knee arthroplasty in 2026 compared 22 patients (25 knees) in the surgical guide group with 25 patients (31 knees) in the conventional group, reporting better prosthesis alignment, partial scores, and range of motion. The retrospective comparison suggests areas worthy of further investigation; case selection and team experience still need to be controlled in future prospective designs. [R10]

Unicompartmental knee arthroplasty preserves more of the original joint structure. Its instrument entry space and alignment targets differ from total knee arthroplasty, making it suitable for establishing evidence independently. Retrospective studies showed simultaneous improvement in some geometric and clinical parameters, providing a clear hypothesis for subsequent prospective comparisons: whether improving placement consistency in key directions can reduce poor recovery outcomes.

Validating this hypothesis requires comparable case selection, surgeon experience, and rehabilitation pathways, and pre-defining the primary endpoint. For bilateral knee cases, intra-patient correlations should be addressed; for multiple scoring and imaging parameters, primary and exploratory outcomes should be distinguished. The focus should be on the magnitude and persistence of improvement, and whether it is concentrated in patients who were initially difficult to locate.

This node is compared with a task-based randomized trial of total knee arthroplasty. Both results suggest that the clinical role of surgical guides varies with surgical technique, objective, and implementation method. Product development can use this information to select the scenario with the most mechanistic plausibility and then conduct targeted validation.
N7 | Execution rates of spinal trajectories (2020–2021)

The clinical study, published online in 2020 and in the journal in 2021, used a patient-specific spinal guide in 15 patients, implementing 76 guide tracks. Some planned tracks were modified due to design or other practical conditions. Guide track usage and mid-track switching are important clinical information in addition to accuracy. [R12]

The plan execution rate reveals the actual usage process beyond accuracy statistics. Some trajectories are cancelled due to changes in treatment decisions, and others are changed due to guide design or intraoperative conditions; both should be recorded separately. Reporting the accuracy of actual completed trajectories using the entire plan as the denominator provides a comprehensive answer to both delivery availability and technical performance.

Continuous case registration can retain the design approval, fitting, drilling, and screw placement status for each trajectory, recording the timing and reason for any changes. This allows for determining whether the problem arose during preoperative communication, contact with the design, or on-site. For cases where guides were not used, the final outcome should still be tracked to ensure that selective success does not obscure the entire process.

Data is also suitable for feedback to companies. If the changes are concentrated on the same bone surface or segment, the design team can modify the structure; if they mainly come from changes in the plan, preoperative discussions and backup plans should be improved to make the product more suitable for actual treatment decisions.
N8 | Evaluating mandibular biopsy access (2022)

The 2022 study of jawbone lesion biopsies involved guide-guided procedures in 8 patients, with freehand manipulation compared to corresponding printed jawbone models. Orientation and axis deviations improved, while depth differences were not significant. The study structure included both clinical feasibility and model comparison, with these two types of results addressing the questions of use and localization, respectively. [R13]

The endpoint of a biopsy includes both reaching the intended location and obtaining tissue sufficient for diagnosis. The clinically guided and model-based freehand controls in the study provide real-world operational and geometric comparisons, respectively; the experimental environment of both should be preserved during analysis. Improvements in orientation and axis while the difference in depth is not significant indicate that the constraints on different degrees of freedom are not the same.

Further research could compare sampling adequacy, repeat biopsies, protection of adjacent structures, and operation time, and clarify whether the model includes soft tissue and actual instrument access limitations. For small lesions or access to adjacent tooth roots, directional improvement may be more meaningful; for deep targets, depth control and tissue deformation may become the main variables.

From a cross-disciplinary perspective, this study illustrates that "precision" must be defined according to the task. Screws focus on intraosseous trajectory, while biopsies focus on effective sampling location. Although both share guiding structures, clinical evaluation still needs to be established separately around their ultimate goals.
N9 | Condylar guides and navigation (2023)

A 2023 study of condylar resection in 21 patients compared titanium guides and navigation, measuring the deviation between the actual resection and the planned resection. Both methods closely approximated the planned resection, but the maximum deviations differed, suggesting that tool selection should also consider the operating space and the need for real-time adjustments. [R14]

Both the navigation and physical guides incorporate preoperative planning into the surgery, but rely on real-time coordinate feedback and mechanical constraints, respectively. The spatial limitations of condylar resection make the accessibility, repositioning, and adjustment capabilities of both methods directly significant. Comparisons should include actual incision deviations along with these steps to explain the origins of accuracy differences.

The study could further stratify tasks based on similar lesion extent and surgeon experience. When the plan is stable and clear bone support is available, physical constraints may simplify execution; when adjustments to the cutting plane or guide placement are required, dynamic information may offer greater flexibility. Selection criteria should be based on case conditions and observable execution outcomes.

This node converges on two paths: efficiency and availability. The most suitable technology should enable the team to identify and correct anomalies in a timely manner while maintaining the target profile. Therefore, the endpoint of comparison should also include error recovery time, temporary conversions, and patient outcomes, rather than simply looking for the minimum average deviation under ideal conditions.

sections.title: Evolution of Commercial Technologies and Products

blocks.text: Can surgical guides reduce operating and fluoroscopy time?

Materialise's osteotomy guide service connects preoperative planning with patient-matched instruments, while its knee joint service revolves around standardized surgical preparation procedures. Smith+Nephew VISIONAIRE also utilizes imaging and physician confirmation to generate patient-matched guides. [R05] [R06] [R07]

These products move some work forward in the supply chain. The value of procurement should be judged by case delivery time, number of plan revisions, instrument tray requirements, and actual intraoperative savings, rather than simply by the "individualized" name used to describe efficiency.
How do guide-assisted and conventional surgery compare in outcomes?

VISIONAIRE and Materialise knee joint solutions exemplify a commercial pathway for patient-matched devices; CORI offers another approach through intraoperative mapping and robot-assisted manipulation. [R07] [R06] [R11]

These routes revolve around similar positioning goals, but differ in the required imaging, preoperative preparation, and intraoperative adjustments. Enterprise evaluations should be based on the same surgical procedures and clinical endpoints to further identify which workflow is suitable for which hospital.
How do guides perform in actual use across specialties?

Mighty Oak’s FIREFLY regulatory records show a product pathway for patient-matched spinal guides. Materialise provides osteotomy and knee-planning services, with commercial delivery organized by procedure. [R15][R16][R05][R06]

The common capabilities across different services are image processing, planning communication, and custom manufacturing; the differences lie in access to anatomy, instrument interfaces, and clinical validation. The latter determines whether a capability can be transferred across specialties.

The product evolution manifests in different clinical organizational routes. FIREFLY established patient-specific trajectory-guidance regulatory milestones in 2016 and 2018; Materialise provides preoperative planning and guide delivery; Smith+Nephew simultaneously presents VISIONAIRE preoperative matching instruments and CORI intraoperative interactive planning routes. They respectively configure decisions and constraints preoperatively or intraoperatively. [R05][R07][R11][R15][R16]

The competitive dimensions of enterprises extend from geometric functions to case turnover, plan validation, and field support. For complex reconstructions, delivery stability can reduce ad-hoc adjustments; for standardized joint procedures, instrument preparation and team learning may be more important. Product evaluation should correlate these service links with specific clinical endpoints, enabling hospitals to determine which types of cases are most effective for investment.

sections.title: Academic–enterprise links: mechanisms to executable schemes

blocks.text: Clinical workflow links through which steps move preoperatively and which remain intraoperative. Maxillofacial, clubfoot, knee and high-tibial studies supply different time, accuracy and use endpoints. Patents make fixation, repeated puncture and image fusion explicit interventions; Materialise, VISIONAIRE, CORI and FIREFLY represent different organizations. Compare preparation, intraoperative changes and patient outcomes within the same procedure.[R01][R02][R03][R04][R05][R07][R11][R15]

headers: Academic evidence, patent scheme and enterprise role
rows: Fixation–plane

Changmugu’s CN110353759A discloses crest fit, K-wire fixation and cutting guidance. It supplies a fixation-to-plane hypothesis; knee randomized/tibial comparative endpoints inform measurement but not hip outcomes. Materialise/VISIONAIRE are workflow references requiring planning, delivery and rescue accounting.[R03][R04][R05][R06][R07][R17]
Single fixation–multiple actions

Putian University hospital group’s CN109602482A discloses sliding plates/grooves and an adjustable tube for repeated transforaminal puncture. Spine trajectory studies share positioning, with added sequence/cumulative disturbance. FIREFLY provides a fixed-trajectory spinal-guide reference for comparing repositioning, imaging use and actual targeting with the sliding-adjustment scheme.[R12][R15][R16][R18]
Fusion–access

Peking University School of Stomatology’s CN108618854A fuses CBCT/intraoral optical scans to design apical length, angle, depth and lesion extent before printing. Jaw-biopsy, condylectomy and reconstruction studies connect accuracy to registration/access. Materialise references organization; evaluation should record localization and extra exposure together.[R01][R05][R13][R14][R19]

sections.title: Translation and validation: variables, controls and decisions

blocks.text: Split the case journey into planning, design exchanges, manufacturing wait, preparation, operation and rescue. Comparisons need matched procedure, difficulty and experience, retaining cancellations/abandoned guides. Radius series and unicompartmental retrospective studies inform endpoints; causality depends on controls. Accuracy without less rescue or better patient outcomes requires reconsidering the benefit target.[R03][R04][R08][R10][R17][R18][R19]

Define timing boundaries and denominator. Outsourcing can reduce local work while adding exchanges/transport; easy-seating selection can shorten surgery while excluding difficult patients. Learning can accelerate later cases. Follow consecutive cases through planning, changes, cancellation, delivery and use, stratifying experience. Later successful-guide cases versus earlier conventional cases confound device, selection, learning and organization.[R01][R03][R04][R05][R07][R17][R19]

headers: Variables, controls, endpoints and failure decisions
rows: Osteotomy workflow

Compare matched, standard and available navigation routes within a procedure; record revisions, trays and rescue. Offset intraoperative savings require total team time/alignment assessment.[R03][R06][R07][R11][R17]
Repeated puncture
Compare repositioning and sliding adjustment at matched targets; record targeting, attempts, imaging and drift. Fewer actions with worse targeting require revised adjustment/locking.[R12][R18]
Oral access

Check fusion, seating and reach against standard/navigation controls; measure localization, exposure and injury. Obstructed access requires window/support redesign, retaining unusable cases.[R13][R14][R19]

blocks.text: Stratify outcomes by intervention distance: seating/tool path/order, then resection/alignment, then function/complications/recovery. Each step needs data; patent time/safety aspirations cannot skip intermediates. Track cases needing imaging, repositioning or alternative routes and whether rescue changes patient outcomes. This distinguishes usability, workflow improvement and clinical benefit.[R08][R10][R12][R13][R14][R15][R17][R18][R19]

Annual scenarios concern case selection and service organization. Materialise/VISIONAIRE move decisions earlier, CORI supports intraoperative interaction and FIREFLY matched spinal guidance. Value depends on uncertainty and team preparation. Fixation, sliding and fusion mechanisms can stratify cases by reduced rescue versus shifted workload.[R05][R07][R11][R15][R17][R18][R19]

rows: Complete case-time/cancellation records could support within-procedure comparisons. Track planning exchanges/exposure; benefits requiring extensive preoperative rework favor selected complexity.[R01][R03][R05][R17][R19]

Repeatable locking/targeting could support joint imaging, accuracy and rescue evaluation. Restrict comparisons with fixed-trajectory products to matched tasks; adjustment variability favors single placement/navigation.[R12][R15][R16][R18]

Consistent net workflow changes across teams could allocate matched versus interactive routes by case. Track outcomes, delay and abandonment. Accuracy alone supports a positioning-tool role without broader clinical-benefit claims.[R03][R04][R11][R14][R17][R19]

blocks.text: Specify who does more, who does less and what the patient receives. Patents define interventions, studies comparators/endpoints, and services delivery/exceptions. Their closure connects efficiency to outcomes.

sections.title: Priorities for Clinical Research and Industry Evaluation

blocks.text: The first priority is to standardize the efficiency endpoint. This involves unifying the definitions of the main time period and imaging exposure, retaining the original procedure records for each case, and analyzing the average and dispersion. This allows for the differentiation between stable savings and significant savings in a few cases, and also determines whether the surgical guide makes surgical scheduling more predictable.

The second priority is a comparison with clearly defined design tasks. Select specific scenarios where conventional positioning is difficult, compare different execution tools under common planning conditions, and then interpret clinical outcomes using mechanism-related geometric endpoints. For low-risk scenarios with mature processes, focus on observing additional investment and user experience.

The third priority is to establish a complete plan execution denominator. All cases entering the design process should retain their outcomes, including cancellations, postponements, unused cases, and intraoperative conversions. Categorizing causes into treatment changes, production delivery, adaptation, and operational factors can directly guide companies and hospitals to improve different aspects.

The fourth priority is to incorporate patient experience into long-term observation. Additional imaging, waiting time, preoperative communication, and recovery all affect the practical value of the technique. Studies can record patients' feelings about the preparation process and treatment recovery in addition to functional follow-up and interpret them together with clinical outcomes.

The most compelling progress should be demonstrated by consistent benefits in target cases: reduced key geometric outliers, more predictable processes, patient recovery meeting predefined goals, and clearly explained additional inputs. Such evidence supports product selection and service configuration, and also provides specific questions for the next round of device design.

P4-05.title: Custom Surgical Instruments
P4-05.subtitle: From patient matching to task matching: guidance, retraction and imaging-compatible instruments
P4-05.thesis: Customized surgical instruments like the translate patient geometry, operating space, and surgical sequence into concrete constraints. Orthopedic guidance, cutting in narrow areas, and continuous retraction each require different validations; parametric design and final product processing together determine whether these instruments can evolve from case-specific use to stable delivery.
