P5-02.title: Sampling Devices
P5-02.subtitle: Connecting collection, release, detection and mechanical safety in a complete performance chain
P5-02.thesis: Research on printed swabs has moved from supply substitution to structural and fluid function design; the true unit of performance is the effective target quantity that is ultimately sent into the detection system after a complete sample, while simultaneously satisfying the consistency of pathway adaptation, expected fracture location, and post-manufacturing state.

questions.question: How can the sampling and testing performance of the printed nasopharyngeal swab be guaranteed?
questions.focus: Distinguishing collection, release, concentration and clinical test agreement

questions.question: How do the structure and materials of sampling supplies meet mechanical safety requirements?
questions.focus: Assessing safety through anatomy, combined bending–torsion–tension loads and the final manufactured state

blocks.text: The sampling device transfers target material from the human body surface to a detection system, studying a continuous material transport chain. The swab first contacts the target site via anatomical pathways, then collects mucus and cells, subsequently retaining sufficient effective target quantity during transport, release, and pretreatment. Printing allows for adjustments to shape, pore size, and microchannels, and also enables the creation of anatomical models to test these designs.

The first issue concerns the sampling and detection performance of the printed nasopharyngeal swabs, requiring separate measurements of the collection volume, release volume, release concentration, and final test results. The second issue concerns mechanical safety, requiring differentiation between head contact, narrow neck bending, handle force transmission, and predetermined breakage after use. These two issues are closely related: structures that easily access the pathway still need to obtain sufficient samples, while increasing surface area or porosity alters strength, cleaning, and material residue conditions.

Ten nodes extend from emergency design and clinical comparisons in 2020 to anatomical testing platforms in 2025. The structural branch examines adaptation to individual anatomical passages, the fluidic branch examines losses during sample transfer, and the clinical branch tests the complete sampling procedure. Arrows connect these research tasks, while the industry section relates studied products and later academic prototypes to their manufacturing routes.
N1 | Hospitals establish swab manufacturing workflows (2020)

A 2020 technical report from USF Health and Northwell describes the development and hospital manufacturing process of an integrated printed swab. The research focuses on design modifications to the head, neck, handle, and break-off area, and integrates cleaning, curing, packaging, and handling into the delivery of the testing kit. [R01]

The one-piece molding simplifies part assembly, but each area still performs a different function. The head needs to contact and retain the sample, the narrow neck needs to adapt to the passage, the handle needs to transmit direction and rotation, and the break-off area needs to fit with the container after sampling. During optimization, the dimensions and stress targets of these areas can be defined separately, and then it can be observed whether new stress concentrations are generated at the joints, so that the structural partitioning is consistent with the overall operation.

The manufacturing process itself is also a design variable. Printing direction affects the forming of slender rods, cleaning determines the smoothness of complex surfaces, and curing and subsequent treatments alter the material state. Comparative studies should use the final delivery state as the starting point for testing, while retaining records of each process. This way, subsequent bending, embrittlement, or inspection interference can be traced back to the specific process, and the design documents, along with the necessary manufacturing conditions, can form a reproducible research object.
N2 | Open prototypes undergo paired validation (2020)

The 2020 open collaboration project progressively screened designs submitted from multiple parties and compared four prototypes with a reference swab in 276 symptomatic outpatient participants. The κ values for paired RT-PCR results ranged from 0.85 to 0.89, demonstrating the feasibility of a shared validation process across multiple designs. [R02]

The common workflow enables different prototypes to be evaluated around the same clinical task, and screening indicators can be extended from mechanical and procedural performance to test results. Paired sampling reduces some of the differences in individual disease states, but it is still necessary to record the sampling order, the interval between two operations, and the operator. These factors are particularly important for samples close to the detection limit, because small changes in the target amount can alter the positive and negative classifications.

The next organizational step is to retain the reasons prototypes are rejected. One design may fail consistency checks during printing, while another may be limited during sampling or sample recovery; each requires a different modification. Recording screening alongside clinical results can identify which bench measurements predict performance. Collaboration then produces comparable knowledge about iteration and provides a basis for validating specific products and platforms.
N3 | Pediatric imaging constrains access-path design (2020)

A 2020 study established a nasopharyngeal pathway model using CT scans of five children aged 11 to 34 months, comparing three printed designs with two commercially available thin swabs. The elliptical cross-section and head shape jointly affected transit time and resistance, and the study used these factors to select the appropriate design; initial cell recovery testing was also performed in two adults. [R03]

The elliptical cross-section exhibits different bending responses in different directions, thus expanding the fitting problem from overall shape reduction to the direction of motion and pathway curvature. The model can control the anatomical environment, allowing the same prototype to repeatedly traverse different pathways and locating areas most prone to contact and deflection. Scale information provided by imaging can also be used to determine the relationship between the neck length, head size, and handle transition.

Subsequent evaluation should cover anatomical variation within the target age group and define model friction, soft-tissue compliance and operating conditions together. Clinical studies in appropriate pediatric populations can separately record sampling completion, experience and test results. These participants must be distinguished from the adults involved in the initial cell-recovery tests. This node asks whether, beyond reducing cross-section, the swab head can be designed to deform in a more favorable direction under pressure.
N4 | Mechanical and functional testing: measuring strength, absorption and sample recovery separately

The 2021 study compared the tensile, torsional, bending, and sampling capabilities of various printed and conventional swabs using a common device. The overall mechanical performance of printed samples was comparable or better, while differences in liquid absorption did not directly translate into similar differences in RNA recovery; processing and short-term aging also altered the strength of some designs. [R04]

Mechanical measurements must be interpreted with failure modes. A higher fracture load indicates greater resistance to pull-off, while a higher bending reaction force can affect contact during insertion through an anatomical passage. Tests should record fracture location, permanent deformation and the head–neck junction so that strength and flexibility can be optimized together. The planned break point requires separate testing to distinguish behavior during sampling from break-off into the collection tube.

Functional testing shows that absorbed volume, retention and release efficiency describe different stages. A structure may absorb less but release more completely, yielding a similar final amount for analysis. Future studies can establish a mass balance for the same sample by measuring the initial amount, collected amount, released amount and residual amount, then relate these to amplification results. This sets design targets for microchannels and open-pore structures and explains why swabs with similar clinical agreement can perform differently on the bench.
N5 | Clinical comparison of two commercial designs (2020–2021)

A prospective study published online in 2020 and in a 2021 journal issue enrolled 70 adults and compared Lattice Swab and Origin KXG with a flocked reference swab. Agreement κ values were 0.90 and 0.84, respectively. For some positive patients, the interval between sampling procedures was as long as 24 hours. [R05]

This study places specific products into a fixed testing platform, thus enabling it to answer questions about the clinical manifestations of corresponding combinations. Comparisons also involve transport media, sampling sequence, and patient status; these conditions should be preserved during analysis. Especially in samples with inconsistent results, tracing the original amplification value and sampling interval is more helpful in explaining where the variation in the target quantity originated than simply recording the overall concordance rate.

Product iterations can be evaluated with paired sampling, counterbalanced sampling order, standardized transport conditions and blinded testing, with a prespecified analysis of low-analyte samples. Sample size should be chosen for the desired precision of agreement estimates, and differences expressed with intervals. Multicenter studies then extend the question from whether one product works to whether its performance relationships persist across institutions, operators and assay platforms.
N6 | Multicenter evaluation across three testing platforms (2020–2021)

A USF-associated study published online in 2020 and in a 2021 journal issue enrolled 291 symptomatic patients at three clinical sites. It compared printed and flocked swabs using three RT-PCR platforms. Overall diagnostic agreement was 95.88%, and κ was 0.901. [R06]

The multiplatform design broadens observation of the complete testing chain. Differences in sample input can be attenuated or amplified by each platform’s preparation and amplification steps. Within-platform results should therefore be retained before interpreting pooled performance. Staffing and logistics at clinical sites can also reveal service-process effects, connecting product validation with actual hospital testing pathways.

The next phase could involve organizing cross-institutional studies into a unified core process with clearly documented local components. Samples from the same batch would be tested on different platforms to observe methodological differences; different manufacturing batches would be tested on the same platform to observe product differences. For samples approaching detection limits, attention should be paid to paired variations and repeatability. The resulting feedback could be returned to a common bench to examine whether a particular release or material specification truly explains changes in clinical outcomes.
N7 | Auxetic structures regulate axial compression (2020–2021)

A study published online in 2020 and in a 2021 journal issue used finite-element analysis and surrogate models to screen swab heads with a negative Poisson’s ratio, then tested printed specimens against the mechanical model. The goal was lateral contraction under axial compression while controlling structural stress. This was a mechanism-based prototype study. [R07]

The flexibility of traditional solid configurations is mainly determined by materials and cross-sections, while structured heads add degrees of freedom such as unit shape, connection angles, and rod diameters. Lateral contraction provides a testable design assumption: when in contact with the path, can the head width change with the load and reduce lateral resistance? This assumption needs to be observed in a model with curvature and friction, and correspond to the calculated response under pure axial compression conditions.

Mechanical optimization must preserve sampling function. More open space can change sample retention, while slender struts and junctions can affect surface treatment and residue removal. Subsequent comparisons can measure insertion resistance, shape recovery and analyte recovery together, weighing deformation benefits against sampling losses. The shared question for microlattice designs is how geometry can tune several functions and how experiments can separate structural from material effects.
N8 | Fluidic swabs integrate flushing and recovery (2023)

The 2023 fluid swab connects the sampling head, microchannel, and syringe, optimizing the inlet using fluid simulation. Spiked samples and eight retained patient samples were used in a printed nasal mold to compare recovery and testing performance; twenty-eight volunteers participated in a separate comfort survey, showing an overall preference for the fluid protocol. [R08]

The fluid-assisted sampling technology revolutionizes the way swabs acquire samples. Traditional surface structures rely on contact, adhesion, and subsequent elution, while channel structures collect target analytes through localized liquid exchange. Comparisons require fixing the initial sample volume and the final total volume, and observing collection efficiency, channel residue, and dilution levels separately. Otherwise, changes in the detection signal may arise simultaneously from increased recovery and changes in liquid ratio, making it difficult to pinpoint the specific mechanism.

When advancing from models to in-vivo evaluation, paired diagnostic sampling and comfort assessment can be combined in one workflow, recording completion and events such as abnormal backflow. Model experiments can vary viscosity, target location and inlet shape to identify conditions favoring fluid-assisted sampling. The next node addresses concentration after transfer: can dilution during release be reduced while keeping output volume controlled?
N9 | Open-cell microlattices enable controlled release (2024)

In 2024, research was conducted on printing three types of perforated microlattice swabs, adjusting sample release through geometric parameters and centrifugation. Dye and honey mucus models demonstrated high recovery and concentration retention. Furthermore, rapid IgG detection and concentration measurement demonstrated the impact of release mode on the detection signal. [R09]

The key to 's research is the integration of release methods into the instrument system. An open space accommodates the liquid, and centrifugation forces it away from the structure, allowing for sample collection with minimal introduction of additional diluent. When comparing different approaches, it's necessary to report both release volume and concentration, and calculate the total amount of the target analyte. Increased concentration may be advantageous for detecting low abundance, while total amount and matrix composition still determine the adequacy of subsequent pretreatment.

The flexibility, liquid storage space, and cleanup accessibility of the microlattice can be altered using the same set of geometric parameters, making it suitable for multi-objective optimization. Studies can fix the material and post-treatment, adjust the pore size and rod diameter separately, and measure residues and mechanical recovery at different viscosities. In the actual testing phase, the release liquid is connected to the target platform to observe whether high-concentration matrix alters the reaction. The anatomical test model thus becomes a subsequent screening tool, helping to verify whether the advantages of the experimental vessel can be maintained in real-world pathways.
N10 | Anatomy and mucus jointly form a test bench (2025)

A 2025 study printed a dual-material nasopharyngeal model with a mucus-mimicking hydrogel and compared injection-molded Heicon swabs with nylon-flocked swabs. Relative to a simple tubular model, the anatomical model changed collection amount, release fraction and RT-qPCR results, demonstrating the effect of the sampling environment on performance assessment. [R10]

The printed object here is a test platform that allows pathway geometry, soft and hard boundaries, and mucus properties to be considered together in experiments. Simple immersion primarily examines material-liquid contact, while the anatomical environment incorporates accessibility, local contact, and operator movement; therefore, the two methods answer different questions. Research can first decompose the simplified environment mechanism and then use the anatomical platform to verify the combined results, avoiding treating model complexity itself as a substitute for realism.

The continued value of the platform depends on its reproducibility and relevance to clinical tasks. Pathway size, surface friction, hydrogel thickness, and rheological properties need to be designed to provide reproducible conditions, and the operation process should be able to record speed, contact path, and completion. By incorporating different age and morphological models for comparison, the location of performance degradation can be traced back to the head and narrow neck design. This provides a common intermediate evaluation environment for the structure, fluid, and detection branches.

sections.title: Evolution of Commercial Technologies and Products

blocks.text: In March 2020, Formlabs, USF Health, Northwell Health, and Tampa General Hospital announced a collaboration to develop printed nasal swabs. The project combined the hospitals' design and validation capabilities with printing equipment, processable resins, and manufacturing support, utilizing existing hospital printing infrastructure for emergency supply. [R11]

The technological shift in this collaboration involves moving from single-piece prototypes to batch manufacturing and testing kits. Hospital technical reports link design, cleaning, curing, and delivery, while subsequent multi-center papers place the same process into specific clinical platforms for comparison. Company materials and equipment constitute the manufacturing conditions, while clinical studies provide the results of the entire sampling and testing combination; these two types of evidence can be mutually interpreted when the product and process are clearly correlated. [R01][R06]

On April 8, 2020, Resolution Medical launched Lattice Swab, using Carbon Digital Light Synthesis and Keystone’s KeySplint Soft Clear material. Its hollow lattice head uses geometric design freedom to provide flexibility and space for sample retention, offering a different route from surface-nodule designs. [R12]

In May of the same year, Carbon's technical exchange focused on the product's design, mechanical testing, clinical evaluation, and manufacturing, and introduced the development plan for pre-sterilized products. This change suggests that the supply model itself also needs to be studied: hospitals receiving unprocessed parts and receiving pre-packaged supplies place different demands on on-site resources and delivery time. [R13]

In 2021, Carbon expanded the user availability of its Design Engine software and listed Lattice Swab as an existing production case for its lattice design technology. The changes at this stage primarily occurred with general-purpose design tools and manufacturing platforms; further research could examine how these tools support dimensional consistency, aperture manufacturability, and rapid iteration. [R14]

This leads to two organizational models for enterprise routes: hospitals collaborate with equipment companies to complete local production, while device manufacturers utilize platforms and supply networks to organize centralized or multi-point delivery. Both require capacity to be measured by qualified, complete supplies usable in the target detection process. Later papers on fluids and microlattices expanded the functional targets, requiring specific materials, release methods, and validation objects to be evaluated individually on their respective prototypes.

sections.title: Direct Links Between Research and Industry

blocks.text: The direct connection is documented in papers and company records: the 2020 USF Health, Northwell Health, Tampa General Hospital and Formlabs announcement identifies joint nasal-swab development. The hospital report connects the one-piece head, neck, handle and breakpoint to cleaning, curing and delivery. The later three-center, 291-patient study evaluates that route on three assay platforms, linking the collection device to the testing workflow. [R01][R06][R11]

Resolution Medical’s Lattice Swab connects Carbon Digital Light Synthesis and KeySplint Soft Clear to a hollow lattice head. Its technical account discusses mechanical and clinical validation. The prospective 70-adult comparison of Lattice Swab, Origin KXG and a flocked reference retains distinct design identities. Carbon’s software expansion explains a design-iteration capability; recovery and comfort still require evidence for the particular manufactured version. [R05][R12][R13][R14]

No direct swab record was found by title-and-abstract searches of the 5,516-record strict patent corpus using swab, nasopharyngeal and related Chinese terms. The patent coverage therefore remains open. Fluidic inlets and channels, microlattice release and auxetic contraction offer specific mechanism-led search entries. Future patent mapping should track collection, retention, release and breakpoint connections against enterprise versions while retaining specific geometry and process versions. [R07][R08][R09]

sections.title: Key Issues in Transformation and Comparative Study Design

blocks.text: Validation should separate sample entry into the head from transfer into the assay liquid. A flocked swab, enterprise lattice and research microlattice could be compared in the same anatomical model using standardized surrogate media for collection, residue, release and operator variation before assay-compatibility assessment. The 2025 model study shows that anatomy changes collection, release and readout rankings; greater absorption alone is insufficient for progression. [R04][R09][R10][R12]

Mechanical comparisons would track neck diameter, head openings, breakpoint position and print orientation while retaining material and postprocessing identity. Outcomes include bending, torsion, fracture location and changes after processing. Pediatric CT work identifies distinct passage and resistance issues. Easier passage with unintended fracture would trigger redesign; progression to a population study requires both mechanical reliability and release against predefined requirements. [R03][R04][R07][R11]

Enterprise-oriented paired studies should fix device version and assay platform, balance sampling order and operators, and report discordance, discomfort, repeat collection and delivery batch. Existing multi-prototype and multicenter studies provide a comparison framework. New fluidic or microlattice systems must establish whether added connections and handling yield consistent benefit. Agreement, operating burden and batch reliability jointly determine progression; surrogate-only gains call for contextual validation. [R02][R06][R08][R09]

In 2027, linking device versions, material batches and processing records to paired outcomes could turn the Formlabs collaboration and Resolution Medical lattice routes into reviewable specialist supply. Batch variation in mechanics and release, rework and assay discordance would be observable signals. If restored flocked supply offers better delivery economics without a sufficient printed-device benefit, printing is more likely to remain emergency capacity or special-geometry development. [R06][R11][R12]

In 2028, reproducible microlattice-release or fluidic-channel gains in anatomical surrogates and the relevant population could support assessment of a structure paired with a specified assay interface. Benefits dependent on extra transfer, centrifugation or expert handling would instead favor laboratory-specific accessories. Detectable input after release, handling steps and invalid outcomes would matter more than maximal porosity or absorption alone. [R08][R09][R10][R13]

By 2029, intellectual-property review should follow product selection: new patents disclosing collection heads, release paths or breakpoints can be matched to paper variables and manufactured versions. Continued absence of direct patent coverage would still allow evaluation from documented collaboration, manufacturing and paired studies. Population-specific designs may coexist with general consumables, or complex designs may return to research because of service costs; sustained supply, workload and real assay performance distinguish these outcomes. [R03][R06][R11][R12]

sections.title: Observation Indicators and Priority Research Tasks

blocks.text: The primary task is to standardize the reporting units for collection and release. Liquid volume, total target amount, and concentration are listed separately, with the amount of release solution used further explained in the test results. For complex viscous environments, the properties of the recovered matrix can be added to observe whether concentration simultaneously alters the detection reaction. This data structure helps connect geometric, fluid, and detection studies to the same performance chain.

The second task is to establish a correspondence between manufacturing variations and failure locations. Dimensional and surface inspections are performed on the neck, grid nodes, neck transition, and fracture zone, and then correlated with combined tensile, torsional, and bending tests. Samples are organized by manufacturing batch, equipment, and material condition to identify the areas most requiring stable control. The yield rate and finished product quantity are reported together to support a comparison between hospital production and supplier deliveries.

The third task is to involve users and operators early in design. Participant experience can be related to contact and force in anatomical models, while operator feedback informs grip, orientation and handling into the collection tube. Sampling interruptions, repositioning and repeat attempts can be recorded to assess their effect on recovered analyte. Repeating the same tasks after each structural revision creates traceable evidence of iteration.

The fourth task is to verify how contingency capabilities are maintained. This involves creating a reusable manufacturing log that includes design versions, material sourcing, printing and post-processing conditions, sampling inspections, and testing compatibility, and periodically verifying its implementation with small batches. Observing the time required to resume production and the percentage of qualified deliveries allows for the conversion of potential equipment capacity into concrete service capacity and facilitates resource allocation between regular production and short-term incremental demand.

P5-03.thesis: Emergency additive manufacturing has value when qualified supplies reach users during shortage windows. Hospital demand records and printing-to-injection-molding cases further show that manufacturing, testing and network scheduling must be coordinated to turn one mobilization into a supply capability that can be restarted.

blocks.text: The core of emergency supply and manufacturing research is to transform modifiable digital designs into qualified supplies that arrive at the point of use on time when demand suddenly surges and regular supply is disrupted. Face shields, sampling swabs, connectors, and breathing apparatus have different functional chains: some rely on geometric coverage, some affect test results, and some continuously withstand cyclic loads. Corresponding manufacturing capabilities should be measured by the ability to deliver these functions. Production volume, validation cycle, and usage conditions collectively determine the value of a technology during a shortage window.
What medical supplies can distributed printing produce when supply is scarce?

Product selection can consider two dimensions: structures achievable with local manufacturing processes and intended-use validation available to hospitals. Face shields combine standard sheets with printed supports; swabs connect structural integrity with sample testing; respiratory-system components connect manufacturing precision with airflow and continuous operation. Studies spanning community supply, paired clinical tests and experimental ventilators create a progression from external protection to diagnostic consumables and complex systems. [R01][R02][R03] This progression can organize a project portfolio: products with established validation tasks can fill early gaps, complex devices follow dedicated test pathways, and actual shortages determine priorities.
How can the quality and clinical suitability of emergency manufacturing be verified?

Quality involves three connected questions: design function, manufacturing repeatability and field performance. Different printers can change internal surfaces and effective dimensions even with the same digital file; different resins can change mechanical and reprocessing behavior despite identical shape. Validation must therefore preserve traceability across product, material, machine and post-processing. Paired swab tests and comparisons between physical flow restrictors and computational models show how test outcomes and manufacturing deviations become observable endpoints. [R02][R06] Wearability and component compatibility belong alongside capacity assessment for protective equipment, while durability and environmental treatment belong in system testing for continuously operating devices.
How do the costs, production capacity, and supply chain performance of emergency printing compare?

The denominator of contingency costs should be the number of items delivered on time and available for the designated task. Beyond material costs, personnel coordination, cleanup, packaging, inspection, rework, and distribution all consume the shortage window. Printing facilitates initial initiation and design modifications, while injection molding facilitates scaling up repetitive production after the design is finalized; the two processes can take turns within the same project. Hospital networks and hybrid production case studies provide a real-world scenario for observing this takeover. [R04][R05] Explanatory comparisons should align demand duration, available manpower, and alternative sources before calculating delivery speeds and total costs for different routes.
How to conduct design and performance verification for the emergency respiratory support device?

Respiratory Support extends the research scale of emergency manufacturing from individual components to complete systems. Material heating, gear cyclic stress, airway resistance, monitoring interfaces, and operator understanding all contribute to its operation. Design validation can sequentially connect computation and bench testing, continuous operation, physiological evaluation in healthy animals, and task assessment with clinical personnel involvement. Each stage answers different questions: bench testing characterizes controllable loads, animal studies observe physiological coupling, and clinical involvement clarifies the working scenario. Therefore, the research framework requires iteratively connecting engineering trials with user requirements to form interpretable design iterations. [R03][R07][R08]
N1 | 2021: testing manufacturing parameters for face-shield capacity

Studders and colleagues varied infill fraction, shell thickness, extrusion width and layer height, assessing face-shield headbands with tensile tests, finite-element analysis and print-time measurements. Increasing layer height and extrusion width reduced printing time by approximately 50% and 39%, respectively. Layer-height changes did not significantly alter strength, while thicker shells and greater infill strengthened specimens. [R01] This separates faster production into parameter changes with different mechanical consequences and provides testable manufacturing settings for community equipment.

The methodology juxtaposes the mechanical results of the specimen with the headband structural analysis, linking material load-bearing capacity with the actual structural stress. Shell thickness, internal filling, and layer height are not equivalent time-saving tools: they respectively alter the load-bearing path, material distribution, and interlayer quantity. Emergency projects thus arrive at a more precise question: under the functional constraints of the target structure, which time can be saved, and which materials must be retained? When reproducing across equipment, this question should be transformed into a remeasured response relationship, forming an acceptable production window for each piece of equipment.

The node shares with swabs and pneumatic components the commonality of treating manufacturing parameters as part of functionality. The difference lies in that headbands can be screened using mechanical parameters, swabs ultimately connect to test results, and pneumatic components connect to flow rate and pressure. From this point, the research chain branches into three paths: face shields move towards large-scale process selection, sampling supplies towards clinical paired evaluation, and respiratory devices towards system load testing. These three paths ultimately converge again based on qualified delivery capabilities.
N2 | 2020: connecting open development with paired clinical swab evaluation

Callahan et al. screened 160 designs and 48 materials, comparing four prototypes with conventional swabs in 276 suspected infection outpatient participants. The κ value for the consistency of detection among the prototypes was 0.85–0.89, and it took 22 days from identifying the shortage to completing the validation of the first prototype; the staff as a whole still preferred conventional swabs. [R02] This case simultaneously retained three dimensions: diagnostic performance, user experience, and development time.

The value of paired design lies in comparing sampling results from the same individual, reducing the interference of pathogen load differences between populations on device evaluation. Materials and structures are screened before entering clinical testing, allowing a large number of candidate solutions to share a common problem definition. Observing consistent testing but different user preferences indicates that result reliability and user experience each have their own areas for improvement. Structural development can iterate separately around sample acquisition, integrity, and acceptability, rather than trying to encompass all functions with a single endpoint.

From a supply organization perspective, multiple prototypes completing the same validation path allows for alternative sourcing options. It's worth extending this to the sharing of evaluation methods: participants can compare the same metrics and then choose a route based on their manufacturing capabilities. The next step in network research should therefore track the replication of validated versions, batch releases, and order allocation, observing how new manufacturers affect delivery times and consistency, and bringing user feedback back to the candidate design selection process.
N3 | 2020: animal studies reveal material failures in cyclic mechanisms

A 2020 rapid-prototype ventilator study combined bench testing with experiments in anesthetized healthy pigs. Early PLA and ABS components failed, prompting redesigned heat-resistant nylon gears. The revised system completed 72 hours of bench operation and maintained stable physiological measurements in crossover comparisons in healthy pigs. [R03] Material and manufacturing-route changes thus turned observed failures directly into engineering revisions.

The analytical value of animal experiments stems from the simultaneous presence of continuous mechanical operation and realistic physiological load. The test bench facilitates input control, while the physiological model links gas exchange, time accumulation, and equipment status. With these two complementing each other, the question shifts from "can a single respiratory waveform be generated?" to "can the required output be maintained under cyclic conditions?" This approach suggests that the time required to manufacture a device and the operating conditions the device will endure during use should be considered in the same design evaluation.

Compared to the face-shield parameter experiment, the failure here is amplified by the overall machine function; compared to the swab pairing comparison, the time dimension becomes the key variable. Further research should bring the failure modes caused by heat, wear, and load variations back into the part design and select suitable processing methods for each part. The convenience of printing in rapid prototyping can be combined with the material and load-bearing advantages of processes such as cutting to form hybrid manufacturing driven by performance requirements.
N4 | Capacity handoff from printing to injection molding (2021)

A case report from the Drexel AJFlex project documented printed-headband production alongside injection molding. The team delivered approximately 33,000 face shields to more than 100 organizations in the region. Clinicians, engineers, manufacturers, distribution teams and volunteers participated, with industrial partners supporting capacity expansion. [R04] Project operations and delivery records show how manufacturing organization changed.

The process relay addresses the issue of misalignment between demand and design status. In the early stages, when quantities are unclear and designs are still being adjusted, digital manufacturing can handle small-batch trial production. Subsequently, as demand becomes concentrated and the structure stabilizes, fixed mold costs can be spread across more products. Running two processes in parallel also preserves a channel for rapid modifications, separating standard batch production from specific localized needs. The actual switchover conditions therefore include remaining orders, mold delivery time, design freeze level, and assembly capacity.

The case extends the single-machine time-saving problem of N1 to the production network: as machine output increases, sheet supply, assembly stations, and last-mile delivery may become bottlenecks. When evaluating a project, waiting times can be recorded by process step to pinpoint where the capacity increase occurs. Subsequent hospital network research further links production capacity with daily consumption, refining process changeover criteria from total order volume to sustainable replenishment needs.
N5 | 2021: hospital networks establish the scale of real deliveries

A single-center observational study documented emergency production from March 14 to May 10, 2020, delivering a total of 17,276 items, of which 57.3% were manufactured by individuals; the study hospital served as a central node connecting 10 other hospitals, receiving daily requests and coordinating production both inside and outside the hospital. [R05] Products cover protective equipment, ventilation support, and diagnostic consumables.

Such records connect distributed manufacturing with specific uses. The central hospital observes demand, while external makers contribute flexible equipment and staffing; orders and deliveries close the loop. Shifting the unit of analysis from an individual item to a replenishment task allows delivery proportion, response time, product gaps and stock-recovery speed to be studied together. Equal output quantities can alleviate shortages to very different degrees, depending on when demand occurs and what clinical task each item serves.

Expanding a network also creates consistency challenges: more equipment, operators and post-processing conditions increase the acceptance-testing workload. Manufacturing-deviation experiments at N6 provide a physical explanation, while version and process records at N9 provide an information-management response. Research on hospital hubs therefore extends from mobilizing resources to allocating validation capacity, matching manufacturing tasks with the receiving department’s inspection capabilities.
N6 | Flow-resistance checks reveal manufacturing deviations (2022)

Duke et al. measured the flow resistance of 30 printed throttling device designs and compared them with computational fluid dynamics models based on actual ventilator flow data. Significant differences were observed between different devices and materials, with internal surface roughness and a reduction in the actual average pore size explaining the deviation of the actual devices from the ideal model. [R06] The study covered fused deposition and photopolymerization equipment, incorporating manufacturing differences into the functional evaluation.

Choosing flow resistance as the connection metric allows geometric errors to be converted into perceptible performance differences within the system. The model describes the ideal shape, while actual measurements reflect the effective channels after forming; subtracting the two reveals the impact of the manufacturing process. For narrow cavities, even with consistent external dimensions, changes in internal pathways may still occur. Therefore, when a distributed network replicates a file, it must also replicate its functional measurement methods and establish a correspondence between the allowable range of variation and the production results.

This node directly explains why N5 requires acceptance testing by source, and also extends the material durability issues of N3 to gas path performance. Computational models are suitable for helping select test conditions and identify sensitive structures, while physical data, in turn, corrects the models and design margins. Research feedback should focus on performance distribution across equipment: by manufacturing at multiple locations with the same geometry, identify which differences can be mitigated by process control and which require structural redesign to reduce sensitivity.
N7 | Durability evaluation after device processing (2022)

The CRISIS study tested a sintered printed device after a 1.83 m drop and autoclaving, and evaluated an extrusion-printed version with a variable-compliance model. Sustained ventilation was generally maintained; the extrusion version delivered minute ventilation of 4.1–12.2 L/min, with respiratory rate inversely related to tidal volume. [R07] Validation addressed treated devices and system output under simulated loads.

Adding transport and reprocessing events before testing covers part of the real path from supply to use, rather than evaluating only newly made prototypes. Variable compliance introduces changing loads and reveals coupling between output variables. The key is test order: expose the device to events that may alter materials or assembly, then measure function. Storage, handling, treatment and operation can therefore form a continuous emergency-device study, with performance recorded separately at each stage.

N3 focuses on failures exposed during operation, while N7 focuses on performance retention after treatment; together, they form durability evidence. Next, N8 needs to be integrated for clinical task analysis, because the device's output range can only be translated into design requirements when it corresponds to a clearly defined use case. Engineering research can then be used to assign tasks such as alarm identification, interface understanding, and continuous monitoring, enabling manufacturability, maintainability, and operator usability to form a unified product evaluation.
N8 | Clinical co-design defines use requirements (2022)

The origami-bag ventilator project held three focus groups with frontline clinicians. Audio transcription and inductive thematic analysis identified needs and collaboration lessons concerning user analysis, use-context understanding, early sustained involvement, prototype communication and educational support. [R08] The findings identified development priorities and human–device interaction issues.

The qualitative approach is suitable for answering product tasks that are not yet clearly defined. Prototyping allows different professionals to communicate around a common, visible object; clinicians can specify the usage environment, patient interaction, and workload, while engineers explain the structure and controllability. Once these two approaches converge, the abstract concept of an "emergency ventilator" can be broken down into specific functional requirements and usage steps. The process of requirements formation itself is also worth documenting, as it explains why a particular parameter becomes a priority design objective.

This path provides an application context for the technical measurements of N6 and N7, and also forms a demand feedback loop back to N3. For supply research, frontline involvement also plays a role: identifying projects where actual needs have changed as early as possible, and reallocating scarce development and testing resources. Requirements, prototypes, and validation results need to be documented in the same version; N9 organizes these relationships into a traceable development process across multiple hardware trials.
N9 | Lifecycle records connect evidence (2021)

Vallatos and colleagues investigated anesthesia-equipment components, leak ports, plastic diagnostic consumables and syringe-pump lockboxes. They found that reproducing shape did not necessarily reproduce function, and developed an Aras Innovator lifecycle workflow from project experience. The paper records replicas that fitted but still leaked; the hardware and system remained under development and evaluation. [R09] Unsuccessful specimens thus became part of the manufacturing knowledge base.

The value of process documentation lies in preserving the causal relationship between design choices and test results. If only the final document is stored, the next manufacturer cannot know whether a certain dimension originated from assembly requirements or machining compensation, nor can they explain which tests should be repeated after a material change. Linking requirements, design versions, manufacturing sources, and acceptance results allows for evidence-based handover in emergency collaborations. Technological changes thus progress from replicating the external form to replicating a set of manufacturing tasks whose applicable conditions are already clearly defined.

The node integrates clinical co-creation, hospital networks, and cross-device testing, feeding back to early product screening. Historical failures help determine more quickly which components are suitable for direct resumption of production during the next shortage, and which require re-validation or process switching. The relationships in the diagram are organized sequentially by problem. Although the lifecycle study was published in 2021, its documentation methods can be used to integrate subsequent flow resistance, durability, and user studies, forming a knowledge loop for the next emergency.
2020: From Open Design to Organized Production Tasks

On March 18, 2020, Prusa Research announced the launch of face shield manufacturing and distribution. The project page disclosed that nearly 200,000 units had been printed and donated, and described the final Prusa PRO Face Shield as meeting EN 166:2001's Class 3 design for droplet and splash protection. [R10] From open documentation to clearly defined uses and product versions, this approach brings broadly participating organizations together for collaborative design. Its industrial value lies in lowering the barrier to entry and reducing redevelopment work at each location through shared versions.

Formlabs' swab project,, was initially designed by USF Health, with Northwell Health collaborating with the company to develop prototypes and conduct testing; project documentation also documents a production network involving hospitals, local medical device manufacturers, and government. [R11] This approach combines equipment, materials, and hospital evaluations into replicable manufacturing capabilities. For industry services, deliverables can include design versions and quality processes, enabling a new location to clearly identify its manufacturing conditions and validation tasks.
April 2020: lattice swabs enter a specialist manufacturing network

On April 8, 2020, Resolution Medical announced Lattice Swab, made using Carbon DLS and Keystone’s KeySplint Soft Clear material. The announcement identified Resolution Medical as the manufacturer and described the product as a Class I, 510(k)-exempt in-vitro diagnostic device. [R12] In this partnership, the manufacturer implements the product, while platform and material partners support structural development around that specific device.

These three enterprise case studies correspond to different organizational scales: Prusa connects the open community, Formlabs connects hospitals and manufacturing resources, and Carbon and its partners connect specialized medical device manufacturers. A common technological shift is expanding geometric files into information packages containing materials, manufacturing processes, and intended uses. Enterprises can then develop different services based on this: the community side emphasizes version communication and component compatibility, the hospital side emphasizes seamless manufacturing processes, and the specialized manufacturing side emphasizes stable batches and supply commitments. Together, they address the issue of replication consistency raised by academic research.

sections.title: How can academia and industry connect?

blocks.text: CN120828529A (2025) defines emergency repair as scanning damage and deformation, optimizing a model, printing and postprocessing, installation testing, and data management. Vallatos and colleagues’ observation of a fitting replica that still leaked identifies the necessary functional closure. Scan accuracy and shape reproduction are inputs; recovery records would be needed to evaluate the patent abstract’s proposed shorter repair cycle. [R14][R09]

The repair chain shares three interfaces with Prusa shields, Formlabs swabs and Carbon/Resolution Medical lattice swabs: version freezing, material availability and delivery of accepted assemblies. Repair restores a specified device function; new consumables validate a complete collection or protection task. These company projects do not establish implementation of the repair patent. The transferable organizational element is a linked record of model, material, postprocessing and acceptance. [R14][R10][R11][R12]

Papers identify where the patent’s ideal sequence needs feedback. Restrictor studies link flow-resistance deviations to bore and inner surface; rapid-ventilator work redesigned failed gears and changed material; AJFlex combined printing and injection molding. These correspond to functional error, durability failure and capacity transition. Academic–enterprise translation should select changes by failure type, since faster printing does not necessarily restore service sooner. [R03][R04][R06][R14]

sections.title: Key Transformation Issue: Turning Resource Mobilization into Stable Delivery

blocks.text: A proposed repair study would start with noncritical accessories having explicit functional boundaries, comparing intact original, damaged and patent-workflow reconstructed parts under the same installation conditions. Fit, load or sealing performance, repeated assembly and postprocessing effects would be measured alongside total restoration time. Geometrical success with functional deviation would return the part to modeling or material selection; both function and assembly repeatability would gate broader evaluation. [R14][R06][R09]

Network validation would distribute the same version across machines and operators, recording print queues, postprocessing, inspection, rework and delivery; capacity would count tested complete products. Hospital-hub and AJFlex studies provide organizational comparators. The patent’s knowledge-management step becomes a versioned record of failure, revision and acceptance. If extra printing sites merely enlarge inspection backlogs, quality and logistics capacity should precede further machine recruitment. [R04][R05][R14]

Surge exercises would compare local printing, centralized printing and established mass production for first accepted delivery, missing-component causes, staff time and post-surge inventory. Frontline-clinician research identifies requirement definition as a development variable; multi-prototype swab validation shows how one workflow can screen designs. A route faster only when acceptance is omitted would not progress; superior stable production would redirect printing toward spares, fixtures and redesign. [R02][R08][R10][R11]

sections.title: 2027-2029: From Incident Response to Routine Preparedness

blocks.text: In 2027, reproducible scan–installation-test–knowledge records for defined accessory classes could support a hospital print service organized by failure type. First-repair success, recurrence, restoration time and engineer interventions would be observable. If manual remodeling still dominates delays, a verified spare-part catalogue is more likely than case-by-case reverse engineering. Enterprise support would center on available materials and accepted versions. [R14][R09][R10]

In 2028, shared material versions and final functional tests could let emergency networks allocate shield and selected consumable work by accepted output. Persistent site differences in roughness, bore and processing would instead favor centralized postprocessing or production. Cross-site rework, failure attribution and inspection backlog would distinguish outcomes. Patent-style data management changes supply efficiency only when it stops replication of defective versions. [R05][R06][R11][R12][R14]

By 2029, routine preparedness may divide between local printing for uncertain, frequently revised accessories and established production for stable, sustained demand. AJFlex provides a manufacturing-transition example; the repair patent retains fault recovery as a separate entry. Exercises showing that catalogues, material reserves and inspection jointly shorten accepted delivery would support expansion. High idle-equipment maintenance costs would instead favor shared regional services. Supply scenarios would also record emergency and transition arrangements from FDA pandemic-device materials. [R04][R08][R10][R13][R14]

The primary priority is to establish a functional database linked to application. Face shield studies retain strength, wearability, and component compatibility metrics; swab studies retain sampling and testing data and user experience; and gas path components retain measured performance and manufacturing conditions. Each result corresponds to a specific version and batch, enabling researchers to differentiate between design variations, manufacturing variations, and usage differences. The value of this shared database lies in supporting cross-site comparisons and providing an interpretable basis for selecting future tasks.

The second priority is to measure the supply recovery process. It is recommended to report the first qualified delivery time, the on-time demand fulfillment rate, the first-pass yield, rework time, and waiting time at each stage. Cost statistics should include coordination, processing, inspection, and distribution, and be grouped by product complexity and demand duration. This combination of metrics can explain why a network is performing well and identify whether adding more printers or strengthening inspection and distribution is more valuable.

The third priority task is design and manufacturing change experiments. Under unified functional requirements, various materials, equipment, or structures are compared, and processing and continuous operating conditions are set up to examine how changes propagate to final performance. Breathing devices are particularly suitable for juxtaposing fluid modeling, durability, and human-machine interface tasks; each experiment is linked through traceable versions, allowing improvements obtained from the experiments to be reintroduced into production. The research can thus progressively establish acceptable ranges of change and evidence-based validation rules.

Finally, the sustainability of the network is studied. This can be observed through repeated drills to assess the initial pass rate after personnel rotation, the speed of resumption of production after a period of inactivity, and whether partners continue to maintain records after supply is restored. The long-term value of emergency manufacturing is reflected in its repeatable startup capability: when demand arises, appropriate products can be selected, corresponding processes can be allocated, necessary verifications can be completed, and the results can be stored again for the next round of preparation.

P6-01.title: Preoperative Planning Models
P6-01.subtitle: From displaying anatomy to traceable models that change decisions
P6-01.thesis: The value of a preoperative model is determined by the specific questions it addresses. Geometric accuracy, spatial representation, material response, and timely delivery constitute a continuous chain of evidence; physical, screen, and virtual reality models support different tasks, and in the future, the appropriate model will need to be selected based on the correspondence between changes in the treatment plan and actual operations.

questions.question: How can personalized physical models help with complex surgical planning?
questions.focus: Complex surgical planning requires understanding lesions, vessels, lumens and adjacent anatomy, and anticipating how instruments or reconstruction structures will reach the target. Physical models make these relationships available for rotation, touch and, in some cases, manipulation.

The choice depends on what needs to be understood, what needs to be changed, and what needs to be practiced.
