blocks.text: Radiotherapy and radionuclide therapy phantoms are experimental subjects with known geometry, materials, and measurement conditions, used for examining imaging, computation, localization, and delivery chains. Printing expands the design capabilities for shape and internal structure; the research focus is on translating these degrees of freedom into traceable physical references. Nine nodes connect individual geometry, low-density transport, end-to-end processes, motion imaging, and organ activity quantification.
How can printed phantoms reproduce tissue density and image features?

The phantom is used to create known, repeatable test conditions. It needs to reproduce relevant characteristics of the target measurement, such as CT attenuation, ultrasound echo, radioactive distribution, or motion, rather than replicating tissue in all aspects.
The performance is determined by the choice of materials, filling, structure, and internal medium.
How can the phantom support radiotherapy dose measurement and verification?

Dose verification compares treatment-plan calculations with measurements. A phantom provides the geometry and material environment for detector placement so that measurements correspond to defined positions, interfaces and treatment workflows.
The question is how phantoms reveal discrepancies and how those discrepancies can be traced to calculation, positioning, equipment or measurement.
How can individualized phantoms be used for quality control of treatment plans?

Treatment plan quality control requires verification of the translation between imaging, models, plans, positioning, and actual delivery. Individualized phantoms can provide a spatial environment similar to the case, allowing for the measurement of key areas.
The need for customization follows from geometries, tissue interfaces, motion or measurement tasks that standard phantoms do not adequately cover.

The three original questions form a progressive relationship. Density and imaging characteristics answer whether the phantom possesses the target physical state; dose measurement answers how the detector provides reliable readings in this state; and individualized quality control answers whether these readings reveal issues not covered by standard procedures. The study should establish references step by step: first confirming the model's state, then evaluating measurements, and finally interpreting differences in the treatment chain.

Task-related equivalence is a guiding principle throughout the study. Imaging contrast, photon transport, motion trajectory, and radioactivity are different physical properties and should be established by corresponding measurements. Designing shape, material, internal medium, and motion separately helps control variables; reassembling them into a complete phantom requires checking whether interfaces and couplings alter the expected function. This preserves patient relevance while maintaining the determinism of experimental conditions.
N1 | Starting patient-specific geometric dose verification (2014)

In 2014, Ehler and colleagues used the head-and-neck region of an anthropomorphic phantom as a patient surrogate to produce a soft-tissue-equivalent printed model for intensity-modulated radiotherapy verification. Relative to conventional phantoms, it revealed larger measurement–calculation differences at shallow depths, showing how geometry changes the problems exposed by a test. [R09]

A known anthropomorphic reference permits direct comparison between printed conversion and existing verification methods. The key is adding anatomical shape to dose checks rather than testing a beam only in a standard block. At shallow depths, electron equilibrium, dose gradients and measurement position can all affect differences. Results should therefore be examined spatially and then separated by material, setup and dosimeter response, creating a verification chain capable of investigating causes.

This node leads to two research branches: N2 combines the patient's shape with the measurement plane, and N3 addresses how to stably manufacture larger structures. A common problem is that the phantom must have a known state. The value of individualization is not in replicating as many shapes as possible, but in allowing errors previously hidden by standard geometry to surface. Subsequent designs should first specify which errors to observe, then arrange the shape, materials, and measurement locations to ensure that the resulting differences have a physical interpretation.
N2 | Planar quality assurance in patient-head phantoms (2017)

In 2017, Yea et al. constructed an FDM phantom based on the patient's head contour, compared calculated and measured doses, and contrasted it with existing quality assurance methods. This study validated the intensity-modulated radiotherapy dose using the patient's relevant spatial morphology, demonstrating the feasibility of combining case geometry and planar analysis. [R01]

The measurement plane makes spatial distribution visible, but its location determines what can be seen. Small positional changes in high-gradient regions can create significant differences, while even if the plane is consistent away from the target, it may not cover the most sensitive parts of the plan. When designing the phantom, the dosimeter space and alignment structure should be considered together so that repeatedly inserted coordinates can be traced back to the planned image. During analysis, absolute dose and shape deviations should be checked separately to avoid a single summary value hiding local problems.

Compared to N1, this step is closer to a real case, but it also introduces sources of error from segmentation, fabrication, and assembly. Subsequent studies can maintain the same plan, applying known small positional or output variations to both the standard phantom and the patient's geometric phantom, comparing which test more readily identifies the target problem. In this way, phantom studies progress from demonstrating that "measurement is close to computation" to explaining "which deviations can be detected," and establishing goals for the end-to-end process of N5.
N3 | Fabricating large phantoms in sections (2017)

Craft and Howell developed a sagittal segmentation manufacturing process in 2017 to produce large-scale patient-specific radiotherapy phantom units, and used post-assembly CT scans to correlate them with the original anatomy. The study focused on workflows addressing print size and warpage issues, using PLA to express soft tissue and bone structures. [R10]

Segment manufacturing breaks down a large model into easily controllable parts, but the assembly interface becomes a new physical boundary. Air in the seams and misalignment between segments can alter the image and dose, therefore geometric errors cannot be evaluated solely on individual segments. Inspection using the assembled image is necessary: the object being measured is in its final irradiated state, and local machining accuracy can only be translated into overall functionality through assembly.

While materials may be identical but shapes may differ, geometry-related tests can be supported first. However, issues with uneven tissue structure require a separate design layer. N4 thus selects low-density regions within the same material to facilitate the separation of material composition and density factors. This connection suggests that phantom complexity should be sequential: first, stabilize manufacturing and positioning; then, introduce heterogeneity requiring verification; and finally, connect the dynamics and the overall process. Each increase in complexity should be accompanied by the addition of measurements that confirm its state.
N4 | Experimental algorithm validation at low density (2018)

In 2018, Zavan et al. fabricated polystyrene phantoms of varying densities using printing parameters to test the Acuros XB algorithm under clinical photon beam and small field conditions. The study used the same material composition to adjust the density, and the calculated and measured results were consistent in most non-penumbra regions. [R02]

Using the same composition is central to method selection. Changing both material and density simultaneously may result in observed differences that mix elemental composition, electron transport, and geometry; using the same material makes it easier to identify the effects of density and interfaces. Printing pores also introduces scale issues: while the macroscopic average density approximates lung tissue, it doesn't guarantee that microscopic channels behave identically in every beam direction. Density uniformity and orientation dependence should be examined to determine what actual structure the algorithm input represents.

Low-density materials and small radiation fields increase sensitivity to local transport conditions, making these phantoms useful for targeted tests of dose calculations. Report where differences occur and under what physical conditions, alongside overall pass rates. Together with N3, this shows that a phantom can approximate patient shape or deliberately simplify it to isolate a mechanism. The approaches meet in N5’s end-to-end tests, explaining material inputs and workflow outcomes. Repeated measurements across pore orientations test the spatial scales over which average density is a valid approximation. If orientation changes response, infill orientation must enter manufacturing records and measurement conditions as a functional property.
N5 | End-to-end breast validation (2020)

A 2020 breast-phantom study attached printed breast structures to an existing thorax phantom, with spaces for an ionization chamber and film in different planes. Scanning, surface-guided positioning, planning and arc-therapy delivery were connected through several treatment-plan measurements and a complete end-to-end test. [R03]

An attachable structure combines relevant anatomy with reusable equipment and concentrates fabrication on what the existing phantom lacks. Predesigned dosimeter locations make measurement part of the model. End-to-end testing checks several transformations together; staged retesting then locates the cause of any discrepancy. The complete workflow reveals combined problems, while local tests explain them, forming an iterative cycle.

Surface positioning further connects the external material with the placement. The printed surface participates in optical recognition and also affects dosing through internal materials; the film slot may also form local air boundaries. The study design should identify these effects separately and incorporate measurement repeatability into the judgment. This node leads to the N8 dynamic thoracic cavity: when motion causes the image input to change over time, the end-to-end chain needs to incorporate temporal consistency, and cannot only verify the plan and delivery when stationary.
N6 | Multitime-point reference data for radionuclides (2023)

In 2023, Robinson et al. established radionuclide therapy dosimetry validation data, arranged multi-timepoint organ activity based on pharmacokinetic models, and obtained SPECT/CT images using printed human phantoms. The filling activity and target activity were consistent within the measurement uncertainty. The data and phantom design were used for multi-center comparisons. [R11]

Radionuclide dose calculation relies not only on a single image but also on time-activity curves and subsequent dose models. Patient data rarely provides independent true values simultaneously, while phantoms with known inputs allow for step-by-step verification of quantification, segmentation, curve fitting, and dose conversion. The significance of choosing a modeled time series lies in controlling the reference, enabling differences obtained from different software or centers to be pinpointed to the processing stage.

Both radionuclide therapy and external-beam radiotherapy require complete-chain validation, but radionuclide calculations depend primarily on activity within the body over time. Future comparisons can hold images constant while varying analysis, then hold analysis constant while varying acquisition, separating algorithm and equipment contributions. N9 adds anatomical organ shapes to test whether calibration from simple geometries transfers to irregular organs, linking temporal and spatial references in a clinically relevant framework.
N7 | Fillable tumor phantoms with adjustable contrast (2024)

A 2024 Micromachines study used a printed tumor phantom with injectable contrast medium to adjust CT radiopacity. The fillable design separates external shape from the imaging medium, allowing different contrast conditions to be constructed. [R04]

This decoupling is suitable for studying the sensitivity of image algorithms: fixing the geometry while changing the contrast allows observation of segmentation or detection performance; fixing the contrast while changing the shape allows observation of the impact of boundary complexity. The contrast medium, shell, and background each affect the image; analysis requires checking whether the shell becomes an additional high-contrast boundary and whether the filling is uniform. The controllability of the phantom comes from the measurability of these states, rather than just from the tunability of the materials.

When shifting from image validation to dosimetry, material equivalence needs to be redefined according to radiation conditions. Similar CT values at diagnostic energies describe an imaging response, while transport at therapeutic energies involves other material properties. These two can be linked through explicit material characterization, rather than using a single appearance similarity value to represent all physical properties. This node contrasts with N4 formation methods: one controls imaging contrast, and the other controls low-density transport, serving different stages of the radiotherapy chain.
N8 | Dynamic thorax and respiratory artifacts (2024)

The 2024 dynamic thoracic cage study used compressible lung and tumor structures to simulate customized respiratory curves. The repeatability of tumor motion amplitude was approximately ±0.2 mm, and it was used for 4D CT artifact studies. The model transforms respiratory irregularities into repeatable test conditions. [R05]

The motion phantom requires simultaneous control of deformation and time. For the same displacement amplitude, different speeds and pauses can lead to different scan phases and reconstruction results. Compressible structures more closely resemble certain respiratory behaviors than rigid body translations, but their deformation distribution still needs independent measurement. Recording the drive signal, actual tumor trajectory, and image reconstruction location allows determination of whether the deviation originates from the drive, scan synchronization, or reconstruction.

The node extends individualization from static anatomy to dynamic input. Four-dimensional imaging provides subsequent target area and motion information, thus upstream artifacts may propagate to the planning stage, while dose delivery testing may only see the final combined error. Causal localization can be established by first reconstructing using known motion verification and then using the same model in subsequent processes. It reflects the N5 end-to-end design: the complete process should maintain references at each stage, allowing the final discrepancies to be traced back along both temporal and spatial axes.
N9 | Organ geometry and SPECT quantification (2025)

A 2025 organ-phantom study created fillable kidney- and parotid-gland-related structures, checked geometry and sealing, and compared known radioactivity with SPECT/CT estimates. Images systematically underestimated activity, and recovery coefficients correlated with surface-area-to-volume ratio, demonstrating an effect of organ shape on quantification. [R06]

The method closely links geometric fabrication with metrological problems. Regular bodies and slender or irregular organs of the same volume have different boundary proportions; limited resolution will cause some signals to be distributed outside the boundaries, so the calibration results need to take shape into account. Fillable phantoms provide independent inputs, but the actual internal volume, residues, leaks, and background will all affect the reference; these factors should be identified before interpreting image underestimation.

After the data is combined with N6 multi-timepoint data, future validation can simultaneously modify organ shape and time-activity trajectories to examine how errors propagate to the final absorbed dose. The value of the phantom lies in quantifying and reproducible biases under known conditions, and in helping to formulate processing strategies. The design principle of feedback to N1 is that patient relevance and reference certainty need to be established simultaneously; only by clearly defining what the phantom itself is can it be used to determine what happened during the imaging, computation, and delivery processes. Real organ contours can also be used to test the stability of segmentation methods. When there is a difference between known cavity boundaries and boundaries on the reconstructed image, quantitative bias may originate from both restoration and region definition; comparing these separately provides clearer improvement targets for subsequent software processing.

sections.title: Evolution of Commercial Technologies and Products

blocks.text: RTsafe provides a traceable example of printed phantoms progressing from research tools to quality-assurance services. In July 2018, the company announced US FDA 510(k) clearance for Personalized PseudoPatient; the attached letter is K180697. The product supports patient-related radiotherapy verification. [R12] This stage connected individual imaging with pretreatment testing as a defined product use.

Official milestones record an independent remote dosimetry service entering the ISRS certification program in 2022 and a collaboration with ZAP Surgical on intracranial radiosurgery in 2024. [R13] The evolution extends from an individual phantom to independent measurements, workflow comparisons and integration with equipment platforms.

The current product portfolio includes phantoms for the head, spine, and abdomen, offering point, two-dimensional, and three-dimensional dose measurement options; Encephalon 3D combines bone equivalent structure with polymer gel readout. [R07] Different products combine geometry, materials, and measurement dimensions to cover equipment inspection, complex planning, and patient-related validation.

The customization service allows users to participate in phantom design, organizing requirements according to body, CT source, detector, measurement direction, and additional features. Official case studies include surface positioning applications and lung measurement inserts. This product logic aligns with the task breakdown in academic research: first, identify the deviations to be discovered, then select the physical structure and readout method. [R08]

From a business value perspective, stable manufacturing is only one part of the equation. Measurement calibration, data feedback, result analysis, and anomaly retesting collectively determine whether a service can help hospitals pinpoint problems. Remote services, in particular, require ensuring consistency in the phantom's state before and after transport, detector tracking, and local execution records to explain central discrepancies as process differences.

Product development for from 2027 to 2029 can be observed along two paths: standard modules expand the comparable testing range, while customized modules cover specific geometric, motion, or imaging conditions. Both share a measurement and analysis foundation, reducing the burden of rebuilding the system for each new scenario. The maturity of the product portfolio should be measured by the ability to detect new errors and the consistency of retests.

Radiotherapy phantom patents connect anatomy to measurable radiation equivalence. CN122455332A (2026) proposes a personalized surface model from body and physiological parameters, tissue-equivalence indices and material formulations for whole-body additive manufacture. The variable-density polystyrene Acuros XB study provides a concrete same-composition density comparator. Equivalence therefore needs definition alongside beam, energy and measurement location. [R02][R14]

RO139161A1 (2025) describes CT-segmented vertebrae printed in bone-density-like resin and embedded in soft-tissue-like gel. This bone–matrix construction complements patient-specific head/neck and sliced-phantom work on superficial dose discrepancies, size limits and warping. RTsafe’s anatomical dosimetry phantoms and customization service provide enterprise interfaces for comparing these manufacturing variables and acceptance tasks. [R01][R09][R10][R07][R08][R15]

RTsafe’s product, service and historical verification announcement describe delivery of anatomy, measurement media and workflow. Breast end-to-end work fixes chamber and film locations; dynamic-thorax work combines compressible lung and tumor motion with 4D CT. These tasks constrain patent materials and assembly through detector positioning, bone–soft-tissue interfaces and geometry under motion. The patents serve as comparators for static materials and personalized geometry within that delivery chain. [R03][R05][R07][R08][R12][R14][R15]

A materials study would compare the whole-body formulations and spine resin–gel construction with standard tissue-equivalent phantoms for density, CT response and dose under selected exposures, sampling interfaces, superficial and homogeneous regions. Similar CT values may arise from different compositions. Energy-specific suitability would restrict use or prompt material revision; stable material, interface and geometry would gate full-plan verification. [R02][R09][R14][R15]

End-to-end comparisons would use the same plan and analysis for conventional, patient-shaped and bone–soft-interface models across scanning, planning, positioning and delivery. Detector repositioning, seams, gel change and reassembly would be tracked. Sliced printing motivates postassembly imaging; breast phantoms motivate fixed detector locations. Assembly-dependent dose deviations trigger connector revision; anatomy-specific discrepancies inform whether customization adds value. [R03][R10][R08][R14][R15]

Dynamic and nuclear-medicine use needs a separate layer. Known motion inputs would test amplitude, phase and artifacts; fillable kidney/parotid work compares known activity with recovery, supported by multicenter reference data. The static whole-body patent contributes shape and material parameters, while motion hardware and activity chambers need separate qualification. Unstable sealing, geometry or reference input would require modular testing before integration. [R05][R06][R11][R14]

In 2027, batch-linked CT and dose records for whole-body formulations and resin–gel spine constructs could support reviewable RTsafe-style customization for defined irradiation uses. Material reproduction, detector repositioning and local dose discrepancies would be signals. Limited-energy suitability favors protocol-specific products. Broader body-shape customization requires additional errors exposed relative to standard phantoms. [R07][R08][R14][R15]

In 2028, shared segmentation, postassembly imaging and end-to-end tests could support intersite comparisons of spine or complex-body models. Dominant gel/seam variation would favor central production or standardized material kits. Same-plan differences, rework and uncertainty components would distinguish routes. Dynamic or fillable extensions first need to preserve established equivalence and detector positioning before broader delivery. [R03][R10][R11][R14][R15]

By 2029, individualized phantoms that repeatedly expose errors missed in complex anatomy, motion or activity quantification could support tiered services. High customization cost with little added information would favor standard phantoms plus local inserts. Additional interpretable discrepancies, verification time and repeat-delivery consistency would distinguish outcomes. The patents’ value depends on maintaining traceable material/geometry links to measurable tasks in supported versions. [R05][R06][R07][R08][R14][R15]

blocks.text: The microfluidic chips transform the transport, mixing, separation, and reaction of liquids into a designable spatial network. The changes brought by the additive manufacturing include overcoming planar wiring constraints, rapid modification of internal structures, and co-designing the chip with interfaces, supports, and drive components. The most noteworthy research task is how these geometric degrees of freedom can improve experimental stability, repeatability, and processing flow.

The four research questions correspond to a complete work chain. Resolution and materials determine whether the chip can form the required channels; droplet and fluid control determine whether the input liquid undergoes a consistent physical process; pretreatment determines whether the target in complex samples can successfully enter the detection process; mold replication determines whether the same function can be continuously manufactured. A change in any of these steps may alter the subsequent results. Therefore, chip comparison requires observing geometry, interfaces, flow rates, and biological tasks within the same system.

There are two parallel manufacturing routes here. Direct printing leaves the 3D internal structure in the finished product, suitable for complex channels, spatial mixers, and integrated interfaces; printing molds and then replicating them leaves the complex machining in the tooling, allowing the final liquid contact material to use systems such as PDMS. They both serve experimental functions, but have different iteration speeds, surface features, and batch replication methods. [R01][R05][R06]

Evaluation units also need to change with the task. The manufacturing stage focuses on actual channel size, connectivity, and surface area; the droplet stage focuses on particle size distribution and continuous operation; the sample stage focuses on recovery rate and inhibition factors; and the replication stage focuses on batch-to-batch consistency. This evaluation chain allows a seemingly simple chip to answer specific questions and enables companies to identify which stages require materials, equipment, or system services.
N1 | Transparent, cell-compatible channels (2016)

Transparency in microchannels is primarily a matter of measurement conditions: cell morphology, flow interfaces, and particle trajectories all depend on stable imaging. Research on PEG-DA transparent devices places stereolithography printing and cell culture in the same evaluation, demonstrating that printed materials can simultaneously participate in structure formation and biological observation. This presents a composite goal for future research: the solid entity left after printing serves as both a fluid boundary and a microscopic observation window and cell contact environment. [R01]

Therefore, "resolution" can be broken down into design size, finished cavity size, and operational size. The fact that a minimal structure can be formed through exposure does not mean that residual material in a closed channel is easily removed; a transparent observation window does not equate to a uniform chemical state of the cell contact surface. Research designs should correlate these quantities with the experimental task, explaining why a geometric change affects flow resistance, image background, or cell response.

Starting from this point, the problem naturally branches into two paths: changing the material to meet direct application requirements, or using printing for the mold while entrusting the final culture interface to another material. The former retains the advantage of integrated three-dimensional structure, while the latter facilitates the use of existing culture and imaging conditions. The most explanatory indicator when choosing a path is the level that geometric accuracy and biological usability can be achieved simultaneously in a single experiment.

The experiment can also set up two sets of comparisons: "same geometry, different materials" and "same materials, different geometry." The former is used to explain interfaces and optics, while the latter is used to explain flow and connectivity. Cross-referencing the results of the two sets is then necessary to identify whether a material's advantages depend on a specific structure. This design allows material selection and structure development to work together and avoids the difficulty of determining the cause when multiple variables change simultaneously.
N2 | Geometry and wettability as two design routes (2021)

Droplet formation requires a continuous phase to stably encapsulate the dispersed phase. A 2021 study examined both hydrophobic resins and three-dimensional annular channels: the former alters the wall surface in contact with the droplets, while the latter utilizes spatial configuration to reduce the contact between the droplets and the wall surface. [R03] Both approaches target the same failure mechanism but address it from the material and geometric entry points, respectively, providing a wider range of design options than simply improving printing accuracy.

The mechanistic implication is that structural design can alter the way interfaces meet. If the target liquid easily wets existing materials, research can first examine whether a continuous phase envelopment can be maintained through channel layout before deciding whether to develop a new formulation. Conversely, even if the resin possesses ideal wettability, inlet fluctuations and local flow fields at bends can still alter droplet formation. Therefore, materials and geometry should be compared as joint variables.

Further research requires observing the droplet behavior throughout the entire process, rather than just recording the moment of generation. Downstream turns, collection, surface aging, and long-term operation can all alter contact conditions. The key leap from node N2 to N4 is transforming stable generation at a single location into consistent output under continuous operation conditions across multiple channels; thus, the evaluation of stability expands from local to the entire network.

Droplet studies also require distinguishing between formation frequency, volume distribution, and merging behavior. The first two reflect generator output, while the last reflects downstream stability. Researchers can observe the inlet, generation zone, and outlet separately, pinpointing a single instability to a specific region. This segmented evidence helps determine whether to improve wetting, contraction geometry, or outlet collection, rather than simply increasing the overall pressure and retesting.
N3 | Mold replication preserves biological interfaces (2023)

The printing mold route separates the high-degree-of-freedom structure from the biological experimental materials. The 2023 LCD mold research used micropores, concentration gradients, and hydrogel devices to conduct cell activity, drug response, and three-dimensional invasion experiments, linking printing quality to actual biological readout. Its significance lies in verifying whether the replicated device can still complete the predetermined experiments. [R05]

The node can be understood on two levels. On a geometric level, the details of the mold surface are transmitted to the replicating device; on an experimental level, the final material comes into contact with the cells, and surface morphology, optical windows, and assembly methods all influence the measurements. By simultaneously comparing structure and response, it's possible to determine whether the difference originates from manufacturing or a biological process. The resulting analytical sequence is to first confirm the replicating structure, then confirm the culture conditions, and finally interpret the experimental results.

The replication method also changes the iterative economy: researchers can focus design modifications on the mold, repeatedly fabricating multiple chips for control. What truly matters is whether the same design can achieve similar environments across multiple experimental batches. This addresses the issue with N6's modular mold library and also provides replaceable fluidic functional units for handling real-world samples in N5.

Replicated structures can be compared at three levels: design, mold and final product. Design–mold differences locate fabrication errors, mold–product differences locate replication errors, and product–experiment differences locate operational effects. Producing multiple devices from one mold separates tooling variation from batch variation and identifies where quality checks belong during scale-up.
N4 | Balancing flow in parallel channels (2020)

Increasing droplet production requires adding more channels, but fluid in a parallel network is not automatically evenly distributed. A 2020 study used computational fluid dynamics and stereolithography to co-design stacked, radially parallel droplet generators and used the output for cell encapsulation. [R02] This shifted the research focus from "how a single generator can work" to "how multiple generators work together".

The technical chain here involves round trips between design and testing. The computational model is used to identify the impact of branch resistance and inlet conditions on distribution; the printed product realizes the network; and experiments are conducted to check whether manufacturing deviations have altered the equilibrium. This allows for more interpretive comparisons: differences between channels under the same flow rate and fluctuations of the same channel at different times should be statistically analyzed separately to distinguish between structural inhomogeneities and drive instability.

The node also illustrates that expanding throughput is not simply a matter of copying modules. Upstream manifolds, interfaces, and outgoing collection become common constraints; with an increase in the number of channels, the average local performance may mask a few failed branches. The next task is to connect the parallel network to a measurable and independently controllable drive system, enabling the identification and maintenance of abnormal branches.

The parallel network can also create distribution maps by channel, rather than just comparing the overall average of all droplets. If some branches continue to deviate, structural asymmetry or resistance differences may warrant priority investigation; if all branches change synchronously over time, the drive and input deserve more attention. This space-time decomposition connects computational design with operational diagnostics, improving the targeting of the next round of modifications.
N5 | Stepwise processing of complex samples (2020)

The chip addresses the challenge of handling complex samples such as whole blood, transforming chip performance into a continuous processing problem. Modular devices from 2020 integrate bacterial pre-enrichment with genomic DNA purification, aiming to improve sample input before molecular detection. Printing here handles the flow path and chamber organization, while detection results depend simultaneously on target recovery, background removal, and step integration. [R04]

This type of research requires a process-oriented perspective. A separation step achieving high purity may become more difficult to detect if a significant amount of the target substance is lost simultaneously; similarly, a rapid step introducing inhibitory factors in subsequent reactions can slow down the overall process. Therefore, the inputs and outputs of each step should be mapped together, recording which stage causes the loss and whether the loss varies with sample composition. This provides a clear target for design optimization.

From a research perspective, pretreatment establishes a substantial link between microfluidics and rapid detection. N2 and N4 provide controllable fluid units, N3 provides fabrication and interface selection, and N5 verifies whether these capabilities can serve real samples. The resulting feedback will re-influence material selection, dead volume, and connection methods, rather than simply adding a detection module.

When processing complex samples, the retained and lost targets at each step should be accounted for separately in the workflow. Research can establish a baseline performance using simpler samples, then increase the background complexity to observe whether capture, elution, or subsequent reactions are the first to become unstable. This approach not only identifies applicable tasks but also clarifies exactly what the added modules improve, helping system development control the number of steps and operational burden.
N6 | Module reconfiguration and replication manufacturing (2023)

The core of the modularity is to allow reusable functions to be incorporated into different experimental combinations. A 2023 study inspired by movable type printing replicated three-dimensional flow paths by assembling molds and combining valves, light sources, and micro-imaging accessories onto the chip, demonstrating concentration gradient, droplet, cell capture, and drug screening platforms. This shifts structural iteration from a complete redesign to functional combination. [R06]

This organizational approach requires maintaining both interface consistency and functional interpretability. Connections of the same shape do not necessarily have the same dead volume and sealing performance; when two independently validated modules are connected, upstream flow and downstream back pressure will affect each other. Therefore, the module library should simultaneously store geometry files, applicable fluid conditions, connection boundaries, and basic performance characteristics, enabling the combined system to be calculated and validated.

The academic value of lies in improving the operability of problem comparisons. For example, replacing the mixing module while keeping the driving and detection constant allows for a clearer observation of the differences caused by the mixing process; replacing the culture material while keeping the geometry constant helps to pinpoint interface factors. Therefore, N6 becomes the convergence point of multiple research paths, leaving the system requirements to N7 and N8.

The function library can be organized according to "input conditions - output behavior". For example, the mixing module stores the input flow ratio and mixed readout, while the capture module stores the sample objects and retrieval performance. Once the interface is clearly defined, the module combination has verifiable expectations; if the whole system deviates, it can be located along the module boundaries. This organizational method allows open designs to evolve from a geometric library into an experimental knowledge base.
N7 | External systems stabilize perfusion (2023)

Sustainable perfusion relies on external devices. The 2023 modular peristaltic pump research integrates printed mechanical components, control electronics, and a user interface to support flow rate settings and pre-programmed flow patterns. [R07] Its research focuses on controllable perfusion systems for everyday experiments, incorporating user adjustment and setting capabilities into the design.

From a fluid dynamics experiment perspective, the nominal setpoints of the pump need to be correlated with the actual environment within the chip. Pipeline elasticity, pump pulsation, and device resistance collectively determine the conditions experienced by the cell or droplet, thus allowing for synchronized recording of drive measurements and chip readouts. By changing the drive while keeping the chip constant, researchers can distinguish between geometry-induced flow differences and variations caused by external equipment.

The industrial opportunity presented by the node lies in delivering a printed chip and an easy-to-use driver system as an experimental workflow. Users are typically most concerned with whether settings can be saved, whether operation can be reproduced, and whether piping can be easily replaced. Programmability further requires open data interfaces to connect imaging, sensing, and driving systems later; this is precisely the research task of N8.

flow control during long-term cultivation should be tested separately from short-term allocation. The former focuses on continuous fluctuations, pipeline conditions, and environmental influences, while the latter focuses on the volume and response of each action. Both types of tasks can share the same mechanical platform but require different calibrations and recordings. Testing separately for each task allows for clearer configuration of the same low-cost pump in multiple research scenarios.
N8 | Independent channels and automation interfaces (2025)

The 2025 open-source multichannel peristaltic pump combines four independent drive channels, quick-change cartridges, and a SiLA 2 interface. Independent channels allow different experiments to run at different speeds; replaceable consumables enable independent maintenance of fluid contact parts; and the software interface allows the device to be integrated into larger automated systems. [R08]

This shows an extension from geometric fabrication to system manageability. In multichip operation, each channel needs its own state and control records, and abnormal flow must be traceable to the corresponding experiment. Total running time alone cannot explain environmental changes experienced by a sample. Connecting experimental identity, control commands and sensor readings enables reproducible parallel experiments.

The feedback path returns to N4: independent control can expose branch differences previously masked by average values, thereby improving manifold and interface design. Another feedback path, from N5 back to N3, focuses on how target losses and background residues in pretreatment are affected by materials and connectors. This forms a complete closed loop—manufacturing provides the structure, experiments verify the functionality, and operational data determines the next round of structure and maintenance plans.

The independent channel adds a new control method to experimental design: different flow programs can be compared simultaneously within the same system, and actual records of each branch are retained. When control, sensing, and sample identity are linked, anomalies are no longer just failures, but become evidence for analyzing structures, piping, and materials. This is also a key aspect of the device platform's transformation from an execution tool to a research feedback tool.

sections.title: How to formulate testable comparisons for the four research questions?

blocks.text: Resolution and materials issues can be addressed by establishing a two-dimensional comparison matrix: one axis represents the finished structure, and the other axis represents the contact materials. For each combination, first check if the channels actually form, then examine the fluid and observed performance. This allows identification whether a material is only effective in wider channels, or whether a fine structure depends on specific processing. The depth of research comes from explaining the interaction between the two, rather than providing a single "best material."

The droplet and fluid control problem can be addressed step-by-step using single-channel, parallel-channel, and independently driven methods. Each stage records spatial distribution and temporal variations to determine the impact of added complexity. For tasks requiring cell encapsulation, the generation process should be linked to subsequent cell states to ensure geometric consistency and shared biological output within the same experimental context.

For sample pretreatment issues, a complete material flow analysis should be employed. The target passes from the raw sample through enrichment, extraction, and detection, with retention, transfer, and loss at each step collectively determining the final performance. Modifications to the printing geometry can correspond to specific steps, such as reducing dead volume at connections, improving contact, or adjusting the collection area. Such optimizations readily generate comparable evidence and are more easily translated into product design.

The mold duplication problem is best addressed by combining repeated use, batch duplication, and different operators for inspection. Multiple duplications of the same mold are used to check for process variations, while duplications of different molds with the same design are used to check for machining variations. Through these two levels of comparison, it can be determined whether quality inspection should be placed at the tooling, finished product, or assembly stage, and a clear process can be established for small-batch manufacturing.

sections.title: Enterprise Technology and Product Roadmap: From Microstructure to Usable System

blocks.text: The Nanoscribe application data for microfluidics focuses on high-resolution three-dimensional microstructures, presented in conjunction with its materials and replication capabilities; the microFAB-3D of Microlight3D utilizes two-photon polymerization direct laser writing, targeting research applications such as microfluidics, micro-optics, and cell culture. Both correspond to the manufacturing platform layer: helping researchers form structures that are difficult to achieve using ordinary planar processes. [R09][R10]

The enterprise capabilities and the aforementioned academic chain can be divided into three delivery layers. The first layer is processing capabilities, including structural dimensions, material compatibility, and substrate adaptation; the second layer is experimental devices, including cleanable channels, optical windows, interfaces, and reproducible molds; the third layer is the operating system, including drives, sensors, software, and maintenance. With each subsequent layer, the product evaluation gets closer to a complete experiment conducted by the user.

On the timeline, direct printing and cell-compatible research in 2016 raised the requirement for integrated materials and experiments; parallel droplets and three-dimensional flow focusing in 2020-2021 advanced the task to fluid functions; replication, assembly, and actuation research in 2023 made devices reusable experimental platforms; and independent channels and automated interfaces in 2025 highlighted multi-experiment management. This is a line of research capability expansion, and enterprise products can form a division of labor along different levels. [R01][R02][R03][R05][R06][R07][R08]

For purchasers and R&D personnel, the most effective technical comparison is to establish a prototype process around the predetermined task. Microstructure equipment provides manufacturing capabilities, mold suppliers provide replication stability, and system integrators provide operation and recording. They can all serve the same chip application, and the value of their collaboration comes from whether the interfaces are clear and whether specific steps can be located when problems occur.

A product signal worth tracking is that the supplier begins to provide reference devices and test data linked to specific experimental tasks. When users can obtain different batches of the same design and compare the outputs using a unified method, the manufacturing platform gradually accumulates transferable application knowledge and is more likely to form long-term cooperation with system integrators.

sections.title: The Connection Between Academia and Industry: How Functional Evidence Enters Products

blocks.text: Microfluidic links begin with whether printing defines molds, flow paths or tissue positions. CN116077230A (2023) describes printed templates, PDMS replication/sealing and surface modification for vascular chips. The LCD-mold paper links replication quality to drug-response and invasion readouts. Both separate fabrication freedom from the final contact material. Template shape, replicated dimensions and surface state define tasks for Nanoscribe components or Microlight3D microFAB-3D. [R05][R09][R10][R11]

CN115891150A (2023) adds a modular variable-channel mixer to extrusion printing for pixelated rigid/flexible precursor distribution. Equal-flow droplet networks and hydrophobic/ring-channel studies identify complementary controls: flow splitting, wall contact and composition. The patented mixer is a comparator for switching lag and spatial error, not an identified paper instrument. Higher-resolution enterprise fabrication should be selected by actual flow and mixing behavior. [R02][R03][R09][R10][R12]

CN110551679A (2019) couples printed liver units to hepatic-artery, portal-vein and central-vein channels. US20240302352A1 (2024) proposes mixing, reservoir, micropore, culture and recovery layers with organized printed constructs inside a chip. These shift evaluation from clear channels to perfusion distribution and observability. Transparent PEG-DA work supplies a material/window starting point; enterprise fabrication needs compatible channel dimensions, optical access and connectors. [R01][R09][R10][R13][R14]

Modular-channel and pump studies supply operating boundaries through assembled paths, independent channels, quick-change cartridges and SiLA 2. Nanoscribe/Microlight3D fabrication complements open control at the interface level. Delivery specifications should include pump connections, venting, observation and replacement alongside feature size. Reusability requires a mixer or organ module to be exchanged while preserving flow calibration and experimental records. [R06][R07][R08][R09][R10][R12][R13]

sections.title: Key translation Issue: Treating the Entire Process as an Evaluation Object

blocks.text: Fabrication studies would compare direct printing, mold replication and microfabricated inserts for the same flow path, measuring dimensions, roughness, transparency, pressure loss, leakage and surface change against established channels. Template and replica dimensions remain separate. Finer structures with unstable flow would trigger sealing/material revision; reproducible manufacture and flow gate subsequent cell-related tasks, with version and processing history retained. [R01][R05][R11]

Inert tracers would test outlet allocation and switching transitions while varying channel impedance, mixer geometry and pump pulsation against single-channel and fixed-ratio controls. The patent’s spatial-distribution target would be compared with deposited boundaries, residence volume and carryover. Greater parallelization variance would trigger network redesign; carryover-limited switching would prioritize mixer and clearing changes over positioning precision. [R02][R03][R07][R12]

Organ-chip validation would first establish cell-free connectivity, flow distribution and optical access, then compare static and perfused models with fixed sources and tasks for function, spatial uniformity and batch variation. Liver and cerebral chips need distinct reference structures. Supply gradients or blocked imaging would trigger engineering revision; reproducible structures and interpretable readouts gate manufacturing-scale evaluation. [R01][R05][R08][R13][R14]

In 2027, consistent replicated channels and surfaces could support specialist fabrication of critical local structures through Nanoscribe- or microFAB-3D-style capabilities. Leakage, dimensional/flow variation and postprocessing time per accepted chip would be signals. Connector errors overwhelming microstructure gains would favor interface improvement in hybrid manufacture. Direct and replicated routes may coexist according to complete-device performance. [R05][R09][R10][R11]

In 2028, agreement between mixer/pump logs and measured distribution could support exchangeable droplet, gradient or material-printing workstations. Persistent carryover and pressure coupling would favor a few fixed configurations. Outlet distributions, switching lag and recalibration after module exchange distinguish outcomes. Open interfaces add value through faster restoration of consistent operation rather than connectivity demonstrations alone. [R02][R06][R08][R09][R12]

By 2029, cross-batch and external-team perfusion/function reproducibility in liver or layered-tissue chips could extend fabrication into defined experimental configurations. Source variability exceeding structural gains would favor standardized fluidic carriers and research customization. Accepted structures, batch readouts and external reproduction time, including materials, pumps and imaging, distinguish outcomes. Vessel classes and layered positions remain inspectable design parameters. [R01][R05][R09][R10][R13][R14]

sections.title: Observation Indicators and Priority Research Tasks

blocks.text: Observe the manufacturing end, recording the success rate of the complete channel, critical dimension fluctuations, post-processing time, and batch consistency. Observe the experimental end, recording droplet distribution, target recovery, sample loss, and continuous operating status. Observe the system end, recording connection time, independent channel control capability, maintenance frequency, and data interface. These three types of indicators together explain the actual progress of a technology.

The preliminary study can set up three sets of controls around the same function: direct printing vs. mold replication; single-channel vs. parallel network; manual drive vs. programmable drive. Each set simultaneously examines the structure and experimental output, providing a clear causal entry point for comparison. Subsequently, complex samples or long-term incubation can be added to incorporate real-world usage requirements into the design.

The core opportunity in this direction lies in transforming spatial design freedom into a reproducible experimental process. The most worthwhile outcomes to follow are those that both explain fluid or biological mechanisms and provide sufficient manufacturing and operational information; the most worthwhile products to follow are systems that enable users to continuously perform the same task and easily identify and correct anomalies.
